Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Niruttidīpanīpāṭha

The Text of the Elucidation of Linguistic Analysis

Ganthārambha

Beginning of the Work

1.

1.

Caturāsītisahassa[M 0.0001], dhammakkhandhāpabhaṅkarā;

Lokamhi yassa jotanti, nantavaṇṇapabhassarā.

Eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma, makers of light, whose boundless splendors shine forth in the world.

2.

2.

Anantavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ, vande niruttipāraguṃ;

Saddhammañcassa saṅghañca, visuddhavaṇṇabhājanaṃ.

I pay homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One of infinite splendor, the master of linguistic analysis; and to his Good Dhamma, and to the Sangha, the vessel for pure qualities.

3.

3.

Moggallāno mahāñāṇī, niruttāraññakesarī;

Nadi byākaraṇaṃnādaṃ, sogatāraññabyāpanaṃ.

Moggallāna, of great wisdom, the lion in the forest of linguistic analysis, sounded the roar of grammar, pervading the wilderness of the Sugata's domain.

4.

4.

Tassatthaṃ dīpayissāmi, nānārāsiṃvibhājayaṃ;

Ogāyha saddasatthāni, navaṅgaṃ satthusāsananti.

I shall illuminate its meaning, analyzing its diverse contents, having delved into the treatises on words and the ninefold teaching of the Master.

1. Sandhikaṇḍa

1. The Chapter on Sandhi

Saññārāsi

The Collection of Terms

Garusaññārāsi

The Collection of Technical Terms

Vaṇṇo[M 0.0002], saro, savaṇṇo, dīgho, rasso, byañjano, vaggo, niggahītaṃ.

Letter, vowel, homogeneous vowel, long, short, consonant, class, niggahīta.

1. Aādayo titālīsaṃ titālīsa (bahūsu) vaṇṇā ka. 2; rū. 2; nī. 1, 2.

1. There are forty-three letters, beginning with 'a'.

Aādayo bindantā tecattālīsakkharā vaṇṇā nāma honti.

The forty-three letters, beginning with 'a' and ending with the dot (bindu), are called 'letters' (vaṇṇā).

A, ā, i, ī, u, ū, eta, e, ota, o. Ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la,va sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ. Atthaṃ vaṇṇenti pakāsentīti vaṇṇā, akkharāti ca vuccanti, nāmapaññattirūpattā nakkharanti khayavayaṃ na gacchantīti akkharā. “Nāmagottaṃ na jīratī”ti saṃ. ni. 1.76 hi vuttaṃ.

a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e (short), e, o (short), o. ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va, sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ. They are called 'letters' (vaṇṇā) because they describe and clarify the meaning. And they are called 'imperishables' (akkharā) because, being of the nature of name-designations, they do not perish—they do not go to destruction and decay. For it has been said: 'Name and lineage do not decay.'

2. Dasādo sarā ka. 3; rū. 3; nī. 3.

2. The first ten are vowels.

Tesu vaṇṇesu ādimhi dasa vaṇṇā sarā nāma honti. Sayameva laddhasarūpā hutvā rājanti virocantīti sarā.

Among these letters, the first ten letters are called 'vowels' (sarā). They are called vowels because, having obtained their own form by themselves, they shine and are brilliant.

3. Dve dve savaṇṇā.

3. In pairs, they are homogeneous.

Tesu saresu dve dvesarā savaṇṇā nāma honti.

Among these vowels, each pair of two is called 'homogeneous' (savaṇṇā).

A, ā avaṇṇo, i, ī ivaṇṇo, u, ū uvaṇṇo, eta, e etavaṇṇo, ota, o otavaṇṇo. Samāno vaṇṇo suti etesanti savaṇṇā, sarūpāti ca vuccanti, samānaṃ rūpaṃ suti etesanti sarūpā.

a, ā are the a-class; i, ī are the i-class; u, ū are the u-class; e (short) and e are the e-class; o (short) and o are the o-class. They are called 'homogeneous' (savaṇṇā) because they have a sound of the same class. They are also called 'of the same form' (sarūpā) because they have the same form and sound.

4. Pubbo rasso ka. 4; rū. 4; nī. 4.22.

4. The former is short.

Dvīsu [M 0.0003] dvīsu savaṇṇesu yo yo pubbo hoti, so so rasso nāma hoti. Rassena kālena vattabbāti rassā, rassakālo nāma akkhidalānaṃ ummisananimmisanasamakālo.

In each pair of homogeneous vowels, whichever is the former is called 'short' (rassa). They are called short because they are to be uttered in a short time. A short time is the time equal to the opening and closing of the eyelids.

Tattha eta, ota iti dve ekapadasaṃyoge pare kvaci labbhanti. Eṭṭhi, seṭṭho, oṭṭho, sotthi.

Therein, the two, short 'e' and short 'o', are sometimes found when a conjunct consonant within the same word follows. For example: eṭṭhi, seṭṭho, oṭṭho, sotthi.

Ekapadasaṃyogeti kiṃ? Padantarasaṃyoge pare rassā mā hontūti. Maṃ ce tvaṃ nikhaṇaṃ vane, jā. 2.22.5 putto tyāhaṃ mahārāja jā. 1.1.7.

Why is 'when a conjunct consonant within the same word follows' specified? So that they are not short when a conjunct consonant in a different word follows. For example: 'Maṃ ce tvaṃ nikhaṇaṃ vane,' 'putto tyāhaṃ mahārāja.'

Kvacīti kiṃ? Ekapadasaṃyogepi vaggantesu vā ya, ra, la, vesu vā paresu rassā mā hontūti. Enti, senti, eyya, bhāseyya, meṇḍo, soṇḍo.

Why is 'sometimes' specified? So that they are not short, even when a conjunct consonant within the same word follows, if that conjunct begins with a final consonant of a class or with y, r, l, or v. For example: enti, senti, eyya, bhāseyya, meṇḍo, soṇḍo.

5. Paro dīgho ka. 5; rū. 5; nī. 5.

5. The latter is long.

Dvīsu dvīsu savaṇṇesu yo yo paro hoti, so so dīgho nāma hoti. Dīghena kālena vattabbāti dīghā, dīghakālo nāma rassehi diguṇakālo.

In each pair of homogeneous vowels, whichever is the latter is called 'long'. They are called 'long' because they are to be spoken in a long time; a long time is twice the time of a short vowel.

6. Kādayo byañjanā ka. 6; rū. 8; nī. 6.

6. Those beginning with 'ka' are consonants.

Tesu vaṇṇesu kādayo bindantā vaṇṇā byañjanā nāma honti. Atthaṃ byañjayantīti byañjanā. Te pana suddhā addhamattikā, rassayuttā diyaddhamattikā, dīghayuttā tiyaddhamattikā.

Among these letters, the letters from 'ka' up to the dot are called 'consonants' (byañjanā). They are called consonants because they make the meaning manifest. When pure, they are half a mora; when joined with a short vowel, one and a half moras; when joined with a long vowel, two and a half moras.

7. Pañcapañcakā vaggā ka. 7; rū 9; nī. 7.

7. The classes consist of five consonants each.

Tesu byañjanesu kādi-mantā pañcabyañjanapañcakā vaggā nāma honti.

Among these consonants, the five groups of five consonants, from 'ka' to 'ma', are called 'classes' (vaggā).

Kādi [M 0.0004] pañcako kavaggo, cādi ca vaggo, ṭādi ṭavaggo, tādi tavaggo, pādi pavaggo. Sesā avaggāti siddhaṃ. Vaṇṇuddese ekaṭṭhānikānaṃ byañjanānaṃ vagge samūhe niyuttāti vaggā.

The group of five beginning with 'ka' is the ka-class; the one beginning with 'ca' is the ca-class; the one beginning with 'ṭa' is the ṭa-class; the one beginning with 'ta' is the ta-class; and the one beginning with 'pa' is the pa-class. It is established that the remaining are 'unclassed' (avaggā). In the exposition of letters, they are called 'classes' (vaggā) because they are appointed to a group, a collection of consonants that share a single place of articulation.

8. Bindu niggahītaṃ ka. 8; rū. 10; nī. 8.

8. The dot is the niggahīta.

Ante bindumatto vaṇṇo niggahītaṃ nāma. Niggayha gayhati uccāriyatīti niggahītaṃ.

The letter at the end that is merely a dot is called 'niggahīta'. It is called 'niggahīta' because it is uttered by being held back and grasped.

Garusaññārāsi niṭṭhito.

Here ends the Collection of Technical Terms.

Byañjanavuttirāsi

The Collection on the Production of Consonants

Ṭhānaṃ, karaṇaṃ, payatanaṃ rū. 2 (piṭṭhe); nī 6 (piṭṭhe); 23 (suttaṅke).

Place, articulator, and effort.

Cha ṭhānāni – kaṇṭhaṭṭhānaṃ, tāluṭṭhānaṃ, muddhaṭṭhānaṃ, dantaṭṭhānaṃ, oṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ, nāsikaṭṭhānaṃ. Tesu byattaṃ vadantena yattha “akkha”nti vuccati, taṃ kaṇṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Yattha “iccha”nti, taṃ tāluṭṭhānaṃ. Yattha “raṭṭha”nti, taṃ muddhaṭṭhānaṃ. Yattha “sattha”nti, taṃ dantaṭṭhānaṃ. Yattha “puppha”nti vuccati, taṃ oṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Nāsapadeso nāsikaṭṭhānaṃ.

There are six places of articulation: the throat, the palate, the crown of the head, the teeth, the lips, and the nose. Among these, when a distinct speaker says 'akkha,' that is the throat-place. Where one says 'iccha,' that is the palate-place. Where one says 'raṭṭha,' that is the head-place. Where one says 'sattha,' that is the teeth-place. Where one says 'puppha,' that is the lip-place. The region of the nose is the nasal-place.

Katthaci pana uraṭṭhānaṃ, siraṭṭhānaṃ, jivhāmūlaṭṭhānantipi āgataṃ. Tattha siraṭṭhānaṃ nāma muddhaṭṭhānameva. Jivhāmūlaṭṭhānaṃ pana sabbavaṇṇānaṃ sādhāraṇanti vadanti.

However, in some treatises the chest-place, the head-place, and the tongue-root-place are also mentioned. Therein, the so-called 'head-place' is the same as the crown-of-the-head-place. But the tongue-root-place, they say, is common to all letters.

Karaṇaṃ catubbidhaṃ – jivhāmūlaṃ, jivhopaggaṃ, jivhaggaṃ, sakaṭṭhānanti.

The articulator is fourfold: the root of the tongue, the blade of the tongue, the tip of the tongue, and the place itself.

Payatanaṃ catubbidhaṃ – saṃvuṭaṃ, vivaṭaṃ, phuṭṭhaṃ, īsaṃphuṭṭhanti. Tattha karaṇānaṃ sakasakaṭṭhānehi saddhiṃ saṃvaraṇādiko visesākāro saṃvuṭādi nāma.

The effort is fourfold: closed, open, contacted, and slightly contacted. Therein, the particular mode, such as closure, of the articulators with their own respective places of articulation, is what is called 'closed,' and so on.

Tattha kaṇṭhapadesānaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭanena uppannā avaṇṇa, kavagga, hakārā kaṇṭhajā nāma. Tālumhi jivhāmajjhasaṅghaṭṭanena uppannā ivaṇṇa, cavagga, yakārā tālujā nāma. Mukhabbhantaramuddhamhi [M 0.0005] jivhopaggasaṅghaṭṭanena uppannā ṭavagga, ra, ḷakārā muddhajā nāma. Upari dantapantiyaṃ jivhaggasaṅghaṭṭanena uppannā tavagga, la, sakārā dantajā nāma. Oṭṭhadvayasaṅghaṭṭanena uppannā uvaṇṇa, pavaggā oṭṭhajā nāma. Niggahītaṃ nāsikajaṃ nāma. Pañcavaggantā pana nāsikaṭṭhānepi sakaṭṭhānepi jāyanti. Ekāro kaṇṭhatālujo. Okāro kaṇṭhoṭṭhajo. Vakāro dantoṭṭhajo. Apica ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā kaṇṭhepi jāyantiyeva. Yadā hakāro vaggantehi vā ya, ra, la, vehi vā yutto hoti, tadā urajoti vadanti. Pañho, tuṇhi, nhāto, vimhito, gayhate, vulhate, avhānaṃ.

Therein, the a-vowel, the ka-class, and the letter h, produced by the mutual contact of the parts of the throat, are called gutturals. The i-vowel, the ca-class, and the letter y, produced by the contact of the middle of the tongue with the palate, are called palatals. The ṭa-class, r, and ḷ, produced by the contact of the blade of the tongue with the crown of the head inside the mouth, are called cerebrals. The ta-class, l, and s, produced by the contact of the tip of the tongue with the upper row of teeth, are called dentals. The u-vowel and the pa-class, produced by the contact of the two lips, are called labials. The niggahīta is called a nasal. The final consonants of the five classes are produced both in the nasal place and in their own respective places. The letter e is guttural-palatal. The letter o is guttural-labial. The letter v is dental-labial. Furthermore, the i-vowel and u-vowel are also produced in the throat. When the letter h is conjoined with the final consonants of the classes or with y, r, l, or v, they say it is 'chest-born.' For example: pañho, tuṇhi, nhāto, vimhito, gayhate, vulhate, avhānaṃ.

Kaṇṭhaṃ saṃvaritvā uccārito akāro saṃvuṭo nāma. Sakasakaṭṭhāna, karaṇāni vivaritvā uccāritā sesasarā ca sa, hakārā ca vivaṭā nāma. Tāniyeva gāḷhaṃ phusāpetvā uccāritā pañcavaggā phuṭṭhā nāma. Thokaṃ phusāpetvā uccāritā ya, ra, la, vā īsaṃphuṭṭhā nāma. Tattha oṭṭhajesu tāva pavaggaṃ vadantānaṃ oṭṭhadvayassa gāḷhaṃ phusanaṃ icchitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Phuṭṭhapayatanikattā pavaggassa. Uvaṇṇaṃ vadantānaṃ pana oṭṭhadvayassa vivaraṇaṃ icchitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Vivaṭapayatanikattā uvaṇṇassa. Esa nayo sesesu sabbesūti.

The letter 'a', pronounced by contracting the throat, is called 'closed' (saṃvuṭa). The remaining vowels and the letters 's' and 'h', pronounced by opening their respective places and articulators, are called 'open' (vivaṭa). The five classes of consonants, pronounced by causing firm contact of those same articulators and places, are called 'contacted' (phuṭṭha). The letters 'y', 'r', 'l', and 'v', pronounced by causing slight contact, are called 'slightly contacted' (īsaṃphuṭṭha). In this regard, for the labials, when pronouncing the pa-class, firm contact of the two lips is required. Why? Because the pa-class has the effort of contact. But when pronouncing the u-vowel, an opening of the two lips is required. Why? Because the u-vowel has the effort of openness. This is the method for all the remaining cases.

Cūḷaniruttiyaṃ pana sabbe rassasarā saṃvuṭā nāma, sabbedīghasarā vivaṭā nāmāti vuttaṃ. Tathā saddasāratthajāliniyaṃ, katthaci sakkaṭaganthe ca. Idaṃ yuttataraṃ. Aññaṭṭhānikabyañjanehi yuttā sarā attano ṭhāna, karaṇāni jahantāpi payatanaṃ na jahanti. Tasmā nānāvaṇṇānaṃ saṃsagge payatanānaṃ saṃsaggabhedopi veditabboti. Tattha “suṇātu me”ti vadanto yadi ṇā-kāraṃ jivhaggena dantaṭṭhāne katvā vadeyya, dantajo nā-kāro eva bhaveyya. Tu-kārañca jivhopaggena muddhaṭṭhāne katvā vadeyya, muddhajo ṭu-kāro eva bhaveyya. Evañca sati akkharavipatti nāma siyā. Esa nayo sesesu muddhajadantajesu. Tasmā kammavācaṃ sāventehi nāma ṭhāna, karaṇa, payatanesu suṭṭhu kusalehi bhavitabbanti.

But in the Cūḷanirutti it is said that all short vowels are called 'closed' and all long vowels are called 'open.' Likewise in the Saddasāratthajālinī and in some Sanskrit treatises. This is more fitting. Vowels conjoined with consonants from other places of articulation, even while abandoning their own place and articulator, do not abandon their effort. Therefore, in the combination of various letters, the distinction in the combination of efforts should also be understood. For instance, if one saying 'suṇātu me' were to pronounce the letter 'ṇā' with the tip of the tongue at the dental place, it would become a dental 'nā.' And if one were to pronounce the syllable 'tu' with the blade of the tongue at the cerebral place, it would become a cerebral 'ṭu.' This being the case, there would be what is called a corruption of the letters. This is the method for the rest of the cerebral and dental sounds. Therefore, those who recite the Kammavācā should indeed be very skilled in place, articulator, and effort.

Sithilañca[M 0.0006], dhanitañca, dīghaṃ, rassaṃ, garuṃ, lahuṃ;

Niggahītaṃ, vimuttañca, sambandhañca, vavatthitaṃ nī. 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16-19, 20, 21 suttesu passitabbaṃ.

Lax and tense, long and short, heavy and light; nasalized and released, connected and separated.

Mudunā vacīpayogena vattabbā vaggapaṭhama, tatiya, pañcamā sithilā nāma. Thaddhena vacīpayogena vattabbā vaggadutiya, catutthā dhanitā nāma. Dīgha, rassā pubbe vuttā. Dīghā ceva saṃyogapubbā ca niggahītantā ca garukā nāma. Sesā lahukā nāma. Yathā saddasahito vāto mukhachiddena bahi anikkhamma nāsasotābhimukho hoti, tathā mukhaṃ avivaṭaṃ katvā vattabbaṃ byañjanaṃ niggahītaṃ nāma. Tena yuttāni sabbabyañjanāni niggahītantāni nāma. Sesā vimuttā nāma. Padasandhivasena vattabbaṃ sambandhaṃ nāma. Padacchedaṃ katvā vattabbaṃ vavatthitaṃ nāma.

The first, third, and fifth consonants of a class, which are to be pronounced with a soft application of speech, are called 'lax.' The second and fourth consonants of a class, which are to be pronounced with a hard application of speech, are called 'tense.' Long and short have been explained before. Syllables that are long, or are preceded by a conjunct consonant, or end with a niggahīta, are called 'heavy.' The rest are called 'light.' A consonant that is to be pronounced with the mouth not open, such that the air accompanied by sound does not exit outwards through the mouth but is directed towards the nasal passage, is called 'nasalized' (niggahīta). All consonants conjoined with it are called 'ending with a niggahīta.' The rest are called 'released.' Pronunciation according to word-juncture is called 'connected.' Pronunciation made with word-division is called 'separated.'

Byañjanavuttirāsi niṭṭhito.

Here ends the Collection on the Production of Consonants.

Lahusaññārāsi

The Section on the Term 'Lahu' (Light)

Jho, lo, po, gho, go.

Jho, lo, po, gho, go.

9. Yuvaṇṇā iyuvaṇṇā (bahūsu) jhalā nāmassante ka. 58; rū. 29; nī. 205.

9. The vowels i and u at the end of a noun are termed 'jhala'.

Anitthiliṅgassa nāmassa ante ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā kamena jhalasaññā honti.

The vowels i and u at the end of a non-feminine noun are respectively termed 'jhala'.

10. Pitthiyaṃ ka. 59; rū. 182; nī. 206.

10. Pitthiyaṃ.

Itthiliṅge nāmassante ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā pasaññā honti.

In the feminine gender, the vowels i and u at the end of a noun are termed 'pa'.

11. Ghā ka. 60; rū. 177; nī. 207.

11. Ghā.

Gho

Gho.

[M 0.0007], Ā iti dvipadaṃ. Itthiliṅge ākāro ghasañño hoti.

This is a two-part rule. In the feminine gender, the vowel ā is termed 'gha'.

12. Go syālapane ka. 57; rū. 71; nī. 214.

12. Go for 'si' in the vocative.

Ālapane si gasañño hoti.

In the vocative, the suffix 'si' is termed 'go'.

Lahusaññārāsi niṭṭhito.

The Section on the Term 'Lahu' is finished.

Saṅketarāsi

The Section on Conventions

13. Vidhi visesanaṃ yaṃ tassa caṃ. 1.1.6; pā. 1.1.72; vidhibbisesanantassa (bahūsu).

13. A grammatical operation applies to that which is specified by a qualifier.

Sutte yaṃ visesanaṃ dissati, tassa vidhi ñātabbo.

In a rule, whatever qualifier is seen, its application should be understood.

‘Ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe’. Narā, nare. Yonanti visesanaṃ. Ṭāṭeti vidhi.

In the rule ‘Ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe,’ the examples are narā and nare. ‘Yonaṃ’ is the qualifier. ‘Ṭāṭe’ is the application.

14. Sattamiyaṃ pubbassa rū. 8 (piṭṭhe); caṃ. 1.1.7; pā. 1.1.66.

14. In the locative, the operation applies to the preceding.

Sattamīniddese pubbavaṇṇasseva vidhi ñātabbo.

When there is a specification in the locative case, the application should be understood as applying only to the preceding element.

‘Saro lopo sare’. Lokaggo apa. thera 1.12.57.

‘A vowel is elided when a vowel follows.’ Example: lokaggo.

15. Pañcamiyaṃ parassa caṃ. 1.1.8; pā. 1.1.67.

15. In the ablative, the operation applies to the following.

Pañcamīniddese parasseva vidhi ñātabbo.

When there is a specification in the ablative case, the application should be understood as applying only to the following element.

‘Ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe’. Narā, nare.

In the rule ‘Ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe,’ the examples are narā and nare.

16. Ādissa caṃ. 1.1.9; pā. 1.1.54.

16. Of the beginning.

Parassa sissamāno dissamāno (mū) vidhi ādivaṇṇassa ñātabbo.

An application prescribed for a following element should be understood as applying to its initial letter.

‘Ra [M 0.0008] saṅkhyāto vā’. Terasa.

In the rule ‘Ra saṅkhyāto vā,’ the example is terasa.

17. Chaṭṭhiyantassa caṃ. 1.1.10; pā. 1.1.52.

17. Of that which is specified by the genitive.

Chaṭṭhīniddese tadantassa vidhi ñātabbo.

When there is a specification in the genitive case, the application should be understood as applying to the end of that which is specified.

‘Rājassi nāmhi’. Rājinā.

In the rule ‘Rājassi nāmhi,’ the example is rājinā.

18. Ṅānubandho caṃ. 1.1.11; pā. 1.1.53.

18. With the indicatory letter ṅ.

Ṅānubandho ādeso chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭhassa antassa ñātabbo.

A substitute with the indicatory letter ṅ should be understood as replacing the final part of that which is specified by the genitive.

‘Gossāvaṅa’. Gavassaṃ.

In the rule ‘Gossāvaṅa,’ the example is gavassaṃ.

19. Ṭānubandhonekavaṇṇo sabbassa caṃ. 1.1.12; pā. 1.1.55; ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassa (bahūsu).

19. A substitute with the indicatory letter ṭ or one that is multilettered replaces the whole.

Yo ca ṭānubandho ādeso, yo ca anekavaṇṇo ādeso, tadubhayaṃ chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭhassa sabbasseva vaṇṇasamudāyassa ñātabbaṃ.

A substitute that has ṭ as an indicatory letter, and a substitute that consists of more than one letter—both of these should be understood as replacing the entire phonemic group of that which is specified by the genitive.

Ṭānubandhe tāva –

Firstly, regarding substitutes with the indicatory letter ṭ:

‘Imassānitthiyaṃ ṭe’. Esu.

In the rule ‘Imassānitthiyaṃ ṭe,’ the example is esu.

Anekavaṇṇe –

Regarding multilettered substitutes:

‘Animi nāmhi’. Anena, iminā.

In the rule ‘Animi nāmhi,’ the examples are anena and iminā.

20. Ñakānubandhā ādyantā caṃ. 1.1.13; pā. 1.1.46.

20. Augments with indicatory ñ or k are prefixed and suffixed.

Ñānubandho āgamo ca kānubandho āgamo ca kamena chaṭṭhīniddiṭṭhassa ādimhi ca ante ca ñātabbo.

An augment with the indicatory letter ñ and an augment with the indicatory letter k should be understood as being added respectively at the beginning and at the end of that which is specified by the genitive.

Ñānubandhe –

Regarding augments with the indicatory letter ñ:

‘Brūto tissiña’. Braviti.

In the rule ‘Brūto tissiña,’ the example is braviti.

Kānubandhe [M 0.0009] –

Regarding augments with the indicatory letter k:

‘Bhūssa vuka’. Babhuva.

In the rule ‘Bhūssa vuka,’ the example is babhuva.

21. Mānubandho sarānamantā paro caṃ. 1.1.14; pā. 1.1.47.

21. An augment with the indicatory letter m comes after the final vowel.

Mānubandho āgamo sarānaṃ antasaramhā paro hoti.

An augment with the indicatory letter m comes after the final vowel of the stem.

‘Najjāyo svāma’. Najjāyo sandanti. ‘Maṃ vā rudhādīnaṃ’. Rundhati. ‘Jara sadānamīma vā’. Jīrati, sīdati.

By ‘Najjāyo svāma’: Najjāyo sandanti. By ‘Maṃ vā rudhādīnaṃ’: Rundhati. By ‘Jara sadānamīma vā’: Jīrati, sīdati.

Imasmiṃ byākaraṇe anekasaratā nāma nadī, purisa iccādīsu liṅgapadesu eva atthi, gamu, pacaiccādīsu dhātupadesu natthi. Sabbadhātuyo byañjanantā eva honti, dhātvantalopakiccaṃ natthi. Tasmā najjāyoti ettha ī-kāro antasaro nāma. Tato ‘najjāyo svāma’ iti suttena ā-kārāgamo. Rundhatīti ettha pana u-kāro antasaro nāma, tato “maṃ vā rudhādīna”nti suttena bindāgamo. Evaṃ jīrati, sīdati iccādīsu. Mrammapotthakesu pana “mānubandho padānamantā paro”ti pāṭho, so sīhaḷapotthakehi na sameti.

In this grammar, the state of having multiple vowels exists only in the section on nominals, in words such as nadī and purisa; it does not exist in the section on roots, such as gamu and paca. All roots are considered to end in a consonant; there is no operation of eliding the final vowel of a root. Therefore, here in najjāyo, the ī is the final vowel. Then, by the rule ‘Najjāyo svāma,’ there is an augment of ā. But here in rundhati, the u is the final vowel, and then by the rule ‘Maṃ vā rudhādīnaṃ,’ there is an augment of the bindu (niggahīta). It is similar in jīrati, sīdati, and so on. However, in the Burmese books, the reading is ‘mānubandho padānamantā paro’ (an augment with indicatory m comes after the end of a word), which does not agree with the Sinhalese books.

22. Vippaṭisedhe caṃ. 1.1.16; pā. 1.4.2.

22. In case of conflict.

Samānavisayānaṃ dvinnaṃ vidhīnaṃ aññamaññapaṭisedharahite ṭhāne yebhuyyena paro vidhi okāsaṃ labhati.

When two rules have the same domain, in a situation where they do not mutually contradict each other, the subsequent rule generally takes precedence.

Cattārome bhikkhave dhammā aṅguttaranikāye -ettha cattārimeti pubbalope sampatte paralopo okāsaṃ labhati.

In `cattārome bhikkhave dhammā`—here, from `cattāro + ime`, when elision of the preceding vowel is possible, the elision of the following vowel takes precedence.

23. Saṅketo nāvayavonubandho caṃ. 1.1.5.

23. An anubandha is a convention, not a component.

Yo vaṇṇo payogassa avayavo na hoti, suttesu saṅketamatto hoti, so anubandho nāma.

A letter that is not a component of the resulting form, but is merely a conventional sign in the rules, is called an anubandha.

‘Gossāva’[M 0.0010]. Gavassaṃ-etena padarūpavidhāne anubandho upayogaṃ na gacchatīti ñāpeti.

In the rule ‘Gossāvaṅa,’ resulting in gavassaṃ—this shows that in the formation of the word-form, the anubandha is not utilized.

24. Vaṇṇaparena savaṇṇopi.

24. By a letter followed by the term 'vaṇṇa', its homogenous counterpart is also included.

Vaṇṇasaddo paro etasmāti vaṇṇaparo, vaṇṇaparena rassasarena savaṇṇopi gayhati sayañca, avaṇṇoti vutte ā-kāropi gayhati a-kāro cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ ivaṇṇuvaṇṇesu.

The term `vaṇṇapara` means 'that which is followed by the word `vaṇṇa`.' By a short vowel that is `vaṇṇapara`, its homogenous long counterpart is also included, as well as itself. This means that when `avaṇṇa` is stated, both the vowel ā and the vowel a are included. The same applies to `ivaṇṇa` and `uvaṇṇa`.

25. Ntuvantumantāvantutavantusambandhī ntu vantumantvāvantutavantu sambandhī (bahūsu).

25. The suffix 'ntu' is related to 'vantu', 'mantu', 'āvantu', and 'tavantu'.

Ntuiti vutte vantu, mantu, āvantu, tavantūnaṃ sambandhībhūto ntukāro gayhati.

When 'ntu' is stated, the 'ntu' that is related to the suffixes 'vantu', 'mantu', 'āvantu', and 'tavantu' is to be understood.

‘Ntantūnaṃ nto yomhi paṭhame’. Guṇavanto, satimanto, yāvanto, bhuttavanto.

In the rule ‘Ntantūnaṃ nto yomhi paṭhame,’ the examples are: guṇavanto, satimanto, yāvanto, bhuttavanto.

Saṅketarāsi niṭṭhito.

The Section on Conventions is finished.

Sandhividhāna

The Method of Sandhi

Atha sandhividhānaṃ dīpiyate.

Now the method of sandhi is explained.

Lopo, dīgho, rasso, vuddhi, ādeso, āgamo, dvibhāvo, vipallāso.

Elision, lengthening, shortening, strengthening, substitution, augment, reduplication, and metathesis.

Loparāsi

The Section on Elision

26. Saro lopo sare ka. 12; rū. 13; nī. 30.

26. A vowel is elided when a vowel follows.

Luppatīti lopo. Sare pare sarūpo vā asarūpo vā pubbo saro lopo hoti.

`Lopa` means 'it is elided.' When a vowel follows, the preceding vowel, whether homogenous or heterogenous, is elided.

Sarūpe tāva –

Firstly, in the case of homogenous vowels:

Avaṇṇe-lokaggo [M 0.0011] apa. thera 1.12.57, bhavāsavo, dha. sa. 1102 avijjāsavo dha. sa. 1102, avijjānusayo vibha. 949.

With the a-vowels: lokaggo, bhavāsavo, avijjāsavo, avijjānusayo.

Ivaṇṇe-munindo, munīrito, varavādīrito, itthindriyaṃ vibha. 219.

With the i-vowels: munindo, munīrito, varavādīrito, itthindriyaṃ.

Uvaṇṇe-bahūpakāro jā. 1.22.588, bahukā ūmi bahūmi, sarabhuyā ūmi sarabhūmi, sarabhuyā udakaṃ sarabhūdakaṃ.

With the u-vowels: bahūpakāro, bahūmi, sarabhūmi, sarabhūdakaṃ.

Asarūpe –

In the case of heterogenous vowels:

Sotindriyaṃ vibha. 219, kāmupādānaṃ, bhavesanā dī. ni. 3.305, bhavogho dha. sa. 1156, so tuṇhassa pārā. 381, diṭṭhānusayo vibha. 949, diṭṭhupādānaṃ, diṭṭhekaṭṭhaṃ, diṭṭhogho dha. sa. 1156, mudindriyaṃ mahāva. 9, puttā matthi dha. pa. 62, urassa dukkho pāci. 402, asantettha na dissanti dha. pa. 304 iccādi.

sotindriyaṃ, kāmupādānaṃ, bhavesanā, bhavogho, so tuṇhassa, diṭṭhānusayo, diṭṭhupādānaṃ, diṭṭhekaṭṭhaṃ, diṭṭhogho, mudindriyaṃ, puttā matthi, urassa dukkho, asantettha na dissanti, and so on.

Iti pubbaloparāsi.

Thus ends the section on the elision of the preceding vowel.

27. Paro kvaci ka. 13; rū. 15; nī. 31.

27. The following vowel is elided sometimes.

Pubbasaramhā sarūpo vā asarūpo vā paro saro kvaci lopo hoti.

After a preceding vowel, the following vowel, whether homogenous or heterogenous, is sometimes elided.

Sarūpe tāva –

Firstly, in the case of homogenous vowels:

Taṃ kadāssu bhavissati jā. 2.22.144 ādayo; taṃ kudassu, kudāssu nāma dummedho, dukkhassantaṃ karissati dha. pa. 376, yadāssa sīlaṃ paññañca jā. 2.22.1474, tadāssu kaṇhaṃ yuñjanti jā. 1.1.29 -kaṇhanti mahākaṇhagoṇaṃ, taṇhāssa vippahīnā, māssu [M 0.0012] kujjha rathesabha, satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyya pārā. 167, 171, āgatāttha tumhe, sotukāmāttha tumhe, māyyo evarūpamakāsi, papaṃ avinduṃ jā. 1.1.2 -pavaḍḍhaṃ āpaṃ labhiṃsūtyattho, nālaṃ kabaḷaṃ padātave jā. 1.1.27 -pa+ādātaveti chedo, gaṇhituntattho, ruppatīti rūpaṃ, bujjhatīti buddho-dīgho, aggīva tappati, itthīva gacchati, nadīva sandati, mātupaṭṭhānaṃ, pitupaṭṭhānaṃ, yete dhammā ādikalyāṇā cūḷava. 399 iccādi.

`Taṃ kadāssu bhavissati`, `kudāssu nāma dummedho, dukkhassantaṃ karissati`, `yadāssa sīlaṃ paññañca`, `tadāssu kaṇhaṃ yuñjanti`—here `kaṇhaṃ` means the great black ox—`taṇhāssa vippahīnā`, `māssu kujjha rathesabha`, `satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyya`, `āgatāttha tumhe`, `sotukāmāttha tumhe`, `māyyo evarūpamakāsi`, `papaṃ avinduṃ`—the meaning is 'they obtained abundant water'—`nālaṃ kabaḷaṃ padātave`—the division is `pa+ādātave`, the meaning is 'to take'—`ruppatīti rūpaṃ`, `bujjhatīti buddho`—with lengthening—`aggīva tappati`, `itthīva gacchati`, `nadīva sandati`, `mātupaṭṭhānaṃ`, `pitupaṭṭhānaṃ`, `yete dhammā ādikalyāṇā`, and so on.

Asarūpe –

In the case of heterogenous vowels:

Itissa pāci. 465, itipi pārā. 1, assamaṇīsi pārā. 135, akataññūsi dha. pa. 383, vandehaṃ, sohaṃ, yassadāni mahāva. 242, chāyāva anapāyinī dha. pa. 2, mādisesu kathāva kā, kinnumāva samaṇiyo madhuvā maññati bālo dha. pa. 69, cakkhundriyaṃ vibha. 219, dveme bhikkhave dhammā a. ni. 2.3, tayome bhikkhave dhammā a. ni. 3.17 iccādi.

`itissa`, `itipi`, `assamaṇīsi`, `akataññūsi`, `vandehaṃ`, `sohaṃ`, `yassadāni`, `chāyāva anapāyinī`, `mādisesu kathāva kā`, `kinnumāva samaṇiyo`, `madhuvā maññati bālo`, `cakkhundriyaṃ`, `dveme bhikkhave dhammā`, `tayome bhikkhave dhammā`, and so on.

Kvacīti kiṃ? Katamā cānanda aniccasaññā a. ni. 10.60.

Why 'sometimes'? For example: `Katamā cānanda aniccasaññā`.

Iti paraloparāsi.

Thus ends the section on the elision of the following vowel.

28. Na dve vā.

28. Or not the two.

Dve pubbaparasarā kvaci lopā na honti vā.

The two vowels, preceding and following, are optionally sometimes not elided.

Appamādo amataṃ padaṃ dha. pa. 21, ko imaṃ pathaviṃvicessati dha. pa. 44.

`Appamādo amataṃ padaṃ`, `ko imaṃ pathaviṃ vicessati`.

Kvacitveva? Sotindriyaṃ vibha. 219, cakkhundriyaṃ vibha. 219,

Why 'sometimes'? For example, `sotindriyaṃ`, `cakkhundriyaṃ`.

Vāti kiṃ[M 0.0013]? Komaṃ vasaliṃ parāmasissati.

Why 'optionally'? For example: `Komaṃ vasaliṃ parāmasissati`.

Ito paṭṭhāya yāvasandhikaṇḍāvasānā yuttaṭṭhānesu sabbattha kvacisaddo, vāsaddo ca vattante. Tattha kvacisaddo nānāpayogaṃ dasseti. Vāsaddo ekapayogassa nānārūpaṃ dasseti. Lopanisedho.

From here on, up to the end of the chapter on sandhi, the words `kvaci` and `vā` apply everywhere in appropriate places. There, the word `kvaci` indicates various applications. The word `vā` indicates various forms of a single application. This is a prohibition of elision.

29. Parasarassa.

29. Of the following vowel.

Niggahītamhā parasarassa kvaci lopo hoti vā.

After a niggahīta, the following vowel is optionally sometimes elided.

Tvaṃsi pe. va. 47; jā. 2.22.764, candaṃva vimalaṃ suddhaṃ dha. pa. 413; su. ni. 642, cakkaṃva vahato padaṃ dha. pa. 1, halaṃdāni pakāsituṃ mahāva. 8, kinti vadeyyaṃ, cīvaranti, pattanti, bhikkhunti.

`tvaṃsi`, `candaṃva vimalaṃ suddhaṃ`, `cakkaṃva vahato padaṃ`, `halaṃdāni pakāsituṃ`, `kinti vadeyyaṃ`, `cīvaranti`, `pattanti`, `bhikkhunti`.

Iti saraloparāsi.

Thus ends the section on vowel elision.

30. Saṃyogādi lopo.

30. Elision of the beginning of a cluster.

Saṃyogassa ādibhūto byañjano kvaci lopo hoti vā.

The initial consonant of a cluster is optionally sometimes elided.

Pupphaṃsā uppajjati pārā. 36 – idha pubbasuttena saralopo, evaṃsa te āsavā pahīnā honti ma. ni. 1.24, sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ, sājīvo garahito mama mi. pa. 6.1.5 - assa+ājīvoti chedo, bhaveyyāti attho.

`Pupphaṃsā uppajjati`—here the vowel is elided by a preceding rule; `evaṃsa te āsavā pahīnā honti`; `sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ`; `sājīvo garahito mama`—the division is `assa+ājīvo`, the meaning is `bhaveyya`.

Tīsu byañjanesu sarūpānaṃ dvinnaṃ ādibyañjanassa lopo – agyāgāraṃ pāci. 326, agyāhito, vutyassa, vityānubhūyate, ekasataṃ khatyā jā. 2.22.594, ratyo, ratyā, ratyaṃ, sakvāhaṃ mārisa devānamindo saṃ. ni. 1.268, iccādi.

Among three consonants, when two are homogenous, the first of the two is elided: `agyāgāraṃ`, `agyāhito`, `vutyassa`, `vityānubhūyate`, `ekasataṃ khatyā`, `ratyo`, `ratyā`, `ratyaṃ`, `sakvāhaṃ mārisa devānamindo`, and so on.

Sarūpānanti [M 0.0014] kiṃ? Titthyā puthuso vadanti su. ni. 897, catutthyantaṃ, chaṭṭhuntaṃ, cakkhvābādhaṃ, vatthvettha.

Why 'homogenous'? For example: `Titthyā puthuso vadanti`, `catutthyantaṃ`, `chaṭṭhuntaṃ`, `cakkhvābādhaṃ`, `vatthvettha`.

Iti byañjanaloparāsi.

Thus ends the section on consonant elision.

31. Lopo.

31. Elision.

Niggahītassa kvaci lopo hoti vā.

The niggahīta is optionally sometimes elided.

Sare pare tāva –

Firstly, when a vowel follows:

Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna bu. vaṃ. 2.27, pupphadānaṃ adāsahaṃ-adāsiṃ+ahanti chedo, bindulopo, puna pubbasaralopo, tuyhatthāya mahāmuni, tuyhevetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ dī. ni. 2.178, tāsāhaṃ santike pāci. 709, tesāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi, pañcannetaṃ dhammānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, channetaṃ dhammānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, samaṇa tveva pucchāmi jā. 2.22.253 samaṇa teva, brāhmaṇa tveva pucchāmi jā. 2.22.258 brāhmaṇa teva -tvaṃ+evāti chedo, vidūnaggamiti.

`Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna`; `pupphadānaṃ adāsahaṃ`—the division is `adāsiṃ+ahaṃ`, with elision of the `bindu` and then elision of the preceding vowel; `tuyhatthāya mahāmuni`; `tuyhevetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ`; `tāsāhaṃ santike`; `tesāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmi`; `pañcannetaṃ dhammānaṃ adhivacanaṃ`; `channetaṃ dhammānaṃ adhivacanaṃ`; `samaṇa tveva pucchāmi`; `brāhmaṇa tveva pucchāmi`—the division is `tvaṃ+eva`; `vidūnaggamiti`.

Byañjane pare –

When a consonant follows:

Taṃ tuyhamūle paṭidesemi.

`Taṃ tuyhamūle paṭidesemi`.

Gāthāyaṃ –

In a verse:

Ariyasaccānadassanaṃ khu. pā. 5.11, etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ dha. pa. 183, khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā.

`Ariyasaccānadassanaṃ`, `etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ`, `khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca`.

Māgame pare –

When the augment 'm' follows:

Garuḷo uragāmiva jā. 1.4.124 supaṇṇo, dhammo arahatāmiva dī. ni. 2.348, āloko passatāmiva su. ni. 769, bako kakkaṭakāmiva jā. 1.1.38, nabhaṃ tārakitāmiva jā. 2.22.1989 tārācitāmiva, padumaṃ [M 0.0015] hatthagatāmiva jā. 2.22.2336 -etesu māgame bindulopo, byañjane pubbasaradīgho ca.

As a Garuḷa to serpents, as the Dhamma to Arahants, as light to those who see, as a heron to crabs, as the sky to the stars, as a lotus in the hand—in these cases, with the augment 'm', there is elision of the bindu, and the preceding vowel is lengthened.

Tathā saṃupasaggassa bindulope antasaradīgho –

Likewise, with the elision of the bindu of the prefix 'saṃ', the final vowel is lengthened:

Sārāgo, sāratto, avisāhāro, sārambho, sāraddho, sāketaṃ nagaraṃ, sādhāraṇaṃ, saṃ assa atthīti sāmī.

Sārāgo (impassioned), sāratto (enamored), avisāhāro (not scattered), sārambho (exertion), sāraddho (resolute), the city of Sāketa, sādhāraṇaṃ (in common); one for whom there is possession (saṃ) is a master (sāmī).

Samāse tumantamhi niccaṃ –

In a compound, when the first member ends in '-tuṃ', the elision of the bindu is obligatory:

Kattukāmo, gantukāmo iccādi.

Kattukāmo (desiring to do), gantukāmo (desiring to go), etc.

Iti binduloparāsi.

Thus ends the section on the elision of the bindu.

32. Syādilopo pubbassekassa.

32. Elision of the case ending of the first of two words.

Vicchāyaṃ ekassa vibhatyantassa padassa dvitte kate pubbapadassa syādilopo hoti.

In repetition, when a single inflected word is doubled, the case ending of the first word is elided.

Ekekaṃ, ekekāni, ekekena, ekekassa iccādi.

Ekekaṃ, ekekāni, ekekena, ekekassa, etc.

Māgame –

In the Māgadhī dialect:

Ekamekaṃ, ekamekāni iccādi.

Ekamekaṃ, ekamekāni, etc.

Iti syādiloparāsi.

Thus ends the section on the elision of case endings.

Appavidhānamuccate.

A miscellaneous rule is stated.

33. Tadaminādīni caṃ. 5.2.1.27; pā. 6.3.109; mu. 2.34; kā. 2.27.

33. Tadaminādīni.

Mahāvuttisuttamidaṃ, tadaminādīni padarūpāni iminā nipātanena sijjhantīti attho.

This is a sutta of wide application. The meaning is that word-forms such as 'tadamina' are accomplished by this rule for irregular formations.

Saralopo byañjane –

Elision of a vowel before a consonant:

Lābu=alābu[M 0.0016], pidhānaṃ=apidhānaṃ, dvāraṃ pidahitvā=apidahitvā, gini=aggini, ratnaṃ=ratanaṃ, nhānaṃ=nahānaṃ, asnāti=asanāti, hanti=hanati, hanti kuddho puthujjano a. ni. 7.64, phalaṃ ve kadaliṃ hanti a. ni. 4.68, sakkāro kāpurisaṃ hanti. Katthaci bahuvacanampi dissati. Vikkosamānā tibbāhi, hanti nesaṃ varaṃ varaṃ jā. 2.22.2370.

Lābu from alābu (gourd); pidhānaṃ from apidhānaṃ (a lid); pidahitvā from apidahitvā (having closed); gini from aggini (fire); ratnaṃ from ratanaṃ (a jewel); nhānaṃ from nahānaṃ (bathing); asnāti from asanāti (eats); hanti from hanati (kills), as in: “An angry worldling kills”; “Fruit indeed kills the plantain tree”; “Honor kills a wicked person.” Sometimes the plural is also seen: “Shouting fiercely, they kill the best among them.”

Ivaṇṇalope –

In the elision of the vowel 'i':

Ārāmarukkhacetyāni=cetiyāni dha. pa. 188, athatthekasataṃ khatyā jā. 2.22.594 =khattiyā, tithyā puthuso vadanti su. ni. 897. Tithyā puthuso niviṭṭhā su. ni. 898 =titthiyā. Viddhasto=viddhaṃsito, utrasto=utrāsito, sneho=sineho, klesavatthūni=kilesavatthūni, kriyā=kiriyā, plavanti=pilavanti.

Cetyāni from cetiyāni (shrines), as in ārāmarukkhacetyāni; khatyā from khattiyā (warriors), as in athatthekasataṃ khatyā; tithyā from titthiyā (sectarians), as in tithyā puthuso vadanti and tithyā puthuso niviṭṭhā; viddhasto from viddhaṃsito (destroyed); utrasto from utrāsito (terrified); sneho from sineho (affection); klesavatthūni from kilesavatthūni (bases of defilement); kriyā from kiriyā (action); plavanti from pilavanti (they float).

Uvaṇṇalope –

In the elision of the vowel 'u':

Paddhāni=padumāni, usmā=usumā iccādi.

Paddhāni from padumāni (lotuses); usmā from usumā (heat), etc.

Saṃyogādibyañjanalopo ca –

And elision of a consonant at the beginning of a conjunct:

Puttānañhi vadho dukho, mātigho labhate dukhaṃ, appassādā kāmā dukhā, natthi kāmaparaṃ dukhaṃ jā. 2.19.118, sekho=sekkho, apekhā=apekkhā, upasampadāpekho=upasampadāpekkho mahāva. 70 iccādi.

Sekho from sekkho (a trainee); apekhā from apekkhā (longing); upasampadāpekho from upasampadāpekkho (one aspiring for higher ordination). Examples: “For the slaughter of sons is suffering (dukho)”; “A matricide obtains suffering (dukhaṃ)”; “Sensual pleasures have little taste and are suffering (dukhā)”; “There is no suffering beyond sensual pleasure (dukhaṃ),” etc.

Sarena saha byañjanalopo –

Elision of a consonant together with its vowel:

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso a. ni. 6.58, akkhāti=akkhāyati, gandhaṃ ghāti=ghāyati, abhiññā=abhiññāya, pariññā=pariññāya, adhiṭṭhā=adhiṭṭhāya, patiṭṭhā=patiṭṭhāya, āvīkatā hissa phāsu mahāva. 134[M 0.0017], assavanatā dhammassa parihāyanti mahāva. 8, vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjati paṭṭhā. 3.1.98, dasāhaparamatā dhāretabbaṃ pārā. 462, nāyaṃ brāhmaṇabhojanatthā, tilodano hehiti jā. 1.8.1, visasenova gārayho, yassatthā rukkharopakā jā. 1.3.54 =visasenovāti evaṃnāmako rājā eva, yassatthā dūramāyanti jā. 1.3.28 – yassāti udarassa, pitu atthā candavatī jā. 1.9.66, upādārūpaṃ, anupādā vimutto, saddhāpabbajito, upanidhāpaññatti. Saṃvidhāvahāro, yāti=yāyati, vāti=vāyati, nibbāti=nibbāyati, nibbanti=nibbāyanti, pahāti=pahāyati, sappatisso=sappatissayo, suhado=suhadayo=sabbattha yalopo,

Paṭisaṅkhā from paṭisaṅkhāya, as in paṭisaṅkhā yoniso; akkhāti from akkhāyati (proclaims); ghāti from ghāyati, as in gandhaṃ ghāti (smells a scent); abhiññā from abhiññāya (for direct knowledge); pariññā from pariññāya (for full understanding); adhiṭṭhā from adhiṭṭhāya (having resolved); patiṭṭhā from patiṭṭhāya (having established); phāsu from phāsuko, as in āvīkatā hissa phāsu (openness is ease for him); assavanatā from assavanatāya, as in assavanatā dhammassa parihāyanti (through not hearing the Dhamma, they decline); tadārammaṇatā from tadārammaṇatāya, as in vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjati (the resultant consciousness with that as its object arises); dasāhaparamatā from dasāhaparamatāya, as in dasāhaparamatā dhāretabbaṃ (it should be kept for a maximum of ten days); atthā from atthāya, as in nāyaṃ brāhmaṇabhojanatthā (this is not for the brahmin’s meal); hehiti from hehissati, as in tilodano hehiti (there will be rice with sesame); gārayho from gārayhova, as in visasenova gārayho (blameworthy like Visasena); yassatthā from yassa atthāya (for the sake of which), as in yassatthā rukkharopakā (for whose sake tree-planters), where Visasena is the name of a king, and yassatthā dūramāyanti (for whose sake they come from afar), where yassa refers to the belly; pitu atthā from pitu atthāya (for the father’s sake), as in pitu atthā candavatī; upādārūpaṃ from upādāyarūpaṃ (derivative matter); anupādā from anupādāya (without clinging), as in anupādā vimutto (liberated without clinging); saddhāpabbajito from saddhāya pabbajito (one gone forth out of faith); upanidhāpaññatti from upanidhāya paññatti (a regulation made in reference to something); saṃvidhāvahāro from saṃvidhāya avahāro (transaction by agreement); yāti from yāyati (goes); vāti from vāyati (blows); nibbāti from nibbāyati (is extinguished); nibbanti from nibbāyanti (they are extinguished); pahāti from pahāyati (abandons); sappatisso from sappatissayo (respectful); suhado from suhadayo (a good-hearted friend). In all these, there is elision of 'ya'.

Mukharo=mukhakharo, vācākaraṇo=vākkaraṇo, vācāpatho=byappatho=vāssa byattaṃ, rassattañca, evaṃ byākho=evaṃ viya kho=vissa byattaṃ, dīgho ca yalopo ca.

Mukharo from mukhakharo (harsh-mouthed); vācākaraṇo from vākkaraṇo (articulation); byappatho from vācāpatho (path of speech), where 'vā' becomes 'bya' and there is shortening; likewise, byākho from 'evaṃ viya kho' (just like), where 'vi' becomes 'by', and there is lengthening and elision of 'ya'.

Lolupo, momuho, kukkuco, susukho, roruvoiccādīsu pana atisayatthadīpanatthaṃ padadvittaṃ katvā pubbapadesu akkharalopo.

Furthermore, in words such as lolupo (very greedy), momuho (utterly deluded), kukkuco (remorseful), susukho (very happy), and roruvo (wailing), the word is doubled to indicate intensity, and then a letter is elided from the first part.

Padalopo ādimajjhantesu –

Elision of a word at the beginning, middle, or end:

Datto=devadatto, assehi yutto ratho=assaratho, rūpabhavo=rūpaṃ, arūpabhavo=arūpaṃ iccādi.

Datto from Devadatto; assaratho from assehi yutto ratho (a chariot yoked with horses); rūpaṃ from rūpabhavo (existence in the form realm); arūpaṃ from arūpabhavo (existence in the formless realm), etc.

Loparāsi niṭṭhito.

The section on elision is finished.

Dīgha, rassarāsi

The Section on Long and Short Vowels

Atha [M 0.0018] dīgha, rassā dīpiyante.

Now long and short vowels are explained.

34. Sesā dīghā.

34. The remaining vowels become long.

Pakkhittamidaṃ suttaṃ. Luttehi vā ādesakatehi vā vaṇṇehi sesā rassasarā kvaci dīghā honti vā.

This is an inserted rule. After letters have been elided or substituted, the remaining short vowels are sometimes optionally made long.

Pubbalutte tāva –

First, in the case of elision of a preceding vowel:

Tatrāyamādi bhavatiṃ dha. pa. 375, tatrābhiratimiccheyya dha. pa. 88; saṃ. ni. 5.198, buddhānussati, saddhīdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ su. ni. 183, anāgārehi cūbhayaṃ dha. pa. 404; su. ni. 633, dhammūpasaṃhitā dī. ni. 2.349, tathūpamaṃ dhammavaraṃ adesayi khu. pā. 6.13, tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho dī. ni. 2.221 iccādi.

'Tatrāyam' from 'tatra ayam'; 'tatrābhiratim' from 'tatra abhiratim', as in 'tatrābhiratimiccheyya'; 'buddhānussati' from 'buddha-anussati'; 'saddhīdha' from 'saddhā idha', as in 'saddhīdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ'; 'cūbhayaṃ' from 'ca ubhayaṃ', as in 'anāgārehi cūbhayaṃ'; 'dhammūpasaṃhitā' from 'dhamma-upasaṃhitā'; 'tathūpamaṃ' from 'tathā upamaṃ', as in 'tathūpamaṃ dhammavaraṃ adesayi'; 'vūpasamo' from 'vi-upasamo', as in 'tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho'; and so on.

Paralutte –

In the case of elision of a following vowel:

Ajitāti bhagavā avoca su. ni. 1039, 1041, sumedho sājāto cāti, ruppatīti rūpaṃ saṃ. ni. 3.79, bujjhatīti buddho, sādhūtipatissuṇitvā dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.4 kāḷayakkhinīvatthu, kiṃsūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ su. ni. 184 iccādi.

'Ajitāti' from 'Ajita iti', as in 'Ajitāti bhagavā avoca'; 'cāti' from 'ca iti', as in 'sumedho sājāto cāti'; 'ruppatīti' from 'ruppati iti', as in 'ruppatīti rūpaṃ'; 'bujjhatīti' from 'bujjhati iti', as in 'bujjhatīti buddho'; 'sādhūti' from 'sādhu iti', as in 'sādhūtipatissuṇitvā'; 'kiṃsūdha' from 'kiṃ su idha', as in 'kiṃsūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ'; and so on.

Bindulutte –

In the case of elision of the bindu:

Tāsāhaṃ pāci. 709, tesāhaṃ jā. 2.22.313.

Tāsāhaṃ, tesāhaṃ.

Ādesesu –

In the case of substitutions:

Myāyaṃdhammo mahāva. 7, svāhaṃ pe. va. 485, vityānubhūyate iccādi.

Myāyaṃdhammo, svāhaṃ, vityānubhūyate, and so on.

Yadipi imāni rūpāni byañjane uparisuttena sijjhanti, luttādesesu pana niccamiva dīghasiddhiñāpanatthaṃ idaṃ suttaṃ pakkhittanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Although these forms are also covered by a subsequent rule concerning consonants, it should be understood that this rule has been inserted here to show that lengthening is almost always obligatory in cases of elision and substitution.

35. Byañjane dīgharassā ka. 25, 26; nī. 35, 36, 64, 71, 165, 179.

35. Lengthening and shortening before a consonant.

Byañjane [M 0.0019] pare rassadīghānaṃ kvaci dīgha, rassā honti vā. Tattha dīghavidhi nāma gāthāvasena vā āgamavasena vā vacanasukhavasena vā buddhisukhavasena vā hoti.

When a consonant follows, short and long vowels may optionally be lengthened or shortened. The rule for lengthening, in particular, is applied for the sake of meter, tradition, euphony, or ease of understanding.

Tattha gāthāvasena tāva –

First, for the sake of meter:

Madhuvāmaññati bālo dha. pa. 69, khantī ca sovacassatā khu. pā. 5.10, evaṃ gāme munī care dha. pa. 49, sakko ujū ca suhujū ca khu. pā. 9.1 iccādi.

“The fool thinks it is like honey (madhuvā)”; “patience (khantī) and compliance”; “thus a sage (munī) should wander in the village”; “able, upright (ujū), and very upright (suhujū),” and so on.

Āgame –

According to tradition:

Uragāmiva jā. 1.7.30, arahatāmiva dī. ni. 2.348, passatāmiva su. ni. 769 iccādi. Gāthāvasenātipi yujjati.

Uragāmiva (like a serpent), arahatāmiva (like Arahants), passatāmiva (like those who see), and so on. This is also suitable for the sake of meter.

Vacanasukhañca buddhisukhañca purime sesadīghepi labbhati.

Ease of pronunciation and ease of understanding are also found in the aforementioned case of the lengthening of the remaining vowel.

Tattha vacanasukhe –

In the case of euphony:

Chārattaṃ mānattaṃ cūḷava. 97, pakaṭṭhaṃ vacanaṃ pāvacanaṃ, pāsādo, pākāro, pāvassi megho, nagaraṃ pāvisi, pāvekkhi, pārisuddhi, pāṭipado, caturāsītisahassāni dha. sa. aṭṭha. 584 iccādi.

Chārattaṃ (probation); mānattaṃ (penance); pāvacanaṃ from pavacanaṃ (scripture), meaning excellent speech; pāsādo (palace); pākāro (wall); pāvassi (it rained); pāvisi (he entered); pāvekkhi (he entered); pārisuddhi (perfect purity); pāṭipado (the first day); caturāsītisahassāni (eighty-four thousand), and so on.

Buddhisukhaṃ nāma padacchedañāṇasukhaṃ. Tattha –

Ease of understanding means the ease of discerning the division of words. For example:

Sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ pārā. 1, sātthikā dhammadesanā, cakkhumāssa yathā andho iccādi.

Sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ (meaningful and well-phrased); sātthikā dhammadesanā (a Dhamma teaching with its benefit); cakkhumāssa yathā andho (as if one who was blind now has sight), and so on.

Bindulutte pana sārāgo, sāratto iccādīni pubbe uddhaṭāniyeva.

In the case of the elision of the bindu, however, sārāgo, sāratto, and so on, have already been cited above.

Iti dīgharāsi.

Thus ends the section on lengthening.

Rassasandhimhi [M 0.0020] gāthāvasena tāva –

Regarding shortening in sandhi, first for the sake of meter:

Yiṭṭhaṃvahutaṃva loke dha. pa. 108, bhovādi nāma so hoti dha. pa. 396; su. ni. 625, yathābhāvi guṇena so iccādi.

Yiṭṭhaṃ va hutaṃ va loke (where vā is shortened to va); bhovādi nāma so hoti (where bhovādī is shortened to bhovādi); yathābhāvi guṇena so (where yathābhāvī is shortened to yathābhāvi), and so on.

Āgame ya, ra, dāgamesu pubbarasso –

According to tradition, when y, r, or d are inserted, the preceding vowel is shortened:

Yathayidaṃ a. ni. 1.1-4, tathayidaṃ, yathariva amhākaṃ bhagavā, tathariva bhikkhusaṅgho, sammadeva samācare saṃ. ni. 1.112, sammadakkhāto mayā satisambojjhaṅgo saṃ. ni. 5.194 iccādi.

Yathayidaṃ (from yathā-idaṃ); tathayidaṃ (from tathā-idaṃ); yathariva (from yathā-iva), as in 'yathariva amhākaṃ bhagavā'; tathariva (from tathā-iva), as in 'tathariva bhikkhusaṅgho'; sammadeva (from sammā-eva), as in 'sammadeva samācare'; sammadakkhāto (from sammā-akkhāto), as in 'sammadakkhāto mayā satisambojjhaṅgo', and so on.

Saṃyogarasso nāma bahulaṃ labbhati –

Shortening before a conjunct consonant is frequently found:

Akkamo, parakkamo, akkhāto, aññā, aññindriyaṃ, aññātaṃ bhagavā, aññātaṃ sugata, attharaṇaṃ, apphoṭeti, alliyati, acchindati, assādo, ābhassaro, pabhassaro, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, jhānassa lābhimhi vasimhi pārā. 203-204.

Akkamo (step) and parakkamo (exertion); akkhāto (declared); aññā (final knowledge); aññindriyaṃ (the faculty of final knowledge); aññātaṃ (understood), as in 'aññātaṃ bhagavā, aññātaṃ sugata'; attharaṇaṃ (a covering); apphoṭeti (snaps the fingers); alliyati (clings); acchindati (cuts off); assādo (gratification); ābhassaro (radiant) and pabhassaro (luminous); sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ (the knowledge of omniscience); lābhimhi (I am a gainer) and vasimhi (I am a master), as in 'jhānassa lābhimhi vasimhi'.

Tā, topaccayesupi rasso –

Shortening also occurs before the suffixes -tā and -to:

Kataññutā, atthaññutā, dhammaññutā, kaññato, nadito, vadhuto.

Kataññutā (gratitude); atthaññutā (knowing the meaning); dhammaññutā (knowing the Dhamma); kaññato (from a girl); nadito (from a river); vadhuto (from a daughter-in-law).

Samāse –

In a compound:

Itthipumaṃ, itthiliṅgaṃ, itthibhāvo, sabbaññubuddho iccādi.

Itthipumaṃ (female and male); itthiliṅgaṃ (feminine gender); itthibhāvo (womanhood); sabbaññubuddho (the omniscient Buddha), and so on.

Iti rassarāsi.

Thus ends the section on shortening.

Dīgha, rassarāsi niṭṭhito.

The section on lengthening and shortening is finished.

Vuddhirāsi

The Section on Vowel Gradation

Atha [M 0.0021] vuddhisandhi dīpiyate.

Now, the vuddhi-sandhi is explained.

36. Yuvaṇṇānameo luttā ka. 14; rū. 16; nī. 34.

36. For i- and u-vowels, e and o are substituted after elision.

Luttā pubbasaramhā vā parasaramhā vā sesānaṃ ivaṇṇuvaṇṇānaṃ kamena e, oādesā honti vā.

When a preceding or following vowel has been elided, for the remaining i-vowels and u-vowels, the substitutions e and o respectively occur, optionally.

Paraivaṇṇe –

When a following i-vowel is involved:

Bandhusseva samāgamo, ateva me acchariyaṃ jā. 2.22.1988, vāteritaṃ, jineritaṃ.

A meeting as if with a relative; exceedingly wonderful to me; stirred by the wind; uttered by the Conqueror.

Parauvaṇṇe –

When a following u-vowel is involved:

Gaṅgodakaṃ, pattaṃ vodakaṃ katvā cūḷava. 376, saṅkhyaṃ su. ni. 754 nopeti vedagū mahāni. 6, udakomiva jātaṃ.

Water of the Ganges; having made the bowl waterless; the one who has attained knowledge does not enter into an enumeration; born like a water-wave.

Kriyāpadesu –

In verb forms:

Veti, apeti, upeti, apekkhā, upekkhā iccādi.

Veti (goes apart); apeti (goes away); upeti (approaches); apekkhā (regard); upekkhā (equanimity); and so on.

Pubbaivaṇṇe –

When a preceding i-vowel is involved:

Rathesabho, janesabho, munelayo iccādi- tattha rathīnaṃ āsabho jeṭṭhakoti rathesabho, rathīnanti rathavantānaṃ ratharuḷhānaṃ yodhānanti attho. Janīnaṃ āsabho janesabho, janīnanti janavantānaṃ issarānaṃ. Munīnaṃ ālayo vihāro munelayo.

Rathesabho (chief of charioteers), janesabho (chief of men), munelayo (abode of sages), and so on. Therein, rathesabho is 'the chief (āsabho), the foremost (jeṭṭhako), of charioteers (rathīnaṃ)'; here 'of charioteers' means of those who have chariots, of warriors mounted on chariots. Janesabho is 'the chief of men (janīnaṃ)'; here 'of men' means of people of substance, of lords. Munelayo is 'the abode (ālayo), the dwelling (vihāro), of sages (munīnaṃ)'.

Pubbauvaṇṇe –

When a preceding u-vowel is involved:

Sundarā itthī sotthi, sundaro attho yassāti sotthi, rassattaṃ, maṅgalaṃ.

Sotthi: that which has a good meaning (sundaro attho) is sotthi (from su + atthi); it involves shortening; it means auspiciousness.

Vuddhirāsi niṭṭhito.

The Section on Vowel Gradation is finished.

Ādesasandhi

Substitution Sandhi

Athādesasandhi [M 0.0022] dīpiyate.

Now the substitution sandhi is explained.

37. Yavā sare ka. 18, 19, 21, 45; nī. 44, 46, 47, 51, 58.

37. Y and v when a vowel follows.

Sare pare ivaṇṇuvaṇṇānaṃ ya, vādesā honti vā.

When a vowel follows, for i-vowels and u-vowels the substitutions y and v occur, optionally.

Ivaṇṇe –

In the case of an i-vowel:

Paṭisanthāravutyassa dha. pa. 376, sabbā vityānubhūyate, kyāhaṃ aparajjhāmi pārā. 383 – idha paṭhamaṃ bindhulopo, sutā ca paṇḍitātyattha, sutā ca paṇḍitātyamhā jā. 2.21.149, ñāto senāpatītyāhaṃ jā. 2.21.94, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ pārā. 411, iccassa vacanīyaṃ dīghanikāye, paccuttaritvā, paccāharati pārā. 305-307, pacceti, paccayo, acceti, accayo dī. ni. 1.251, accāyaṃ majjhimo khaṇḍo jā. 1.7.33 – atireko ayaṃ majjhimo khaṇḍotyattho, apuccaṇḍatā – aputiaṇḍatātyattho, jaccandho, jaccaghānako, jacceḷako, abbhuggacchati, abbheti, abbhokāso dī. ni. 1.191, ajjhokāso ajjhāgamā iccādi.

Paṭisanthāravutyassa (paṭisanthāravutti + assa): his practice is friendliness; sabbā vityānubhūyate (vīti + anubhūyate): all is experienced as passed beyond; kyāhaṃ aparajjhāmi (ki + ahaṃ): do I offend?—here first there is elision of the bindu; sutā ca paṇḍitātyattha (iti + attha): the meaning is 'the learned and wise'; sutā ca paṇḍitātyamhā (iti + amhā): from us who are learned and wise; ñāto senāpatītyāhaṃ (senāpati + iti + ahaṃ): I am known as the general; iccetaṃ kusalaṃ (iti + etaṃ): this is skillful; iccassa vacanīyaṃ (iti + assa): this should be said to him; paccuttaritvā (paṭi + uttaritvā): having replied; paccāharati (paṭi + āharati): brings back; pacceti (paṭi + eti): returns; paccayo (paṭi + ayo): condition; acceti (ati + eti): transgresses; accayo (ati + ayo): transgression; accāyaṃ majjhimo khaṇḍo (ati + ayaṃ): this middle section is excessive—the meaning is 'this middle section is excessive (atireko)'; apuccaṇḍatā: not being harsh in return—the meaning is 'a-paṭi-caṇḍatā'; jaccandho (jāti + andho): blind from birth; jaccaghānako (jāti + aghānako): unable to smell from birth; jacceḷako (jāti + eḷako): mute from birth; abbhuggacchati (abhi + uggacchati): rises up; abbheti (abhi + eti): approaches; abbhokāso (abhi + okāso): open space; ajjhokāso (adhi + okāso): open space; ajjhāgamā (adhi + āgamā): arrival; and so on.

Vātveva? Itissa muhuttampi pāci. 465, atisigaṇo, adhīritaṃ.

And in the optional case? Itissa muhuttampi (iti + assa): for him even for a moment; atisigaṇo: very swift; adhīritaṃ: placed upon.

Ettha ca iccetantiādīsu iminā suttena iti, pati, atiputi, jāti, abhi, adhisaddānaṃ ivaṇṇassa yattaṃ, ‘tavagga, varaṇāna’…nti suttena yamhi tavaggassa cattaṃ, ‘vagga, la, sehi te’ti suttena yassa pubbarūpattaṃ, abhi, adhisaddesu pana ‘catutthadutiyesvesa’…nti suttena vaggacatutthānaṃ tatiyattaṃ.

And here, in iccetaṃ and so on, by this rule the i-vowel of the words iti, pati, atipati, jāti, abhi, and adhi becomes y; by the rule beginning 'tavagga...', the t-group becomes the c-group when y follows; by the rule beginning 'vagga...', the y is assimilated to the preceding form; but in the words abhi and adhi, by the rule beginning 'catutthadutiyesvesa...', the fourth consonant of a group becomes the third.

Uvaṇṇe [M 0.0023] –

In the case of a u-vowel:

Cakkhvābādhamāgacchati, pātvākāsi ma. ni. 2.308, vatthvettha vihitaṃ niccaṃ, dvākāro mahāva. 9, madhvāsavo pāci. 328, anvayo, anveti, svākkhāto mahāva. 26, 62, svākāro mahāva. 9, bahvābādho iccādi.

Cakkhvābādhamāgacchati (cakkhu + ābādhaṃ): an eye-disease comes; pātvākāsi (pātu + akāsi): he made manifest; vatthvettha vihitaṃ niccaṃ (vatthu + ettha): the object here is always prescribed; dvākāro (du + ākāro): duality; madhvāsavo (madhu + āsavo): honey-liquor; anvayo (anu + ayo): consequence; anveti (anu + eti): follows; svākkhāto (su + akkhāto): well-proclaimed; svākāro (su + ākāro): of good form; bahvābādho (bahu + ābādho): much affliction; etc.

38. Eonaṃ ka. 17, 18; rū. 19, 20; nī. 43, 44.

38. Of e and o.

Sare pare e, onaṃ ya, vādeso hoti vā.

When a vowel follows, for e and o the substitutions y and v occur, optionally.

Kyassa byapathayo assu su. ni. 967, kyassu idha gocarā su. ni. 967 -ke+assa puggalassāti attho, byapathayoti vacanapathā, yathā nāmaṃ tathā jhassa-ce+assāti chedo, tyāhaṃ evaṃ vadeyyaṃ ma. ni. 1.30, tyassa pahīnā honti, putto tyāhaṃ mahārāja jā. 1.1.7, pabbatyāhaṃ gandhamādane jā. 2.22.397, adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo mahāva. 7, yyassa vippaṭisārajā, yyassa te honti anatthakāmā, yyassu maññāmi samaṇe-ettha ca avisiṭṭhepi vacanasadde ye+assāti padacchedabuddhisukhatthaṃ ‘yyassā’ti potthakāropanaṃ yujjatiyeva, yathā taṃ? ‘Yadāssa sīlaṃ paññañca’ jā. 2.22.1474 iccādīsu viya, kvatthosi jīvitena me, yāvatakvassa kāyo, tāvatakvassa byāmo dī. ni. 2.35, atha khvassa, atthi khvetaṃ brāhmaṇa, yatvādhikaraṇaṃ dī. ni. 1.213, yvāhaṃ, svāhaṃ iccādi.

Kyassa byapathayo assu, kyassu idha gocarā: the meaning is 'for which person' (ke + assa); byapathayo means 'paths of speech'; yathā nāmaṃ tathā jhassa: the division is ce + assa; tyāhaṃ evaṃ vadeyyaṃ (te + ahaṃ): I would say to you; tyassa pahīnā honti (te + assa): they are abandoned for him; putto tyāhaṃ mahārāja (te + ahaṃ): I am your son, O great king; pabbatyāhaṃ gandhamādane (pabbate + ahaṃ): I am on Mount Gandhamādana; adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo (me + ayaṃ): this Dhamma has been attained by me; yyassa vippaṭisārajā (ye + assa): for whom there are regrets; yyassa te honti anatthakāmā (ye + assa): for whom there are those who wish harm; yyassu maññāmi samaṇe (ye + assu): whom I consider to be ascetics—and here, even in the case of an ambiguous word, for ease of understanding the word division ye + assa, the writing 'yyassā' in books is indeed appropriate, just as in 'Yadāssa sīlaṃ paññañca' (yadā + assa), etc.; kvatthosi jīvitena me (ko + atthosi): for what purpose is my life?; yāvatakvassa kāyo (yāvatako + assa): as large as his body is; tāvatakvassa byāmo (tāvatako + assa): so large is his fathom; atha khvassa (kho + assa): then indeed for him; atthi khvetaṃ brāhmaṇa (kho + etaṃ): there is indeed this, brahmin; yatvādhikaraṇaṃ (yato + adhikaraṇaṃ): because of which; yvāhaṃ (yo + ahaṃ): I who; svāhaṃ (so + ahaṃ): I who am he; etc.

Vātveva? So ahaṃ vicarissāmi su. ni. 194, so ahaṃ bhante.

And in the optional case? So ahaṃ vicarissāmi: I, that one, will wander; so ahaṃ bhante: I, that one, venerable sir.

39. Yuvaṇṇānamiyaṅauvaṅa moga. 5-136 (yuvaṇṇāna miyaṅuvaṅa sare).

39. Iyaṅ and uvaṅ for i- and u-vowels.

Sare pare ivaṇṇuvaṇṇantānaṃ padānaṃ iyaṅa, uvaṅaādesā honti vā. Ṅānubandho antādesattho. Evaṃ sabbattha.

When a vowel follows, for words ending in i-vowels and u-vowels, the substitutions iyaṅ and uvaṅ occur, optionally. The anubandha ṅ indicates that the substitution is of the final part. Thus everywhere.

Idha [M 0.0024] ekekassa padassa rūpadvayaṃ vuccate.

Here, a pair of forms for each word is stated.

Ivaṇṇe –

In the case of an i-vowel:

Tiyantaṃ tyantaṃ – tattha tiyantanti iminā suttena siddhaṃ, tyantanti ‘yavā sare’ti suttena. Evaṃ sesesu. Aggiyāgāre agyāgāre, catutthiyatthe mahāva. 37 catutthyatthe, pañcamiyatthe pañcamyatthe, pathaviyākāso pathabyākāso, viyañjanaṃ byañjanaṃ, viyākato byākato, viyākaṃsu byākaṃsu, viyatto byatto, viyūḷho byūḷho, dhammaṃ adhiyeti ajjheti, patiyeti pacceti pattiyāyati vā, pariyaṅko pallaṅko, vipariyāso vipallāso, idha ekarūpaṃ hoti – pariyatti, pariyatto, pariyāyo, pallaṅkoiccādīsu parisadde rassa lattaṃ katvā issa ‘yavā sare’ti yatte kate yassa pubbarūpattaṃ.

Tiyantaṃ / tyantaṃ (ti + antaṃ): here, tiyantaṃ is formed by this rule, and tyantaṃ by the rule 'yavā sare'. Thus for the rest. Aggiyāgāre / agyāgāre (aggi + āgāre); catutthiyatthe / catutthyatthe (catutthī + atthe); pañcamiyatthe / pañcamyatthe (pañcamī + atthe); pathaviyākāso / pathabyākāso (pathavī + ākāso); viyañjanaṃ / byañjanaṃ (vi + añjanaṃ); viyākato / byākato (vi + ākato); viyākaṃsu / byākaṃsu (vi + ākaṃsu); viyatto / byatto (vi + atto); viyūḷho / byūḷho (vi + ūḷho); dhammaṃ adhiyeti / ajjheti (adhi + eti); patiyeti / pacceti or pattiyāyati (paṭi + eti); pariyaṅko / pallaṅko (pari + aṅko); vipariyāso / vipallāso (vipari + āso). Here only one form occurs: pariyatti, pariyatto, pariyāyo. In pallaṅko, etc., in the word pari, the r is changed to l, the i is changed to y by 'yavā sare', and the y is assimilated to the preceding form.

Uvaṇṇe –

In the case of a u-vowel:

Bhikkhuvāsane, sayambhuvāsane, idhapi rūpadvayaṃ labbhati – duvaṅgikaṃ=dvaṅgikaṃ, bhuvādigaṇo=bhvādigaṇo iccādi.

Bhikkhuvāsane (bhikkhu + āsane); sayambhuvāsane (sayambhū + āsane). Here too a pair of forms is found: duvaṅgikaṃ / dvaṅgikaṃ (du + aṅgikaṃ); bhuvādigaṇo / bhvādigaṇo (bhū + ādi-gaṇo); etc.

40. Vitisseve vā rū. 33 (piṭṭhe).

40. Optionally, v for the i of iti before eva.

Evasadde pare itisaddassa i-kārassa vo hoti vā.

When the word eva follows, the i-sound of the word iti optionally becomes v.

Itveva coro aṅgulimālo, samuddotveva saṅkhyaṃ udā. 45 gacchati, mahāudakakkhandhotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati, mahāsammatotveva paṭhamaṃ akkharaṃ nibbattaṃ dī. ni. 3.131, isigilitveva samaññā ahosi ma. ni. 3.133.

Itveva coro aṅgulimālo: thus indeed was the robber Aṅgulimāla; samuddotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati: it is reckoned just as 'ocean'; mahāudakakkhandhotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati: it is reckoned just as 'a great mass of water'; mahāsammatotveva paṭhamaṃ akkharaṃ nibbattaṃ: the first letter arose as just 'Mahāsammata'; isigilitveva samaññā ahosi: the designation was just 'Isigili'.

Vāti kiṃ? Iccevattho, samuddoteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati.

Why 'optionally'? Iccevattho (iti + eva + attho): this is the meaning. Samuddoteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati: it is reckoned as 'ocean'.

Suttavibhattena [M 0.0025] evasadde pare aññati-kārassa vattaṃ. Vilapatveva so dijo jā. 1.6.103, anusetvevassa kāmarāgo, anusetvevassa rūparāgo – anuseti+eva+assāti chedo, hotveva kāriyasanniṭṭhānaṃ, hoteva vā.

By extension of the rule, the change to v occurs for the i-sound of other words ending in ti before eva. Vilapatveva so dijo (vilapati + eva): that bird laments indeed; anusetvevassa kāmarāgo (anuseti + eva + assa): sensual lust indeed lies latent in him; anusetvevassa rūparāgo: lust for form indeed lies latent in him—the division is anuseti + eva + assa; hotveva kāriyasanniṭṭhānaṃ (hoti + eva): the conclusion of the matter is indeed; or hoteva.

41. Eonama vaṇṇe ka. 27; rū 39; nī. 66, 163-4.

41. A for e and o before a letter.

Sarabyañjanabhūte vaṇṇe pare e, onaṃ attaṃ hoti vā. Tattha essa attaṃ yebhuyyena ma, dāgamesveva hoti.

When a letter, whether vowel or consonant, follows, the substitution a for e and o occurs, optionally. Therein, the substitution of a for e occurs mostly with the augments m and d.

Akaramhasa te kiccaṃ jā. 1.4.29 – akaramhasetyattho, disvā yācakamāgate jā. 1.7.58; 2.22.2261, disvā paṇḍitamāgate jā. 2.22.783, yamāhu natthi vīriyanti jā. 2.18.162 – ye+āhutyattho. Kadassu – ke+assu, yadeva te jātinissitā, tadeva te jarānissitāye+eva, te+evāti chedo, sve bhavo svātanaṃ pārā. 22 – byañjane dīgho.

Akaramhasa te kiccaṃ: the meaning is akaramhase; disvā yācakamāgate (yācake āgate): seeing the beggars who have come; disvā paṇḍitamāgate (paṇḍite āgate): seeing the wise who have come; yamāhu natthi vīriyanti (ye + āhu): those who say 'there is no effort'; kadassu (ke + assu): who indeed?; yadeva te jātinissitā (ye + eva): whatever things are dependent on birth; tadeva te jarānissitā (te + eva): those things are dependent on aging—the division is ye + eva, te + eva; svātanaṃ (from sve): belonging to tomorrow—the vowel is lengthened before a consonant.

Omhi –

In the case of o:

Sa sīlavā dha. pa. 84, sa paññavā, sa ve kāsāvamarahati dha. pa. 10, esa attho, esa dhammo dha. pa. 5, dinnamāsi janindena jā. 2.22.2161 (dinnamhāti janindena) – dinno+āsīti chedo, maggamatthi vibha. aṭṭha. 189 – maggo+atthi, aggamakkhāyati a. ni. 1.47, paccayākārameva ca vibha. aṭṭha. 225, saṅgho pabbatamiva, saddo cicciṭamiva, hiyyo bhavo hiyyattanaṃ, pāto asanaṃ pātarāso, pātamanusiṭṭho, kakusandha koṇāgamano, thera vādānamuttamo – kakusandhoti ca theroti ca chedo, theravādoti attho.

Sa sīlavā (so sīlavā): he is virtuous; sa paññavā (so paññavā): he is wise; sa ve kāsāvamarahati (so ve): he indeed is worthy of the ochre robe; esa attho (eso attho): this is the meaning; esa dhammo (eso dhammo): this is the Dhamma; dinnamāsi janindena (dinno āsi): it was given by the lord of men—the division is dinno + āsi; maggamatthi (maggo atthi): there is a path; aggamakkhāyati (aggo akkhāyati): it is called the highest; paccayākārameva ca (paccayo ākāraṃ): and the mode of conditions; saṅgho pabbatamiva (cf. pabbatova from pabbato iva): the Sangha is like a mountain; saddo cicciṭamiva (cf. cicciṭova from cicciṭo iva): the sound is like a chirp; hiyyattanaṃ (hiyyo attanaṃ): belonging to yesterday; pātarāso (pāto asanaṃ): morning meal; pātamanusiṭṭho (pāto anusiṭṭho): instructed in the morning; Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana; thera vādānamuttamo (thero): the elder, best of the traditions—the division is kakusandho iti and thero iti, and the meaning is theravādo.

Suttavibhattena [M 0.0026] animittepi hoti. Tuvañca dhanusekha ca jā. 1.16.239, paccayamahāpadeso hesa, ekakoṭṭhāso esa, abhilāpamattabhedo esa iccādi.

By extension of the rule, it occurs even without a following cause. Tuvañca dhanusekha ca (dhanusekho): you and Dhanusekha; paccayamahāpadeso hesa (hi eso): for this is the great section on conditions; ekakoṭṭhāso esa (eso): this is one portion; abhilāpamattabhedo esa (eso): this is a difference of mere expression; etc.

42. Gossāvaṅa ka. 22, 78; rū. 28; nī. 52, 229.

42. Avaṅ for go.

Sare pare gossa antassa avaṅa hoti.

When a vowel follows, the substitution avaṅ occurs for the final part of go.

Go ca asso ca gavāssaṃ.

Go ca asso ca gavāssaṃ (go + asso): a cow and a horse.

Suttavibhattena byañjanepi. Sagavacaṇḍo a. ni. 4.108, paragavacaṇḍo.

By extension of the rule, also before a consonant. Sagavacaṇḍo, paragavacaṇḍo.

Appavidhānamuccate.

Miscellaneous rules are stated.

Mahāvuttinā avaṇṇassa uttaṃ, ottañca –

According to the Mahāvutti, for the a-vowel, the substitutions u and o:

Puthujjano, puthubhūto-puthūti vā eko pāṭipadiko, puthunā puthunītipi dissati, apekkhiyāno apekkhiyānaapekkhitvātyattho. Evaṃ anumodiyāno, marīcikūpamaṃ abhisambuddhāno, mā maṃ pisācā khādantu, jīva tvaṃ saradosataṃ jā. 1.2.9, rattidivova so dibbo, mānusaṃ saradosataṃ-vassasatantyattho, anuyanti disodisaṃ dī. ni. 3.281, sampatanti disodisaṃ-taṃ taṃ disantyattho, parosataṃ, parosahassaṃ, aññoññaṃ aññamaññaṃ, ponopuññaṃ punappunaṃ, ponobbhavikā taṇhā-punoti vā eko nipāto, puno tassa mahe sino, puno pattaṃ gahetvāna, na ca dāni puno atthi, mama tuyhañca saṅgamo, na puno amatākāraṃ, passissāmi mukhaṃ tava apa. therī 2.2.235.

Puthujjano; puthubhūto—or puthu is a single nominal stem, as seen in puthunā and puthunīti; apekkhiyāno—the meaning is apekkhitvā (having expected); similarly anumodiyāno (rejoicing); abhisambuddhāno (awakening); mā maṃ pisācā khādantu (let not the demons devour me); jīva tvaṃ saradosataṃ (sarada-sataṃ): may you live a hundred autumns; rattidivova so dibbo (rattidivo): that divine one, day and night; mānusaṃ saradosataṃ: a hundred human autumns—the meaning is 'a hundred years'; anuyanti disodisaṃ (disā-disaṃ): they follow in every direction; sampatanti disodisaṃ: they fall in every direction—the meaning is 'that and that direction'; parosataṃ (para-sataṃ): over a hundred; parosahassaṃ (para-sahassaṃ): over a thousand; aññoññaṃ (añña-aññaṃ): one another; ponopuññaṃ (puna-punaṃ): again and again; ponobbhavikā taṇhā (puna-bhavikā): craving leading to renewed existence—or puna is a single particle, as in: puno tassa mahesino (again, of that great seer); puno pattaṃ gahetvāna (again, having taken the bowl); na ca dāni puno atthi, mama tuyhañca saṅgamo (and now there is again no meeting for me and you); na puno amatākāraṃ, passissāmi mukhaṃ tava (I will not again see your deathless-like face).

Ivaṇṇassa attaṃ, uttaṃ, ettañca –

For the i-vowel, the substitutions a, u, and e:

Tadamināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ-taṃ etaṃ atthajātaṃ iminā pariyāyena veditabbanti attho, sakiṃ āgacchati sīlenāti [M 0.0027] sakadāgāmī, itthiyā bhāvo itthattaṃ, evumaṃ – evaṃ+imanti chedo, tvaṃ no satthā mahāmune, atthadhammavidū ise.

Tadamināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ: the meaning is 'that collection of meanings (taṃ etaṃ atthajātaṃ) should be understood by this method (iminā pariyāyena)'; sakiṃ āgacchati sīlenāti sakadāgāmī (sakiṃ + āgāmī): a once-returner is one who returns once by means of virtue; itthiyā bhāvo itthattaṃ (itthi + ttaṃ): womanhood is the state of a woman; evumaṃ: the division is evaṃ + imaṃ; tvaṃ no satthā mahāmune, atthadhammavidū ise (isi): you are our teacher, O great sage, O seer (ise) who knows the goal and the Dhamma.

Uvaṇṇassa ittaṃ, ottañca –

For the u-vowel, the substitutions i and o:

Mātito dī. ni. 1.303, pitito, mātipakkho, pitipakkho, mātigho jā. 2.19.118, pitigho, mattikaṃ dhanaṃ pārā. 34, pettikaṃ dhanaṃ, api no lacchasi, kacci no tumhe yāpetha, kathaṃ no tumhe yāpetha, sotukāmattha no tumhe bhikkhave, na no samaṃ atthi khu. pā. 6.3, na hi no saṅkarantena ma. ni. 3.272, natthi no koci pariyāyo jā. 1.5.110 (na hi no koci pariyāyo) – imesu tīsu nusaddo ekaṃsatthe, sosito sotatto ceva jā. 1.1.94 sotatto sosindo ceva; ma. ni. 1.157 – suṭṭhu sītalo suṭṭhu santattotyattho, jambunadiyā jātaṃ jambonadaṃ.

From mother, from father; mother's side, father's side; matricide, patricide; maternal wealth, paternal wealth. 'Will you indeed obtain it?'; 'Are you indeed maintaining yourselves?'; 'How indeed do you maintain yourselves?'; 'Bhikkhus, are you indeed desirous of listening?'; 'We have nothing equal'; 'For there is no association with us'; 'There is no way for us.' In these three, the particle 'nu' has the sense of certainty. 'Sosita' and 'sotatta' mean 'well cooled' and 'well heated' respectively. Born from the Jambu river is 'jambonada' gold.

Essa ittaṃ –

The substitution of 'i' for 'e'—

Okandāmasi bhūtāni, pabbatāni vanāni ca jā. 2.22.2173 – avakandāmasetyattho, yaṃ karomasi brahmuno, tadajja tuyhaṃ dassāma dī. ni. 2.370, idha hemantagimhisu dha. pa. 286, buddhapaccekabuddhisu, cetehi cetaputtihi cariyā. 1.106 – cetaputtehi saddhintyattho.

'We call down upon the beings, the mountains, and the forests'—the meaning is 'we call down upon.' 'What we do for Brahma, that today we shall give to you, here in winter and summer, among Buddhas and Solitary Buddhas, with the sons of the Cetis'—this means 'together with the sons of the Cetis.'

Ossa uttaṃ –

The substitution of 'u' for 'o'—

Manuññaṃ, na tenatthaṃ abandhisu jā. 1.6.7 – so tena vacanena atthaṃ na abandhi na labhītyattho. Avhāyantu su yuddhena jā. 2.22.871 – so [M 0.0028] pahāravacanena maṃ avhayantotyattho. Api nu hanukā santā jā. 1.1.146 – no hanukā ekantaṃ khinnā dukkhapattātyattho.

'Pleasant.' 'By that they did not grasp the meaning'—the meaning is: by that speech he did not grasp, did not obtain the meaning. 'Let them indeed challenge me to battle'—the meaning is: he challenges me with words of assault. 'Are the jaws indeed tranquil?'—the meaning is: no, the jaws are utterly weary, afflicted with suffering.

Vikārasandhipi ādesasandhirūpattā idha saṅgayhati.

Modification sandhi is also included here because it has the nature of substitution sandhi.

Iti sarādesarāsi.

Thus the section on vowel substitution.

Kavaggato paṭṭhāya vaggāvaggabyañjanānaṃ ādeso dīpiyate.

Beginning with the k-group, the substitution of grouped and ungrouped consonants is explained.

43. Vaggalasehi te.

43. By the groups, l, and s, they [are substituted for ya].

Pañcavaggehi ca la, sehi ca parassa ya-kārassa kvaci te eva vagga la, sā honti vā yathākkamaṃ, ya-kāro pubbarūpattaṃ āpajjatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Following the five consonant groups and the letters `l` and `s`, a `y` is sometimes optionally substituted by those very group consonants, or by `l` and `s`, respectively. This is to say that the letter `y` is assimilated to the preceding form.

Nipaccatīti nipako, nipakassa bhāvo nepakkaṃ, vipāko eva vepakkaṃ, vattabbanti vākkaṃ, vākyaṃ vā. Pamukhe sādhu pāmokkhaṃ – yassa pubbarūpatte kate ādidutiyassa paṭhamattaṃ, subhagassa bhāvo sobhaggaṃ, dobhaggaṃ, bhuñjitabbanti bhoggaṃ, yuñjitabbanti yoggaṃ, kukkucabhāvo kukkuccaṃ, vattabbanti vāccaṃ, vuccate, paccate, vaṇijānaṃ kammaṃ vāṇijjaṃ, bhuñjitabbanti bhojjaṃ, yuñjitabbanti yojjaṃ.

'One who is prudent' is `nipaka`; the state of being prudent is `nepakkaṃ`. `Vipāka` itself is `vepakkaṃ`. 'What is to be said' is `vākkaṃ`, or `vākyaṃ`. 'Good at the head' is `pāmokkhaṃ`—for which, when assimilation to the preceding form has occurred, the first of the initial two syllables is lengthened. The state of being fortunate is `sobhaggaṃ`; also `dobhaggaṃ`. 'What is to be enjoyed' is `bhoggaṃ`. 'What is to be yoked' is `yoggaṃ`. The state of remorse is `kukkuccaṃ`. 'What is to be said' is `vāccaṃ`; `vuccate` (is said); `paccate` (is cooked). The work of merchants is `vāṇijjaṃ`. 'What is to be eaten' is `bhojjaṃ`. 'What is to be yoked' is `yojjaṃ`.

44. Tavaggavaraṇānaṃ ye cavaggabayañā ka. 269, 41; nī. 104, 106, 119, 121-5.

44. For the t-group, v, r, and ṇ, followed by y: the c-group, b, y, and ñ.

Ādesabhūte vā vibhattibhūte vā paccayabhūte vā ya-kāre pare tavaggānaṃva, ra, ṇānañca cavagga, ba, ya, ñādesā honti vā yathākkamaṃ.

When the letter `y`—whether as a substitute, an inflection, or a suffix—follows, for the consonants of the t-group, and for `v`, `r`, and `ṇ`, the substitutes are optionally the consonants of the c-group, and `b`, `y`, and `ñ`, respectively.

Pokkharañño, pokkharaññā, pokkharaññaṃ, samaṇassa bhāvo sāmaññaṃ, evaṃ brahmaññaṃ, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ pārā. 411 iccādīni ‘yavā sare’ti sutte udāhaṭāni.

`Pokkharañño, pokkharaññā, pokkharaññaṃ`. The state of a recluse is `sāmaññaṃ`; similarly, `brahmaññaṃ`. '`iccetaṃ kusalaṃ`' and so on are cited under the rule 'yavā sare'.

Paṇḍitassa [M 0.0029] bhāvo paṇḍiccaṃ, santassa bhāvo saccaṃ, tathassa bhāvotacchaṃ, yajjevaṃ-yadi+evaṃ, najjo, najjā, najjaṃ, suhadassa bhāvo sohajjaṃ, vattabbanti vajjaṃ, jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati dha. sa. 160, upasampajjati, ajjhokāso, bojjhaṅgo, bojjhā, bodhiyā vā, bujjhitabbanti bojjhaṃ, bujjhati, ponopuññaṃ, thanato sambhūtaṃ thaññaṃ.

The state of a learned one is `paṇḍiccaṃ` (learning). The state of being is `saccaṃ` (truth). The state of being so is `tacchaṃ` (reality). `Yajjevaṃ` from `yadi evaṃ` (if so). `Najjo, najjā, najjaṃ` (river). The state of a good heart is `sohajjaṃ` (friendship). 'What is to be said' is `vajjaṃ` (fault). 'He dwells having attained jhāna' (`upasampajja`). `Upasampajjati` (he attains). `Ajjhokāso` (open space). `Bojjhaṅgo` (factor of enlightenment). `Bojjhā`, or `bodhiyā` (of enlightenment). 'What is to be awakened to' is `bojjhaṃ`; `bujjhati` (he awakens). `Ponopuññaṃ` (repeatedly). 'Born from the breast' is `thaññaṃ` (breast-milk).

Pavagge yassa pubbarūpaṃ –

Assimilation of `y` to the preceding consonant in the p-group—

Vappate, luppate, abbhuggato, abbhokāso, usabhassa bhāvo osabbhaṃ, labhiyateti labbhaṃ, labbhate, gāme hitaṃ gammaṃ, opammaṃ, sokhummaṃ, āgamma, upagamma, gamiyateti gammo, evaṃ dammo, rammo, gammate, rammate.

`Vappate` (is sown), `luppate` (is cut off). `Abbhuggato` (gone up). `Abbhokāso` (open space). The state of a bull is `osabbhaṃ`. 'What is to be obtained' is `labbhaṃ`; `labbhate` (is obtained). 'Beneficial to the village' is `gammaṃ`. `Opammaṃ` (comparison). `Sokhummaṃ` (subtlety). `Āgamma` (having come), `upagamma` (having approached). 'What is to be gone to' is `gammo`; similarly `dammo` (to be tamed), `rammo` (delightful). `Gammate` (is gone to), `rammate` (is delighted in).

‘Tavagga varaṇāna…’nti iminā suttena yamhi rassa yattaṃ –

According to the rule 'Tavaggavaraṇāna...', the substitution of `y` for `r`—

Kayyate kariyate, ayyo ariyo.

`Kayyate` from `kariyate` (is done). `Ayyo` from `ariyo` (noble).

‘Vaggalasehi te’ti lato yassa pubbarūpaṃ –

According to the rule 'Vaggalasehi te', the assimilation of `y` to a preceding `l`—

Pallaṅko, vipallāso, kosallaṃ, pattakallaṃ.

`Pallaṅko` (couch), `vipallāso` (perversion), `kosallaṃ` (skill), `pattakallaṃ` (proper time).

‘Tavaggavaraṇāna…’nti yamhi vassa battaṃ –

According to the rule 'Tavaggavaraṇāna...', the substitution of `b` for `v`—

Puthabyā, puthabyaṃ, bhātu apaccaṃ bhātabyo, korabyo, dive bhavaṃ dibbaṃ dibyaṃ.

`Puthabyā, puthabyaṃ` (of the earth). 'A brother's offspring' is `bhātabyo` (nephew). `Korabyo` (a Kaurava). 'Existing in heaven' is `dibbaṃ` or `dibyaṃ` (divine).

‘Vaggalasehi te’ti sato yassa pubbarūpaṃ –

According to the rule 'Vaggalasehi te', the assimilation of `y` to a preceding `s`—

Rahasi bhavaṃ rahassaṃ, somanassaṃ, domanassaṃ, sovacassaṃ, dovacassaṃ-manogaṇattā majjhe sāgamo, bhāsitabbanti bhassaṃ, ādissa=ādisitvā, uddissa=uddisitvā, upavassa=upavasitvā, samphussa=samphusitvā, tussati, dussati, nassatiiccādi.

That which exists in secret is `rahassaṃ` (a secret). `Somanassaṃ` (joy), `domanassaṃ` (sorrow), `sovacassaṃ` (docility), `dovacassaṃ` (indocility)—because they belong to the `manas` group, there is an insertion of `s` in the middle. 'What is to be spoken' is `bhassaṃ`. `Ādissa` for `ādisitvā` (having pointed out). `Uddissa` for `uddisitvā` (having specified). `Upavassa` for `upavasitvā` (having dwelt near). `Samphussa` for `samphusitvā` (having touched). `Tussati` (is pleased), `dussati` (is corrupted), `nassati` (perishes), etc.

45. Tathanarānaṃ [M 0.0030] ṭaṭhaṇalā rū. 3 (piṭṭhe).

45. For `t`, `th`, `n`, and `r`, [the substitutions are] `ṭ`, `ṭh`, `ṇ`, and `l`.

Tādīnaṃ ṭādiādesā honti vā.

For `t` and the others, the substitutions `ṭ` and the others optionally occur.

Tassa ṭattaṃ –

The substitution of `ṭ` for `t`—

Paṭihaññati, paṭaggi dātabbo, paṭicchanno, paṭippanno, byāvaṭo, udāhaṭo, dukkaṭaṃ iccādi.

`Paṭihaññati` (is struck back), `paṭaggi dātabbo` (a counter-fire is to be set), `paṭicchanno` (covered), `paṭippanno` (entered upon), `byāvaṭo` (engaged), `udāhaṭo` (spoken), `dukkaṭaṃ` (wrongdoing), etc.

Thassa ṭhattaṃ –

The substitution of `ṭh` for `th`—

Pīḷanaṭṭho paṭi. ma. 1.17, saṅkhataṭṭho paṭi. ma. 1.17, aṭṭhiṃkatvā suṇeyya jā. 2.17.92, aṭṭhakathā iccādi.

`Pīḷanaṭṭho` (for the purpose of oppressing), `saṅkhataṭṭho` (for the purpose of the conditioned), `aṭṭhiṃkatvā suṇeyya` (one should listen, giving one's full attention), `aṭṭhakathā` (commentary), etc.

Nassa ṇattaṃ –

The substitution of `ṇ` for `n`—

Gāmaṃ netīti gāmaṇi, senaṃ netīti senāṇi, paṇidhi, paṇidhānaṃ, paṇihitaṃ, paṇāmo, pariṇāmo, oṇāmo, uṇṇāmo, karaṇīyaṃ, karaṇaṃ, ñāṇaṃ, tāṇaṃ, pamāṇaṃ, saraṇaṃ, gahaṇaṃ iccādi.

'One who leads a village is a `gāmaṇi` (village leader)'; 'one who leads an army is a `senāṇi` (general)'; `paṇidhi` (aspiration), `paṇidhānaṃ` (aspiration), `paṇihitaṃ` (applied), `paṇāmo` (veneration), `pariṇāmo` (maturation), `oṇāmo` (bending down), `uṇṇāmo` (raising up), `karaṇīyaṃ` (to be done), `karaṇaṃ` (doing), `ñāṇaṃ` (knowledge), `tāṇaṃ` (protection), `pamāṇaṃ` (measure), `saraṇaṃ` (refuge), `gahaṇaṃ` (grasping), etc.

Rassa lattaṃ –

The substitution of `l` for `r`—

Paligho, palibodho, palipanno, pallaṅko, taluṇo taruṇo, kalunaṃ paridevayi jā. 2.22.2151, mahāsālo, aṭṭhasālinī, nayasālinī iccādīni.

`Paligho` (bar), `palibodho` (obstruction), `palipanno` (fallen into), `pallaṅko` (couch), `taluṇo` for `taruṇo` (young), `kalunaṃ` for `karuṇaṃ` (pitifully) `paridevayi` (he lamented), `mahāsālo` (a man of great wealth), `Aṭṭhasālinī`, `Nayasālinī`, etc.

Idāni mahāvuttividhānamuccate.

Now the method of irregular substitutions is stated.

Kassa khattaṃ –

The substitution of `kh` for `k`—
