Nikkhamati, nikkhanto, nekkhamo, rājakiccaṃ karotīti khattā, kattā vā.

`Nikkhamati` (goes out), `nikkhanto` (gone out), `nekkhamo` (renunciation). 'One who performs royal duties' is a `khattā`, or `kattā`.

Dattañca –

And `d` for `t`—

Sadatthapasuto siyā dha. pa. 166.

'One should be intent on the true goal.'

Yattañca [M 0.0031] –

And `y` for `t`—

Sayaṃ raṭṭhaṃ hitvāna, pupphadānaṃ dadātīti pupphadāniyo pupphadāniko, sippalivane vasatīti sippalivaniyo sippalivaniko, kumāriyā kumārikā.

'Having himself abandoned the kingdom.' 'Because he gives flower-offerings,' he is a `pupphadāniyo` or `pupphadāniko`. 'Because he dwells in Sippalivana,' he is a `sippalivaniyo` or `sippalivaniko`. From `kumārī` is derived `kumārikā` (a young girl).

Khassa gattaṃ –

The substitution of `g` for `kh`—

Eḷamūgo eḷamūkho.

`Eḷamūgo` for `eḷamūkho` (a dumb mute).

Gassa kattaṃ –

The substitution of `k` for `g`—

Lujjatīti loko, ārogyaṃ abhisajjetīti bhisakko, kulūpako kulūpago, khīrūpako khīrūpago, gīvūpakaṃ gīvūpagaṃ.

'Because it disintegrates, it is the `loko` (world).' 'Because he restores health,' he is a `bhisakko` (physician). `Kulūpako` for `kulūpago` (one who frequents families). `Khīrūpako` for `khīrūpago` (one who approaches for milk). `Gīvūpakaṃ` for `gīvūpagaṃ` (that which is near the neck).

Ghassa hattaṃ –

The substitution of `h` for `gh`—

Sīghajavatāya sīho.

Because of its swiftness (`sīghajavatā`), it is a `sīho` (lion).

Cassa chattaṃ –

The substitution of `ch` for `c`—

Vinicchayo, acchariyaṃ, macchariyaṃ, raṃsiyo niccharanti-nigacchantīti attho.

`Vinicchayo` (decision), `acchariyaṃ` (wonderful), `macchariyaṃ` (stinginess). 'Rays issue forth' (`niccharanti`)—the meaning is 'they go out' (`nigacchanti`).

Chassa sattaṃ –

The substitution of `s` for `ch`—

Atthi sāhassa jīvitaṃ jā. 2.22.314 -chāhaṃ+assāti chedo, saḷāyatanaṃ.

'There is life for six days'—this is parsed as `chāhaṃ + assa`. `Saḷāyatanaṃ` (the six sense bases).

Jassa dattaṃ –

The substitution of `d` for `j`—

Parasenaṃ jinātītipassenadī-mahāvuttinā saralopo, rassa pararūpaṃ.

'Because he conquers the enemy army,' he is `Pasenadi`—by an irregular rule, there is elision of a vowel and assimilation of `r` to the following form.

Yattañca –

And the state of being 'y'—

Nissāya jāyatīti niyo, niyako vā, niyaṃ puttaṃ.

'Because it is born from dependence,' it is `niyo`, or `niyako`. `Niyaṃ puttaṃ` (one's own son).

Ñassaṇattaṃ – [M 0.0032]

The substitution of `ṇ` for `ñ`—

Paṇṇatti paññatti, paṇṇāsaṃ paññāsaṃ. Paṇṇavīsati pañcavīsati.

`Paṇṇatti` for `paññatti` (designation). `Paṇṇāsaṃ` for `paññāsaṃ` (fifty). `Paṇṇavīsati` for `pañcavīsati` (twenty-five).

Nattañca –

And `n` for `ñ`—

Nāmamattaṃ na nāyati, animittā na nāyare visuddhi. aṭṭha. 1.228 – na paññāyantīti attho.

'A mere name does not lead.' 'The signless are not led'—the meaning is 'they are not known.'

Tassa kattaṃ –

The substitution of `k` for `t`—

Niyako niyato.

`Niyako` for `niyato` (fixed, certain).

Thattañca –

And `th` for `t`—

Nitthiṇṇo, nittharaṇaṃ, netthāraṃ.

`Nitthiṇṇo` (crossed over), `nittharaṇaṃ` (crossing over), `netthāraṃ` (a guide).

Nattañca –

And `n` for `t`—

Jino, pino, lino, paṭisallino, paḷino, malino, supino, pahīno, dhuno, puno, luno, āhunaṃ, pāhunaṃ.

`Jino` (victor), `pino` (fat), `lino` (sluggish), `paṭisallino` (secluded), `palino` (grey-haired), `malino` (stained), `supino` (dream), `pahīno` (abandoned), `dhuno` (shaken off), `puno` (again), `luno` (cut), `āhunaṃ` (oblation), `pāhunaṃ` (guest-gift).

Dassa ḍattaṃ –

The substitution of `ḍ` for `d`—

Chavaḍāho, disāḍāho, kāyaḍāho.

`Chavaḍāho` (corpse-burning), `disāḍāho` (conflagration), `kāyaḍāho` (burning of the body).

Ḷattañca –

And `ḷ` for `d`—

Pariḷāho, āgantvā chavaṃ dahanti etthāti āḷahanaṃ, susānaṃ.

`Pariḷāho` (fever, burning). 'Having come, they burn a corpse here,' thus it is `āḷahanaṃ` (cremation ground), a `susānaṃ` (cemetery).

Tattañca –

And `t` for `d`—

Sugato, tathāgato, kusito, udati pasavatīti utu.

`Sugato` (Well-gone), `Tathāgato` (Thus-gone), `kusito` (lazy). 'It arises and brings forth,' thus it is `utu` (season).

Dhassa dattaṃ –

The substitution of `d` for `dh`—

Ekamidāhaṃ bhikkhave samayaṃ ma. ni. 1.501 -idhāti vā nipāto.

'Ekamidāhaṃ, bhikkhave, samayaṃ' (At one time, monks, I...)—or, it is the particle `idha`.

Hattañca [M 0.0033] –

And `h` for `dh`—

Sāhu dassanamariyānaṃ dha. pa. 206, saṃhitaṃ, vihitaṃ, pihitaṃ, abhihitaṃ, sannihitaṃ, paṇihitaṃ, saddahati, vidahati, pidahati.

'Good is the sight of the noble ones.' `Saṃhitaṃ` (connected), `vihitaṃ` (arranged), `pihitaṃ` (closed), `abhihitaṃ` (spoken), `sannihitaṃ` (stored up), `paṇihitaṃ` (directed). `Saddahati` (has faith), `vidahati` (arranges), `pidahati` (closes).

Nassa uttaṃ –

The substitution of `u` for `n`—

Upaññāso=upanyāso, ñāyo=nyāyo-niccaṃ eti phalaṃ etenāti ñāyo, ñeyyaṃ=neyyaṃ.

`Upaññāso` for `upanyāso` (introduction). `Ñāyo` for `nyāyo` (method)—'because one constantly goes to the fruit by this,' it is `ñāyo`. `Ñeyyaṃ` for `neyyaṃ` (what is to be led/understood).

Yattañca –

And `y` for `n`—

Thenassa kammaṃ theyyaṃ, therādhinanti therādheyyaṃ, pātimokkhaṃ, parādheyyakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

The work of a thief (`thena`) is `theyyaṃ` (theft). `Therādheyyaṃ` means 'under the authority of the elders.' `Pātimokkhaṃ`. `Parādheyyakaṃ dukkhaṃ` (suffering dependent on another).

Passa phattaṃ –

The substitution of `ph` for `p`—

Nipphajjati, nipphatti, nipphannaṃ.

`Nipphajjati` (is produced), `nipphatti` (production), `nipphannaṃ` (produced).

Battañca –

And `b` for `p`—

Sambahulaṃ=sampahulaṃ, bahusanto na bharati su. ni. 98 =pahu santo na bharati.

`Sambahulaṃ` for `sampahulaṃ` (very many). 'Though having much, he does not support' for 'though able, he does not support.'

Bhassa phattaṃ –

The substitution of `ph` for `bh`—

Anantaṃ sabbatopaphaṃ dī. ni. 1.499.

“Endless, shining all around.”

Massa pattaṃ –

The substitution of `p` for `m`—

Cirappavāsiṃ dha. pa. 219, hatthippabhinnaṃ dha. pa. 326.

`Cirappavāsiṃ` (one who has been away for a long time); `hatthippabhinnaṃ` (an elephant in rut).

Yassa vattaṃ –

The substitution of `v` for `y`—

Dīghāvu kumāro mahāva. 459 =dīghāyu kumāro, āyuṃ dhāretīti āvudhaṃ=āyudhaṃ, āyu assa atthīti atthe ‘āvuso’ti nipāto, kasāvo=kasāyo, kāsāvaṃ=kāsāyaṃ, sāliṃ lunātīti sālilāyako, tiṇalāyako.

Prince `Dīghāvu` for Prince `Dīghāyu`; `āvudhaṃ` for `āyudhaṃ` because it protects life (`āyuṃ dhāreti`); in the sense ‘he has life’ (`āyu assa atthi`), there is the particle `āvuso`; `kasāvo` for `kasāyo`; `kāsāvaṃ` for `kāsāyaṃ`; `sālilāyako` is one who cuts rice (`sāliṃ lunāti`); `tiṇalāyako`.

Lassa rattaṃ [M 0.0034] –

The substitution of `r` for `l`—

Nīlaṃ jalaṃ etthāti nerañjarā, jalaṃ gaṇhituṃ alanti arañjaro, sassataṃ pareti, ucchedaṃ pareti-paletīti attho.

`Nerañjarā`, because ‘there is dark (`nīla`) water (`jala`) here’; `arañjaro`, because ‘they are able (`alaṃ`) to take water (`jala`)’; ‘he goes towards (`pareti`) eternalism,’ ‘he goes towards (`pareti`) annihilationism’—the meaning is ‘he goes away’ (`paleti`).

Vassa pattaṃ –

The substitution of `p` for `v`—

Pipāsati pivāsati.

`Pipāsati` for `pivāsati`.

Battañca –

And the substitution of `b` for `v`—

Byākato, byatto, byañjanaṃ, sīlabbataṃ, nibbānaṃ, nibbutaṃ, dibbaṃ, dibbati, sibbati, kubbati, kubbanto, krubbati, krubbanto, asevitabbattā vāretabboti bālo, pabbajito, pabbajjā iccādi.

`Byākato`, `byatto`, `byañjanaṃ`, `sīlabbataṃ`, `nibbānaṃ`, `nibbutaṃ`, `dibbaṃ`, `dibbati`, `sibbati`, `kubbati`, `kubbanto`, `krubbati`, `krubbanto`; a `bālo` (fool) is so called because he is not to be associated with (`asevitabba`) and is to be avoided (`vāretabbo`); `pabbajito`, `pabbajjā`, etc.

Sassa chattaṃ –

The substitution of `ch` for `s`—

Ucchiṭṭhaṃ-avasiṭṭhantyattho, “dibbā saddā niccharanti, raṃsiyo vi. va. 730 niccharantī”ti etthāpi sassa chattaṃ icchanti.

`Ucchiṭṭhaṃ` means ‘what remains’ (`avasiṭṭhaṃ`); in “divine sounds emanate, rays emanate,” here too the substitution of `ch` for `s` is intended.

Tattañca –

And the substitution of `t` for `s`—

Uttiṭṭhapattaṃ upanāmenti mahāva. 64, “uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyyā” ti ettha pana uddissa tiṭṭhanaṃ uttiṭṭhanti attho. “Uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyāna yācanā jā. 1.7.59”ti vuttaṃ.

They bring forward `uttiṭṭhapattaṃ` (a bowl of leftovers). However, in “one should rise up, one should not be heedless,” the meaning of `uttiṭṭha` is ‘standing for a purpose.’ It is said: “The noble ones stand for a purpose; this is the entreaty of the noble ones.”

Hassa ghattaṃ –

The substitution of `gh` for `h`—

Niccaṃ dahati etthāti nidāgho, laghu lahu.

`Nidāgho` (summer heat), because it constantly burns (`niccaṃ dahati`) here; `laghu` becomes `lahu`.

Ḷassa ḍattaṃ –

The substitution of `ḍ` for `ḷ`—

Garuḍo garuḷo.

`Garuḍo`; `garuḷo`.

Iti byañjanādesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on consonant substitutions.

Missakādeso [M 0.0035] vuccate.

Mixed substitutions will now be explained.

Avassa uttaṃ –

The substitution of `u` for `ava`—

Uddhammo, ubbinayo, uppatho, ummaggo, uññā avaññā, uññātaṃ avaññātaṃ, ujjhānasaññī.

`Uddhammo`, `ubbinayo`, `uppatho`, `ummaggo`; `uññā` for `avaññā`; `uññātaṃ` for `avaññātaṃ`; `ujjhānasaññī`.

Ottañca –

And the substitution of `o` for `ava`—

Onaddho, okāso, ovādo, olokanaṃ iccādi.

`Onaddho`, `okāso`, `ovādo`, `olokanaṃ`, etc.

Vassa ottaṃ –

The substitution of `o` for `va`—

Uposatho – upavasathoti ṭhiti, nonītaṃ navanītaṃ, nivatthakoco nivatthakavaco, ko te balaṃ mahārāja, ko nu te rathamaṇḍalaṃ jā. 2.22.1880 – kvati attho. Ko te diṭṭho vā suto vā, vānaro dhammiko iti, ko nume gotamasāvakā gatā-kva nu+imeti chedo, soṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ iccādi.

`Uposatho`—the form is `upavasatho`; `nonītaṃ` for `navanītaṃ`; `nivatthakoco` for `nivatthakavaco`; “O great king, what is your strength? What now is your chariot-circle?”—here `ko` means `kva` (where). “Where have you seen or heard of a righteous monkey?”; “Where now have these disciples of Gotama gone?”—the analysis is `kva nu ime`; `soṇṇaṃ` for `suvaṇṇaṃ`, etc.

Kussa kruttaṃ –

The substitution of `kr` for `k`—

Krubbati kubbati.

`Krubbati` for `kubbati`.

Ttassa trattaṃ –

The change of `tt` to `tr`:

Atrajo putto, khetrajo putto attajo, khettajo, gotrabhū, vatrabhū, citraṃ, vicitraṃ, cittaṃ, vicittaṃ, utrastamidaṃ cittaṃ saṃ. ni. 1.98, utrāsī palāyī saṃ. ni. 1.249, yātrā ca me bhavissati ma. ni. 1.23 iccādi.

`Atrajo putto` from `attajo putto` (a son born of oneself); `khetrajo putto` from `khettajo putto` (a son born of the field); `gotrabhū` from `gottabhū` (one who belongs to the lineage); `vatrabhū` from `vattabhū` (one who maintains a practice); `citraṃ`, `vicitraṃ` from `cittaṃ`, `vicittaṃ` (variegated, diverse); `utrastamidaṃ cittaṃ` (this mind is terrified), where `utrastaṃ` is from `uttastaṃ`; `utrāsī palāyī` (terrified, he fled), where `utrāsī` is from `uttāsī`; `yātrā ca me bhavissati` (and I will have a journey), where `yātrā` is from `yattā`; and so on.

Dassa drattaṃ –

The change of `d` to `dr`:

Indriyaṃ, sukho udayo yassāti sukhudrayaṃ, dukkhudrayaṃ kammaṃ ma. ni. 2.109, pathavī undriyyati saṃ. ni. 1.158 – bhijjatītyattho, mittadrubbho mittaddubbho.

`Indriyaṃ` (faculty). `Sukhudrayaṃ` from `sukho udayo yassa` (that which has a happy arising). `Dukkhudrayaṃ kammaṃ` (an action with a painful arising). `Pathavī undriyyati`, which means 'the earth splits apart.' `Mittadrubbho` from `mittaddubbho` (one who injures a friend).

Ddassa drattaṃ [M 0.0036] –

The change of `dd` to `dr`:

Bhadraṃ bhaddaṃ, asso bhadro dha. pa. 143, sadā bhadrāni passati dī. ni. 2.153, sabbe bhadrāni passantu jā. 1.2.105, bhadrāni bhadrāni yānāni yojetvā, ludraṃ dī. ni. 2.43 luddaṃ.

`Bhadraṃ` from `bhaddaṃ` (auspicious). `Asso bhadro` (an excellent horse). `Sadā bhadrāni passati` (one always sees good things). `Sabbe bhadrāni passantu` (may all see good things). `Bhadrāni bhadrāni yānāni yojetvā` (having yoked excellent, excellent vehicles). `Ludraṃ` from `luddaṃ` (cruel).

Bassa brattaṃ –

The change of `b` to `br`:

Brahāvanaṃ, brahantaṃ vā vanappatiṃ jā. 1.1.14, brahmā, brāhmaṇo – bāhitapāpattā arahā brāhmaṇoti vuccati, brahmuno apaccanti jātibrāhmaṇo vuccati.

`Brahāvanaṃ` (a great forest), or `brahantaṃ vanappatiṃ` (a great tree). `Brahmā`, `brāhmaṇo` (a brahmin). An Arahant is called a brahmin because he has expelled evil (`bāhitapāpattā`). One is called a brahmin by birth because he is a descendant of Brahmā (`brahmuno apaccaṃ`).

Va, vīnaṃ byattaṃ –

The change of `va` or `vi` to `bya`:

Byayo=vayo-vināsotyattho, kiccākiccesu byāvaṭo=vāvaṭo, paṅke byasanno=visanno, byamhito=vimhito, byamhaṃ=vimānaṃ-mānassa mhattaṃ.

`Byayo` from `vayo`, meaning 'destruction.' `Byāvaṭo` from `vāvaṭo` (engaged in duties and non-duties). `Byasanno` from `visanno` (sunk in the mud). `Byamhito` from `vimhito` (astonished). `Byamhaṃ` from `vimānaṃ` (celestial mansion), explained as 'greatness of pride/measure' (`mānassa mhattaṃ`).

Kkhassa cchattaṃ –

The change of `kkh` to `cch`:

Acchi=akkhi, sacchi=sakkhi-saha akkhinā vattatīti atthe nipāto, paccakkhanti attho. Nibbānaṃ sacchikaroti mi. pa. 5.3.12, macchikā=makkhikā, lacchī=lakkhī-sirīti attho.

`Acchi` from `akkhi` (eye). `Sacchi` from `sakkhi` (eyewitness); this is a particle in the sense of 'acting with the eye' (`saha akkhinā vattati`), meaning 'directly perceived' (`paccakkhaṃ`). `Nibbānaṃ sacchikaroti` (one realizes Nibbāna). `Macchikā` from `makkhikā` (fly). `Lacchī` from `lakkhī`, meaning 'prosperity' (`sirī`).

Mahāvuttinā akkharasaṃkhittaṃ hoti –

According to the Mahāvutti, there is also abbreviation of syllables:

Ācero ācariyo, na mātāpitarasaṃvaḍḍho, anācerakule vasaṃ jā. 1.1.9, āceramhi susikkhitā jā. 1.7.82, brahmacero brahmacariyo, tiṇhaṃ tikhiṇaṃ, taṇhā tasiṇā, suṇhā suṇisā, abhiṇhaṃ abhikkhaṇaṃ, paṇho pubbaṇho, paṇhe vajjho mahosadho jā. 1.15.324, surāmerayo-surāmereyyo, surāmereyyapānāni, yo naro anuyuñjati dha. pa. 247. Kammadhārayo= kammadhāreyyo[M 0.0037], pāṭihīraṃ pāṭiheraṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ, accheraṃ acchariyaṃ, maccheraṃ maccharaṃ macchariyaṃ iccādi.

`Ācero` from `ācariyo` (teacher), as in `na mātāpitarasaṃvaḍḍho, anācerakule vasaṃ` (not raised by mother and father, living in a family without a teacher) and `āceramhi susikkhitā` (well-trained by the teacher). `Brahmacero` from `brahmacariyo` (one who lives the holy life). `Tiṇhaṃ` from `tikhiṇaṃ` (sharp). `Taṇhā` from `tasiṇā` (craving). `Suṇhā` from `suṇisā` (daughter-in-law). `Abhiṇhaṃ` from `abhikkhaṇaṃ` (repeatedly). `Paṇho` (question) and `pubbaṇho` (forenoon), as in `paṇhe vajjho mahosadho` (Mahosadha is to be consulted in questions). `Surāmerayo` from `surāmereyyo` (liquor and spirits), as in `surāmereyyapānāni, yo naro anuyuñjati` (the man who indulges in drinking liquor and spirits). `Kammadhārayo` from `kammadhāreyyo` (karmadhāraya compound). `Pāṭihīraṃ` and `pāṭiheraṃ` from `pāṭihāriyaṃ` (miracle). `Accheraṃ` from `acchariyaṃ` (wonderful). `Maccheraṃ` and `maccharaṃ` from `macchariyaṃ` (stinginess), and so on.

Akkharavaḍḍhipi hoti –

There is also addition of syllables:

Ekacciyo ekacceyyo ekacco, mātiyo macco, kiccayaṃ kiccaṃ, paṇḍitiyaṃ paṇḍiccaṃ, suvāmi sāmi, suvāmini sāmini, suvakehi puttehi sakehi puttehi, sattavo satto, tvañca uttamasattavo jā. 2.21.76, evaṃ uttamasattavo jā. 2.21.79 iccādi.

`Ekacciyo` and `ekacceyyo` from `ekacco` (a certain one). `Mātiyo` from `macco` (mortal). `Kiccayaṃ` from `kiccaṃ` (duty). `Paṇḍitiyaṃ` from `paṇḍiccaṃ` (wisdom). `Suvāmi` from `sāmi` (lord). `Suvāmini` from `sāmini` (lady). `Suvakehi puttehi` from `sakehi puttehi` (with one's own sons). `Sattavo` from `satto` (a being), as in `tvañca uttamasattavo` (and you are the highest being) and `evaṃ uttamasattavo` (thus the highest being), and so on.

Iti missakādesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on mixed substitutions.

Bindādeso dīpiyate.

Substitutions for the Niggahīta will now be explained.

46. Vagge vagganto ka. 31; rū. 49; nī. 138-9.

46. Before a stop, it becomes the corresponding nasal.

Vaggabyañjane pare niggahītassa sakavaggantabyañjanādeso hoti vā.

When a niggahīta is followed by a stop consonant, it is optionally replaced by the nasal of that consonant's class.

Dīpaṅkaro, saṅkhāro, saṅgaho, sañcāro, sañjāto, saṇṭhitaṃ, attantapo, parantapo, amatandado, purindado, sandhi, sannidhi, sampatti, sambuddho, sambhavo, sambhāro, sambhinno, sammato iccādīsu niccaṃ, taṅkaro, taṃkaro iccādīsu aniccaṃ, buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi khu. pā. 1.saraṇattaya, na taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu iccādīsu dha. pa. 67 natthi.

The change is obligatory in cases such as: `Dīpaṅkaro`, `saṅkhāro`, `saṅgaho`, `sañcāro`, `sañjāto`, `saṇṭhitaṃ`, `attantapo`, `parantapo`, `amatandado`, `purindado`, `sandhi`, `sannidhi`, `sampatti`, `sambuddho`, `sambhavo`, `sambhāro`, `sambhinno`, and `sammato`. The change is optional in cases such as `taṅkaro` or `taṃkaro`. The change does not occur in phrases such as `buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi` or `na taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu`.

Mahāvuttividhānamuccate.

The method of the Mahāvutti will now be explained.

Vaggāvaggesu byañjanesu paresu niggahītaṃ pararūpaṃ gacchati –

When followed by stop or non-stop consonants, the niggahīta is assimilated to the following consonant:

Sakkaroti, sakkato, sakkāro, sakkaccaṃ, takkattā, takkaro, takkhaṇaṃ taṅkhaṇaṃ taṃ khaṇaṃ, taggatikaṃ taṃ gatikaṃ, tanninno, tappoṇo, tappabbhāro, tappadhāno, etapparamo, yagguṇo yaṃguṇo, talleṇā, malleṇā, sallekho, paṭisallīno, tabbaṇṇanā taṃvaṇṇanā, tassamo taṃsamo, idappaccayatā[M 0.0038], cirappavāsiṃ, hatthippabhinnaṃ iccādi. Imasmiṃ ganthe ekattha siddhampi taṃ taṃ rūpaṃ tattha tattha punappunampi vidhiyyati ñāṇavicittatthaṃ.

`Sakkaroti`, `sakkato`, `sakkāro`, `sakkaccaṃ`, `takkattā`, `takkaro`, `takkhaṇaṃ` (also `taṅkhaṇaṃ` or `taṃ khaṇaṃ`), `taggatikaṃ` (also `taṃ gatikaṃ`), `tanninno`, `tappoṇo`, `tappabbhāro`, `tappadhāno`, `etapparamo`, `yagguṇo` (also `yaṃguṇo`), `talleṇā`, `malleṇā`, `sallekho`, `paṭisallīno`, `tabbaṇṇanā` (also `taṃvaṇṇanā`), `tassamo` (also `taṃsamo`), `idappaccayatā`, `cirappavāsiṃ`, `hatthippabhinnaṃ`, and so on. In this book, even if a particular form is established in one place, it is prescribed again and again in various places for the sake of developing a versatile knowledge.

47. Mayadā sare ka. 34, 35; rū. 34, 52; nī. 142-5.

47. Before a vowel, it becomes `m`, `y`, or `d`.

Sare pare niggahītassa kvaci ma, ya, dā honti vā.

When a vowel follows, the niggahīta optionally and in some cases becomes `m`, `y`, or `d`.

Tattha dādeso ya, ta, etasaddehi napuṃsake dissati –

Among these, the substitution of `d` is seen after the pronouns `ya`, `ta`, and `eta` in the neuter:

Yadabravi jā. 1.2.143, tadaniccaṃ ma. ni. 2.19, etadavoca satthā su. ni. dvayatānupassanāsutta.

`Yadabravi` (what he said); `tadaniccaṃ` (that is impermanent); `etadavoca satthā` (the Teacher said this).

Samāse pana dādeso tiliṅge dissati –

In a compound, however, the substitution of `d` is seen in all three genders:

Yadanantaraṃ, tadanantaraṃ, etadatthā kathā a. ni. 2.68. Etadatthā mantanā a. ni. 2.68 -tattha yassa atthassa vā yassa padassa vā yassā kathāya vā anantaraṃ yadanantaraṃ.

`Yadanantaraṃ` (immediately after which), `tadanantaraṃ` (immediately after that), `etadatthā kathā` (a talk for this purpose), `etadatthā mantanā` (a council for this purpose). Here `yadanantaraṃ` means 'immediately after which meaning, or which word, or which talk.'

Kvacitveva? Yametaṃ vārijaṃ pupphaṃ, adinnaṃ upasiṅghasi jā. 1.6.115.

And in what case? 'This water-born flower, which you smell, has not been given.'

Mādeso ya, ta, etasaddehi pumitthiliṅgesu dissati –

The substitution of `m` is seen after the pronouns `ya`, `ta`, and `eta` in the masculine and feminine genders:

Yamāhu devesu sujampatīti jā. 1.15.54, tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā jā. aṭṭha. 1.20.35, etamatthaṃ viditvā mahāva. 2-3.

`Yamāhu devesu sujampatīti` (whom they call Sujampati among the gods); `tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā` (the Teacher, explaining that meaning); `etamatthaṃ viditvā` (having understood this meaning).

Aññasaddehi pana dve ādesā tiliṅge dissanti –

With other words, however, both substitutions are seen in all three genders:

Sakadāgāmī, evametamabhiññāya su. ni. 1221 iccādi.

`Sakadāgāmī` (once-returner); `evametamabhiññāya` (having thus fully understood this), and so on.

Yādeso idaṃsadde pare tasaddamhā eva kvaci dissati –

The substitution of `y` is sometimes seen only after the pronoun `taṃ` when `idaṃ` follows:

Tayidaṃ na sādhu jā. 2.22.279, tayidaṃ na suṭṭhu jā. 2.22.279.

`Tayidaṃ na sādhu` (that is not good); `tayidaṃ na suṭṭhu` (that is not right).

48. Yevahisu ño

48. Before `ya`, `eva`, and `hi`, it becomes `ñ`.

Ya[M 0.0039], eva, hisaddesu paresu niggahītassa ño hoti. Yassa pubbarūpattaṃ.

When the words `ya`, `eva`, or `hi` follow, the niggahīta becomes `ñ`. The following `y` is then assimilated to it.

Ānantarikaññamāhu khu. pā. 6.5 – ānantarikaṃ + yaṃ + āhūti chedo, yaññadeva-yaṃ + yaṃ + eva, taññeva taṃ+eva, purisaññeva, paccattaññeva, tañhi, purisañhi, atthasañhito atthasaṃhito, dhammasañhito dhammasaṃhito.

`Ānantarikaññamāhu`, the analysis of which is `ānantarikaṃ yaṃ āhu` (which they call an immediately effective kamma); `yaññadeva`, from `yaṃ yaṃ eva` (whatever); `taññeva`, from `taṃ eva` (that very thing); `purisaññeva`; `paccattaññeva`; `tañhi`, from `taṃ hi` (for that); `purisañhi`, from `purisaṃ hi`; `atthasañhito` from `atthasaṃhito` (connected with the meaning); `dhammasañhito` from `dhammasaṃhito` (connected with the Dhamma).

49. Ye saṃssa ka. 33; rū. 51; nī. 141.

49. Of the prefix `saṃ` before `y`.

Yamhi pare saṃ upasaggassa niggahītassa ño hoti. Yassa pubbarūpattaṃ.

When `y` follows, the niggahīta of the prefix `saṃ` becomes `ñ`. The `y` is then assimilated to it.

Saññogo saṃyogo, saññutto saṃyutto. Saṃyojanaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, saññamo saṃyamo, saññato saṃyato, saññamati saṃyamati, saññācikā saṃyācikā kuṭiṃ pārā. 348 iccādi.

`Saññogo` from `saṃyogo` (conjunction); `saññutto` from `saṃyutto` (conjoined); `saññojanaṃ` from `saṃyojanaṃ` (fetter); `saññamo` from `saṃyamo` (restraint); `saññato` from `saṃyato` (restrained); `saññamati` from `saṃyamati` (one restrains); `saññācikā kuṭiṃ` from `saṃyācikā kuṭiṃ` (requesting a hut), and so on.

Iti bindādesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on substitutions for the Niggahīta.

Ādesasandhirāsi niṭṭhito.

The section on euphonic combination by substitution is concluded.

Āgamasandhi

Conjunction by Augmentation

Athāgamasandhi dīpiyate.

Now conjunction by augmentation is explained.

Mahāvuttinā sarāgamo –

According to the Mahāvutti, vowel augmentation:

A –

A –

Paṇṇasālaṃ amāpetvā jā. 2.22.1913, paṇṇasālaṃ amāpiya jā. 1.1.148 – māpetvā iccevattho, na cāpi apunappunaṃ, hatthibondiṃ pavekkhāmi jā. 1.1.148 -punappunaṃ iccevattho[M 0.0040], natthi loke anāmataṃ jā. 1.2.31 – amata pubbaṃ ṭhānanti attho, anavajjaṃ, anamataggo, jaccandho, jaccabadhiro, jaccamūgo, jaccapaṇḍako.

`Paṇṇasālaṃ amāpetvā`, `paṇṇasālaṃ amāpiya`—the meaning is simply `māpetvā` ('having caused to be built'). `Na cāpi apunappunaṃ, hatthibondiṃ pavekkhāmi`—here `apunappunaṃ` means `punappunaṃ` ('again and again'). `Natthi loke anāmataṃ`—the meaning is `amata pubbaṃ ṭhānaṃ` ('a state not previously experienced'). `Anavajjaṃ`, `anamataggo`, `jaccandho`, `jaccabadhiro`, `jaccamūgo`, `jaccapaṇḍako`.

Ā –

Ā –

Aḍḍhe ājāyare kule saṃ. ni. 1.49, manussesu paccājāto, āpūrati tassa yaso pari. 386.

He is born into a wealthy family; he is reborn among humans; his fame increases.

I –

I –

Dhammikathaṃ katvā pārā. 39, sarantā sapanti gacchantīti sarisapā.

`Dhammikathaṃ katvā`. `Sarisapā`: so called because they move along creeping.

Ī –

Ī –

Kabaḷīkāro, manasīkāro, manasīkaroti, tappākaṭīkaroti, dūrībhūto, abyayībhāvo.

The making of morsels, attention, he attends, he makes it manifest, become distant, the state of being indeclinable.

U –

U –

Ñātiparijinassa bhāvo ñātipārijuññaṃ, evaṃ bhogapārijuññaṃ- parijinassāti parihānassa, parikkhayassa.

The state of one who has lost relatives is loss of relatives; similarly, loss of wealth. “Lost” here means decline, destruction.

O –

O –

Parosataṃ, saradosataṃ, disodisaṃ dha. pa. 42 iccādi.

Over a hundred, a hundred autumns, from direction to direction, etc.

‘Atippago kho tāva piṇḍāya caritu’ dī. ni. 3.1 nti ettha pātottho pagosaddo eva.

“It is too early to wander for alms-food”—here the word `pago` has the meaning of “early morning.”

Iti sarāgamarāsi.

Thus ends the section on vowel augmentation.

50. Vanataragācāgamā

50. Consonant Augmentation

Sare pareva na, ta, ra, gā ca ma, ya, dā ca āgamā honti.

When a vowel follows, n, t, r, g, c, m, y, and d may be augments.

Go, to, do, no, mo, yo, ro, vo,

Go, to, do, no, mo, yo, ro, vo.

Tattha [M 0.0041] go –

Among these, go –

Ariyehi puthagevāyaṃ janoti puthujjano mahāniddese, idha pana pagosaddo eva, pageva vutyassa, pageva manussitthiyāti pārā. 55.

A `puthujjano` (a common person) is so called because this person is separate from the noble ones. Here, however, the word `pago` is simply `eva`; `pageva` is said of him, and `pageva` of a human woman.

To –

To –

Ajjatagge dī. ni. 1.250, tasmātiha ma. ni. 1.29, katamo nāma so rukkho, yassa tevaṃ gataṃ phalaṃ jā. 2.18.10 -tevanti evaṃ.

`Ajjatagge` (from this day forth); `tasmātiha` (therefore here); “What, pray, is the name of that tree, whose fruit has become so?”—here `tevaṃ` means “so.”

Do –

Do –

Udaggo, udabbahi, udapādi, udayo, udāhaṭo, udito, udīrito, dubhato vuṭṭhānaṃ paṭisambhidāmagge; visuddhimagge, dubhayāni viceyya paṇḍarāni su. ni. 531, todeyya, kappā dubhayo su. ni. 1131 – dve isayoti attho. Kiñcideva, kocideva, kismiñcideva, yāvadeva, tāvadeva, valutte-yāvade, tāvadeti siddhaṃ, punadeva, sakideva, sammadeva-dāgame rasso, sammadakkhāto saṃ. ni. 5.195, sammadaññā vimutto ma. ni. 2.234, bahudeva rattiṃ a. ni. 3.101, ahudeva bhayaṃ dī. ni. 1.159 iccādi.

`Udaggo` (elevated), `udabbahi` (he drew out), `udapādi` (it arose), `udayo` (arising), `udāhaṭo` (spoken), `udito` (risen), `udīrito` (uttered). `Dubhato vuṭṭhānaṃ` (rising from both). `Dubhayāni viceyya paṇḍarāni` (having examined both white things). `Todeyya`. `Kappā dubhayo`—the meaning is “the two seers.” `Kiñcideva` (anything at all), `kocideva` (anyone at all), `kismiñcideva` (in anything at all). `Yāvadeva` (just as much), `tāvadeva` (just so much)—in the Valutta grammar, `yāvade` and `tāvade` are also found. `Punadeva` (again indeed), `sakideva` (once indeed), `sammadeva` (rightly indeed)—with the `d` augment, the preceding long vowel is shortened. `Sammadakkhāto` (well proclaimed), `sammadaññā vimutto` (liberated by perfect direct knowledge). `Bahudeva rattiṃ` (for much of the night indeed). `Ahudeva bhayaṃ` (there was indeed fear), etc.

No –

No –

Ito nāyati, ciraṃ nāyati, kamme sādhu kammaniyaṃ kammaññaṃ, attano idaṃ attaniyaṃ, addhānaṃ khamatīti addhaniyaṃ, lobhassa hitaṃ lobhaniyaṃ lobhaneyyaṃ, dosaniyaṃ dosaneyyaṃ, mohaniyaṃ mohaneyyaṃ, oghaniyaṃ, yoganiyaṃ, ganthaniyaṃ, niddhunanaṃ, niddhunanako, sañjānanaṃ, sañjānanako, saññāpanako iccādi.

`Ito nāyati` (he comes from here), `ciraṃ nāyati` (he comes for a long time). `Kamme sādhu kammaniyaṃ`, `kammaññaṃ` (suitable for work). `Attano idaṃ attaniyaṃ` (belonging to oneself). `Addhānaṃ khamatīti addhaniyaṃ` (suitable for a journey). `Lobhassa hitaṃ lobhaniyaṃ`, `lobhaneyyaṃ` (conducive to greed). `Dosaniyaṃ`, `dosaneyyaṃ` (conducive to aversion). `Mohaniyaṃ`, `mohaneyyaṃ` (conducive to delusion). `Oghaniyaṃ` (conducive to floods), `yoganiyaṃ` (conducive to yokes), `ganthaniyaṃ` (conducive to fetters). `Niddhunanaṃ` (shaking off), `niddhunanako` (one who shakes off). `Sañjānanaṃ` (perceiving), `sañjānanako` (one who perceives), `saññāpanako` (one who causes to perceive), etc.

Mo [M 0.0042] –

Mo –

Tathā kena te idha mijjhati pe. va. 181, rūpāni manupassati dha. sa. aṭṭha. 596, ākāse mabhipūjaye, aññamaññassa ma. ni. 3.40, ekamekassa pārā. aṭṭha. 1.23, samaṇamacalo a. ni. 4.87, adukkhamasukhā vedanā saṃ. ni. 4.250 iccādi.

`Lahumessati` (it will become light), `garumessati` (it will become heavy), `maggamatthi` (there is a path), `aggamakkhāyati` (it is called the highest), `uragāmiva` (like snakes), `arahatāmiva` (like arahants), etc. Likewise: `Kena te idha mijjhati` (By what are you attached here?), `rūpāni manupassati` (one contemplates forms), `ākāse mabhipūjaye` (one should worship in the sky), `aññamaññassa` (to one another), `ekamekassa` (to each one), `samaṇamacalo` (the unmoving ascetic), `adukkhamasukhā vedanā` (neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling), etc.

Yo –

Nayimassa vijjā mayamatthi jā. 1.3.25, yathayidaṃ a. ni. 1.21-22, tathayidaṃ, chayime dhammā a. ni. 6.11, navayime dhammā a. ni. 9.9, dasayime dhammā a. ni. 10.16, mamayidaṃ, soyeva, teyeva, taṃyeva taññeva, tehiyeva, tesaṃyeva tesaññeva, tasmiyeva, buddhoyeva, buddhesuyeva, bodhiyāyeva kāraṇā cariyā. 1.65, hotiyeva, atthiyeva iccādi. Tiyantaṃ, aggiyāgāre, catutthīyatthe iccādīni ivaṇṇantarūpāni yāgamenāpi sijjhantiyeva.

`Nayimassa vijjā mayamatthi` (For this one there is no knowledge...), `yathayidaṃ` (as this is), `tathayidaṃ` (so this is), `chayime dhammā` (these six principles), `navayime dhammā` (these nine principles), `dasayime dhammā` (these ten principles). `Mamayidaṃ` (this is mine). `Soyeva` (that very one), `teyeva` (those very ones), `taṃyeva`/`taññeva` (that very thing), `tehiyeva` (by those very ones), `tesaṃyeva`/`tesaññeva` (of those very ones), `tasmiyeva` (in that very one). `Buddhoyeva` (the Buddha himself), `buddhesuyeva` (among the Buddhas themselves), `bodhiyāyeva kāraṇā` (for the sake of enlightenment itself). `Hotiyeva` (it is indeed), `atthiyeva` (it exists indeed), etc. Forms ending in `i`, such as `tiyantaṃ`, `aggiyāgāre`, `catutthīyatthe`, etc., are also formed by means of the `y` augment.

And here, just as in “`atiriva kallarūpā`” (exceedingly beautiful form), “`ativiya lābhaggayasaggapatto`” (attained the highest gain and renown), “`paraṃviya mattāya`” (beyond measure), etc., the words `iva` and `viya` are used in the sense of `eva` (indeed). Likewise, in “`yathariva`,” “`tathariva`,” “`varamhākaṃ bhusāmiva`” (better for us indeed), “`netaṃ ajjatanāmiva`” (this is not like today), etc., the word `iva` is used in the sense of `eva`.

51. Chā ḷo.

51. After `cha`, `ḷ`.

Sare pare chamhā ḷāgamo hoti.

When a vowel follows, the augment `ḷ` comes after `cha`.

Chaḷaṅgaṃ, chaḷāyatanaṃ, chaḷāsītisahassāni pe. va. 374, atthassa dvārā pamukhā chaḷete jā. 1.1.84, chaḷevānusayā honti abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā bu. vaṃ. 3.5.

`Chaḷaṅgaṃ` (six factors), `chaḷāyatanaṃ` (the six sense bases), `chaḷāsītisahassāni` (eighty-six thousand). “These six are the foremost doors to the goal.” “There are just six underlying tendencies.” “The six superknowledges are of great power.”

Mahāvuttividhānamuccate.

The method according to the Mahāvutti is stated.

Sare [M 0.0044] pare manādīhi sāgamo –

When a vowel follows, the augment `s` comes after words such as `manas`.

When a vowel follows, the augment `h` is often inserted.

Māhevaṃ ānanda dī. ni. 2.95, nohetaṃ bhante dī. ni. 1.185-186, nohidaṃ bho gotama dī. ni. 1.263, nahevaṃ vattabbe kathā. 1, hevaṃ vattabbe, hevaṃ vadati, ujū ca suhujūca khu. pā. 9.1, suhuṭṭhitaṃ sukhaṇo iccādi.

`Māhevaṃ ānanda` (Not so, Ānanda!), `nohetaṃ bhante` (It is not so, venerable sir), `nohidaṃ bho gotama` (It is not so, good Gotama), `nahevaṃ vattabbe` (it should not be said so), `hevaṃ vattabbe` (it should be said so), `hevaṃ vadati` (he says so), `ujū ca suhujū ca` (straight and very straight), `suhuṭṭhitaṃ` (well-established), `sukhaṇo`, etc.

Iti byañjanāgamarāsi.

Thus ends the section on consonant augmentation.

Dvibhāvasandhi

Conjunction by Doubling

Atha dvibhāvasandhi dīpiyate.

Now conjunction by doubling will be explained.

Dvibhāvo tividho. Tattha pakkamo, parakkamo iccādi byañjanadvittaṃ nāma. Rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ siñcati iccādi vibhatyantapadadvittaṃ nāma. Titikkhā, tikicchā, jagamā, jagamu iccādi dhātupadadvittaṃ nāma.

Doubling is threefold. Therein, `pakkamo`, `parakkamo`, etc., are called the doubling of a consonant; `rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ siñcati`, etc., are called the doubling of an inflected word; `titikkhā`, `tikicchā`, `jagamā`, `jagamu`, etc., are called the doubling of a root.

53. After a vowel, two.

Why 'after a vowel'? For `sampayutto`.

Kī, kudha, kamu, kusa, gaha, juta, ñā, si, su, sambhu, sara, sasa iccādīnaṃ dhātūnañca, u, du, nipubbānaṃ padānañca ādibyañjanassa dvittaṃ.

54. Catutthadutiyesvesaṃ tatiyapaṭhamā ka. 44, 29; rū. 24; nī. 57, 68, 74, 77-8, 80, 82-3, 91, 122.

54. Of these fourth and second consonants, they become third and first consonants respectively.

Vagge catuttha, dutiyesu paresu kamena tatiya, paṭhamā esaṃ catuttha, dutiyānaṃ dvibhāvaṃ gacchanti, dutiyabhāvaṃ gacchantīti attho. ‘Saramhā dve’ti suttena vā ‘vaggalasehi te’iccādīhi vā dutiya, catutthānampi sadisatte jāte puna iminā suttena [M 0.0049] ādidutiyassa paṭhamattaṃ, ādicatutthassa tatiyattañca jātaṃ.

When fourth and second consonants of a class follow, of these fourth and second consonants that have undergone doubling, they become a third and a first respectively; this is the meaning. When a second or fourth consonant has been made similar (i.e., doubled) by the rule 'saramhā dve' or by 'vaggalasehi te', etc., then by this present rule the initial second (of the pair) becomes a first, and the initial fourth becomes a third.

Tattha kavagge –

Therein, in the Guttural Class (kavagga):

Ākkhātaṃ, pakkhittaṃ, pakkhepo, rūpakkhandho, vedanākkhandho, dhātukkhobho, āyukkhayo, nakkhamati.

Ākkhātaṃ, pakkhittaṃ, pakkhepo, rūpakkhandho, vedanākkhandho, dhātukkhobho, āyukkhayo, nakkhamati.

‘Vaggalasehi te’ti suttavidhāne –

By the provision of the rule 'vaggalasehi te':

Pamukhe sādhu pāmokkhaṃ, paggharati, ugghosati, nigghoso.

Pamukhe sādhu pāmokkhaṃ, paggharati, ugghosati, nigghoso.

Cavagge –

In the Palatal Class (cavagga):

Acchādeti, acchindati-saṃyoge rassattaṃ, pacchādeti, pacchindati, setacchattaṃ, rukkhacchāyā, tathassa bhāvo tacchaṃ, rathassa hitā racchā, pajjhāyati, ujjhāyati, nijjhāyati, paṭhamajjhānaṃ, dutiyajjhānaṃ, ajjhokāso, bojjhaṅgo, dummedhassa bhāvo dummejjhaṃ, bujjhati, bujjhitabbaṃ, bojjhaṃ, paṭivijjha, paṭivijjhiya, paṭivijjhitvā iccādi.

Acchādeti, acchindati (with shortening in conjunction), pacchādeti, pacchindati, setacchattaṃ, rukkhacchāyā; the state of 'tathā' is tacchaṃ; what is good for a chariot (ratha) is a road (racchā); pajjhāyati, ujjhāyati, nijjhāyati, paṭhamajjhānaṃ, dutiyajjhānaṃ, ajjhokāso, bojjhaṅgo; the state of the unwise (dummedha) is dummejjhaṃ; bujjhati, bujjhitabbaṃ, bojjhaṃ, paṭivijjha, paṭivijjhiya, paṭivijjhitvā, etc.

Ṭavagge –

In the Retroflex Class (ṭavagga):

Yatraṭṭhitaṃ, tatraṭṭhito, uṭṭhito, niṭṭhito, thalaṭṭho, jalaṭṭho, vuḍḍho iccādi.

Yatraṭṭhitaṃ, tatraṭṭhito, uṭṭhito, niṭṭhito, thalaṭṭho, jalaṭṭho, vuḍḍho, etc.

Tavagge –

In the Dental Class (tavagga):

Sumanatthero, yasatthero, avatthā, avatthānaṃ, vitthāro, abhitthuto, vitthambhito, uddharati, uddharaṇaṃ, uddhaṭaṃ, niddhāreti, niddhāraṇaṃ, niddhāritaṃ, niddhano, niddhuto, niddhoto iccādi.

Sumanatthero, yasatthero, avatthā, avatthānaṃ, vitthāro, abhitthuto, vitthambhito, uddharati, uddharaṇaṃ, uddhaṭaṃ, niddhāreti, niddhāraṇaṃ, niddhāritaṃ, niddhano, niddhuto, niddhoto, etc.

Pavagge –

In the Labial Class (pavagga):

Vippharati, vippharaṇaṃ, vipphāro, apphoṭeti, mahapphalaṃ, nipphalaṃ, madhupphāṇitaṃ, vibbhamati, vibbhamo, ubbhataṃ, nibbhayaṃ, dubbharo, sabbhāvo[M 0.0050], usabhassa bhāvo osabbhaṃ, labbhati, ārabbho, ārabbha, ārabbhitvā iccādi.

Vippharati, vippharaṇaṃ, vipphāro, apphoṭeti, mahapphalaṃ, nipphalaṃ, madhupphāṇitaṃ, vibbhamati, vibbhamo, ubbhataṃ, nibbhayaṃ, dubbharo, sabbhāvo; the state of a bull (usabha) is osabbhaṃ; labbhati, ārabbho, ārabbha, ārabbhitvā, etc.

Idhapi u, du, nito parapadānaṃ ādibyañjanassa dvittaṃ visesato icchanti.

Here too, the doubling of the initial consonant of a word following 'u', 'du', and 'ni' is especially intended.

Iti visadisadvittarāsi.

Thus the section on the doubling of dissimilar consonants.

55. Vicchābhikkhaññesu dve caṃ. 6.3-1; pā. 8.1.1, 4.

55. A word is doubled in the sense of pervasion (vicchā) and repetition (abhikkhañña).

Vicchāyaṃ abhikkhaññe ca anekatthassa ekapadassa dve rūpāni honti. Bhinne atthe kriyāya vā dabbena vā guṇena vā byāpituṃ icchā vicchā. Punappunakriyā abhikkhaññaṃ.

In the sense of pervasion (vicchā) and repetition (abhikkhañña), a single word referring to multiple things takes two forms. Pervasion (vicchā) is the wish to encompass distinct items, whether by action, substance, or quality. Repetition (abhikkhañña) is an action done again and again.

Vicchāyaṃ tāva –

First, in the sense of pervasion:

Rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ siñcati. Gāme gāme sataṃkumbhā, gāmo gāmo ramaṇiyo, gehe gehe issaro, rasaṃ rasaṃ bhakkhayati, kriyaṃ kriyaṃ ārabhate.

He waters tree after tree. In village after village there are a hundred pots. Village after village is delightful. In house after house there is a master. He enjoys flavor after flavor. He undertakes action after action.

Ānupubbiyepi vicchāva gamyate –

Pervasion (vicchā) is also understood in the sense of sequence:

Mūle mūle thūlā, agge agge sukhumā, jeṭṭhaṃ jeṭṭhaṃ anupavesetha, imesaṃ devasikaṃ māsakaṃ māsakaṃ dehi, mañjūsakarukkho pupphaṃ pupphaṃ pupphati, ime janā pathaṃ pathaṃ accenti, sabbe ime aḍḍhā, katarā katarā imesaṃ aḍḍhatā, katamā katamā imesaṃ aḍḍhatā.

Thick at every root, fine at every tip. Let them enter according to seniority. Give to these a māsaka each day, each month. The coral tree blossoms flower by flower. These people pass along path after path. All these are wealthy; which among them is wealthier, which among them is wealthiest?

Abhikkhaññe –

In the sense of repetition:

Bhattaṃ pacati pacati, apuññaṃ pasavati pasavati, bhutvā bhutvā nippajjanti, paṭaṃ paṭaṃ karoti, paṭapaṭāyati, ekamekaṃ, ekamekāni iccādīsu vicchāsu pubbapade syādilopo.

He cooks and cooks a meal. He produces demerit again and again. Having eaten again and again, they lie down. He makes cloth after cloth. It crackles repeatedly. In 'ekamekaṃ', 'ekamekāni', etc., which are in the sense of pervasion, the case ending of the first word is elided.

56. Sabbādīnaṃ vītihāre.

56. Of 'sabba' and other pronouns, in the sense of reciprocity.

Atikkamma [M 0.0051] haraṇaṃ atihāro, na atihāro vītihāro, aññamaññassa antoyeva haraṇantiattho, vītihāratthe gamyamāne sabbādīnaṃ sabbanāmānaṃ dve rūpāni honti, pubbassekassa ca syādilopo.

Taking by surpassing is 'atihāra'; not 'atihāra' is 'vītihāra', which means taking within one another. When the sense of reciprocity (vītihāra) is understood, pronouns such as 'sabba' take two forms, and the case ending of the first is elided.

Ime dve janā aññamaññassa upakārakā, itarītarassa upakārakā, aññamaññaṃ passanti, aññamaññassa denti, aññamaññassa apenti, aññamaññassa dhanaṃ, aññamaññe nissitā.

These two people are helpful to each other; helpful to one another; they see each other; they give to each other; they take from each other; each other's wealth; they are dependent on each other.

57. Yāvatātāvaṃ sambhame caṃ. 6.3.14; pā. 8.1.12; yāvabodhaṃ sambhame (bahūsu).

57. As many times as is necessary, in agitation.

Yaṃ parimāṇamassāti yāvaṃ. Taṃ parimāṇamassāti tāvaṃ. Punappunaṃ bhamanaṃ pavattanaṃ sambhamo. Turitena vacīpayogena taṃ taṃ upāyadīpanaṃ sambhamo, āmeḍitameva vuccati, sambhame gamyamāne yāvatā yattakena padena so attho paññāyati, tattakaṃ padaṃ payujjate, dvikkhattuṃ vā tikkhattuṃ vā taduttari vā udīriyatetyattho. Yathābodhaṃ sambhametipi pāṭho, soyevattho.

`Yāvaṃ` means 'that which has a certain measure.' `Tāvaṃ` means 'that which has that measure.' `Sambhama` is repeated movement or occurrence. `Sambhama` is also the indication of some state by hurried speech; this is called `āmeḍita` (repetition). When `sambhama` is to be conveyed, a word is used as many times as is needed to make the meaning known; that is, it is uttered two times, three times, or more. There is also the reading `yathābodhaṃ sambhame`, with the same meaning.

Bhaye, kodhe, pasaṃsāyaṃ, turite, kotūhale’cchare.

In fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, and wonder;

Hāse, soke, pasāde ca, kare āmeḍitaṃ budho.

also in laughter, sorrow, and satisfaction, the wise person should make a repetition (`āmeḍita`).

Tattha bhaye –

Therein, in fear:

Sappo sappo, coro coro –

`Sappo, sappo!` (A snake, a snake!); `Coro, coro!` (A thief, a thief!).

Kodhe –

In anger:

Vijjha vijjha, pahara pahara.

`Vijjha, vijjha!` (Pierce, pierce!); `Pahara, pahara!` (Strike, strike!).

Pasaṃsāyaṃ –

In praise:

Sādhu sādhu.

`Sādhu, sādhu!` (Good, good!).

Turite [M 0.0052] –

In haste:

Gaccha gaccha.

`Gaccha, gaccha!` (Go, go!).

Kotūhale –

In curiosity:

Āgaccha āgaccha.

`Āgaccha, āgaccha!` (Come, come!).

Acchare –

In wonder:

Aho buddho aho buddho.

`Aho buddho, aho buddho!` (Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Buddha!).

Hāse –

In laughter:

Abhikkamatha vāseṭṭhā abhikkamatha vāseṭṭhā dī. ni. 2.210.

`Abhikkamatha vāseṭṭhā, abhikkamatha vāseṭṭhā!` (Go forward, Vāseṭṭhas, go forward, Vāseṭṭhas!).

Soke –

In sorrow:

Kahaṃ ekaputtaka kahaṃ ekaputtaka saṃ. ni. 4.120.

`Kahaṃ ekaputtaka, kahaṃ ekaputtaka?` (Where is my only son, where is my only son?).

Pasāde –

In satisfaction:

Abhikkantaṃ bho gotama abhikkantaṃ bho gotama ma. ni. 2.106 iccādi. Tikkhattuṃudānaṃ udānesi “namo tassa bhagavato” ma. ni. 2.357 iccādi.

`Abhikkantaṃ bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ bho gotama!` (Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Excellent, Venerable Gotama!), and so on. Three times he uttered the inspired utterance: “Homage to the Blessed One,” and so on.

Iti padavākyadvittarāsi.

Thus the collection on the doubling of words and phrases.

Dvibhāvasandhirāsi niṭṭhito.

The chapter on connection by reduplication is finished.

Vipallāsasandhi

The Connection by Inversion

Atha vipallāsasandhi dīpiyate.

Now the connection by inversion is explained.

Padakkharānaṃ pubbāparavipariyāyo vipallāso.

Inversion (`vipallāsa`) is the reversal of the former and latter order of letters of a word.

58. Hassa vipallāso.

58. The inversion of 'h'.

Yamhi pare hassa pubbāparavipallāso hoti vā.

When followed by 'y', the letter 'h' is optionally inverted with it.

Dayhati, saṅgayhati, sannayhati, vuyhati, duyhati, muyhati.

For example: `dayhati`, `saṅgayhati`, `sannayhati`, `vuyhati`, `duyhati`, `muyhati`.

Vātveva[M 0.0053]? Saṅgaṇhiyati, evaṃ saṅgayha saṅgaṇhitvā, āruyha āruhitvā, ogāyha ogāhitvā. Pasayha pasahitvā.

Why 'optionally'? For example: saṅgaṇhiyati. Similarly: saṅgayha and saṅgaṇhitvā; āruyha and āruhitvā; ogāyha and ogāhitvā; pasayha and pasahitvā.

59. Ve vā rū. 40 (piṭṭhe).

59. Optionally with 'v'.

Vamhi pare hassa vipallāso hoti vā.

When followed by 'v', the letter 'h' is optionally inverted with it.

Bavhābādho bahvābādho, bavhettha nhāyatī jano udā. 9 =bahvettha nhāyatī jano.

For example: bavhābādho for bahvābādho; bavhettha nhāyatī jano for bahvettha nhāyatī jano.

Mahāvuttividhānaṃ vuccate.

The explanation from the Mahāvutti is stated.

Ya, rānaṃ vipallāso –

Inversion of 'y' and 'r'—

Kuṭi me kayirati pārā. 358, vacanaṃ payirudāhāsi, garuṃ payirūpāsati, vandāmi te ayyire pasannacitto jā. 2.17.54 -yassa dvittaṃ.

For example: kayirati (for kariyate); payirudāhāsi (for pariyudāhāsi); payirūpāsati (for pariyupāsati); vandāmi te ayyire pasannacitto (for ariye), where 'y' is doubled.

Niggahītassa vipallāso –

Inversion of the niggahīta (ṃ)—

Nirayamhi apaccisuṃ jā. 2.22.60, te me asse ayācisuṃ jā. 2.22.1863. Imā gāthā abhāsisuṃ.

For example: nirayamhi apaccisuṃ (for apacciṃsu); te me asse ayācisuṃ (for ayāciṃsu); imā gāthā abhāsisuṃ (for abhāsiṃsu).

Sarānampi vipallāso –

Inversion of vowels also occurs—

Haññayyevāpi koci naṃ jā. 2.22.1193 – haññeyyāti ṭhiti, amūlamūlaṃ gantvā-mūlamūlaṃ agantvāti attho. Evaṃ paratra. Anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā pārā 389, animittaṃ katvā, saddhaṃ na bhuñjatīti asaddhabhoji, disvā padamanuttiṇṇaṃ jā. 1.1.20 – uttiṇṇaṃ adisvāti attho.

For example: 'Haññayyevāpi koci naṃ' (Even if someone were to kill him), where the established meaning is 'he should be killed.' 'Amūlamūlaṃ gantvā' (going to the rootless root), where the meaning is 'not going to the root of the root.' Similarly elsewhere. 'Anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā' (having caused a non-opportunity to be made); 'animittaṃ katvā' (having made it signless); 'asaddhabhoji' means 'one who does not eat with faith' (saddhaṃ na bhuñjati). 'Disvā padam anuttiṇṇaṃ' (seeing the unsubmerged foot), where the meaning is 'not seeing it submerged' (uttiṇṇaṃ adisvā).

Padānampi vipallāso –

Inversion of words also occurs—

Navaṃ pana bhikkhunā cīvaralābhena, nāgakaññā caritaṃ gaṇena jā. 1.15.268 -nāgakaññāgaṇena caritanti ṭhiti.

For example: 'Navaṃ pana bhikkhunā cīvaralābhena, nāgakaññā caritaṃ gaṇena' (But when a monk has received a new robe, conduct with a group of nāga maidens), where the established interpretation is 'conduct with a group of nāga maidens' (nāgakaññāgaṇena caritaṃ).

Iti vipallāsarāsi.

Thus the chapter on inversion.

60. Bahulaṃ caṃ. 1.1.130; pā. 3.3.113.

60. By General Application.

Sandhividhānaṃ [M 0.0054] nāma bahulaṃ hoti, yebhuyyena hotīti attho. Adhikārasuttaṃ. Yāvaganthapariyosānā yuttaṭṭhānesu sabbattha vattate. Etena sabbasaddasuttesu aniṭṭhanivatti ca iṭṭhapariggaho ca kato hoti.

The rules of sandhi are general (bahulaṃ); the meaning is that they apply for the most part (yebhuyyena). This is a governing rule (adhikārasutta). It is valid everywhere in suitable places up to the end of the text. By means of it, in all grammatical rules, the exclusion of unintended forms and the inclusion of intended forms is accomplished.

Iti niruttidīpaniyā nāma moggallānadīpaniyaṃ

Thus in the Moggallānadīpanī, the section named the Niruttidīpanī.

Sandhikaṇḍo niṭṭhito.

The Chapter on Sandhi is concluded.

2. Nāmakaṇḍa

2. The Chapter on Nouns

Vibhattirāsi

The Chapter on Inflections

Atha [M 0.0055] liṅgamhā syādivibhattividhānaṃ dīpiyate.

Now the rule for the inflections beginning with 'si' after a nominal stem (liṅga) is explained.

Liṅgaṃ, nāmaṃ, pāṭipadikanti atthato ekaṃ, dabbābhidhānassa purisādikassa pakatirūpassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tañhi sattannaṃ vibhattīnaṃ vasena vibhāgaṃ patvā kiñci visadarūpaṃ hoti, kiñci avisadarūpaṃ, kiñci majjhimarūpanti evaṃ tividhena liṅgarūpena yuttattā liṅganti vuccati.

Nominal stem (liṅga), noun (nāma), and base (pāṭipadika) are one in meaning. This is the name for the natural form of a term designating a substance, such as 'person.' For that stem, having undergone division by means of the seven inflections, becomes in some cases clear in form, in some unclear, and in some intermediate. Thus, because it is endowed with a threefold form of gender (liṅga), it is called a 'nominal stem' (liṅga).

Tadeva kiñci saddaliṅgānurūpaṃ, kiñci atthaliṅgānurūpañca pariṇamantaṃ pavattati, tasmā nāmanti ca vuccati.

That same stem proceeds by transforming, conforming partly to grammatical gender and partly to natural gender. Therefore, it is also called a 'noun' (nāma).

Tadeva dhātu, paccaya, vibhattipadehi cevasaddapadatthakapadehi ca ‘visuṃ bhūtaṃ pada’nti katvā pāṭipadikanti ca vuccati.

That same stem, being considered a 'term separate' from the terms that are roots, suffixes, and inflections, and also from terms that are mere sounds, is also called a 'base' (pāṭipadika).

Tattha dhātupadaṃ nāma brū, bhū, hūiccādi.

Therein, the term 'root' (dhātupada) refers to 'brū,' 'bhū,' 'hū,' and so on.

Paccayapadaṃ nāma ṇa, tabba, anīya iccādi.

The term 'suffix' (paccayapada) refers to 'ṇa,' 'tabba,' 'anīya,' and so on.

Vibhattipadaṃ nāma si, yo, aṃ, yo,ti, anti iccādi.

The term 'inflection' (vibhattipada) refers to 'si,' 'yo,' 'aṃ,' 'yo,' 'ti,' 'anti,' and so on.

Saddapadatthakapadāni nāma rājassa, sakhassa, pumassa iccādīni. Ettha ca rājassaiccādīni saddasutte saddapadatthakāni honti, payoge atthapadatthakāni. Dhātupaccayavibhattipadāni pana niccaṃ saddapadatthakāni eva honti, saddasuttesveva ca labbhanti, na payogeti, idaṃ dvinnaṃ nānattaṃ.

Terms that are mere sounds are, for example, 'rājassa,' 'sakhassa,' 'pumassa,' and so on. Here, in a grammatical rule, forms like 'rājassa' are terms that are mere sounds; in actual usage, they are terms that have meaning. Roots, suffixes, and inflections, however, are always only terms that are mere sounds and are found only in the grammatical rules, not in usage. This is the difference between the two.

Yadievaṃ bhussa, brussa, bhūto, hūto, ṇe, tabbe, simhi, timhi iccādinā tehi kathaṃ vibhattuppatti hotīti? Anukaraṇapadāni nāma tāni atthissa, karotissa iccādīni viya, tasmā tāni ca rājassa iccādīni ca anukaraṇaliṅgabhāvena ettha saṅgayhanti, na ekantaliṅgabhāvenāti. Evañca katvā ‘dhātu- paccaya[M 0.0056], vibhattivajjitamatthavaṃ liṅga’nti avocuṃ. Tattha atthavanti atthapadatthakaṃ vuccati, rājassaiccādikaṃ saddapadatthakaṃ vivajjeti, etena atthapadatthake sati taddhita, samāsa, kitakapadānampi ekantaliṅgabhāvaṃ sādhenti. Na hi tesaṃ liṅganāmabyapadesakiccaṃ atthi, yāni ca nāmassa visesanāni bhavituṃ arahanti, tāni upasagga, nipātapadāni tvāntādipadāni ca idha visesananāmabhāvena saṅgayhantīti.

If so, how can inflections be generated from such forms as 'bhussa,' 'brussa,' 'bhūto,' 'hūto,' 'ṇe,' 'tabbe,' 'simhi,' 'timhi,' and so on? They are 'imitative terms' (anukaraṇapadāni), like 'atthissa,' 'karotissa,' etc. Therefore, they and forms like 'rājassa' are included here as 'imitative nominal stems,' not as having a definitive nature as a stem. Thus it was said: 'A nominal stem (liṅga) is that which is meaningful and devoid of root, suffix, and inflection.' Here, 'meaningful' refers to a term with semantic content, which excludes terms like 'rājassa' that are mere sounds. By this, they establish the definitive status as nominal stems for secondary derivatives (taddhita), compounds (samāsa), and primary derivatives (kitaka) when they have semantic content. For these, there is no need for a separate designation as a nominal stem. And those terms that can be qualifiers of a noun—prefixes, particles, and terms ending in '-tvā,' etc.—are included here as 'qualifying nouns'.

61. Dve dvekānekesu nāmasmā si yo aṃyo nā hi sa naṃ smāhi sanaṃsmiṃsu ka. 55; rū. 63; nī. 200.

61. From a noun, in singular and plural meanings respectively, the following pairs of inflections occur: si, yo; aṃ, yo; nā, hi; sa, naṃ; smā, hi; sa, naṃ; smiṃ, su.

Ekasmiṃ atthe ca anekesu atthesu ca pavattā nāmasmā dve dve si, yo…pe… smiṃ, suvibhattiyo honti.

From a noun, occurring in a singular meaning and in plural meanings respectively, the inflections 'si,' 'yo,' and so on up to 'smiṃ,' 'su,' occur in pairs.

Vibhajantīti vibhattiyo, ekamekaṃ pakatināmapadaṃ nānārūpavibhāgavasena kattu, kammādinānāatthavibhāgavasena ekatta, bahuttasaṅkhyāvibhāgavasena ca vibhajantīti attho. Si, lo iti paṭhamā nāma…pe… smiṃ, su iti sattamī nāma. Dvīsu dvīsu pubbaṃ pubbaṃ ‘ekasmiṃ atthe pavattaṃ vacana’nti ekavacanaṃ nāma. Paraṃ paraṃ ‘anekesu atthesu pavattaṃ vacana’nti anekavacanaṃ nāma. Bahuvacananti ca puthuvacananti ca etassa nāmaṃ. Sabbamidaṃ iminā suttena siddhaṃ.

They are called 'inflections' (vibhattiyo) because they 'divide' (vibhajanti). The meaning is that they divide each base noun-term by way of various forms, by way of various meanings such as agent and object, and by way of number, i.e., singular and plural. 'Si,' 'yo' is the first inflection; ... up to ... 'smiṃ,' 'su' is the seventh inflection. Of each pair, the former is called the 'singular number' (ekavacana), being 'the expression occurring in a single meaning.' The latter is called the 'plural number' (anekavacana), being 'the expression occurring in multiple meanings.' 'Bahuvacana' and 'puthuvacana' are also names for this. All this is established by this rule.

62. Paṭhamātthamatte ka. 284; rū. 65; nī. 577; caṃ. 2.1.93; pā. 2.3.46.

62. The first [inflection] is in the sense of the stem-meaning only.

Kattu, kammādikaṃ bāhiratthaṃ anapekkhitvā liṅgatthamatte pavattā nāmasmā paṭhamāvibhatti hoti.

Without reference to any external meaning such as agent or object, the first inflection occurs after a nominal stem to express the meaning of the stem alone.

Ayaṃ mama puriso, ime mama purisā.

Ayaṃ mama puriso (this is my man); ime mama purisā (these are my men).

63. Āmantane ka. 285; rū. 70; nī. 578; caṃ. 2.1.94; pā. 2.3.47.

63. In address.

Āmantanaṃ [M 0.0057] vuccati ālapanaṃ. Āmantanavisaye liṅgatthamatte pavattā nāmasmā paṭhamāvibhatti hoti.

Address (āmantana) is called 'calling out' (ālapana). In the sense of address, the first inflection occurs after a nominal stem to express the meaning of the stem alone.

Bho purisa, bhonto purisā.

Bho purisa (O man!); bhonto purisā (O men!).

64. Kamme dutiyā ka. 297; rū. 76, 284; nī. 580; caṃ. 2.1.43; pā. 1.4.49-51.

64. The second [inflection] is in the sense of the object.

Nāmasmā kammatthe dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

The second inflection occurs after a nominal stem in the sense of the object.

Purisaṃ passati, purise passanti.

Purisaṃ passati (he sees the man); purise passanti (they see the men).

65. Kattukaraṇesu tatiyā ka. 286, 288; rū. 83; nī. 591, 594; caṃ. 2.1.62, 63; pā. 2.3.18.

65. The third [inflection] is in the sense of the agent and the instrument.

Nāmasmā kattari ca karaṇe ca tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

The third inflection occurs after a nominal stem in the sense of the agent and in the sense of the instrument.

Purisena kataṃ, purisehi kataṃ, purisena kulaṃ sobhati, purisehi kulaṃ sobhati.

Purisena kataṃ (done by the man); purisehi kataṃ (done by the men); purisena kulaṃ sobhati (the family shines by the man); purisehi kulaṃ sobhati (the family shines by the men).

66. Catutthī sampadāne ka. 293; rū 85, 301; nī. 605; caṃ. 2.1.73; pā. 2.3.13.

66. The fourth [inflection] is in the sense of the recipient.

Nāmasmā sampadānatthe catutthīvibhatti hoti.

The fourth inflection occurs after a nominal stem in the sense of the recipient.

Purisassa deti, purisānaṃ deti.

Purisassa deti (he gives to the man); purisānaṃ deti (he gives to the men).

67. Pañcamyāvadhismiṃ ka. 295; rū. 89, 307; nī. 607 caṃ. 2.1.81; pā. 2.3.28; 1.4.24 pañcamyavadhismā (bahūsu).

67. The fifth [inflection] is in the sense of the point of departure.

Avadhi vuccati apādānaṃ. Nāmasmā avadhiatthe pañcamīvibhatti hoti.

The point of departure (avadhi) is called the ablative (apādāna). The fifth inflection occurs after a nominal stem in the sense of the point of departure.

Purisasmā apeti, purisehi apeti.

Purisasmā apeti (he goes away from the man); purisehi apeti (he goes away from the men).

68. Chaṭṭhī [M 0.0058] sambandhe ka. 30; rū. 92, 315; nī. 609; caṃ. 2.1.95; pā. 2.3.50.

68. The sixth [inflection] is in the sense of relation.

Nāmasmā sambandhatthe chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti.

The sixth inflection occurs after a nominal stem in the sense of relation.

Purisassa dhanaṃ, purisānaṃ dhanaṃ.

Purisassa dhanaṃ (the man's wealth); purisānaṃ dhanaṃ (the men's wealth).

69. Sattamyādhāre ka. 312; rū. 94, 319; nī. 630; caṃ. 2.1.88; pā. 2.3.36; 1.3.45.

69. The seventh [inflection] is in the sense of location.

Nāmasmā ādhāratthe sattamīvibhatti hoti.

The seventh inflection occurs after a nominal stem in the sense of location.

Purisasmiṃ tiṭṭhati, purisesu tiṭṭhati.

Purisasmiṃ tiṭṭhati (he stands in/on the man); purisesu tiṭṭhati (he stands among the men).

Vibhattirāsi niṭṭhito.

The Chapter on Inflections is concluded.

Itthipaccayarāsi

The Section on Feminine Affixes.

70. Itthiyamatvā ka. 237; rū. 176; nī. 466; caṃ. 2.3.15; pā. 4.1.4.

70. In the feminine, the affix -ā follows -a.

Itthiyaṃ+ato+āti chedo. Akārantanāmamhā itthiyaṃ āpaccayo hoti.

The division of the rule is: itthiyaṃ + ato + ā + iti. The affix -ā occurs in the feminine from a noun ending in -a.

Abhāsitapumehi kehici saññāsaddehi niccaṃ –

Always, from certain nouns that are not used in the masculine:

Kaññā, paññā, saññā, nāvā, sālā, taṇhā, icchā, bhikkhā, sikkhā, gīvā, jivhā, vīsā, tiṃsā, cattālīsā, paññāsā iccādi.

Kaññā (maiden), paññā (wisdom), saññā (perception), nāvā (boat), sālā (hall), taṇhā (craving), icchā (desire), bhikkhā (almsfood), sikkhā (training), gīvā (neck), jivhā (tongue), vīsā (twenty), tiṃsā (thirty), cattālīsā (forty), paññāsā (fifty), etc.

Bhāsitapumehipi sabbanāmehi tabbā, nīya, tapaccayantehi ca niccaṃ –

Always, also from pronouns that are used in the masculine, and from stems ending in the suffixes -tabba, -nīya, and -ta:

Sabbā, katarā, katamā, anubhavitabbā, anubhavanīyā, gatā, jātā, bhūtā, hūtā iccādi.

Sabbā (all), katarā (which of two), katamā (which of many); anubhavitabbā (to be experienced), anubhavanīyā (to be experienced); gatā (gone), jātā (born), bhūtā (become), hūtā (offered), etc.

Aññehi [M 0.0059] pana aniccaṃ –

But from others, optionally:

Kalyāṇā, kalyāṇī, sundarā, sundarī, sobhaṇā, sobhaṇī, kumbhakārā, kumbhakārī, kumbhakārinī, atthakāmā, atthakāmī, atthakāminī, paribbājikā, paribbājikinī, ekākā, ekākinī, dīpanā, dīpanī iccādi.

Beautiful (forms: kalyāṇā, kalyāṇī), lovely (sundarā, sundarī), fair (sobhaṇā, sobhaṇī), female potter (kumbhakārā, kumbhakārī, kumbhakārinī), well-wisher (atthakāmā, atthakāmī, atthakāminī), female wanderer (paribbājikā, paribbājikinī), solitary (ekākā, ekākinī), illuminating (dīpanā, dīpanī), etc.

Suttavibhattena samāse mātu, dhītu iccādīhi āpaccayo hoti. Nandamātā, uttaramātā, devadhītā, rājadhītā, assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā iccādi.

By a special provision of a rule, in a compound, the affix -ā occurs after stems such as mātu (mother) and dhītu (daughter). For example: Nandamātā (Nanda's mother), Uttaramātā (Uttara's mother), devadhītā (a deva's daughter), rājadhītā (a king's daughter); as in the Pāḷi, 'assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā' (she is not an ascetic, not a Sakyan's daughter), etc.

Ettha ca ‘itthiya’nti katthaci saddamattassa vā, katthaci atthamattassa vā itthibhāve jotetabbeti attho. Evañca sati itthipaccayāpi syādayo viya jotakamattā eva honti, na vācakāti siddhaṃ hoti.

And here, the meaning of the term 'itthiyam' (in the feminine) is that the feminine state is to be indicated, sometimes of the word-form alone, and sometimes of the meaning alone. This being so, it is established that feminine affixes, like the case endings beginning with 'si', are merely indicators, not primary signifiers.

71. Nadādīhi ṅī ka. 238; rū. 187; nī. 467; nadādito vī (bahūsu).

71. From stems of the nadī-group, the affix Ṅī.

Nadādīhi itthiyaṃ ṅī hoti. Ṅānubandho ‘ntantūnaṃ ṅīmhi to vā’ti ettha visesanattho.

From stems of the nadī-group, the affix Ṅī occurs in the feminine. The indicatory letter Ṅ serves for specification in the rule 'Ntantūnaṃ ṅīmhi to vā'.

Nadī, mahī, itthī, kumārī, taruṇī, vāseṭṭhī, gotamī, kaccānī, kaccāyanī, māṇavī, sāmaṇerī, nāvikī, pañcamī, chaṭṭhī, catuddasī, pañcadasī, sahassī, dasasahassī, satasahassī, kumbhakārī, mālakārī, cakkhukaraṇī, ñāṇakaraṇī, dhammadīpanī iccādi.

Nadī (river), mahī (earth), itthī (woman), kumārī (maiden), taruṇī (young woman), Vāseṭṭhī (a woman of the Vāseṭṭha clan), Gotamī (a woman of the Gotama clan), Kaccānī/Kaccāyanī (a woman of the Kaccāna/Kaccāyana clan), māṇavī (young woman), sāmaṇerī (novice nun), nāvikī (female sailor), pañcamī (the fifth), chaṭṭhī (the sixth), catuddasī (the fourteenth), pañcadasī (the fifteenth), sahassī (a group of a thousand), dasasahassī (a group of ten thousand), satasahassī (a group of a hundred thousand), kumbhakārī (female potter), mālakārī (female garland-maker), cakkhukaraṇī (producing vision), ñāṇakaraṇī (producing knowledge), dhammadīpanī (illuminating the Dhamma), etc.

72. Ntantūnaṃ ṅīmhi to vā ka. 239, 241; rū. 190, 191; nī. 468, 471.

72. Of stems in -nta and -ntu, optionally 't' before Ṅī.

Nta, ntūnaṃ to hoti vā ṅīmhi pare.

Of stems ending in -nta and -ntu, 't' optionally occurs when Ṅī follows.

Gacchatī, gacchantī, satī, santī, bhavissatī, bhavissantī, guṇavatī, guṇavantī, satimatī, satimantī, sabbāvatī, sabbāvantī, yāvatī, yāvantī, tāvatī, tāvantī, bhuttavatī, bhuttavantī.

Going (fem. forms: gacchatī, gacchantī), being (satī, santī), about to be (bhavissatī, bhavissantī), virtuous (guṇavatī, guṇavantī), mindful (satimatī, satimantī), possessing all (sabbāvatī, sabbāvantī), as great as (yāvatī, yāvantī), so great as (tāvatī, tāvantī), one who has eaten (bhuttavatī, bhuttavantī).

73. Goto vā ka. 238; rū. 187; nī. 467.

73. From 'go', optionally.

Gosaddamhā [M 0.0060] itthiyaṃ vī hoti vā.

From the stem 'go', the affix -vī optionally occurs in the feminine.

Gāvī.

Gāvī (a cow).

Vāti kiṃ? Gokāṇā pariyantacārinīti pāḷi. Tattha kāṇāti andhā.

Why 'optionally'? The Pāḷi text has: 'Gokāṇā pariyantacārinī' (A one-eyed cow wandering at the edge). Therein, 'kāṇā' means one-eyed.

74. Yakkhādīhinī ca ka. 238, 240; rū. 287, 193; nī. 467, 469; yakkhāditvinī ca (bahūsu).

74. From 'yakkha' etc., also -inī.

Yakkhādīhi akārantehi itthiyaṃ vī ca hoti inī ca.

From a-stems such as 'yakkha', in the feminine, both the affix -ī and the affix -inī occur.

Yakkhī, yakkhinī, nāgī, nāginī, mahiṃsī, mahiṃsinī, migī, miginī, sīhī, sīhinī, dīpī, dīpinī, byagghī, byagghinī, kākī, kākinī, kapotī, kapotinī, mānusī, mānusinī iccādi.

Female yakkha (yakkhī, yakkhinī), female nāga (nāgī, nāginī), female buffalo (mahiṃsī, mahiṃsinī), doe (migī, miginī), lioness (sīhī, sīhinī), leopardess (dīpī, dīpinī), tigress (byagghī, byagghinī), female crow (kākī, kākinī), female dove (kapotī, kapotinī), human female (mānusī, mānusinī), etc.

75. Ārāmikādīhi ka. 240; rū. 193; nī. 469.

75. From 'ārāmika' etc.

Ārāmikādīhi akārantehi itthiyaṃ inī hoti.

From a-stems such as 'ārāmika' (monastery attendant), the affix -inī occurs in the feminine.

Ārāmikinī, antarāyikinī, nāvikinī, olumbikinī, paṃsukūlikinī, paribbājikinī, rājinī, ekākinī iccādi.

Ārāmikinī (female monastery attendant), antarāyikinī (a woman who is an obstacle), nāvikinī (female sailor), olumbikinī, paṃsukūlikinī (a female rag-robe wearer), paribbājikinī (female wanderer), rājinī (queen), ekākinī (solitary woman), etc.

Saññāyaṃ –

As a specific designation:

Mānusinī mānusā vā, aññatra mānusī sampatti.

The forms are 'mānusinī' or 'mānusā'; but 'mānusī' is used elsewhere, as in 'mānusī sampatti' (human attainment).

76. Gharaṇyādayo ka. 240; rū. 193; nī. 469.

76. Gharaṇī and so on.

Gharaṇīiccādayo itthiyaṃ nīpaccayantā sijjhanti.

The words 'gharaṇī', etc., are formed as feminine stems ending in the suffix -nī.

Gharaṇī, vetraṇī, pokkharaṇī-esu nassa ṇattaṃ. Ācarinīyalopo, ācariyā vā.

In gharaṇī, vetraṇī, and pokkharaṇī, 'n' becomes 'ṇ'. For 'ācariya' (teacher), 'ācarinī' is formed by elision, or alternatively the form is 'ācariyā'.

77. Mātulāditvānī [M 0.0061] bhariyāyaṃ ka. 98; rū. 189; nī. 261.

77. From 'mātula' etc., the suffix -ānī, in the sense of 'wife'.

Mātulādīhi akārantehi bhariyāyaṃ ānī hoti.

From a-stems such as 'mātula', the affix -ānī occurs in the sense of 'wife'.

Mātubhātā mātulo, tassa bhariyā mātulānī, evaṃ varuṇānī, gahapatānī, ācariyānī, khattiyānī.

A mother's brother is a 'mātula'; his wife is a 'mātulānī'. Similarly: varuṇānī (Varuṇa's wife), gahapatānī (a householder's wife), ācariyānī (a teacher's wife), khattiyānī (a khattiya's wife).

‘Bahulā’dhikārā khattiyī khattiyā ca.

By the authority of the governing rule 'bahulaṃ' (variously), the forms 'khattiyī' and 'khattiyā' also occur.

78. Yuvaṇṇehi nī.

78. From stems ending in -i and -u, the affix Nī.

Ivaṇṇantehi uvaṇṇantehi ca itthiyaṃ nī hoti.

From stems ending in the letter -i and from those ending in the letter -u, the affix Nī occurs in the feminine.

Chattapāṇinī, daṇḍapāṇinī, daṇḍinī, chattinī, hatthinī, mālinī, māyāvinī, medhāvinī, piyapasaṃsinī, brahmacārinī, bhayadassāvinī, atthakāminī, hitacārinī, bhikkhunī, khattiyabandhunī, paṭunī, paracittavidunī, mattaññunī, atthaññunī, dhammaññunī iccādi.

Chattapāṇinī (a woman with an umbrella in hand), daṇḍapāṇinī (a woman with a staff in hand), daṇḍinī (a woman with a staff), chattinī (a woman with an umbrella), hatthinī (a female elephant), mālinī (a woman with a garland), māyāvinī (a deceitful woman), medhāvinī (a wise woman), piyapasaṃsinī (a woman who praises what is dear), brahmacārinī (a woman living the holy life), bhayadassāvinī (a woman who sees danger), atthakāminī (a woman who desires the good), hitacārinī (a woman who acts for the welfare of others), bhikkhunī (a nun), khattiyabandhunī (a female relative of a khattiya), paṭunī (a clever woman), paracittavidunī (a woman who knows the minds of others), mattaññunī (a woman who knows moderation), atthaññunī (a woman who knows the meaning), dhammaññunī (a woman who knows the Dhamma), etc.

79. Timhāññatthe ktimhāññatthe (bahūsu), moggallāne 31 suttaṅke.

79. From a stem in -ti, in the sense of another word.

Aññapadatthasamāse tipaccayantamhā itthiyaṃ nī hoti.

In a bahubbīhi compound (a compound signifying another word), from a stem ending in the suffix -ti, the affix Nī occurs in the feminine.

Ahiṃsāratinī, dhammaratinī, vacchagiddhinī, puttagiddhinī, muṭṭhassatinī, micchādiṭṭhinī, sammādiṭṭhinī, attaguttinī iccādi.

Ahiṃsāratinī (she whose delight is in non-harming), dhammaratinī (she whose delight is in the Dhamma), vacchagiddhinī (she who is greedy for calves), puttagiddhinī (she who is greedy for children), muṭṭhassatinī (she who is of confused mindfulness), micchādiṭṭhinī (she who holds wrong view), sammādiṭṭhinī (she who holds right view), attaguttinī (she who has a guarded self), etc.

Aññattheti kiṃ? Dhamme rati dhammarati.

Why the specification 'in the sense of another word'? (To exclude cases like:) 'delight in the Dhamma' (dhamme rati), which is 'dhammarati'.

80. Yuvāti.

80. From 'yuvan', the affix -ti.

Yuvato itthiyanti hoti.

From the stem 'yuvan', the affix -ti occurs in the feminine.

Yuvati.

Yuvati (a young woman).

Ettha ca ‘ti’ iti suttavibhattena vīsa, tiṃsatopiti hoti vā. Vīsati, vīsaṃ, tiṃsati, tiṃsaṃ.

And here, by analysis of the rule specifying '-ti', this affix also optionally occurs after 'vīsa' (twenty) and 'tiṃsa' (thirty). Hence the forms: vīsati or vīsaṃ (twenty); tiṃsati or tiṃsaṃ (thirty).

81. Upamā [M 0.0062] saṃhita sahita saññata saha sapha vāmalakkhaṇāditūrutvū caṃ. 2.3.79; pā. 4.1.69, 70 tūrutū (bahūsu).

81. From ūru, when preceded by upamā, saṃhita, sahita, saññata, saha, sapha, vāma, lakkhaṇa, etc., the affix ū.

Lakkhaṇādito+ūruto+ūti chedo.

The division of the rule is: lakkhaṇādito + ūruto + ū + iti.

Aññapadatthasamāse upamādipubbā ūrusaddamhā itthiyaṃ ū hoti.

In a bahubbīhi compound, from the word 'ūru' (thigh) when it is preceded by 'upamā' etc., the affix -ū occurs in the feminine.

Nāgassa nāsā viya ūrū yassāti nāganāsūrū, saṃhitā sambandhā ūrū yassāti saṃhitorū, sahitā ekabaddhā ūrū yassāti sahitorū, saññatā alolā ūrū yassāti saññatorū, ūruyā ūrunā? saha vattatīti sahorū, sapho vuccati khuro, saṃsiliṭṭhatāya saphabhūtā ūrū yassāti saphorū, vāmā sundarā ūrū yassāti vāmorū, lakkhaṇasampannā ūrū yassāti lakkhaṇorū.

Nāganāsūrū: she whose thighs (ūrū) are like an elephant's (nāgassa) trunk (nāsā). Saṃhitorū: she whose thighs are well-joined (saṃhitā). Sahitorū: she whose thighs are joined together (sahitā). Saññatorū: she whose thighs are restrained (saññatā). Sahorū: she who is with (saha) thighs. Saphorū: she whose thighs are like hoofs (sapha), that is, smooth. Vāmorū: she whose thighs are beautiful (vāmā). Lakkhaṇorū: she whose thighs possess auspicious marks (lakkhaṇa).

Suttavibhattena brahmabandhūti sijjhati.

By analysis of the rule, the form 'brahmabandhū' (a kinswoman of Brahmā) is accounted for.

“Sace maṃ nāganāsūrū, olokeyya pabhāvatī”ti jā. 2.20.14 ca “ekā tuvaṃ tiṭṭhasi sahitūrū”ti jā. 1.16.297 ca “saññatūrū mahāmāyā, kumāri cārudassanā”ti jā. 2.17.109 ca “vāmorū saja maṃ bhadde”ti dī. ni. 2.348 ca “kāraṇaṃ nappajānāmi, sammatto lakkhaṇūruyā”ti dī. ni. 2.348 ca “gārayhassaṃ brahmabandhuyā”ti jā. 2.22.2109 ca pāḷipadāni dissanti.

The following Pāḷi passages are seen: 'Sace maṃ nāganāsūrū, olokeyya pabhāvatī' (If she of the elephant-trunk thighs, the radiant one, should look at me); 'ekā tuvaṃ tiṭṭhasi sahitūrū' (You stand alone, O you of the well-joined thighs); 'saññatūrū mahāmāyā, kumāri cārudassanā' (Mahāmāyā of the restrained thighs, the maiden of lovely sight); 'vāmorū saja maṃ bhadde' (O you of the beautiful thighs, embrace me, good lady); 'kāraṇaṃ nappajānāmi, sammatto lakkhaṇūruyā' (I do not know the reason, I am intoxicated by her of the auspiciously-marked thighs); and 'gārayhassaṃ brahmabandhuyā' (I would be censured by the kinswoman of Brahmā).

Tattha ‘sajā’ti āliṅgāhi, ‘gārayhassa’nti ahaṃ gārayho bhaveyyaṃ.

Therein, 'sajā' means 'embrace'; 'gārayhassaṃ' means 'I would be censurable'.

Ettha ca tāpaccayantā sabhāvaitthiliṅgā eva – lahutā, mudutā, gāmatā, janatā, devatā iccādi.

And here, stems ending in the suffix -tā are inherently feminine in gender: lahutā (lightness), mudutā (softness), gāmatā (a group of villagers), janatā (a group of people), devatā (a deity), etc.

Tathā tipaccayantā – gati, mati, ratti, sati, tuṭṭhi, diṭṭhi, iddhi, siddhi iccādi, tathā yāgu, dhātu, dhenu, kaṇḍu, kacchu, mātu, dhītu[M 0.0063], duhitu iccādi, jambū, vadhū, camū, sutanū, sarabū iccādi ca. Sakkataganthesu pana sutanū, sarabū iccādīsupi ūpaccayaṃ vidahanti.

Similarly, stems ending in the suffix -ti: gati (going), mati (thought), ratti (night), sati (mindfulness), tuṭṭhi (satisfaction), diṭṭhi (view), iddhi (psychic power), siddhi (success), etc. Likewise, yāgu (rice-gruel), dhātu (element), dhenu (cow), kaṇḍu (itching), kacchu (scabies), mātu (mother), dhītu/duhitu (daughter), etc.; and jambū (rose-apple tree), vadhū (daughter-in-law, bride), camū (army), sutanū (a woman with a beautiful body), sarabū (a doe), etc. In Sanskrit works, however, they posit the suffix -ū even for words like sutanū and sarabū.

Tattha itthiliṅgabhūtā sabbe ‘ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā pitthiya’nti suttena niccaṃ pasaññā honti. ‘Ākāro ca ghā’ti suttena niccaṃ ghasañño.

Therein, all stems that are feminine and end in -i or -u are always designated 'Pa' by the rule 'Ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā p'itthiyaṃ'. By the rule 'Ākāro ca ghā', a stem in -ā is always designated 'Gha'.

Itthipaccayarāsi niṭṭhito.

The Section on Feminine Affixes is concluded.

Ākārantitthiliṅgarāsi

The Group of Feminine Nouns Ending in -ā

Itthiliṅgaṃ chabbidhaṃ ākārantaṃ, ikārantaṃ, īkārantaṃ, ukārantaṃ, ūkārantaṃ, okārantaṃ. Tattha kaññāsaddamhā atthamatte paṭhamā.

The feminine gender is of six kinds: ending in -ā, -i, -ī, -u, -ū, and -o. Therein, from the word 'kaññā', the first case ending is used in the sense of the mere meaning of the stem.

82. Gasīnaṃ ka. 220; rū. 74; nī. 447.

82. Of Ga and Si.

Kenaci suttena aladdhavidhīnaṃ gasīnaṃ lopo hotīti silopo.

Of Ga and Si, for which no operation has been prescribed by any rule, elision occurs; thus, the elision of Si.

Kaññā tiṭṭhati.

The maiden stands.

83. Jantuhetvīghapehi vā ka. 118; rū. 146; nī. 293.

83. Jantuhetvīghapehi vā.

Jantu, hetūhi ca punnapuṃsakesu īkārantehi ca ghato ca pasaññehi ivaṇṇuvaṇṇehi ca yonaṃ lopo hoti vā.

After `jantu` and `hetu` in the masculine and neuter genders, and after stems ending in `ī`, and after `gha`- and `pa`-designated nouns, and after stems ending in `i` and `u`, the ending `yo` is optionally elided.

Kaññā tiṭṭhanti, kaññāyo tiṭṭhanti.

The maidens stand, the maidens stand.

Āmantanatthe paṭhamā, ‘gosyālapane’ti gasaññā.

The first case ending is used in the sense of addressing. The designation `ga` is given to `si` in the sense of calling.

84. Ghabrahmāditve ka. 114, 193; rū. 122, 178; nī. 288; ghabrahmādite (bahasu).

84. Ghabrahmāditve.

Ghato ca brahmādito ca gassa e hoti vā. Ādisaddena isi, muni, revatī, kattu, khattuiccāditopi.

After a `gha`-designated noun and after `brahmā` and so on, the vocative singular ending `ga` optionally becomes `e`. By the word `ādi` (etc.), this also applies after `isi`, `muni`, `revatī`, `kattu`, `khattu`, and so on.

Bhoti [M 0.0064] kaññe, bhoti kaññā, bhotiyo kaññāyo, bhotī kaññāyo, “uṭṭhehi puttika pabbajjā dukkarā puttika” iti therīpāḷi therīgā. 465, tasmā ge pare mahāvuttinā rassopi yujjati. Kusajātake “na me akāsi vacanaṃ, atthakāmāya puttike”tipi jā. 2.20.47 atthi.

O good maiden (`kaññe`), O good maiden (`kaññā`); O good maidens (`bhotiyo kaññāyo`), O good maidens (`bhotī kaññāyo`). 'Arise, my daughter, the going forth is difficult, my daughter'—thus in the Therīpāḷi. Therefore, when the vocative ending `ge` follows, shortening is also suitable according to the Mahāvutti. In the Kusajātaka there is also: 'She did not heed my word, though I desired her welfare, O my daughter.'

Kammatthe dutiyā, ‘saro lopo sare’ti pubbasaralopo.

The second case ending is used in the sense of the object. By the rule 'a vowel is elided when a vowel follows,' the preceding vowel is elided.

Kaññaṃ passati, kaññā passati, kaññāyo passati.

He sees a maiden (`kaññaṃ`); he sees maidens (`kaññā`); he sees maidens (`kaññāyo`).

Kattari tatiyā.

The third case ending is used in the sense of the agent.

85. Ghapatekasmiṃ nādīnaṃ yayā ka. 111, 112; rū. 179, 183 nī. 283, 284.

85. Ghapatekasmiṃ nādīnaṃ yayā.

Ghato ca pasaññehi ivaṇṇuvaṇṇehi ca ekatte pavattānaṃ nādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ ekavacanānaṃ kamena ya, yā honti.

After `gha`- and `pa`-designated nouns, and stems ending in `i` and `u`, for the five singular case endings beginning with `nā`, `ya` and `yā` are the respective substitutions.

Kaññāya kataṃ, kaññāhi kataṃ. Ettha ca ghatopi yāādeso dissati. “Te ca tattha nisīditvā, tassa rukkhassa chāyayā” jā. 1.14.182 ti ca “samantā parivāriṃsu, tassa rukkhassa chāyayā” jā. 1.14.189 ti ca pāḷi, tathā “sakkharopamayā vade” saccasaṅkhepa 176 gāthā, “bāladārakalīlayā”ti vibhāvinī 154 ca dissanti. Mahāvuttinā ghassa rasso.

Done by the maiden (`kaññāya`); done by the maidens (`kaññāhi`). Here the substitution of `yā` is also seen for `gha`-designated nouns. 'And having sat down there, in the shade (`chāyayā`) of that tree' and 'They surrounded him on all sides, in the shade (`chāyayā`) of that tree' are Pāli passages. Likewise, 'one should speak with a simile of gravel (`sakkharopamayā`)' and 'with the play of a young child (`bāladārakalīlayā`)' are seen. According to the Mahāvutti, there is shortening of the vowel of a `gha`-designated noun.

86. Smāhismiṃnaṃ mhābhimhi vā ka. 99; rū. 81.

86. Smāhismiṃnaṃ mhābhimhi vā.

Tesaṃ kamena mhā, bhi, mhi honti vā. Ete ādesā gāthāsu bahulaṃ dissanti.

For them (`smā`, `hi`, `smiṃ`), the respective optional substitutes are `mhā`, `bhi`, and `mhi`. These substitutions are seen frequently in verses.

Kaññāhi kataṃ, kaññābhi kataṃ.

Done by the maidens (`kaññāhi`); done by the maidens (`kaññābhi`).

Sampadāne [M 0.0065] catutthī, kaññāya deti, kaññānaṃ deti, kaññāya ābhataṃ vatthaṃ, kaññānaṃ ābhataṃ vatthaṃ.

The fourth case ending is used in the sense of the recipient. He gives to the maiden; he gives to the maidens. A cloth brought for the maiden; a cloth brought for the maidens.

Apādāne pañcamī, kaññāya apeti, kaññamhā apetirassattaṃ, kaññāhi kaññābhi apeti.

The fifth case ending is used in the sense of the point of departure. He goes away from the maiden (`kaññāya`); he goes away from the maiden (`kaññamhā`)—with shortening; he goes away from the maidens (`kaññāhi`, `kaññābhi`).

Sambandhe chaṭṭhī, kaññāya santakaṃ, kaññānaṃ santakaṃ.

The sixth case ending is used in the sense of relation. Belonging to the maiden; belonging to the maidens.

Okāse sattamī, kaññāya tiṭṭhati.

The seventh case ending is used in the sense of location. He stands on or at the maiden.

87. Yaṃ ka. 116; rū. 180; nī. 443.

87. Yaṃ.

Ghato ca pasaññehi ivaṇṇuvaṇṇehi ca smiṃno yaṃ hoti vā.

After `gha`- and `pa`-designated nouns, and after stems ending in `i` and `u`, the ending `smiṃ` optionally becomes `yaṃ`.

Kaññāyaṃ tiṭṭhati, kaññāya tiṭṭhati, kaññāsu tiṭṭhati.

He stands on or at the maiden (`kaññāyaṃ`); he stands on or at the maiden (`kaññāya`); he stands among the maidens (`kaññāsu`).

Saddhā medhā paññā vijjā, cintā mantā vīṇā taṇhā.

Faith, intelligence, wisdom, knowledge, thought, counsel, lute, craving.

Icchā mucchā ejā māyā, mettā mattā sikkhā bhikkhā.

Desire, infatuation, agitation, illusion, loving-kindness, measure, training, alms-food.

Jaṅghā gīvā jivhā vācā, chāyā āsā gaṅgānāvā.

Shin, neck, tongue, speech, shadow, hope, the river Ganges, boat.

Gāthā senā lekhā sākhā, mālā velā pūjā khiḍḍā.

Verse, army, writing, branch, garland, time, offering, play.

Pipāsā vedanā saññā, cetanā tasiṇāpajā.

Thirst, feeling, perception, volition, craving, offspring.

Devatā vaṭṭakā godhā, balākā parisā sabhā.

Deity, quail, iguana, crane, assembly, hall.

Ūkā sephālikā laṅkā, salākā vālikā sikhā.

Louse, jasmine, island, ticket, sand, crest.

Visākhā visikhā sākhā, gacchā vañjhā jaṭā ghaṭā.

Visākhā, street, branch, plant, barren woman, matted hair, throng.

Jeṭṭhā soṇḍā vitaṇḍā ca, varuṇā vanitā latā.

Jeṭṭhā, elephant's trunk, and sophistry; Varuṇa tree, woman, creeper.

Kathā niddā sudhā rādhā, vāsanā sīsapā papā.

Talk, sleep, nectar, Rādhā, impression, sissoo tree, water-booth.

Pabhā sīmā khamā jāyā, khattiyā sakkharā surā.

Light, boundary, patience, wife, noblewoman, gravel, liquor.

Dolā tulā silā līlā, lāle’lā mekhalā kalā.

Swing, balance, stone, play, saliva, cardamom, girdle, art.

Vaḷavā’ [M 0.0066] lambusā mūsā, mañjūsā sulasā disā.

Mare, Alambusā, crucible, casket, Sulasā, direction.

Nāsā juṇhā guhā īhā, lasikā vasudhādayo.

Nose, moonlight, cave, effort, lymph, earth, and so on.

88. Nambādīhi nambādīhi (bahūsu).

88. Not for `amba` and so on.

Gasaññehi amba, anna, ammaiccetehi gassa e na hoti.

After `amba`, `anna`, and `amma`, the vocative singular `ga` does not become `e`.

89. Rasso vā.

89. Optional shortening.

Ambādīnaṃ rasso hoti vā ge pare.

For `amba` and so on, there is optional shortening when the vocative ending `ge` follows.

Bhoti amba, bhoti ambā, bhoti anna, bhoti annā, bhoti amma, bhoti ammā, sesaṃ kaññāsamaṃ.

O good mother (`amba`), O good mother (`ambā`); O good mother (`anna`), O good mother (`annā`); O good mother (`amma`), O good mother (`ammā`). The rest is like `kaññā`.

Ettha visesavidhānamuccate.

Here a special rule is stated.

90. Ti sabhāparisāya.

90. `ti` for `sabhā` and `parisā`.

Sabhāparisāhi smiṃnoti hoti. ‘Gho ssaṃssāssāya tīsū’ti suttena timhi rasso.

After `sabhā` and `parisā`, `smiṃ` becomes `ti`. By the rule 'Gho ssaṃssāssāya tīsū,' the preceding vowel is shortened.

Sabhati, sabhāya, sabhāyaṃ, sabhāsu, parisati, parisāya, parisāyaṃ, parisāsu, tamaddasa mahābrahmā, nisinnaṃ samhi parisati, iti bhagavā tasmiṃ parisati suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ kāyaṃ vivari ma. ni. 1.359.

Forms: `sabhati`, `sabhāya`, `sabhāyaṃ`, `sabhāsu`; `parisati`, `parisāya`, `parisāyaṃ`, `parisāsu`. 'The Great Brahmā saw him seated in his own assembly (`parisati`).' 'Thus the Blessed One in that assembly (`parisati`) revealed his golden-colored body.'

Nandamātā, rājadhītāiccādīsu ‘ghabrahmāditve’ti ghassa ettaṃ.

In words such as `Nandamātā` and `rājadhītā`, by the rule 'ghabrahmāditve,' the final vowel of the stem is changed to `e` in the vocative.

Acchariyaṃ nandamāte, abbhutaṃ nandamāte a. ni. 7.53, bhoti devadhīte, bhoti sakyadhītare-mahāvuttinā samāse syādīsu ārattaṃ rassattañca. Ltupaccayantā pana yebhuyyena tīsu liṅgesu samānarūpā honti, “atthadhammaṃ paripucchitā ca uggahetā [M 0.0067] ca dhammānaṃ sotā ca payirūpāsitā cā”ti therīpāḷi. Tathā kvaci gacchantādisaddāpi. Tamokhandhaṃ padālayaṃ, evaṃ dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇaṃ iccādi-tattha padālayanti padālayantī, bhaṇanti bhaṇantīti attho.

'Wonderful, O mother of Nanda! Marvelous, O mother of Nanda!' 'O good daughter of the devas!' 'O good daughter of the Sakyans!' According to the Mahāvutti, in a compound, for the case endings `si` and so on, there is lengthening and shortening.
