When it denotes a substance possessing a substance, as in 'daṇḍī puriso' (the staff-bearing man), then sound, substance, class, and relation are the qualifier.

Pācakasaddo yadā jātimattaṃ vadati pācako jātīti, tadā suti ca kriyā ca visesanaṃ. Yadā kriyānipphādakaṃ dabbaṃ vadati pācako purisoti, tadā suti ca kriyā ca jāti ca kriyākārakasambandho ca visesanaṃ.

The word 'pācaka' (cook), when it merely indicates a class as in 'pācako jāti' (a cook is a class), then sound and activity are qualifiers. When it indicates a substance performing an action as in 'pācako puriso' (a cook is a man), then sound, activity, class, and the relation of action and agent are qualifiers.

Tissasaddo yadā nāmamattaṃ vadati tisso nāmanti, tadā suti visesanaṃ. Yadā nāmavantaṃ dabbaṃ vadati, tisso bhikkhūti, tadā suti ca nāmajāti ca sambandho ca visesanaṃ.

The word 'Tissa,' when it merely expresses a name, as in 'tisso nāmaṃ' (Tissa is a name), then sound is the qualifier. When it expresses a name-possessing entity, as in 'tisso bhikkhu' (Tissa is a monk), then sound, name-class, and relation are qualifiers.

Sabbattha yaṃ yaṃ vadatīti vuttaṃ, taṃ taṃ visesyanti ca dabbanti ca veditabbaṃ. Ettha ca suti nāma saddasabhāvā eva hoti, saddapakkhikā [M 0.0165] eva. Sabbo saddo paṭhamaṃ sattābhidhāyakoti ca ñāse vuttaṃ. Tasmā sabbattha sutiṭṭhāne sattā eva yuttā vattunti. Sattāti ca tassa tassa atthassa vohāramattenapi loke vijjamānatā vuccati, taṃ taṃ saddaṃ suṇantassa ca ñāṇaṃ taṃtadatthassa atthitāmattaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ jānāti, tato paraṃ jātisadde jātiṃ jānāti. Guṇasadde guṇanti evamādi sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Liṅga, saṅkhyā, parimāṇānipi visesanatthe saṅgayhanti.

In all cases, that which is said to be spoken of should be understood as both the thing qualified and the substance. Here, `suti` (sound) is indeed the very nature of the word, belonging only to the side of the word. It is said in the commentary that every word first denotes a being. Therefore, in all places of sound, it is fitting to speak only of beings. And by 'being' is meant the existence in the world of that particular meaning merely by way of convention. For one hearing a particular word, knowledge first knows merely the existence of that particular meaning; thereafter, in the case of a class-word, one knows the class; in the case of a quality-word, one knows the quality—and so on, all should be stated. Gender, number, and measure are also included among the meanings of a qualifier.

Tattha liṅgaṃ nāma ye itthi, purisānaṃ liṅga, nimitta, kuttā’kappā nāma abhidhamme vuttā, ye ca napuṃsakānaṃ liṅga, nimitta, kuttā’kappā nāma avuttasiddhā, ye ca saddesu ceva atthesu ca visadā’visadākāra, majjhimākārā sandissanti, sabbametaṃ liṅgaṃ nāma.

Here, 'gender' (liṅga) refers to the marks, signs, demeanour, and appearances of women and men, as stated in the Abhidhamma; and those marks, signs, demeanour, and appearances of neuters, though not explicitly stated, are established by implication. Whatever appears distinctly, indistinctly, or in an intermediate manner in words and meanings—all of this is called gender.

Evaṃ visesana, visesyavasena duvidho attho pubbe vuttassa saddaliṅgassa attho nāma, so saliṅgo, sasaṅkhyo, saparimāṇo cāti tividho hoti.

Thus, the meaning of the previously mentioned word-gender is twofold, by way of being a qualifier and a thing qualified. That meaning is threefold: having gender, having number, and having measure.

Tattha saliṅgo yathā? Saññā, phasso, cittaṃ. Kaññā, puriso, kulaṃ. Mālā, rukkho, dhananti.

Here, what is an example of having gender? Perception, contact, mind. A maiden, a man, a family. A garland, a tree, wealth.

Sasaṅkhyo yathā? Eko, dve, tayo, bahū iccādi.

What is an example of having number? One, two, three, many, and so forth.

Saparimāṇo yathā? Vidatthi, hattho, doṇo, āḷhakaṃ iccādi.

What is an example of having measure? A span, a cubit, a doṇa, an āḷhaka, and so forth.

Api ca suddho, saṃsaṭṭhoti duvidho liṅgattho. Tattha kammādisaṃsaggarahito suddho nāma. So saliṅgo, sasaṅkhyo, saparimāṇo, upasaggattho, nipātattho, pāṭi-padikatthoti chabbidho. Atthi, sakkā, labbhāiccādi idha pāṭipadikaṃ nāma. Tuna, tvāna, tvā, tave, tuṃ, khattuṃpaccayantāpi nipātesu gayhanti.

Moreover, the meaning of the stem is twofold: pure and mixed. Here, that which is devoid of association with action and so forth is called pure. It is sixfold: having gender, having number, having measure, the meaning of prefixes, the meaning of particles, and the meaning of a nominal stem. Here, 'atthi' (exists), 'sakkā' (is possible), 'labbhā' (is obtainable), and so forth, are called a nominal stem. Those ending in the suffixes 'tuna', 'tvāna', 'tvā', 'tave', 'tuṃ', and 'khattuṃ' are also included among particles.

Saṃsaṭṭho [M 0.0166] vuttasaṃsaṭṭho, avuttasaṃsaṭṭhoti duvidho. Tattha vuttasaṃsaṭṭho catubbidho samāsena vuttasaṃsaṭṭho, taddhitena, ākhyātena, kitenāti. Tattha samāsena vutto chakārakasambandhavasena sattavidho, bhāvena saddhiṃ aṭṭhavidho vā, tathā taddhitena vutto. Ākhyātena vutto kattu, kamma, bhāvavasena tividho. Kitena vutto chakāraka, bhāvavasena sattavidho. Sabbo suddho ceva vuttasaṃsaṭṭho ca paṭhamāya visayo.

The mixed is twofold: the stated mixed and the unstated mixed. Therein, the stated mixed is fourfold: that stated by a compound, by a secondary derivative, by a verb, and by a primary derivative. Therein, that stated by a compound is sevenfold based on the relation with the six grammatical functions, or eightfold including abstract quality. Similarly is that stated by a secondary derivative. That stated by a verb is threefold: by agent, by object, and by abstract quality. That stated by a primary derivative is sevenfold based on the six grammatical functions and abstract quality. All pure meanings and those stated mixed meanings are the domain of the first case.

Avuttasaṃsaṭṭhopi kattusaṃsaṭṭho, kammasaṃsaṭṭhotiādinā anekavidho. So dutiyādīnaṃ eva visayoti. Ettha ca vibhattiyā vinā kevalo saddo payogaṃ nārahatīti katvā payogārahatthameva chabbidhe suddhe catubbidhe ca vuttasaṃsaṭṭhe paṭhamā payujjati, na atthajotanatthaṃ.

The unstated mixed is also manifold, such as mixed with agent, mixed with object, and so on. It pertains only to the second case and others. Here, since a mere word without an inflection is not fit for use, the first case is applied to the sixfold pure and fourfold stated mixed only for the sake of fitness for use, not for illuminating meaning.

Kenaci vācakena avuttāni pana kammādīni vibhattīhi vinā viditāni na hontītikatvā atthajotanatthampi kammādīsu dutiyādayo payujjanti. Tasmā atthamatteti idha desantarāvacchedake visayamatte bhummaṃ. Kamme dutiyāiccādīsu pana nipphādetabbe payojane bhummanti evaṃ dvinnaṃ bhummānaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbanti.

However, since the grammatical roles of object, etc., when unstated by any denotative word, are not known without inflections, the second case and others are used with the object, etc., also for the sake of illuminating the meaning. Therefore, here, in 'merely in the meaning' (atthamatte), the locative case is in the sense of mere scope, delimiting a particular domain. But in instances such as 'the second case [applies] to the object,' the locative case is used in the sense of the purpose to be accomplished. Thus, the difference between these two uses of the locative case should be understood.

290. Āmantane ka. 285; rū. 70; nī. 578; caṃ. 2.1.94; pā. 2.3.47; āmantaṇe (bahūsu).

290. In Addressing

Pageva siddhassa vatthuno nāmena vā nipātena vā attano abhimukhīkaraṇaṃ āmantanaṃ nāma. Adhikāmantane atthamatte paṭhamā hoti. Ettha ca āmantanapadaṃ nāma kriyāpekkhaṃ na hoti, tasmā kārakasaññaṃ na labhati.

The directing of an already established thing towards oneself by name or particle is called addressing. In the specific sense of addressing, in its mere meaning, the first case is used. Here, the word used in addressing does not depend on a verb; therefore, it does not acquire the designation of a grammatical function.

Taṃ pana duvidhaṃ sādarā’nādaravasena. Ehi samma, ehi jeti.

It is twofold, however: by way of respect and disrespect. For example: 'Come, friend,' 'Come, you!'

Tathā [M 0.0167] sajīva, nijjīvavasena, bho purisa, vadehi bho saṅkha, vadehi bho saṅkha dī. ni. 2.426. Ummujja bho puthusile, ummujja bho puthusileti saṃ. ni. 4.358.

Likewise, by way of animate and inanimate. For example: 'O man.' 'Speak, O conch, speak, O conch.' 'Emerge, O broad stone, emerge, O broad stone.'

Tathā paccakkhā’paccakkhavasena, bho purisa, kahaṃ ekaputtaka, kahaṃ ekaputtakāti saṃ. ni. 2.63; dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.2.

Likewise, by way of present and not present. For example: 'O man.' 'Where are you, O only son, where are you, O only son?'

Tathā niyamā’niyamavasena, bho purisa, acchariyaṃ vata bho abbhutaṃ vata bho dī. ni. 2.192. Yatra hi nāma saññī samānotiādi dī. ni. 2.192. Idaṃ āmantanaṃ nāma pageva siddhe eva hoti, na vidhātabbe, na hi pageva rājabhāvaṃ vā bhikkhubhāvaṃ vā appattaṃ janaṃ “bho rājā”ti vā “bho bhikkhū”ti vā āmantentīti.

Likewise, by way of specific and non-specific addressing. For example: 'O man.' 'O, wonderful indeed! O, marvelous indeed!' 'Where indeed one who is percipient is equal,' and so on. This addressing, indeed, occurs only in what is already established, not in what is to be brought into being. For one does not address a person who has not already attained kingship or monkhood as 'O king' or 'O monk.'

Paṭhamāvibhattirāsi niṭṭhito.

The Section on the First Case is Concluded.

Dutiyāvibhattirāsi

The Section on the Second Case

Kasmiṃ atthe dutiyā?

In what sense does the second case occur?

291. Kamme dutiyā ka. 297; rū. 284; nī. 580; caṃ. 2.1.43; pā. 1.4.49-51.

291. The second case occurs in the sense of object.

Kammatthe dutiyā hoti. Kariyateti kammaṃ, taṃ nibbattikammaṃ, vikatikammaṃ, pattikammanti tividhaṃ hoti.

The second case occurs in the sense of object. `Kamma` is that which is done; it is threefold: the productive object, the modifying object, and the attainable object.

Tattha nibbattikammaṃ yathā? Iddhimā hatthivaṇṇaṃ māpeti, rājā nagaraṃ māpeti, mātā puttaṃ vijāyati, bījaṃ rukkhaṃ janeti, kammaṃ vipākaṃ janeti, āhāro balaṃ janeti, jano puññaṃ karoti, pāpaṃ karoti, buddho dhammaṃ desesi, vinayaṃ paññapesi, bhikkhu jhānaṃ uppādeti, maggaṃ uppādeti iccādi.

Here, what is the productive object? For example: One with psychic power creates an elephant form, a king builds a city, a mother gives birth to a son, a seed produces a tree, kamma produces its result, food produces strength, a person does merit, does evil, the Buddha taught the Dhamma, laid down the discipline, a monk develops jhāna, develops the path, and so on.

Vikatikammaṃ [M 0.0168] yathā? Gehaṃ karoti, rathaṃ karoti, ghaṭaṃ karoti, paṭaṃ vāyati, odanaṃ pacati, bhattaṃ pacati, kaṭṭhaṃ aṅgāraṃ karoti, suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ karoti, gehaṃ jhāpeti, rukkhaṃ chindati, pākāraṃ bhindati, vihayo lunāti, pāṇaṃ hanati, bhattaṃ bhuñjati iccādi.

What is the modifying object? For example: One builds a house, makes a chariot, makes a pot, weaves a cloth, cooks rice, cooks a meal, turns wood into charcoal, makes a bracelet from gold, burns down a house, cuts down a tree, breaks a wall, harvests grain, kills a living being, eats a meal, and so on.

Pattikammaṃ yathā? Gāmaṃ gacchati, gehaṃ pavisati, rukkhaṃ ārohati, nadiṃ tarati, ādiccaṃ passati, dhammaṃ suṇāti, buddhaṃ vandati payirupāsati iccādi.

What is the attainable object? For example: One goes to a village, enters a house, climbs a tree, crosses a river, sees the sun, hears the Dhamma, pays respects to the Buddha, attends upon him, and so on.

Pakatikammaṃ, vikatikammanti duvidhaṃ. Suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ karoti, kaṭṭhaṃ aṅgāraṃ karoti, purisaṃ ṭhitaṃ passati, purisaṃ gacchantaṃ passati, bhikkhuṃ passati sataṃ, sampajānaṃ, abhikkamantaṃ, paṭikkamantaṃ, ālokentaṃ, vilokentaṃ, samiñjentaṃ, pasārentaṃ.

It is of two kinds: the natural object and the modifying object. For example: One makes gold into a bracelet, turns wood into charcoal, sees a man standing, sees a man walking, sees a monk mindful and clearly comprehending, going forward, going backward, looking ahead, looking around, contracting, stretching.

Ettha ‘purisaṃ, bhikkhu’nti pakatikammaṃ, ‘ṭhitaṃ, sataṃ’iccādīni vikatikammāni.

Here, 'a man' and 'a monk' are the natural object (pakatikamma), while 'standing' and 'mindful,' etc., are the modifying objects (vikatikamma).

Dhātukammaṃ, kāritakammanti duvidhaṃ. Gāmaṃ gacchati, purisaṃ gāmaṃ gameti.

It is of two kinds: the root-object and the causative-object. For example: One goes to the village; one causes a man to go to the village.

Dhātukammañca dvikammikadhātūnaṃ duvidhaṃ padhānakammaṃ, appadhānakammanti. Ajapālo ajaṃ gāmaṃ neti, puriso bhāraṃ gāmaṃ vahati, harati, gāmaṃ sākhaṃ kaḍḍhati, gāviṃ khīraṃ dohati, brāhmaṇaṃ kambalaṃ yācati, brāhmaṇaṃ bhattaṃ bhikkhati, gāviyo vajaṃ avarundhati, bhagavantaṃ pañhaṃ pucchati, rukkhaṃ phalāni ocināti, sissaṃ dhammaṃ bravīti, bhagavā bhikkhū etadavoca udā. 23 (thokaṃ visadisaṃ), sissaṃ dhammaṃ anusāsati iccādi.

And the object of dual-object verbs is twofold: the primary object and the secondary object. For example: the goatherd leads the goat to the village; the man carries the load to the village, or transports it; one drags the branch to the village; one milks milk from the cow; one asks the brahmin for a blanket; one begs the brahmin for food; one confines the cows to the pen; one asks the Blessed One a question; one picks fruits from the tree; the teacher tells the disciple the Dhamma; the Blessed One said this to the monks; the teacher instructs the disciple in the Dhamma, and so on.

Ettha ca ‘ajaṃ, khīraṃ’ iccādi padhānakammaṃ nāma kattārā pariggahetuṃ iṭṭhatarattā. ‘Gāmaṃ, gāviṃ’iccādi appadhānakammaṃ nāma tathā aniṭṭhatarattā.

Here, 'the goat,' 'milk,' and so on, are called the primary object because they are more desired to be taken by the agent. 'The village,' 'the cow,' and so on, are called the secondary object because they are similarly less desired.

Tattha [M 0.0169] padhānakammaṃ kathinakammaṃ nāma, kammabhāve thirakammanti vuttaṃ hoti. Appadhānakammaṃ akathinakammaṃ nāma, athirakammanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tañhi kadāci sampadānaṃ hoti, kadāci apādānaṃ, kadāci sāmi, kadāci okāso. Yathā – so maṃ dakāya neti, gāvito khīraṃ dohati, gāviyā khīraṃ dohahi, gāviyaṃ khīraṃ dohati iccādi.

Therein, the primary object is called the 'kathina object,' meaning it is said to be a firm object in its objective capacity. The secondary object is called the 'akathina object,' meaning it is said to be a non-firm object. For it is sometimes the dative, sometimes the ablative, sometimes the genitive, sometimes the locative. For example: 'He leads me for water'; 'He milks milk from the cow' (ablative); 'He milks milk of the cow' (genitive); 'He milks milk from the cow' (locative), and so on.

Kamme dutiyāti vattate.

The rule 'in the object, the second case' is carried forward.

292. Gatibodhāhārasaddatthā kammaka bhajjādīnaṃ payojje ka. 300; rū. 286; nī. 587; caṃ. 2.1.44; pā. 1.4.52.

292. In the case of the agent of the causative of verbs with the meaning of going, knowing, eating, and sounding, and of intransitive verbs such as bhajj and others.

Niccavidhisuttamidaṃ. Gamanatthānaṃ bodhanatthānaṃ āhāratthānaṃ saddatthānaṃ akammakānaṃ bhajjādīnañca dhātūnaṃ payojje kammani dutiyā hoti. Ettha ca payojjakammaṃ nāma kāritakammaṃ vuccati.

This is a rule of invariable application. The second case occurs in the object which is the agent of the causative of verbs with the meaning of going, knowing, eating, and sounding, and of intransitive verbs such as bhajj and others. Here, the object which is the agent of the causative is called the instigated object.

Puriso purisaṃ gāmaṃ gamayati, sāmiko ajapālaṃ ajaṃ gāmaṃ nayāpeti, ācariyo sissaṃ dhammaṃ bodheti, puriso purisaṃ bhattaṃ bhojeti, ācariyo sissaṃ dhammaṃ pāṭheti, puriso purisaṃ sayāpeti, acchāpeti, uṭṭhāpeti, puriso purisaṃ dhaññaṃ bhajjāpeti, koṭṭāpeti, uddharāpeti.

A man causes a man to go to the village; the owner causes the goatherd to lead the goat to the village; the teacher causes the disciple to understand the Dhamma; a man causes a man to eat a meal; the teacher causes the disciple to recite the Dhamma; a man causes a man to lie down, to sit, or to rise up; a man causes a man to fry grain, to thresh, or to lift up.

Etesamīti kiṃ? Puriso purisena odanaṃ pāceti.

Why specify 'of these verbs'? A man causes rice to be cooked by a man.

Ettha ca gamanatthādīnaṃ payojje tatiyāpi rūpasiddhiyaṃ 141 piṭṭhe saddanītiyañca sutta-148 piṭṭhe vuttā. Saddanītiyaṃ tatiyāpayogepi kammatthameva icchati. Ñāsādīsu katvatthaṃ icchanti.

Here, for the agent of the causative of verbs with the meaning of going and so on, the third case is also stated in the Rūpasiddhi and the Saddanīti. In the Saddanīti, even with the use of the third case, the meaning of object is still desired. In the case of verbs such as `ñā` (to know), they desire the meaning of agent.

Yadā [M 0.0170] pana paṭhamaṃ payojakaṃ añño dutiyo payojeti, tadā paṭhamo payojjo nāma. Tasmiṃ tatiyāevāti vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Attanā vippakataṃ kuṭiṃ parehi pariyosāpeti pārā. 363.

But when a second instigator causes the first instigator to act, then the first is called the instigated agent. It is stated in the commentary that for that instigated agent, only the third case is used. For example: one causes a hut, begun by oneself, to be finished by others.

293. Harādīnaṃ vā ka. 300; rū. 286; nī. 587; caṃ. 2.1.45; pā. 1.4.53.

293. Optionally, in the case of `har` and other verbs.

Harādīnaṃ payojje kammani vikappena dutiyā hoti.

For the agent of the causative of `har` and other verbs, the second case optionally occurs.

Sāmiko purisaṃ bhāraṃ hāreti purisena vā, purisaṃ āhāraṃ ajjhohāreti purisena vā, purisaṃ kammaṃ kāreti purisena vā, rājā purisaṃ attānaṃ dasseti purisena vā, purisaṃ buddhaṃ vandāpeti purisena vā.

The master causes a man to carry a burden (or: by a man); causes a man to consume food (or: by a man); causes a man to perform work (or: by a man); the king causes a man to see himself (or: by a man); causes a man to pay homage to the Buddha (or: by a man).

194. Na khādādīnaṃ ka. 300; rū. 286; nī. 587; caṃ. 2.1.47; pā. 1.4.57.

194. Not in the case of `khād` and other verbs.

Khādādīnaṃ payojje kammani na dutiyā hoti.

For the agent of the causative of `khād` and other verbs, the second case does not occur.

Sāmiko purisena khajjaṃ khādāpeti, ada-bhakkhane, bhattaṃ ādeti, sāmiko dāsena purisaṃ avhāpeti, saddāyāpeti, kandayati, nādayati. Ettha ca ‘saddāyāpetī’ti saddaṃ kārāpeti, nāmadhātu cesā. Kanda, nadāpi saddatthāyeva.

The master causes food to be eaten by a man. (The root) `ad` is in the sense of eating: he causes rice to be eaten. The master causes a slave to summon a man, to make a sound, to cry, or to roar. And here, `saddāyāpeti` means 'causes a sound to be made,' and this is a denominative verb. `Kand` and `nad` also have the meaning of sound.

295. Vahissāniyantuke ka. 300; rū. 286; nī. 587; caṃ. 2.1.48; pā. 1.4.52.

295. Of the root `vah`, when the agent is uncontrolled.

Vahissāti dhātuniddeso i-kāro, niyāmeti payojetīti niyantā, natthi niyantā etassāti aniyantuko. Yassa aññena payojakena kiccaṃ natthi, sayameva ñatvā vahati, so aniyantuko nāma, vahadhātussa tādise aniyantuke payojje kammani dutiyā na hoti.

In `vahissa`, the `i`-vowel is an indication of the root. A `niyantā` is one who directs or instigates; an `aniyantuko` is one for whom there is no controller. One who has no task from another instigator, but carries, knowing by himself, is called an `aniyantuko`. For the root `vah`, when the instigated agent is such an `aniyantuko`, the second case does not occur.

Sāmiko [M 0.0171] dāsena bhāraṃ vāheti.

The master causes a burden to be carried by a slave.

Aniyantuketi kiṃ? Balībadde bhāraṃ vāheti.

Why specify 'when the agent is uncontrolled'? He causes oxen to carry a burden.

296. Bhakkhissāhiṃsāyaṃ ka. 300; rū. 286; nī. 587; caṃ. 2.1.49; pā. 1.4.5.

296. Of the root `bhakkh`, in the sense of non-harming.

Bhakkhituṃ icchantassa bhakkhāpanaṃ hiṃsā nāma na hoti, anicchantassa bhakkhāpanaṃ hiṃsā nāma, bhakkhadhātussa payojje kammani ahiṃsāvisaye dutiyā na hoti.

Causing one who wishes to eat to eat is not called harming; causing one who does not wish to eat to eat is called harming. For the agent of the causative of the root `bhakkh`, in the sphere of non-harming, the second case does not occur.

Sāmiko purisena modake bhakkhāpeti.

The master causes sweets to be eaten by a man.

Ahiṃsāyanti kiṃ? Balībadde sassaṃ bhakkhāpeti. Ettha ‘sassa’nti thūlataraṃ sassanti vadanti.

Why specify 'in the sense of non-harming'? He causes oxen to eat the crops. Here, they say that by 'crops' is meant coarser crops.

Pāḷiyaṃ “sabbesaṃ viññāpetvāna apa. thera 1.1.438, tosenti sabbapāṇinaṃ apa. thera 1.1.300. Therassa patto dutiyassa gāhetabbo” iccādinā pārā. 615 payojje chaṭṭhīpi dissati.

In the Pāli Canon, the sixth case is also seen for the instigated agent, as in 'sabbesaṃ viññāpetvāna, tosenti sabbapāṇinaṃ' and 'Therassa patto dutiyassa gāhetabbo,' and so forth.

297. Jhādīhi yuttā ka. 299; rū. 288; nī. 582, 586; caṃ. 2.1.50; pā. 2.3.2.

297. In connection with `dhī` and other particles.

Dhīiccādīhi nipātopasaggehi yuttā liṅgamhā dutiyā hoti.

When connected with particles and prefixes such as `dhī`, the second case occurs after the nominal stem.

Dhī brāhmaṇassa hantāraṃ dha. pa. 389, dhīratthu’maṃ pūtikāyaṃ jā. 1.3.129, dhīratthu taṃ dhanalābhaṃ jā. 1.4.36, dhīratthu bahuke kāme. Tatiyāpi dissati, dhīratthu jīvitena me jā. 2.17.135. Antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandaṃ dī. ni. 1.1, abhito gāmaṃ vasati, paritogāmaṃ vasati, nadiṃ nerañjaraṃ pati su. ni. 427, etesu chaṭṭhyatthe dutiyā.

Fie upon the brahmin's killer! Fie upon this foul body! Fie upon that gain of wealth! Fie upon many desires! The third case is also seen: 'Fie upon my life!' 'Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā'; 'he dwells near the village'; 'he dwells around the village'; 'towards the Nerañjarā River'—in these, the second case is used in the sense of the sixth case.

Tathā [M 0.0172] paṭibhāti maṃ bhagavā udā. 45; saṃ. ni. 1.217, apissu maṃ tisso upamāyo paṭibhaṃsu ma. ni. 1.374, paṭibhātu taṃ bhikkhu dhammo bhāsituṃ mahāva. 258. Paṭibhantu taṃ cunda bojjhaṅgā saṃ. ni. 3.79 – ‘ma’nti mama, ‘ta’nti tava, sampadānatthe dutiyā. ‘Ma’nti mamañāṇe, ‘ta’nti tavañāṇetipi vaṇṇesuṃ. Na upāyamantarena atthassa siddhi, natthi samādānamantarena sikkhāpaṭilābho, nevidha na huraṃ na ubhayamantarena, esevanto dukkhassa ma. ni. 3.393; udā. 74. Tattha ‘antarenā’ti nipātapadametaṃ, vajjetvātyattho. Pubbena gāmaṃ, dakkhiṇena gāmaṃ, uttarena gāmaṃ, gāmassa pubbeti attho.

Thus the Blessed One appears to me; and three similes have occurred to me. May the Dhamma, O monk, occur to you for speaking. May the factors of enlightenment, O Cunda, occur to you. Here, `maṃ` means 'to me' (genitive: `mama`), and `taṃ` means 'to you' (genitive: `tava`); this is the second case in the dative sense. They also explained `maṃ` as 'in my knowledge' and `taṃ` as 'in your knowledge.' 'Without the means, there is no success of the purpose'; 'without undertaking, there is no acquisition of the training precepts'; 'neither here nor hereafter nor in between the two—this is the end of suffering.' Therein, `antarena` is a particle meaning 'except for.' 'East of the village,' 'south of the village,' 'north of the village'; the meaning is 'to the east of the village.'

Upasaggapubbānaṃ akammakadhātūnaṃ payoge ādhāre dutiyā, pathaviṃ adhisessati, gāmaṃ adhitiṭṭhati, rukkhaṃ ajjhāvasati, mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā abhinisīdeyya vā abhinipajjeyya vā pāci. 130, gāmaṃ upavasati, gāmaṃ anuvasati, pabbataṃ adhivasati, gharaṃ āvasati, agāraṃ ajjhāvasati dī. ni. 1.258; pārā. 519, uposathaṃ upavasati, kāmāvacaraṃ upapajjati, rūpāvacaraṃ upapajjati, arūpāvacaraṃ upapajjati, sakkassa sahabyataṃ upapajjati, nipannaṃ vā upanipajjeyya dī. ni. 3.282, nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya dī. ni. 3.282, ṭhitaṃ vā upatiṭṭheyya dī. ni. 3.282 iccādi.

In the use of intransitive verbs preceded by prefixes, the second case is used for the location: he will lie upon the earth; he stands over the village; he dwells by the tree; he may sit down upon or lie down upon a couch or a stool; he lives near the village; he dwells near the village; he dwells on the mountain; he inhabits the house; he resides in the house; he observes the Uposatha; he is reborn in the sense-sphere; he is reborn in the form-sphere; he is reborn in the formless-sphere; he is reborn into companionship with Sakka; he may lie down near one who is lying down; he may sit near one who is sitting; he may stand near one who is standing, and so forth.

Tappāna, cārepi dutiyā, nadiṃ pivati, samuddaṃ pivati, gāmaṃ carati, araññaṃ carati, nadiyaṃ, gāmeti attho.

With verbs of drinking and wandering, the second case is also used: 'He drinks the river,' 'he drinks the ocean,' 'he wanders through the village,' 'he wanders through the forest.' The meaning is 'in the river,' 'in the village.'

Kāla, disāsupi ādhāre eva dutiyā, taṃ khaṇaṃ, taṃ muhuttaṃ, taṃ kālaṃ, ekamantaṃ khu. pā. 5.1, ekaṃ samayaṃ khu. pā. 5.1; dī. ni. 1.1, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ pārā. 16, sāyanhasamayaṃ, taṃ divasaṃ, imaṃ rattiṃ dī. ni. 3.285, dutiyampi, tatiyampi, catutthaṃ vā pañcamaṃ vā appeti, tato pubbaṃ, tato paraṃ, purimaṃ disaṃ dī. ni. 2.336, dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ dī. ni. 2.336, pacchimaṃ disaṃ dī. ni. 2.336, uttaraṃ disaṃ dī. ni. 2.336, imā dasa [M 0.0173] disāyo, katamaṃ disaṃ tiṭṭhati nāgarājā jā. 1.16.104, imāsu disāsu katamāya disāya tiṭṭhati chaddantanāgarājāti atthoiccādi.

With time and directions also, the second case is used in the sense of location: 'that moment,' 'that instant,' 'that time,' 'to one side,' 'at one time,' 'at the time of morning,' 'at the time of evening,' 'that day,' 'this night,' 'a second time,' 'a third time,' 'he applies a fourth or a fifth time,' 'before that,' 'after that,' 'the eastern direction,' 'the southern direction,' 'the western direction,' 'the northern direction,' 'these ten directions,' 'in which direction does the nāga king stand?' The meaning is, 'among these directions, in which direction does the six-tusked nāga king stand?', and so forth.

298. Lakkhaṇitthambhūtavicchāsvabhinā ka. 299; rū. 288; nī. 582, 586; caṃ. 2.1.54; pā. 1.4.90, 91; 2.3.8.

298. With abhi in the senses of characteristic, thus-become, and pervasion.

Lakkhaṇādīsu atthesu pavattena abhinā yuttā liṅgamhā dutiyā hoti.

When connected with abhi occurring in meanings such as characteristic, the second case occurs from the nominal stem.

Lakkhīyati lakkhitabbaṃ anenāti lakkhaṇaṃ. Ayaṃ pakāro itthaṃ, īdiso visesoti attho. Itthaṃ bhūto pattoti itthambhūto. Bhinne atthe byāpituṃ icchā vicchā.

‘Characteristic’ is that by which something is recognized or is to be recognized; the meaning is: this is the manner, such is the distinctive feature. ‘Thus-become’ means ‘having attained such a state.’ ‘Vicchā’ is the desire to pervade a distinct meaning.

Tattha lakkhaṇe –

Therein, in the sense of characteristic:

Rukkhamabhi vijjotate vijju, rukkhaṃ abhi byāpetvā vijjotateti attho, vijjobhāsena byāpito rukkho vijjuppādassa lakkhaṇaṃ saññāṇaṃ hoti.

The lightning flashes upon the tree. The meaning is, 'having pervaded the tree, it flashes.' The tree, pervaded by the radiance of the lightning, becomes a characteristic or a sign of the lightning's appearance.

Itthambhūte –

In the sense of thus-become:

Sādhu devadatto mātaramabhi, mātaraṃ abhi visiṭṭhaṃ katvā sādhūti attho, devadatto sakkaccaṃ mātupaṭṭhāne aggapurisoti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato pārā. 1. Ettha ca ‘abbhuggato’ti abhi visiṭṭhaṃ katvā uggatoti attho, ayaṃ kittisaddo bhoto gotamassa sakalalokaggabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā uggatoti vuttaṃ hoti, kittisaddasambandhe pana tassa kho pana bhoto gotamassāti attho.

Devadatta is good towards his mother. The meaning is, 'he is good, acting in a distinguished manner towards his mother'; it is said that Devadatta is the foremost person in diligently attending to his mother. And indeed, such a glorious reputation has arisen concerning the venerable Gotama. Here, ‘abbhuggato’ means 'it has arisen in a distinguished manner'; it is said that this reputation has arisen proclaiming the venerable Gotama's supreme status in the entire world. However, in connection with the reputation, the meaning is 'of that venerable Gotama.'

Vicchāyaṃ –

In the sense of pervasion:

Rukkhaṃ [M 0.0174] rukkhaṃ abhi vijjotate cando, byāpetvā vijjotatetyattho.

The moon shines upon tree after tree. The meaning is, 'having pervaded, it shines.'

Ettha ca lakkhaṇādiatthā abhisaddena jotanīyā piṇḍatthā eva, na vacanīyatthā, byāpanādiatthā eva vacanīyatthāti.

And here, meanings such as characteristic are to be indicated by the word abhi; they are only implied meanings, not expressed meanings. Meanings such as pervasion are indeed expressed meanings.

299. Patiparīhi bhāge ca ka. 299; rū. 288; nī. 582, 586; caṃ. 2.1.55; pā. 1.4.90.

299. With pati and pari, and in the sense of division.

Lakkhaṇi’tthambhūta, vicchāsu ca bhāge ca pavattehi pati, parīhi yuttā liṅgamhā dutiyā hoti.

When connected with pati and pari occurring in the senses of characteristic, thus-become, pervasion, and division, the second case occurs from the nominal stem.

Lakkhaṇe –

In the sense of characteristic:

Rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate vijju, rukkhaṃ pari vijjotate vijju. Tattha ‘patī’ti paṭicca, ‘parī’ti pharitvā.

The lightning flashes towards the tree; the lightning flashes around the tree. Therein, ‘pati’ means 'on account of,' and ‘pari’ means 'having pervaded.'

Itthambhūte –

In the sense of thus-become:

Sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ pati, sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ pari.

Devadatta is good towards his mother; Devadatta is good concerning his mother.

Vicchāyaṃ –

In the sense of pervasion:

Rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate cando, rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pari vijjotate cando.

The moon shines towards tree after tree; the moon shines around tree after tree.

Bhāge –

In the sense of division:

Taṃ dīyatu, yadettha maṃ pati siyā, taṃ dīyatu, yadettha maṃ pari siyā. Tattha ‘patī’ti paṭicca, ‘parī’ti paricca, uddissāti attho, ‘ṭhapita’nti pāṭhaseso. Ettha maṃ uddissa yaṃ [M 0.0175] vatthu ṭhapitaṃ siyā, taṃ me dīyatūtyattho, etesu bahūsu bhāgesu yo mama bhāgo, so mayhaṃ dīyatūti vuttaṃ hotīti.

Let that be given, whatever here may fall to me; let that be given, whatever here may pertain to me. Therein, ‘pati’ means 'on account of,' ‘pari’ means 'encompassing,' and the meaning is 'designated for'; ‘ṭhapitaṃ’ is the remainder of the reading. Here, the meaning is: whatever thing may have been set aside designated for me, let that be given to me. It is said: among these many portions, whatever is my share, let that be given to me.

300. Anunā ka. 299; rū. 288; nī. 582, 586; caṃ. 2.1.56; pā. 1.4.84, 90.

300. With anu.

Lakkhaṇi’tthambhūta, vicchāsu ca bhāge ca pavattena anunā yuttā liṅgamhā dutiyā hoti.

When connected with anu occurring in the senses of characteristic, thus-become, pervasion, and division, the second case occurs from the nominal stem.

Lakkhaṇe –

In the sense of characteristic:

Rukkhaṃ anu vijjotate vijju, rukkhaṃ anu pharitvāti attho. Caturāsītisahassāni, sambuddhamanupabbajuṃ bu. vaṃ. 21.5, ‘sambuddha’nti bodhisattaṃ, anu gantvā pabbajiṃsūti attho, vipassibodhisatte pabbajite sati tānipi caturāsītikulaputtasahassāni pabbajiṃsūti vuttaṃ hoti. Saccakriyamanu vuṭṭhi pāvassi, ‘anū’ti anvāya, paṭiccāti attho, saccakriyāya sati saccakriyahetu devo pāvassīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Hetu ca lakkhaṇaṃ bhavatī”ti vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Saccakriyāya sahevātipi yujjati. “Saha sacce kate mayha”nti cariyā. 3.82 hi vuttaṃ.

The lightning flashes along the tree; the meaning is, 'having pervaded along the tree.' Eighty-four thousand went forth after the Sambuddha. ‘Sambuddha’ means the Bodhisatta; the meaning is, 'having gone after, they went forth.' It is said that when the Bodhisatta Vipassī went forth, those eighty-four thousand sons of good families also went forth. Rain fell following the act of truth. ‘Anu’ means 'in accordance with,' 'on account of'—this is the meaning. It is said that when the act of truth was performed, the god rained because of the act of truth. It is stated in the commentary, 'A cause also becomes a characteristic.' It is also fitting to say 'together with the act of truth.' For it is said, 'When my truth was made...'

Itthambhūte –

In the sense of thus-become:

Sādhu devadatto mātaramanu. Tattha ‘anū’ti anvāya paṭicca.

Devadatta is good towards his mother. Therein, ‘anu’ means 'in accordance with,' 'on account of.'

Vicchāyaṃ –

In the sense of pervasion:

Rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ anu vijjotate cando. Tattha ‘anū’ti anu pharitvā.

The moon shines along tree after tree. Therein, ‘anu’ means 'pervading along.'

Bhāge –

In the sense of a share:

Yadettha [M 0.0176] maṃ anu siyā, taṃ dīyatu. Tattha ‘anū’ti anvāya. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Whatever here may be my share, let that be given. Herein, ‘anu’ means 'in accordance with.' The rest is just as explained.

301. Sahatthe ka. 299; rū. 288; nī. 582, 586; caṃ. 2.1.57; pā. 1.4.85.

301. In the sense of concomitance.

Sahatthe anunā yuttā liṅgamhā dutiyā hoti.

When connected with `anu` in the sense of concomitance, the second case occurs from the nominal stem.

Pabbataṃ anu tiṭṭhati pabbatamanusenā tiṭṭhati (moggallānavuttiyaṃ). Nadiṃ anvāvasitā bārāṇasī. ‘Anū’ti anugantvā, nadiyā saha ābaddhā tiṭṭhatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

He stands along the mountain. Bārāṇasī is settled along the river. ‘Anu’ means 'having gone along'; it is said that it stands connected with the river.

302. Hīne ka. 299; rū. 288; nī. 582, 586; caṃ. 2.1.58; pā. 1.4.86.

302. In the sense of inferiority.

Hīne pavattena anunā yuttā liṅgamhā dutiyā hoti.

When connected with `anu` occurring in the sense of inferiority, the second case occurs from the nominal stem.

Anu sāriputtaṃ paññavanto, anugatā pacchato gatāti attho, sabbe paññavanto sāriputtato hīnāti vuttaṃ hoti.

The wise are inferior to Sāriputta. The meaning is: 'they have gone after, gone behind.' It is said that all the wise are inferior to Sāriputta.

303. Upena ka. 299; rū. 288; nī. 582, 586; caṃ. 2.1.59; pā. 1.4.87.

303. With `upa`.

Hīne upena yuttā liṅgamhā dutiyā hoti.

When connected with `upa` in the sense of inferiority, the second case occurs from the nominal stem.

Upa sāriputtaṃ paññavanto, upecca gatā samīpe gatāti attho, hīnātveva vuttaṃ hoti.

The wise are inferior to Sāriputta. The meaning is: 'having approached, they have gone near.' It is indeed said in the sense of inferiority.

Ettha ca abhiiccādayo kammappavacanīyāti saddasatthesu vuttā. Tattha pakārena vuccatīti pavacanīyaṃ, pakāro ca lakkhaṇi’tthambhūta, vicchādiko piṇḍattho vuccati, kammanti byāpanādikriyā, kammaṃ pavacanīyaṃ yehi te kammappavacanīyā.

Here, moreover, `abhi` and so forth are stated as 'kammappavacanīya' in the grammatical treatises. Therein, `pavacanīya` is so called because something is stated by way of a manner; and manner—such as characteristic, state, distinction, and so forth—is called a condensed meaning. `Kamma` means action, such as pervading. Those by which action is stated are `kammappavacanīya`.

Tattha [M 0.0177] byāpanādikriyāvisesavācīhi upasaggehi sambandhesati kammatthe dutiyā hoti, asambandhe pana ādhāra, sāmyādiatthesu hoti, lakkhaṇādayo pana sāmatthiyasiddhā piṇḍatthā evāti.

Therein, when connected with prefixes denoting specific actions such as pervasion, the second case is used in the sense of the object. However, when not so connected, it occurs in meanings such as location, similarity, and so forth. Characteristics and the like, however, are indeed condensed meanings established by their own capacity.

304. Kāladdhānamaccantasaṃyoge ka. 298; rū. 287; nī. 581; pā. 2.3.5

304. In continuous connection with time and distance.

Kālassa vā addhuno vā dabba, guṇa, kriyāhi accantaṃ nirantaraṃ saṃyoge kāla’ddhānavācīhi liṅgehi paraṃ dutiyā hoti.

When there is a continuous, uninterrupted connection of time or distance with substance, quality, or action, the second case occurs after nominal stems denoting time or distance.

Kāle –

In the sense of time:

Sattāhaṃ gavapānaṃ, māsaṃ maṃsodanaṃ, saradaṃ ramaṇīyā nadī, sabbakālaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ nandanaṃ, māsaṃ sajjhāyati, vassasataṃ jīvati, tayo māse abhidhammaṃ deseti.

For seven days, the drinking of milk; for a month, rice with meat; throughout the autumn, the river is delightful; at all times, the Nandana Grove is delightful; for a month, he recites; he lives for a hundred years; for three months, he teaches the Abhidhamma.

Addhāne –

In the sense of distance:

Yojanaṃ vanarāji, yojanaṃ dīgho pabbato, kosaṃ sajjhāyati.

A yojana of forest-line; a mountain a yojana long; for a kosa he recites.

Accantasaṃyogeti kiṃ? Māse māse bhuñjati, yojane yojane vihāro.

Why is 'in continuous connection' stated? He eats month by month; there is a monastery yojana by yojana.

Ettha ca kriyāvisesanampi kattārā sādhetabbattā kammagatikaṃ hoti, tasmā tampi ‘kamme dutiyā’ti ettha kammasaddena gayhati.

And here, since even an adverbial qualification of an action is to be accomplished by the agent, it partakes of the nature of an object. Therefore, that too is included by the word 'kamma' in the rule 'the second case in the sense of the object.'

Sukhaṃ seti, dukkhaṃ seti, sīghaṃ gacchati, khippaṃ gacchati, dandhaṃ gacchati, muduṃ pacati, garuṃ essati, lahuṃ essati, sannidhikārakaṃ bhuñjati, samparivattakaṃ otāpeti, kāyappacālakaṃ gacchati pāci. 590, hatthappacālakaṃ [M 0.0178] gacchati, sīsappacālakaṃ gacchati pāci. 594-595, surusurukārakaṃ bhuñjati pāci. 627, avagaṇḍakārakaṃ bhuñjati pāci. 622, piṇḍukkhepakaṃ bhuñjati pāci. 620, hatthaniddhunakaṃ bhuñjati pāci. 623, hatthanillehakaṃ bhuñjati pāci. 628, candimasūriyā samaṃ pariyāyanti, visamaṃ pariyāyanti iccādi.

He sleeps happily; he sleeps unhappily; he goes quickly; he goes swiftly; he goes slowly; he cooks gently; he will come heavily; he will come lightly; he eats having stored it; he warms himself by turning over; he goes shaking his body; he goes shaking his hand; he goes shaking his head; he eats making a 'surusuru' sound; he eats with bulging cheeks; he eats tossing up lumps of food; he eats shaking his hand; he eats licking his hand; the moon and sun revolve evenly; they revolve unevenly, and so on.

Dutiyāvibhattirāsi niṭṭhito.

The section on the second case is concluded.

Tatiyāvibhattirāsi

The Section on the Third Case

Kasmiṃ atthe tatiyā?

In what sense is the third case used?

305. Kattukaraṇesu tatiyā ka. 286, 288; rū. 291, 293; nī. 591, 594; caṃ. 2.1.62-3; pā. 2.3.18.

305. The third case is used in the sense of the agent and the instrument.

Kattari karaṇe ca tatiyā hoti. Kattāti ca kārakoti ca atthato ekaṃ “karotīti kattā, karotīti kārako”ti, tasmā “kattukārako”ti vutte dvinnaṃ pariyāyasaddānaṃ vasena ayameva kriyaṃ ekantaṃ karoti, sāmī hutvā karoti, attappadhāno hutvā karotīti viññāyati, tato kriyā nāma kattuno eva byāpāro, na aññesanti ca, aññe pana kriyāsādhane kattuno upakārakattā kārakā nāmāti ca, tathā anupakārakattā akārakā nāmāti ca viññāyantīti.

The third case occurs in the sense of the agent and the instrument. The agent (`kattā`) and the doer (`kāraka`) are one in meaning: 'one who acts is the agent; one who acts is the doer.' Therefore, when 'agent-doer' is said, by means of these two synonymous terms it is understood that this very one performs the action exclusively, performs it as a master, performs it as the principal. Hence, action is indeed the function of the agent alone, and not of others; but others are called 'doers' (`kāraka`) because they are helpful to the agent in accomplishing the action, and similarly, they are called 'non-doers' (`akāraka`) because they are not helpful.

Tattha kattā tividho sayaṃkattā, payojakakattā, kammakattāti.

Therein, the agent is of three kinds: the self-agent, the instigating agent, and the object-as-agent.

Tattha dhātvatthaṃ sayaṃ karonto sayaṃkattā nāma, puriso kammaṃ karoti.

Therein, one who himself performs the action denoted by the root is called the self-agent; for example, 'a man does a deed.'

Paraṃ [M 0.0179] niyojento payojakakattā nāma, puriso dāsaṃ kammaṃ kāreti.

One who employs another is called the instigating agent; for example, 'a man makes a slave do a deed.'

Kammakattā nāma payojjakakattāpi vuccati, puriso dāsena kammaṃ kāreti dāsassa vā, yo ca aññena kataṃ payogaṃ paṭicca kammabhūtopi sukarattā vā kammabhāvena avattukāmatāya vā ajānanatāya vā vañcetukāmatāya vā kattubhāvena voharīyati, so kammakattā nāma, kusūlo sayameva bhijjati, ghaṭo sayameva bhijjati. Apica sukaro vā hotu dukkaro vā, yo kammarūpakriyāpade paṭhamanto kattā, so kammakattāti vuccati. Saddarūpena kammañca taṃ attharūpena kattā cāti kammakattā, kusūlo bhijjati, ghaṭo bhijjati, paccati munino bhattaṃ, thokaṃ thokaṃ ghare ghare iccādi.

The agent-as-object is also called the instigating agent, as when 'a man makes a slave do work' or 'of the slave.' And one who, in dependence on an action performed by another, though being an object, is spoken of as an agent—either because of ease, or unwillingness to be in the state of an object, or ignorance, or a wish to deceive—is called the agent-as-object. For example, 'the granary breaks by itself,' 'the pot breaks by itself.' Moreover, whether it is easy or difficult, whoever is the agent in the nominative case in a verb with a passive form, is called the agent-as-object. Formally, it is an object, but semantically, it is an agent—thus, it is the agent-as-object. Examples include: 'the granary breaks,' 'the pot breaks,' 'the sage's food is cooked,' 'little by little in each house,' and so on.

Ettha ca saddattho duvidho paramattho, paññattatthoti. Tattha paramattho ekantena vijjamānoyeva. Paññattattho pana koci vijjamānoti sammato. Yathā? Rājaputto, govisāṇaṃ, campakapupphanti. Koci avijjamānoti sammato. Yathā? Vañjhāputto, sasavisāṇaṃ, udumbarapupphanti. Saddo ca nāma vatticchāpaṭibaddhavuttī hoti, vattamāno ca saddo atthaṃ na dīpetīti natthi, saṅkete sati suṇantassa atthavisayaṃ buddhiṃ na janetīti natthīti adhippāyo. Iti avijjamānasammatopi attho saddabuddhīnaṃ visayabhāvena vijjamāno eva hoti. Itarathā ‘vañjhāputto’ti padaṃ suṇantassa tadatthavisayaṃ cittaṃ nāma na pavatteyyāti, saddabuddhīnañca visayabhāvena vijjamāno nāma attho saddanānātte buddhinānātte ca sati nānā hoti, visuṃ visuṃ vijjamāno nāma hotīti adhippāyo. Evaṃ saddabuddhivisayabhāvena vijjamānañca nānābhūtañca atthaṃ paṭicca kārakanānāttaṃ kriyākārakanānāttañca hoti[M 0.0180], na pana sabhāvato vijjamānameva nānābhūtameva ca atthanti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Tasmā “saṃyogo jāyate” iccādīsu saddabuddhīnaṃ nānāttasiddhena atthanānāttena dvinnaṃ saddānaṃ dvinnaṃ atthānañca kriyākārakatāsiddhi veditabbāti.

Here, the meaning of a word is twofold: ultimate meaning and conventional meaning. Among these, the ultimate meaning is absolutely existent. The conventional meaning, however, is considered to exist in some cases. For example: 'a prince,' 'an ox's horn,' 'a champak flower.' It is also considered non-existent in some cases. For example: 'a barren woman’s son,' 'a hare’s horn,' 'an udumbara flower.' A word, indeed, has a usage bound by the speaker's intention. There is no case where a word, being uttered, does not convey a meaning; that is, when a convention exists, it is not the case that it does not generate in the listener an understanding concerning the meaning—this is the intention. Thus, even a meaning considered non-existent becomes existent as the object of word and cognition. Otherwise, for one hearing the term 'a barren woman’s son,' a thought concerning its meaning would not arise. Moreover, a meaning that exists as the object of word and cognition is diverse when there is a diversity of words and a diversity of cognitions; it is understood as existing separately—this is the intention. Thus, depending on a meaning that exists as the object of word and cognition and is diverse, there arises a diversity of case roles and a diversity of actions and case roles. However, it should not be concluded here that meaning exists and is diverse by its own nature. Therefore, in phrases like 'a union arises,' the establishment of the action and case role of two words and two meanings is to be understood through the diversity of meaning established by the diversity of word and cognition.

Kayirate anenāti karaṇaṃ, kriyāsādhane kattuno sahakārīkāraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ duvidhaṃ ajjhattikakaraṇaṃ, bāhirakaraṇanti.

That by which something is done is an instrument. It is said to be a cooperative cause of the agent in accomplishing the action. It is of two kinds: the internal instrument and the external instrument.

Tattha kattuno aṅgabhūtaṃ karaṇaṃ ajjhattikaṃ nāma, puriso cakkhunā rūpaṃ passati, manasā dhammaṃ vijānāti, hatthena kammaṃ karoti, pādena maggaṃ gacchati, rukkho phalabhārena oṇamati.

In this context, an instrument that is a part of the agent is called internal. A person sees forms with the eye, cognizes mental objects with the mind, performs actions with the hand, walks the path with the foot, a tree bends with the weight of fruit.

Kattuno bahibhūtaṃ bāhiraṃ nāma, puriso yānena gacchati, pharasunā parasunā (sakkataganthesu) chindati, rukkho vātena oṇamati.

That which is external to the agent is called external. A man goes by vehicle, cuts with an axe, a tree bends with the wind.

306. Sahatthena ka. 287; rū. 296; nī. 592; caṃ. 2.1.65; pā. 2.3.19.

306. In the sense of 'with'.

Sahasaddassa attho yassa soti sahattho, sahatthena saddena yuttā liṅgamhā tatiyā hoti. Sahasaddassa attho nāma samavāyattho.

That which has the meaning of the word 'saha' is 'sahattho.' The third case occurs from a noun connected with a word having the meaning of 'saha.' The meaning of the word 'saha' is indeed the meaning of combination.

So tividho dabbasamavāyo, guṇasamavāyo, kriyāsamavāyoti. Puttena saha dhanavā pitā, puttena saha thūlo pitā, puttena saha āgato pitā. Saha, saddhiṃ, samaṃ, nānā, vināiccādiko sahatthasaddo nāma.

It is of three kinds: combination of substance, combination of quality, and combination of action. A father with his son is wealthy; a father with his son is stout; a father with his son has arrived. Words such as 'saha' (with), 'saddhiṃ' (together with), 'samaṃ' (together with), 'nānā' (without), and 'vinā' (without) are called words with the meaning of 'saha'.

Nisīdi bhagavā saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena mahāva. 59, sahassena samaṃ mitā saṃ. ni. 1.32, piyehi nānābhāvo vinābhāvo dī. ni. 2.183, 207, saṅgho saha vā gaggena vinā vā gaggena uposathaṃ kareyya mahāva. 167.

The Blessed One sat down together with the community of monks; measured equal with a thousand; being apart from dear ones, being without them; the Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha either with Gagga or without Gagga.

307. Lakkhaṇe rū. 147 piṭṭhe; nī. 598; caṃ. 2.1.66; pā. 2.3.21.

307. In the sense of characteristic.

Lakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0181] vuccati itthambhūtalakkhaṇaṃ, tasmiṃ tatiyā hoti.

A characteristic is called 'itthambhūtalakkhaṇa' (a characteristic of being such); in that sense, the third case is used.

Assupuṇṇehi nettehi, pitaraṃ so udikkhati jā. 2.22.2123. Brahmabhūtena attanā viharati a. ni. 3.67, asambhinnena vilepanena rājānamadakkhi, tidaṇḍakena paribbājakamadakkhi, ūnapañcabandhanena pattena aññaṃ pattaṃ cetāpeti pārā. 612 (thokaṃ visadisaṃ), bhikkhu pāsādikena abhikkantena paṭikkantena ālokitena vilokitena samiñjitena pasāritena gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi, sā kāḷī dāsī bhinnena sīsena lohitena galantena pativissakānaṃ ujjhāpesi ma. ni. 1.226, ukkhittakāya antaraghare gacchanti pāci. 584, pallatthikāya antaraghare nisīdanti pāci. 599.

With eyes full of tears, he looked at his father. He dwells with himself become Brahmā. He saw the king with unbroken anointment; he saw the wanderer with a triple staff. With a bowl lacking five bindings, he procures another bowl. The monk, with dignified going forward and turning back, looking ahead and looking around, contracting and extending his limbs, entered the village for alms. That dark slave woman, with a broken head and flowing blood, caused the neighbors to complain. With body held high, they go inside the house; with legs crossed, they sit inside the house.

Aṅgavikāropi idha saṅgayhati ka. 291; rū. 299; nī. 603, akkhinā kāṇaṃ passati, ‘akkhī’ti idaṃ ‘kāṇa’nti pade visesanaṃ, vikalena cakkhuaṅgena so kāṇo nāma hoti. Hatthena kuṇiṃ passati, pādena khañjaṃ passati.

Deformity of a limb is also included here. By the eye, one perceives a one-eyed person; this 'eye' is a qualifier for the word 'one-eyed.' By means of a defective eye-organ, he is called one-eyed. By the hand, one perceives a person with a crippled arm; by the foot, one perceives a lame person.

308. Hetumhi ka. 289; rū. 297; nī. 601.

308. In the sense of cause.

Hinoti pavattati phalaṃ etenāti hetu, tasmiṃ tatiyā hoti.

That by which a result is produced or occurs is a cause; in that sense, the third case is used.

Annena vasati, vijjāya sādhu, kammunā vattati loko, kammunā vattati pajā ma. ni. 2.460; su. ni. 659 (vattatī pajā). Kammunā vasalo hoti, kammunā hoti brāhmaṇo su. ni. 136. Kenaṭṭhena dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā, kena nimittena, kena vaṇṇena [M 0.0182] saṃ. ni. 1.234 kena paccayena, kena hetunā jā. 2.22.2097, kena kāraṇena jā. aṭṭha. 4.15 mātaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā iccādi.

One lives by food; one is good by knowledge. The world exists by action; beings exist by action. By action, one becomes an outcast; by action, one becomes a brahmin. By what meaning, by what sign, by what appearance, by what condition, by what cause, by what reason, and so on.

Ettha ca karaṇaṃ tividhaṃ kriyāsādhakakaraṇaṃ, visesanakaraṇaṃ, nānāttakaraṇanti.

Here, the instrument is of three kinds: the instrument of action accomplishment, the instrument of distinction, and the instrument of diversity.

Tattha kriyāsādhakaṃ pubbe vuttameva.

Among these, the instrument for accomplishing action is indeed as previously stated.

Visesanakaraṇaṃ yathā? Ādicco nāma gottena, sākiyo nāma jātiyā su. ni. 425. Gottena gotamo nātho apa. thera 1.1.253 (visadisaṃ), sāriputtoti nāmena apa. thera 1.1.251, vissuto paññavā ca so, jātiyā khattiyo buddho dī. ni. 2.92, jātiyā sattavassiko mi. pa. 6.4.8, sippena naḷakāro so, ekūnatiṃso vayasā dī. ni. 2.214, vijjāya sādhu, tapasā uttamo, suvaṇṇena abhirūpo, pakatiyā abhirūpo, pakatiyā bhaddako, yebhuyyena mattikā pāci. 86, dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāreti, samena dhāvati, visamena dhāvati, sukhena sukhito homi, pāmojjena pamudito bu. vaṃ. 2.78. Dvidoṇena dhaññaṃ kiṇāti, sahassena asse vikkiṇāti, attanāva attānaṃ sammannati pārā. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā (sammanni) iccādi.

The instrument of distinction is as follows: Ādicca by clan, Sākiya by birth. By clan, the protector is Gotama; by name, Sāriputta, renowned and wise is he. By birth a khattiya, the Buddha; seven years old by birth; by craft, he is a reed-worker; twenty-nine by age; good by knowledge; supreme by austerity; handsome by gold; naturally handsome; naturally excellent; mostly clay. He rules the kingdom justly and evenly by Dhamma; he runs evenly; he runs unevenly. I am happy with happiness; I am delighted with joy. He buys grain for two doṇas; he sells horses for a thousand; he appoints himself by himself, and so on.

Nānāttakaraṇaṃ yathā? Kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇena, purisena thāmadassinā bu. vaṃ. 2.56. Kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedha, kiṃ te ajinasāṭiyā dha. pa. 394. Alaṃ te idha vāsena pārā. 436, alaṃ me buddhena pārā. 52, kinnumebuddhena pārā. 52, na mamattho buddhena pārā. 52, maṇinā me attho pārā. 344, vadeyyātha bhante yenattho, pānīyena pāṇiyena (mū.) attho, mūlehi bhesajjehi attho mahāva. 263, seyyena atthiko, mahagghena [M 0.0183] atthiko, māsena pubbo, pitarā sadiso, mātarā samo, kahāpaṇena ūno, dhanena vikalo, asinā kalaho, vācāya kalaho, ācārena nipuṇo, vācāya nipuṇo, guḷena missako, tilena missako, vācāya sakhilo iccādi.

The instrument of diversity is as follows: What use to me is one who has crossed over, a man seeing strength? What use to you are matted locks, dull-witted one? What use to you is an antelope hide cloak? Enough for you living here. Enough of the Buddha for me. What then of the Buddha? I have no need of the Buddha. I have need of a jewel. You should say, venerable sir, what your need is. I need water. I need roots for medicine. One in need of a bed; one in need of great price; earlier by a month; like a father; equal to a mother; less by a kahāpaṇa; lacking in wealth; a quarrel with a sword; a quarrel with speech; skilled in conduct; skilled in speech; mixed with molasses; mixed with sesame; amiable in speech, and so on.

Tathā kammā’vadhi, ādhāra’ccantasaṃyoga, kriyāpavaggāpi nānāttakaraṇe saṅgayhanti.

Likewise, the object, the limit, continuous connection with the locus, and the completion of an action are also included under the instrument of diversity.

Kamme tāva –

Firstly, in the sense of the object—

Tilehi khette vappati, tantavāyehi cīvaraṃ vāyāpeti, sunakhehi khādāpenti iccādi.

Sesame is sown in the field; he has a robe woven by weavers; they have something eaten by dogs, and so on.

Avadhimhi –

In the limit—

Sumuttā mayaṃ tena mahāsamaṇena cūḷava. 437, muttomhi kāsirājena, cakkhu suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā saṃ. ni. 4.85, ottappati kāyaduccaritena a. ni. 5.2, hirīyati kāyaduccaritena a. ni. 5.2, jigucchati sakena kāyena, pathabyā ekarajjena, saggassa gamanena vā. Sabbalokādhipaccena, sotāpattiphalaṃ varaṃ dha. pa. 178 iccādi.

We are well freed by that great ascetic; I am freed by the king of Kāsi. The eye is empty of self or of what belongs to self. One has moral dread of bodily misconduct; one has moral shame of bodily misconduct; one is disgusted with one's own body. The fruit of stream-entry is superior to sole sovereignty over the earth, to going to heaven, or to lordship over all the world, and so on.

Ādhāre –

In the sense of location—

Tena khaṇena tena layena tena muhuttena mahāva. 17, tena samayena pārā. 1, kālena dhammassavanaṃ khu. pā. 5.9. So vo mamaccayena satthā dī. ni. 2.216, tiṇṇaṃ māsānaṃ accayena dī. ni. 2.168; udā. 51, pubbena gāmaṃ, dakkhiṇena gāmaṃ, puratthimena dhataraṭṭho, dakkhiṇena virūḷhako pacchimena virūpakkho dī. ni. 2.336, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami khu. pā. 5.1 iccādi.

At that moment, at that instant, at that brief period, at that time, it was time for hearing the Dhamma. He is your Teacher after my passing. After the lapse of three months, to the east of the village, to the south of the village, in the east is Dhataraṭṭha, in the south is Virūḷhaka, in the west is Virūpakkha; he approached where the Blessed One was, and so forth.

Accantasaṃyoge –

In the sense of continuous duration—

Māsena bhuñjati, yojanena dhāvati iccādi.

He eats for a month; he runs for a league, and so on.

Kriyāpavaggo [M 0.0184] nāma kriyāya sīghataraṃ niṭṭhāpanaṃ, tasmiṃ jotetabbe tatiyā, ekāheneva bārāṇasiṃ pāpuṇi, tīhi māsehi abhidhammaṃ desesi, navahi māsehi vihāraṃ niṭṭhāpesi, gamanamattena labhati, oṭṭhapahaṭamattena paguṇaṃ akāsi.

The term 'completion of action' means the swift completion of an action. When this is to be illustrated, the third case is used. In a single day, he reached Bārāṇasī. In three months, he taught the Abhidhamma. In nine months, he completed the monastery. He attains by merely going. He mastered it by mere recitation.

Tatiyāvibhattirāsi niṭṭhito.

The section on the third case ending is completed.

Catutthīvibhattirāsi

The section on the fourth case ending.

Kasmiṃ atthe catutthī?

In what sense is the fourth case used?

309. Sampadāne catutthī ka. 293; rū. 301; nī. 605; catutthī sampadāne (bahūsu), caṃ. 2.1.73; pā. 2.3.13.

309. The fourth case is used in the dative sense.

Sampadāne catutthī hoti. Sammā padīyate assāti sampadānaṃ, sampaṭicchakanti vuttaṃ hoti.

The fourth case is used in the dative sense. 'That to which something is properly given' is the dative; this is to say, the recipient.

Taṃ vatthusampaṭicchakaṃ, kriyāsampaṭicchakanti duvidhaṃ. Bhikkhussa cīvaraṃ deti, buddhassa silāghate.

This is twofold: the recipient of an object and the recipient of an action. One gives a robe to a monk; one praises the Buddha.

Puna anirākaraṇaṃ, anumati, ārādhananti tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha na nirākaroti na nivāretīti anirākaraṇaṃ, diyyamānaṃ na paṭikkhipatīti attho. Asati hi paṭikkhipane sampaṭicchanaṃ nāma hotīti. Kāyacittehi sampaṭicchanākāraṃ dassetvā paṭiggaṇhantaṃ sampadānaṃ anumati nāma. Vividhehi āyācanavacanehi parassa cittaṃ ārādhetvā sampaṭicchantaṃ ārādhanaṃ nāma. Bodhirukkhassa jalaṃ deti, bhikkhussa annaṃ deti, yācakassa annaṃ deti.

Again, it is threefold: non-rejection, consent, and propitiation. Herein, 'non-rejection' means not rejecting, not preventing; the meaning is not rejecting what is being given. For when there is no rejection, it is called acceptance. The dative of one who receives by showing the manner of acceptance with body and mind is called 'consent'. The dative of one who accepts after having propitiated another's mind with various words of entreaty is called 'propitiation'. One gives water to the Bodhi tree, one gives food to a monk, one gives food to a beggar.

Kriyāsampaṭicchakaṃ nānākriyāvasena bahuvidhaṃ.

The recipient of an action is of many kinds according to the variety of actions.

Tattha [M 0.0185] rocanakriyāyoge –

Therein, in connection with the action of pleasing—

Tañca amhākaṃ ruccati ceva khamati ca ma. ni. 1.179; ma. ni. 2.435, pabbajjā mama ruccati jā. 2.22.43, kassa sāduṃ na ruccati, na me ruccati bhaddante, ulūkassābhisecanaṃ jā. 1.3.60. Gamanaṃ mayhaṃ ruccati, māyasmantānampi saṅghabhedo ruccittha pārā. 418, yassāyasmato na khamati, khamati saṅghassa pārā. 438, bhattaṃ mayhaṃ chādeti, bhattamassa nacchādeti cūḷava. 282, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ lūkhāni bhojanāni nacchādenti mahāva. 261 (thokaṃ visadisaṃ). Tattha ‘chādetī’ti icchaṃ uppādetīti attho.

And that is both pleasing and acceptable to us; ordination is pleasing to me; to whom is a pleasant thing not pleasing?; the consecration of an owl is not pleasing to me, venerable sir. Going is pleasing to me; may schism in the Sangha not be pleasing even to the venerable ones; to whichever venerable one it is not acceptable...; it is acceptable to the Sangha. The meal pleases me; the meal does not please him; coarse food does not please those monks. Herein, 'chādeti' means 'it arouses desire'.

Dhāraṇappayoge –

In connection with the verb 'to hold' or 'to owe'—

Chattaggāho rañño chattaṃ dhāreti, sampatijātassa bodhisattassa devā chattaṃ dhārayiṃsu.

The umbrella-bearer holds an umbrella for the king; the gods held an umbrella for the newly-born Bodhisatta.

Buddhassa silāghate, thometīti attho, tuyhaṃ hanute, tuṇhibhāvena vañcetīti attho, bhikkhunī bhikkhussa bhuñjamānassa pānīyena vā vidhūpanena vā upaṭṭhāti pāci. 816 (visadisaṃ). Dutiyāpi hoti, rañño upaṭṭhāti, rājānaṃ upaṭṭhāti, ahaṃ bhotiṃ upaṭṭhissaṃ jā. 2.22.1934, ahaṃ taṃ upaṭṭhissāmi, mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ khu. pā. 5.6, tuyhaṃ sapate, sapassu me vepacitti saṃ. ni. 1.253, sapathampi te samma ahaṃ karomi jā. 2.21.407, tava mayi saddahanatthaṃ saccaṃ karomīti attho, rañño sataṃ dhāreti, idha kulaputto na kassaci kiñci dhāreti a. ni. 4.62, tassa rañño mayaṃ nāgaṃ dhārayāma. Tattha ‘rañño sataṃ dhāretī’ti sataṃ balidhanaṃ vā daṇḍadhanaṃ vā nidetīti nidhetīti, nidhema (keci) attho, “iṇaṃ katvā gaṇhātī”ti ca vadanti. ‘Dhārayāmā’ti puna nidema nidhetīti, nidhema (keci), tuyhaṃ saddahati, mayhaṃ saddahati, saddahāsi siṅgālassa, surāpītassa brāhmaṇa jā. 1.1.113.

One praises the Buddha, meaning one extols him. He conceals from you, meaning he deceives by silence. A nun attends to a monk who is eating with water or a fan. The accusative is also used: one attends to the king (dative), one attends to the king (accusative). I will attend to the lady; I will attend to you. Attending to mother and father. One swears to you; 'Swear to me, Vepacitti!'; 'I also make an oath for you, friend,' meaning, 'I make a vow for the purpose of your having faith in me.' One owes the king a hundred; here a clansman does not owe anything to anyone; we owe that king a nāga. Herein, 'one owes the king a hundred' means one deposits a hundred as tribute-money or fine-money, and they also say, 'he takes it as a loan.' 'We owe' means we deposit again. He has faith in you; he has faith in me; you had faith in Siṅgāla, the drunken brahmin.

Devāpi [M 0.0186] te pihayanti tādino dha. pa. 94 (tassa pihayanti), devāpi tesaṃ pihayanti, sambuddhānaṃ satīmataṃ dha. pa. 181, ‘pihayantī’ti punappunaṃ daṭṭhuṃ patthentīti attho. Dutiyāpi hoti, sace maṃ pihayasi, dhanaṃ piheti, hiraññaṃ piheti, suvaṇṇaṃ piheti. Tatiyāpi dissati, rūpena piheti, saddena piheti iccādi.

Even the gods long for them, for such ones; even the gods long for them, the mindful, fully enlightened ones. 'They long for' means they desire to see again and again. The accusative is also used: if you long for me; he longs for wealth; he longs for gold; he longs for silver. The third case is also seen: he longs on account of form; he longs on account of sound, and so on.

Tassa kujjha mahāvīra jā. 1.4.49, mā me kujjha rathesabha jā. 2.22.1696 (kujjhi), yadihaṃ tassa kuppeyyaṃ, mātu kuppati, pitu kuppati, yo appaduṭṭhassa narassa dussati dha. pa. 125; su. ni. 667; jā. 1.5.94, duhayati disānaṃ megho, pūreti vināseti vāti attho, akāle vassanto hi vināseti nāma, yo mittānaṃ na dubbhati jā. 2.22.19, aduṭṭhassa tuvaṃ dubbhi jā. 1.16.295, mittānaṃ na dubbheyya, titthiyā issanti samaṇānaṃ, ussūyanti dujjanā guṇavantānaṃ, pativissakānaṃ ujjhāpesi ma. ni. 1.226 (ujjhāpesi), mā tumhe tassa ujjhāyittha udā. 26 (visadisaṃ), mahārājānaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ viravitabbaṃ vikkanditabbaṃ, kyāhaṃ ayyānaṃ aparajjhāmi pārā. 383 ayye vā, rañño aparajjhati rājānaṃ vā, ārādho me rājā hoti.

Be angry with him, O great hero! Do not be angry with me, O lord of chariots! If I were to be angry with him... He is angry at his mother; he is angry at his father. He who harms an innocent person... The cloud harms the directions, meaning it fills or destroys; for raining at the wrong time is indeed a form of destruction. One who does not betray friends... You harmed the innocent. One should not betray friends. Heretics are jealous of ascetics; the wicked are envious of the virtuous. He made the neighbors complain. Do not complain about him. One should complain to the great kings, cry out, and wail. In what way do I offend the noble sirs, or the noble lady? One offends the king (dative) or the king (accusative). The king is pleased with me.

Pati, āpubbassa su-dhātussa anu, patipubbassa ca gī-dhātussa yoge sampadāne catutthī. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi “bhikkhavo”ti, “bhaddante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ a. ni. 1.1. Ettha ca pubbavākye āmantanakriyāya kattā bhagavā, so paravākye paccāsuyoge sampadānaṃ hoti, ‘paccassosu’nti bhaddanteti paṭivacanaṃ adaṃsūti attho. Bhikkhū buddhassa āsuṇanti, rājā bimbisāro pilindavacchattherassa ārāmikaṃ paṭissutvā mahāva. 270, amacco rañño bimbisārassa paṭissutvā mahāva. 270, sampaṭicchitvāti attho, bhikkhu janaṃ dhammaṃ sāveti[M 0.0187], jano tassa bhikkhuno anugiṇāti paṭigiṇāti, sādhukāraṃ detīti attho.

The fourth case is used in the dative sense in connection with the root `su` when preceded by `paṭi` or `ā`, and with the root `gī` when preceded by `anu` or `paṭi`. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks!' 'Venerable sir!' those monks responded to the Blessed One. Here, in the preceding sentence, the agent of the act of addressing is the Blessed One; in the following sentence, in connection with responding, he is the recipient. 'They responded' means they gave the answer 'Venerable sir!' The monks listen to the Buddha. King Bimbisāra, having promised a park-keeper to the Elder Pilindavaccha; the minister, having promised King Bimbisāra—meaning, having accepted. A monk makes the people hear the Dhamma; the people approve of and agree with that monk, meaning, they give their assent.

Ārocanatthayoge –

In connection with the sense of declaring—

Ārocayāmi vo bhikkhave ma. ni. 1.416, paṭivedayāmi vo bhikkhave ma. ni. 1.416, āmantayāmi vo bhikkhave dī. ni. 2.218 (visadisaṃ), dhammaṃ vo desessāmi ma. ni. 3.105, bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ deseti, yathā no bhagavā byākareyya, niruttiṃ te pavakkhāmi, ahaṃ te ācikkhissāmi, ahaṃ te kittayissāmi, bhikkhūnaṃ etadavoca.

I declare to you, O monks; I announce to you, O monks; I address you, O monks; I will teach you the Dhamma. He teaches the Dhamma to the monks; as the Blessed One would explain to us. I will explain the etymology to you; I will tell you; I will proclaim it to you. He said this to the monks.

310. Tadatthe ka. 277; rū. 303; nī. 554.

310. In the sense of 'for that purpose'.

Tassā tassā kriyāya atthoti tadattho, tadatthe sampadāne catutthī hoti.

'The purpose of each respective action' is the meaning of `tadattho`. In the sense of 'for that purpose', the fourth case is used in the dative.

311. Sassāya catutthiyā ka. 109; rū. 304; nī. 279-80.

311. Āya for the `sa` of the fourth case.

Akārantato catutthībhūtassa sassa āyo hoti vā.

After a noun ending in 'a', the fourth case ending `sa` is optionally replaced by `āya`.

Vinayo saṃvaratthāya, saṃvaro avippaṭisāratthāya, avippaṭisāro pāmujjatthāya, pāmujjaṃ pītatthāya, pīti passaddhatthāya, passaddhi sukhatthāya, sukhaṃ samādhatthāya, samādhi yathābhūtañāṇadassanatthāya, yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ nibbidatthāya, nibbidā virāgatthāya, virāgo vimuttatthāya, vimutti vimuttiñāṇadassanatthāya, vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ anupādāparinibbānatthāya pari. 366, atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ ma. ni. 1.50, alaṃ kukkuccāya pārā. 38, alaṃ sammohāya, pākāya vajati, yuddhāya gacchati, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ pāci. 902.

Discipline is for the sake of restraint, restraint is for the sake of freedom from remorse, freedom from remorse is for the sake of joy, joy is for the sake of rapture, rapture is for the sake of tranquility, tranquility is for the sake of happiness, happiness is for the sake of concentration, concentration is for the sake of knowledge and vision of things as they are, knowledge and vision of things as they are is for the sake of disenchantment, disenchantment is for the sake of dispassion, dispassion is for the sake of liberation, liberation is for the sake of the knowledge and vision of liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation is for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging; for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans; enough of anxiety, enough of delusion; it proceeds to maturity, goes to battle, I entered the village for alms.

Tumatthopi [M 0.0188] tadatthe saṅgayhati, alaṃ mitte sukhāpetuṃ, amittānaṃ dukhāya ca jā. 2.17.13. Lokānukampāya buddho loke uppajjati, alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati mahāva. 13.

The sense of the infinitive is also included in that purpose; it is enough to please friends and for the suffering of enemies. Out of compassion for the world, a Buddha arises in the world. It is enough for a pleasant dwelling; it leads to higher knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.

Alamatthayoge –

In connection with the sense of 'enough'—

Alaṃ mallo mallassa, arahati mallo mallassa, alaṃ te idha vāsena pārā. 436, alaṃ te hiraññasuvaṇṇena, kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇena bu. vaṃ. 2.56, kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedha, kiṃ te ajinasāṭiyā dha. pa. 394.

A wrestler is a match for a wrestler. A wrestler is fit for a wrestler. Enough of your dwelling here. Enough of your silver and gold. What use to me is one who has crossed over? What use are your matted locks, O dullard? What use is your antelope-skin cloak?

Maññanāpayoge anādare apāṇismimeva catutthī, kaṭṭhassa tuvaṃ maññe, kaliṅgarassa kaḷiṅgarassa, kaḷaṅgarassa (ka.) tuvaṃ maññe, jīvitaṃ tiṇāyapi na maññati.

In connection with the verb 'to think', in the sense of disrespect, and only for inanimate objects, the dative case is used. 'I consider you a piece of wood'; 'I consider you a worthless log'; 'he does not consider life worth even a blade of grass.'

Anādareti kiṃ? Suvaṇṇaṃ taṃ maññe.

Why the specification 'in the sense of disrespect'? 'I consider it to be gold.'

Apāṇisminti kiṃ? Gadrabhaṃ tuvaṃ maññe.

Why the specification 'for inanimate objects'? 'I consider you a donkey.'

Gatyatthānaṃ nayanatthānañca dhātūnaṃ kammani catutthī, appo saggāya gacchati dha. pa. 174, yo maṃ dakāya neti jā. 1.6.97, nirayāyupakaḍḍhati dha. pa. 311, mūlāya paṭikasseyya cūḷava. 111.

The dative case is used for the object of verbs with the meaning of going and leading. Few go to heaven; one who leads me to water; one drags another to hell; one would drag it back to the root.

Āsīsanakriyāyoge –

In connection with the action of blessing—

Āyu bhavato hotu, bhaddaṃ te hotu, bhaddamatthu te jā. 1.8.15; jā. 2.17.1, kusalaṃ te hotu, anāmayaṃ te hotu, sukhaṃ te hotu, atthaṃ te hotu, hitaṃ te hotu, kalyāṇaṃ te hotu, svāgataṃ te hotu, sotthi te hotu sotthi gabbhassa ma. ni. 2.351, maṅgalaṃ te hotu.

May you have long life, may good befall you, may good be yours, may there be well-being for you, may you be free from illness, may you be happy, may there be benefit for you, may there be welfare for you, may there be good fortune for you, welcome to you, may there be safety for you, safety for the womb, may there be auspiciousness for you.

Sammutiyoge [M 0.0189] kammatthe [chaṭṭhī], itthannāmassa bhikkhuno rūpiyachaḍḍakassa sammuti pārā. 590, pattagāhāpakassa sammutiiccādi pārā. 614.

In connection with a formal act, in the sense of the object [the genitive case is used]: the formal appointment of a monk named so-and-so as a rejector of money, the formal appointment of a bowl-receiver, and so on.

Āvikaraṇādiyoge –

In connection with disclosure, and so on—

Tuyhañcassa āvi karomi, tassa me sakko pāturahosi, tassa pahiṇeyya, bhikkhūnaṃ dūtaṃ pāhesi, kappati bhikkhūnaṃ āyogo, vaṭṭati bhikkhūnaṃ āyogo, patthodano dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ nappahoti, ekassa pahoti, ekassa pariyatto, upamaṃ te karissāmi ma. ni. 1.258; jā. 2.19.24, añjaliṃ te paggaṇhāmi jā. 2.22.327, tathāgatassa phāsu hoti, āvikatā hissa phāsu mahāva. 134, lokassa attho, lokassa hitaṃ, maṇinā me attho pārā. 344, na mamattho buddhena pārā. 52, namatthu buddhānaṃ namatthu bodhiyā jā. 1.2.17, vipassissa ca namatthu dī. ni. 3.277, namo karohi nāgassa ma. ni. 1.249, namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama apa. thera 1.2.129. Sotthi pajānaṃ dī. ni. 1.274, suvatthi pajānaṃ iccādi.

I declare this to you; Sakka appeared to me; he should send to him; he sent a messenger to the monks; it is suitable for the monks to make an effort; it is proper for the monks to make an effort; a pot of rice is not enough for two or three, it is enough for one, it is sufficient for one; I will make a comparison for you; I raise my joined hands to you; the Tathāgata is comfortable; being in the open is indeed a comfort for him; for the benefit of the world, for the welfare of the world; I have a need for the jewel; I have no need of the Buddha; homage to the Buddhas, homage to enlightenment, and homage to Vipassī; pay homage to the Nāga; homage to you, O thoroughbred of men; homage to you, O supreme man. Safety to the people, well-being to the people, and so on.

Catutthīvibhattirāsi niṭṭhito.

The section on the fourth case ending is concluded.

Pañcamīvibhattirāsi

The Section on the Fifth Case Ending

Kasmiṃ atthe pañcamī?

In what sense is the fifth case used?

312. Pañcamyāvadhismiṃ ka. 295; rū. 307; nī. 607; caṃ. 2.1.81; pā. 2.3.28; 1.4.24.

312. The fifth case is used in the sense of a limit.

Avadhiyati vavatthiyati padattho etasmāti avadhi, tasmiṃ pañcamī hoti, avadhīti ca apādānaṃ vuccati.

That from which the meaning of a word is limited and determined is called a boundary (avadhi); in that sense, the fifth case is used, and a boundary is also called the ablative (apādāna).

Apanetvā ito aññaṃ ādadāti gaṇhātīti apādānaṃ. Taṃ tividhaṃ niddiṭṭhavisayaṃ, uppāṭavisayaṃ, anumeyyavisayanti.

That from which one takes or receives something, having separated it, is the ablative (apādāna). It is threefold: the sphere of the expressed, the sphere of the supplied, and the sphere of the inferred.

Tattha [M 0.0190] yasmiṃ apādānavisayabhūto kriyāviseso sarūpato niddiṭṭho hoti, taṃ niddiṭṭhavisayaṃ. Yathā? Gāmā apenti munayo, nagarā niggato rājā.

Therein, where a specific action, which is the sphere of the ablative, is expressed in its own form, that is the sphere of the expressed. For example: The sages depart from the village; the king went out from the city.

Yasmiṃ pana so pāṭhasesaṃ katvā ajjhāharitabbo hoti, taṃ uppāṭavisayaṃ. Yathā? Valāhakā vijjotate vijju, agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitoti mahāva. 30. Ettha hi ‘nikkhamitvā’ti padaṃ ajjhāharitabbaṃ.

But where that action must be supplied by way of ellipsis, that is the sphere of the supplied. For example: Lightning flashes from the clouds; one has gone forth from the home to homelessness. Here, indeed, the word 'having gone out' must be supplied.

Yasmiṃ pana so niddiṭṭho ca na hoti, ajjhāharituñca na sakkā, atha kho atthato anumānavasena so viññeyyo hoti, taṃ anumeyyavisayaṃ. Yathā? Māthurā pāṭaliputtakehi abhirūpatarā, sīlameva sutā seyyo jā. 1.5.65, mayā bhiyyo na vijjati, aggohamasmi lokassa, jeṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, seṭṭhohamasmi lokassa iccādi ma. ni. 3.207. Kriyaṃ vinā kārakaṃ nāma na sijjhatītikatvā ukkaṃsanakriyā ettha anumetabbā hoti. Evaṃ kriyāpadarahitesu dūrayogādīsupi avinābhāvikriyānumānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

But where that action is neither expressed nor can be supplied, but rather is to be understood from the meaning by way of inference, that is the sphere of the inferred. For example: The people of Mathurā are more beautiful than those of Pāṭaliputta; virtue is indeed better than learning; there exists none better than me; I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world, and so on. Because a grammatical case is not established without an action, here an action of surpassing is to be inferred. Thus, even in expressions lacking a verb, such as those involving 'far from', etc., the inference of an inseparable action should be understood.

Puna calā’calavasena duvidhaṃ.

Again, it is twofold: moving and unmoving.

Calaṃ yathā? Puriso dhāvatā assā patati, dve meṇḍā yujjhitvā aññamaññato apasakkanti. Ettha ca yadi calaṃ siyā, kathaṃ avadhi nāma bhaveyya. Accutilakkhaṇo hi avadhīti? Vuccate-dve meṇḍā sakasakakriyāya calanti, itarītarakriyāya avadhī hontīti natthi ettha avadhilakkhaṇavirodhoti.

The moving, for example: A man falls from a running horse; two rams, having fought, retreat from each other. And here, if the ablative source were moving, how could it be a boundary? For a boundary is characterized by being fixed. It is said: the two rams move by their own respective actions; by the action relative to the other, they become boundaries. Thus, there is no contradiction with the characteristic of a boundary here.

Acalaṃ yathā? Gāmā apenti munayo, nagarā niggato rājā.

The unmoving, for example: Sages depart from the village; a king departs from the city.

Puna kāyasaṃsaggapubbakaṃ, cittasaṃsaggapubbakanti duvidhaṃ hoti, gāmā apenti munayo, corā bhayaṃ jāyate. Ettha ca “kiṃva [M 0.0191] dūro ito gāmo, ito sā dakkhiṇā disā dī. ni. 3.279. Ito ekanavutikappe”ti dī. ni. 2.4 ādīsu vadantassa cittasaṃsaggapubbakampi veditabbaṃ. “Na mātā puttato bhāyati, na ca putto mātito bhāyati, bhayā bhīto na bhāsasī”ti jā. 2.21.138 pāḷi. Atthi te ito bhayaṃ ma. ni. 2.350, natthi te ito bhayaṃ, yato khemaṃ tato bhayaṃ jā. 1.9.58, corā bhāyati, corā bhīto. Chaṭṭhī ca, corassa bhāyati, corassa bhīto. Dutiyā ca, “kathaṃ paralokaṃ na bhāyeyya, evaṃ paralokaṃ na bhāyeyya, bhāyasi maṃ samaṇa su. ni. sūcilomasutta, nāhaṃ taṃ bhāyāmi su. ni. sūcilomasutta, bhāyitabbaṃ na bhāyati, nāhaṃ bhāyāmi bhoginaṃ jā. 2.22.835, na maṃ migā uttasantī”ti jā. 2.22.307 pāḷipadāni dissanti. Tattha “bhogina’nti nāgaṃ, corā tasati uttasati corassa vā, sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa dha. pa. 129, pāpato ottappati jigucchati harāyati pāpena vā.

Again, it is twofold: preceded by bodily contact and preceded by mental contact. For example: The sages depart from the village; fear arises from a thief. And here, in such phrases as, 'How far is the village from here? From here, that is the southern direction. From here, ninety-one eons ago,' that which is preceded by mental contact should also be understood. The Pāli states: 'A mother does not fear her son, nor does a son fear his mother. Afraid because of fear, you do not speak.' There is fear for you from this; there is no fear for you from this. From where there is safety, from there comes fear. One fears a thief; one is afraid of a thief. And the genitive case: one fears a thief; one is afraid of a thief. And the accusative case: 'How should one not fear the next world? Thus, one should not fear the next world. You fear me, ascetic. I do not fear you. One does not fear what should be feared. I do not fear the serpent. The deer are not terrified of me'—these Pāli phrases are seen. There, 'bhoginaṃ' means a serpent. One trembles at a thief, is terrified of a thief (ablative), or of a thief (genitive). All tremble at punishment. One has moral dread of evil (ablative), is disgusted by it, is ashamed of it, or by evil (instrumental).

Yato kiñci sippaṃ vā vijjaṃ vā dhammaṃ vā gaṇhāti, tasmiṃ akkhātari pañcamī, upajjhāyā adhīte, upajjhāyā sippaṃ gaṇhāti, dvāsīti buddhato gaṇhiṃ, dve sahassāni bhikkhuto. Caturāsītisahassāni, yeme dhammā pavattino theragā. 1027.

From whomever one receives any craft, knowledge, or Dhamma, the ablative case is used with reference to that teacher. One learns from the preceptor; one receives a craft from the preceptor. Eighty-two I received from the Buddha, two thousand from the monks. Eighty-four thousand are these teachings of mine that are in circulation.

Yato suṇāti, tasmiṃ pañcamī, chaṭṭhī ca, ito sutvā, imassa sutvā vā, yamhā dhammaṃ vijāneyya, sammāsambuddhadesitaṃ dha. pa. 392.

From whomever one hears, in that case the ablative and also the genitive are used: having heard from this one, or having heard of this one. 'From whom one might know the Dhamma, taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.'

Yato labhati, tasmiṃ pañcamī, saṅghato labhati, gaṇato labhati.

From whomever one obtains, in that case the ablative is used: one obtains from the Sangha; one obtains from the group.

Yato parājayati, yato pabhavati, yato jāyati, tasmiṃ pañcamī, buddhasmā parājayanti aññatitthiyā, pāḷiyaṃ pana parājiyoge apādānaṃ pāṭhasesavasena labbhati, tasmiṃ kho [M 0.0192] pana saṅgāme devā jiniṃsu, asurā parājiniṃsu. Ettha devehi parājiniṃsūti pāṭhaseso. “Mayaṃ jitāmhā ambakāya. Himavantā pabhavanti pañca mahānadiyo a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.8.19, ayaṃ bhāgīrathī gaṅgā, himavantā pabhāvitā”ti pāḷi apa. thera 1.1.255, corā bhayaṃ jāyate, kāmato jāyate bhayaṃ dha. pa. 215, jātaṃ saraṇato bhayaṃ jā. 1.1.36; 1.2.13; 1.9.56, 57, 59, yaṃkiñci bhayaṃ vā veraṃ vā upaddavo vā upasaggo vā jāyati, sabbaṃ taṃ bālato jāyati, no paṇḍitato, kāmato jāyatī soko dha. pa. 214, ubhato sujāto putto dī. ni. 1.311, urasmā jāto, ure jāto vā, cīvaraṃ uppajjeyya saṅghato vā gaṇato vā ñātimittato vā pārā. 500 (thokaṃ visadisaṃ).

From where one is defeated, from where one arises, from where one is born—in that case, the fifth case ending is used. The followers of other sects are defeated by the Buddha. However, in the Pāli texts, the ablative in connection with defeat is obtained by way of textual remainder. In that very battle, the gods were victorious, and the asuras were defeated. Here, the textual remainder is 'they were defeated by the gods.' 'We are conquered by Ambakā.' 'Five great rivers arise from the Himalayas—this Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā originates from the Himalayas' is a Pāli text. Fear arises from thieves. Fear arises from desire. Fear is born from a refuge.
