For example: `dussīlo` (immoral) and `duppañño` (unwise). Here, in the grammars of words, the statement of meaning for 'sampannaṃ brahma' and so on is merely a clarification of the word's sense. However, in the suttas, having understood the appropriate primary meaning of these terms, one should also understand the statement of meaning accordingly.

Yathāsaddatthe –

In the sense of correspondence—

Rūpassa sabhāvassa yogyaṃ anurūpaṃ, attānaṃ attānaṃ paṭicca pavattaṃ paccattaṃ, aḍḍhamāsaṃ aḍḍhamāsaṃ anugataṃ anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ, gharaṃ gharaṃ anugataṃ anugharaṃ, vassaṃ vassaṃ anugataṃ anuvassaṃ, jeṭṭhānaṃ [M 0.0220] anupubbaṃ anujeṭṭhaṃ, sattiyā anurūpaṃ yathāsatti, balassa anurūpaṃ yathābalaṃ, kamassa anurūpaṃ yathākkamaṃ. Evaṃ yathāsaṅkhyaṃ, yathālābhaṃ. Sotassa paṭilomaṃ paṭisotaṃ, paṭivātaṃ, paṭisaddaṃ.

Suitable to the intrinsic nature of form is `anurūpaṃ`; what occurs depending on each self is `paccattaṃ`; following every half-month is `anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ`; going from house to house is `anugharaṃ`; year after year is `anuvassaṃ`; following the elders in succession is `anujeṭṭhaṃ`; suitable to one's ability is `yathāsatti`; suitable to strength is `yathābalaṃ`; suitable to order is `yathākkamaṃ`. Similarly, `yathāsaṅkhyaṃ` (according to number), `yathālābhaṃ` (according to gain). Against the current is `paṭisotaṃ`; against the wind is `paṭivātaṃ`; against the sound is `paṭisaddaṃ`.

Pacchāpadatthe –

In the sense of 'after'—

Rathassa pacchā anurathaṃ.

Behind the chariot is `anurathaṃ`.

Yugabhūto padattho yugapadattho, sahabhāvīatthadvayassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tattha asaniphalena saha pavattaṃ cakkaṃ sacakkaṃ, gadāvudhena yugaḷapavattaṃ vāsudevassa cakkāvudhantipi vadanti yugapadatthe sacakkaṃ nidhehi, (moggallānavuttiyaṃ). cakkena yugapata dhehi sacakkaṃ, (mugdhabodhavuttiyaṃ). he bisaṇu! cakkena saha yugapadekakāle gadaṃ dhāraya. (mugdhabodhaṭīkāyaṃ 226 piṭṭhe), sahassa sattaṃ.

A word that has become a pair has the meaning of a pair; this is the name for the coexistence of two meanings. Here, a wheel that functions together with a thunderbolt is `sacakkaṃ`. They also call the wheel-weapon of Vāsudeva, which functions as a pair with the mace-weapon, `cakkāvudhaṃ`. The substitution of `sa` for `saha` is applied.

339. Yathā natulye ka. 319; rū. 330; nī. 696; caṃ. 2.2.3; pā. 2.1.7.

339. `Yathā` is used when not in the sense of equality.

Tulyato aññasmiṃ atthe pavatto yathāsaddo syādinā saha ekattho hoti moggallāne aññathāvutti dassitā.

The word `yathā`, occurring in a meaning different from equality, becomes one in meaning with a `syādi` form.

Yathāsatti, yathābalaṃ, yathākkamaṃ, ye ye vuḍḍhā yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, vuḍḍhānaṃ paṭipāṭi vā yathāvuḍḍhaṃ.

`Yathāsatti` (according to ability), `yathābalaṃ` (according to strength), `yathākkamaṃ` (according to order). Whichever elders, `yathāvuḍḍhaṃ` (according to seniority); or the succession of elders is `yathāvuḍḍhaṃ`.

Natulyeti kiṃ? Yathā devadatto, tathā yaññadatto.

What is the purpose of saying 'not in the sense of equality'? As Devadatta, so Yaññadatta.

340. Yāvāvadhāraṇe ka. 319; rū. 330; nī. 696; caṃ. 2.2.4; pā. 2.1.8.

340. `Yāva` is used in the sense of delimitation.

Avadhāraṇaṃ vuccati paricchindanaṃ, avadhāraṇe pavatto yāvasaddo syādinā saha ekattho bhavati.

`Avadhāraṇa` is called `paricchindana` (delimitation); the word `yāva`, occurring in the sense of delimitation, becomes one in meaning with a `syādi` form.

Yattakaṃ [M 0.0221] attho vattatīti yāvadatthaṃ, dāgamo. Yattakaṃ jīvo vattatīti yāvajīvaṃ, yattakaṃ āyu vattatīti yāvatāyukaṃ, takāra, kakārā āgamā.

As much as the meaning extends is `yāvadatthaṃ`; `da` is an augment. As long as life lasts is `yāvajīvaṃ`; as long as the life-span lasts is `yāvatāyukaṃ`; `ta` and `ka` are augments.

341. Parāpābahitiropurepacchā vā pañcamyā ka. 319; rū. 330; nī. 696; caṃ. 2.2.7; pā. 2.1.12, 13; ‘payyapā…’ (bahūsu).

341. Optionally with the fifth case, the words `pari`, `ā`, `apa`, `bahi`, `tiro`, `pure`, and `pacchā`.

Pari, apa, āiccādayo saddā pañcamyantena syādinā saha ekatthā bhavanti vā.

The words `pari`, `apa`, `ā`, and so on, optionally become one in meaning with a `syādi` form ending in the fifth case.

Pabbatato pari samantā vassīti devo paripabbataṃ paripabbatā vā, pabbataṃ vajjetvā vassīti attho. Pabbatato bahiddhā apapabbataṃ apapabbatā vā, pāṭaliputtato bahiddhā vassīti devo āpāṭaliputtaṃ āpāṭaliputtā vā, ākumārehi kaccāyanassa yaso vattatīti ākumāraṃ ākumārā vā, ābhavaggā bhagavato yaso vattatīti ābhavaggaṃ ābhavaggā vā, āpāṇakoṭiyā saraṇagamanaṃ vattatīti āpāṇakoṭikaṃ, kāgamo. Gāmato bahi bahigāmaṃ bahigāmā vā, evaṃ bahinagaraṃ, bahileṇaṃ, pabbatato tiro tiropabbataṃ tiropabbatā vā, evaṃ tiropākāraṃ, tirokuṭṭaṃ. Ettha ca ‘tiro’ti parabhāgo vuccati. Bhattamhā pure purebhattaṃ purebhattā vā, aruṇamhā pure purāruṇaṃ purāruṇā vā, bhattassa pacchā pacchābhattaṃ pacchābhattā vā.

Excluding the mountain, the god rains, thus `paripabbataṃ` or `paripabbatā`; the meaning is 'it rains avoiding the mountain'. Outside the mountain is `apapabbataṃ` or `apapabbatā`. Outside Pāṭaliputta, the god rains, thus `āpāṭaliputtaṃ` or `āpāṭaliputtā`. Kaccāyana's fame spreads up to the youths, thus `ākumāraṃ` or `ākumārā`. The Blessed One's fame spreads up to the summit of existence, thus `ābhavaggaṃ` or `ābhavaggā`. The going for refuge occurs up to the last moment of life, thus `āpāṇakoṭikaṃ`; `ka` is an augment. Outside the village is `bahigāmaṃ` or `bahigāmā`; likewise `bahinagaraṃ` (outside the town), `bahileṇaṃ` (outside the cave). Beyond the mountain is `tiropabbataṃ` or `tiropabbatā`; likewise `tiropākāraṃ` (beyond the wall), `tirokuṭṭaṃ` (beyond the rampart). Here, `tiro` is said to mean the 'other side'. Before the meal is `purebhattaṃ` or `purebhattā`; before dawn is `purāruṇaṃ` or `purāruṇā`; after the meal is `pacchābhattaṃ` or `pacchābhattā`.

342. Samīpāyāmesvanu ka. 319; rū. 330; nī. 696; caṃ. 2.2.9; pā. 2.1.15, 16.

342. Anu is used in the senses of proximity and extent.

Samīpe āyāme ca pavatto anusaddo syādinā saha ekattho bhavati vā.

The word 'anu', occurring in the senses of proximity and extent, optionally becomes one in meaning with syādi (case endings).

Vanassa samīpaṃ anuvanaṃ, asani anuvanaṃ gatā, gaṅgaṃ anuyātā anugaṅgaṃ, bārāṇasī.

Near the forest is 'anuvanaṃ'; the thunderbolt went near the forest. Along the Ganges is 'anugaṅgaṃ', as in Bārāṇasī.

343. Oro [M 0.0222] pari paṭi pāre majjhe heṭṭhuddhādhonto vā chaṭṭhiyā ka. 319; rū. 330; nī. 696; caṃ. 2.2.11; pā. 2.1.18; ‘orepari…’ (bahūsu).

343. Ora, pari, paṭi, pāra, majjha, heṭṭhā, uddha, adho, and anto are used optionally with the sixth case.

Orādayo saddā chaṭṭhīyantena syādinā saha ekatthā bhavanti vā.

The words beginning with 'ora' optionally become one in meaning with syādi (case endings) ending in the sixth case.

Ettha ca ore, pāre, majjhesaddesu ‘tadaminādīnī’ti suttena ekāro, gaṅgāya oraṃ oregaṅgaṃ, sikharassa upari uparisikharaṃ. Evaṃ uparipāsādaṃ, uparimañcaṃ, uparipabbataṃ, sotassa paṭilomaṃ paṭisotaṃ. Evaṃ paṭivātaṃ, yamunāya pāraṃ pāreyamunaṃ, gaṅgāya majjhaṃ majjhegaṅgaṃ, pāsādassa heṭṭhā heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ, heṭṭhāmañcaṃ, gaṅgāya uddhaṃ uddhaṃgaṅgaṃ, gaṅgāya adho adhogaṅgaṃ, pāsādassa anto antopāsādaṃ. Evaṃ antogāmaṃ, antonagaraṃ, antovassaṃ.

Here, in the words 'ore', 'pāre', and 'majjhe', the vowel 'e' occurs by the rule 'tadaminādīnī'. Near the Ganges is 'oregaṅgaṃ'; above the peak is 'uparisikharaṃ'. Likewise, 'uparipāsādaṃ' (above the palace), 'uparimañcaṃ' (above the couch), 'uparipabbataṃ' (above the mountain). Against the stream is 'paṭisotaṃ'. Likewise, 'paṭivātaṃ' (against the wind). The far side of the Yamunā is 'pāreyamunaṃ'. The middle of the Ganges is 'majjhegaṅgaṃ'. Below the palace is 'heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ'; below the couch is 'heṭṭhāmañcaṃ'. Above the Ganges is 'uddhaṃgaṅgaṃ'. Below the Ganges is 'adhogaṅgaṃ'. Inside the palace is 'antopāsādaṃ'. Likewise, 'antogāmaṃ' (inside the village), 'antonagaraṃ' (inside the town), 'antovassaṃ' (during the rainy season).

Vāti kiṃ? Gaṅgāoraṃ, majjhesamuddasmiṃ iccādi.

What is the purpose of saying 'optionally'? As in 'Gaṅgāoraṃ' (near the Ganges), 'majjhesamuddasmiṃ' (in the middle of the ocean), and so on.

344. Tiṭṭhagvādīni ka. 319; rū. 330; nī. 697; caṃ. 2.2.10; pā. 2.1.17.

344. Tiṭṭhagu and so forth.

Tiṭṭhaguiccādīni asaṅkhyekatthe sijjhanti.

'Tiṭṭhagu' and so forth are formed in a non-numeral sense.

Tiṭṭhanti gāvo yasmiṃ kāle tiṭṭhagu, vahanti gāvoyasmiṃ kāle vahagu, ‘gossū’ti suttena ossa uttaṃ. Āyatiṃ yavo yasmiṃ kāleti āyatiyavo, khale yavo yasmiṃ kāleti khaleyavaṃ. Pubbapade vibhattialopo. Lunā yavā yasmiṃ kāleti lunayavaṃ, ettha ‘lunā’ti lāvitā, luyamānā yavā yasminti luyamānayavaṃ iccādi.

The time when cows stand is 'tiṭṭhagu'; the time when cows carry is 'vahagu'. By the rule 'gossū', 'o' becomes 'u'. The time when barley is in the future is 'āyatiyavo'; the time when barley is on the threshing floor is 'khaleyavaṃ'. Elision of the case ending occurs in the first word. The time when barley is reaped is 'lunayavaṃ'; here, 'lunā' means 'harvested'. The time when barley is being reaped is 'luyamānayavaṃ', and so on.

Tathā pāto nahānaṃ yasmiṃ kāleti pātanahānaṃ. Evaṃ sāyanahānaṃ, pāto kammakaraṇakālo yasminti [M 0.0223] pātakālaṃ. Evaṃ sāyakālaṃ, pāto vassati megho yasminti pātameghaṃ. Evaṃ sāyameghaṃ, pāto gantabbo maggo yasminti pātamaggaṃ. Evaṃ sāyamaggaṃ iccādi. Mahāvuttinā pātosaddassa pātattaṃ. Ettha ca ‘tiṭṭhagu’ iccādīni viggahatthavasena aññapadatthe siddhāni viya dissanti, aññapadassa pana liṅgādīnaṃ vasena tesaṃ rūpavikāro nāma natthi, tasmā abyayarūpattā idha gahitāni, sabbañcetaṃ asaṅkhyasamāsapadaṃ nāma napuṃsakaṃ eva hoti, rassantameva hoti. Sabbavibhattīnañca akārantamhā bahulaṃ aṃ hoti, ikārukārantehi lopo hoti.

Similarly, the time when bathing is done in the morning is 'pātanahānaṃ'. Likewise, 'sāyanahānaṃ' (evening bathing). The time when work is done in the morning is 'pātakālaṃ'. Likewise, 'sāyakālaṃ' (evening time). The cloud that rains in the morning is 'pātameghaṃ'. Likewise, 'sāyameghaṃ' (evening cloud). The path to be taken in the morning is 'pātamaggaṃ'. Likewise, 'sāyamaggaṃ' (evening path), and so on. According to the Mahāvutti, the word 'pāto' becomes 'pāta'. Here, words like 'tiṭṭhagu' and so forth appear to be established in the sense of another word by way of grammatical analysis, but there is no change in their form according to the gender, etc., of that other word. Therefore, because they are indeclinable in form, they are included here. And all such non-numeral compound words (asaṅkhyasamāsapada) are indeed neuter and end in a short vowel. For all case endings, 'aṃ' frequently occurs after stems ending in 'a'; elision occurs after stems ending in 'i' and 'u'.

Abyayībhāvasamāso niṭṭhito.

The chapter on the Indeclinable Compound is concluded.

Tappurisasamāsa

Tappurisa Compound (Determinative Compounds)

Dutiyātappurisa

The Accusative Tappurisa Compound

Atha amādisamāso vuccate, so tappurisoti ca vuccati. Tassa puriso tappuriso, tappurisasaddena sadisattā ayaṃ samāso tappurisoti vuccati. Yathā hi tappurisasaddo visesanapadatthaṃ jahitvā visesyapadatthe tiṭṭhati, evaṃ ayaṃ samāsopīti.

Now the amādi compound is explained; it is also called a Tappurisa. 'His man' is a 'tappuriso'; because this compound is similar to the word 'tappurisa', it is called 'Tappurisa'. Just as the word 'tappurisa' abandons the meaning of the qualifying word and stands in the meaning of the qualified word, so too does this compound.

345. Amādi ka. 327; rū. 351; nī. 704; caṃ. 2.2.16.

345. Amādi.

Amādivibhattiyuttaṃ syādyantapadaṃ paṭhamantena syādyantapadena saha ekatthaṃ bhavati, ayañca samāso anvatthavasena “amādisamāso”ti ca “tappurisasamāso”ti ca vuccati. Iminā amādisahitassa vākyassa amādekatthasaññaṃ katvā vuttatthānaṃ vibhattīnaṃ lopo, tato ekatthapadante syādyuppatti hoti.

A word ending in a case termination that is associated with a case termination beginning with 'aṃ' combines into a single meaning with a word ending in a case termination in the first case. This compound is called both 'amādisamāsa' and 'tappurisasamāsa' according to its meaning. By this rule, having designated the phrase associated with 'amādi' as having a single meaning, there is elision of the case endings of the expressed meanings, and then a case ending arises at the end of the single-meaning word.

So [M 0.0224] pana samāso dutiyātappuriso, tatiyātappuriso, catutthītappuriso, pañcamītappuriso, chaṭṭhītappuriso, sattamītappurisoti chabbidho. Ekamekasmiñcettha “niccasamāso, aniccasamāso”ti ca “luttasamāso, aluttasamāso”ti ca duvidho.

That compound, moreover, is of six kinds: the Accusative Tappurisa, Instrumental Tappurisa, Dative Tappurisa, Ablative Tappurisa, Genitive Tappurisa, and Locative Tappurisa. And each of these is of two kinds: 'obligatory compound' (niccasamāso) and 'optional compound' (aniccasamāso), as well as 'elided compound' (luttasamāso) and 'unelided compound' (aluttasamāso).

Tattha dutiyātappuriso kattuvācakesu gata, nissita,-atīta, atikkanta, patta, āpannaiccādīsu paresu hoti.

Among these, the Accusative Tappurisa occurs when agentive words such as `gata` (gone), `nissita` (dependent), `atīta` (past), `atikkanta` (surpassed), `patta` (reached), `āpanna` (entered), and so on, follow.

Gāmaṃ gatoti gāmagato gāmaṃ gato vā. Evaṃ araññagato, bhūmigato, rājānaṃ nissitoti rājanissito. Evaṃ atthanissito, dhammanissito. Bhavaṃ atīto bhavātīto. Evaṃ bhayātīto, kālātīto, khaṇātīto, pamāṇaṃ atikkantoti pamāṇātikkanto, sukhaṃ pattoti sukhappatto. Evaṃ dukkhappatto, sotaṃ āpannoti sotāpanno. Evaṃ nirodhasamāpanno, addhānamaggaṃ paṭipannoti addhānamaggappaṭipanno, rukkhaṃ ārūḷhoti rukkhārūḷho, rathārūḷho, oghaṃ tiṇṇoti oghatiṇṇo oghaṃ tiṇṇo vā iccādi.

One who has gone to the village (gāmaṃ gato) is 'gāmagato', or optionally 'gāmaṃ gato'. Likewise, 'araññagato' (forest-gone), 'bhūmigato' (ground-gone). One dependent on the king (rājānaṃ nissito) is 'rājanissito'. Likewise, 'atthanissito' (meaning-dependent), 'dhammanissito' (Dhamma-dependent). One who has passed beyond existence (bhavaṃ atīto) is 'bhavātīto'. Likewise, 'bhayātīto' (fear-beyond), 'kālātīto' (time-beyond), 'khaṇātīto' (moment-beyond). One who has exceeded the measure (pamāṇaṃ atikkanto) is 'pamāṇātikkanto'. One who has attained happiness (sukhaṃ patto) is 'sukhappatto'. Likewise, 'dukkhappatto' (suffering-attained). One who has attained the stream (sotaṃ āpanno) is 'sotāpanno'. Likewise, 'nirodhasamāpanno' (cessation-attained). One who has entered upon the long road (addhānamaggaṃ paṭipanno) is 'addhānamaggappaṭipanno'. One who has climbed a tree (rukkhaṃ ārūḷho) is 'rukkhārūḷho'; 'rathārūḷho' (chariot-climbed). One who has crossed the flood (oghaṃ tiṇṇo) is 'oghatiṇṇo', or optionally 'oghaṃ tiṇṇo', and so on.

Kammupapadavihitehi kitantapadehi pana niccasamāsoyeva, kumbhaṃ karotīti kumbhakāro, rathakāro, pattaṃ gaṇhātīti pattaggāho, atthaṃ kāmetīti atthakāmo, dhammakāmo, vinayaṃ dhāretīti vinayadharo, dhammadharo, brahmaṃ carati sīlenāti brahmacārī, bhavapāraṃ gacchati sīlenāti bhavapāragū, sabbaṃ jānātīti sabbaññū, atthaññū, dhammaññūiccādi.

However, with verbal derivatives formed with an object as the preceding member, the compounding is always obligatory: one who makes a pot (kumbhaṃ karoti) is a 'kumbhakāro' (pot-maker); 'rathakāro' (chariot-maker). One who takes a bowl (pattaṃ gaṇhāti) is a 'pattaggāho' (bowl-taker). One who desires meaning (atthaṃ kāmeti) is an 'atthakāmo' (meaning-desirer); 'dhammakāmo' (Dhamma-desirer). One who bears the discipline (vinayaṃ dhāreti) is a 'vinayadharo' (discipline-bearer); 'dhammadharo' (Dhamma-bearer). One who lives the holy life by virtue (brahmaṃ carati sīlena) is a 'brahmacārī'. One who goes to the far shore of existence by virtue (bhavapāraṃ gacchati sīlena) is a 'bhavapāragū'. One who knows all (sabbaṃ jānāti) is 'sabbaññū' (all-knower); 'atthaññū' (meaning-knower); 'dhammaññū' (Dhamma-knower), and so on.

Bahulādhikārattā ta, tavantu, tāvī, anta, māna, tuna, tvāna, tvā, tuṃ, tavepaccayantesu paresu samāso na hoti, vassaṃ vuttho, odanaṃ bhutto, odanaṃ bhuttavā, odanaṃ bhuttāvī, dhammaṃ suṇanto, dhammaṃ suṇamāno [M 0.0225] dhammaṃ sotuna, dhammaṃ sutvāna, dhammaṃ sutvā, dhammaṃ sotuṃ, dhammaṃ sotave.

Due to the governing rule of 'bahula' (various applicability), compounding does not occur when words ending in the suffixes `ta`, `tavantu`, `tāvī`, `anta`, `māna`, `tuna`, `tvāna`, `tvā`, `tuṃ`, and `tave` follow. For example: `vassaṃ vuttho` (having lived through the rains), `odanaṃ bhutto` (having eaten rice), `odanaṃ bhuttavā` (having eaten rice), `odanaṃ bhuttāvī` (having eaten rice), `dhammaṃ suṇanto` (hearing the Dhamma), `dhammaṃ suṇamāno` (hearing the Dhamma), `dhammaṃ sotuna` (to hear the Dhamma), `dhammaṃ sutvāna` (having heard the Dhamma), `dhammaṃ sutvā` (having heard the Dhamma), `dhammaṃ sotuṃ` (to hear the Dhamma), `dhammaṃ sotave` (to hear the Dhamma).

Iti dutiyātappuriso.

Thus concludes the Accusative Tappurisa.

Tatiyātappurisa

Instrumental Tappurisa Compound

Tatiyātappuriso kammavācakesu kitantesu ca sampanna, sahagatādīsu ca pubba, sadisa, sama, ūnattha, kalaha, nipuṇa,-missaka, sakhilādīsu ca paresu hoti.

The Instrumental Tappurisa Compound occurs with verbal derivatives (kitanta) expressing the object, and with words such as `sampanna` (endowed), `sahagata` (accompanied), and so on, and with words such as `pubba` (before), `sadisa` (similar), `sama` (equal), `ūnattha` (deficient in meaning), `kalaha` (strife), `nipuṇa` (skilled), `missaka` (mixed), `sakhila` (intimate), and so on, when they follow.

Buddhena bhāsito buddhabhāsito. Evaṃ buddhadesito, buddhapaññatto, buddharakkhito, satthārā vaṇṇito satthuvaṇṇito, viññūhi garahito viññugarahito, viññupasattho, issarena kataṃ issarakataṃ, attanā kataṃ sayaṃkataṃ, parehi kataṃ paraṃkataṃ, bindāgamo. Sukehi āhaṭaṃ sukāhaṭaṃ, raññā hato rājahato, rogena pīḷito rogapīḷito, agginā daḍḍho aggidaḍḍho, sappena daṭṭho sappadaṭṭho, sallena viddho sallaviddho, icchāya apakato abhibhūto icchāpakato.

Spoken by the Buddha (Buddhena bhāsito) is 'buddhabhāsito'. Likewise, 'buddhadesito' (Buddha-taught), 'buddhapaññatto' (Buddha-ordained), 'buddharakkhito' (Buddha-protected). Praised by the Teacher (satthārā vaṇṇito) is 'satthuvaṇṇito'. Blamed by the wise (viññūhi garahito) is 'viññugarahito'; 'viññupasattho' (wise-praised). Done by the lord (issarena kataṃ) is 'issarakataṃ'. Done by oneself (attanā kataṃ) is 'sayaṃkataṃ'. Done by others (parehi kataṃ) is 'paraṃkataṃ'. `bindāgamo` (insertion of a nasal). Brought by parrots (Sukehi āhaṭaṃ) is 'sukāhaṭaṃ'. Killed by the king (raññā hato) is 'rājahato'. Afflicted by disease (rogena pīḷito) is 'rogapīḷito'. Burned by fire (agginā daḍḍho) is 'aggidaḍḍho'. Bitten by a snake (sappena daṭṭho) is 'sappadaṭṭho'. Pierced by a dart (sallena viddho) is 'sallaviddho'. Removed or overcome by desire (icchāya apakato abhibhūto) is 'icchāpakato'.

Sīlena sampanno sīlasampanno. Evaṃ sukhasahagataṃ, ñāṇasampayuttaṃ, mittasaṃsaggo, piyasampayogo, piyavippayogo, jātiyā andho jaccandho, guṇahīno, guṇavuḍḍho, catuvaggena saṅghena karaṇīyaṃ kammaṃ catuvaggakaraṇīyaṃ. Evaṃ pañcavaggakaraṇīyaṃ, kākehi peyyā kākapeyyā, nadī.

Endowed with virtue (sīlena sampanno) is 'sīlasampanno'. Likewise, 'sukhasahagataṃ' (accompanied by happiness), 'ñāṇasampayuttaṃ' (conjoined with knowledge), 'mittasaṃsaggo' (association with friends), 'piyasampayogo' (union with the beloved), 'piyavippayogo' (separation from the beloved). Blind from birth (jātiyā andho) is 'jaccandho'. 'guṇahīno' (devoid of virtues), 'guṇavuḍḍho' (grown in virtues). A formal act to be done by a community of four (catuvaggena saṅghena karaṇīyaṃ kammaṃ) is 'catuvaggakaraṇīyaṃ'. Likewise, 'pañcavaggakaraṇīyaṃ' (a formal act for a community of five). A river drinkable by crows (kākehi peyyā nadī) is 'kākapeyyā nadī'.

Ekakkharesu parapadesu niccasamāso, urena gacchatīti urago, pādena pivatīti pādapo iccādi.

When the subsequent words are monosyllabic, the compounding is obligatory: one that goes on its chest (urena gacchati) is an 'urago' (snake); one that drinks with its foot (pādena pivati) is a 'pādapo' (tree), and so on.

Kvaci majjhepadalopo, guḷena saṃsaṭṭho odano guḷodano. Evaṃ khīrodano, assena yutto ratho assaratho. Evaṃ ājaññaratho, maggena sampayuttaṃ cittaṃ maggacittaṃ[M 0.0226], jambuyā paññāto dīpo jambudīpo, ekena adhikā dasa ekādasa iccādi.

Sometimes there is elision of the middle word: rice mixed with molasses (guḷena saṃsaṭṭho odano) becomes 'guḷodano'. Likewise, 'khīrodano' (milk-rice). A chariot yoked with a horse (assena yutto ratho) becomes 'assaratho'. Likewise, 'ājaññaratho' (thoroughbred-chariot). The mind associated with the path (maggena sampayuttaṃ cittaṃ) becomes 'maggacittaṃ'. The island known by the rose-apple tree (jambuyā paññāto dīpo) becomes 'jambudīpo'. Ten increased by one (ekena adhikā dasa) becomes 'ekādasa' (eleven), and so on.

Pubbādīsu – māsena pubbo māsapubbo, mātarā sadiso mātusadiso. Evaṃ mātusamo, pitusamo, ekena ūnā vīsati ekūnavīsati, sīlena vikalo sīlavikalo, asinā kalaho asikalaho, vācāya nipuṇo vācānipuṇo. Evaṃ yāvakālikasammissaṃ, vācāsakhilo, satthārā sadiso satthukappo, puññena attho puññattho, puññena atthiko puññatthiko. Evaṃ seyyatthiko, mahagghatthiko, guṇena adhiko guṇādhiko iccādi.

With `pubba` (before) and so on: a month before (māsena pubbo) becomes 'month-before' (māsapubbo); similar to the mother (mātarā sadiso) becomes 'mother-similar' (mātusadiso). Likewise, 'mother-equal' (mātusamo), 'father-equal' (pitusamo); twenty less one (ekena ūnā vīsati) becomes 'nineteen' (ekūnavīsati); lacking in virtue (sīlena vikalo) becomes 'virtue-lacking' (sīlavikalo); a quarrel with a sword (asinā kalaho) becomes 'sword-quarrel' (asikalaho); skilled in speech (vācāya nipuṇo) becomes 'speech-skilled' (vācānipuṇo). Likewise, 'mixed with what is for a limited time' (yāvakālikasammissaṃ), 'gentle in speech' (vācāsakhilo); similar to the teacher (satthārā sadiso) becomes 'teacher-like' (satthukappo); a need for merit (puññena attho) becomes 'merit-purpose' (puññattho); one needing merit (puññena atthiko) becomes 'merit-needing' (puññatthiko). Likewise, 'needing comfort' (seyyatthiko), 'needing great value' (mahagghatthiko); superior in virtue (guṇena adhiko) becomes 'virtue-superior' (guṇādhiko), and so on.

Bahulādhikārā kvaci samāso na hoti, pharasunā chinnaṃ, kākehi pātabbā, dassanena pahātabbā dhammā, bhāvanāya pahātabbā dhammā iccādi.

Due to the 'bahula' rule (variable application), compounding sometimes does not occur: `pharasunā chinnaṃ` (cut by an axe), `kākehi pātabbā` (to be drunk by crows), `dassanena pahātabbā dhammā` (states to be abandoned by seeing), `bhāvanāya pahātabbā dhammā` (states to be abandoned by development), and so on.

Iti tatiyātappuriso.

Thus concludes the Third Tappurisa Compound.

Catutthītappurisa

Fourth Tappurisa Compound

Catutthītappuriso tadatthe vā attha, hita, deyyādīsu vā paresu hoti.

The Fourth Tappurisa compound is formed with subsequent words such as `attha`, `hita`, `deyya`, and so on, or when it is for the purpose of that first member.

Kathinassa dussaṃ kathinadussaṃ, kathinatthāya ābhaṭaṃ dussanti attho. Evaṃ kathinacīvaraṃ, kathināya dussaṃ, kathināya cīvarantipi yujjati, kathinatthārāyāti attho. Cīvarāya dussaṃ cīvaradussaṃ. Evaṃ cīvaramūlaṃ cīvaramūlyaṃ (rū. nī.), saṅghassa ābhaṭaṃ bhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ, saṅghatthāya vā paṭiyattaṃ bhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ. Evaṃ āgantukabhattaṃ, gamikabhattaṃ, gilānabhattaṃ.

Cloth for the Kathina is `kathinadussaṃ`; the meaning is cloth brought for the purpose of the Kathina. Similarly, `kathinacīvaraṃ` (Kathina robe); `kathināya dussaṃ` (cloth for the Kathina) or `kathināya cīvaraṃ` (robe for the Kathina) are also correct, the meaning being 'for the purpose of the Kathina spreading'. Cloth for a robe is `cīvaradussaṃ`. Similarly, `cīvaramūlaṃ` (price of a robe). Food brought for the Saṅgha is `saṅghabhattaṃ`, or food prepared for the Saṅgha is `saṅghabhattaṃ`. Similarly, `āgantukabhattaṃ` (food for guests), `gamikabhattaṃ` (food for travelers), `gilānabhattaṃ` (food for the sick).

Saṅghassa [M 0.0227] attho saṅghattho, lokassa hito lokahito, buddhassa deyyaṃ buddhadeyyaṃ, buddhassa paṇāmo buddhappaṇāmo. Evaṃ buddhathomanā, buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ, suttassa anulomaṃ suttānulomaṃ. Evaṃ suttānurūpaṃ, suttānukūlaṃ, suttānuguṇaṃ, ṭhānassa arahaṃ ṭhānārahaṃ, rañño arahaṃ rājārahaṃ. Evaṃ rājagghaṃ, rājadeyyaṃ, kattuṃ kāmetīti kattukāmo. Evaṃ gantukāmo, kathetukāmo, daṭṭhukāmo, sotukāmo. Ettha ca tumantassa asaṅkhyattā ‘asaṅkhyehi sabbāsa’nti tato niccaṃ catutthīlopo hoti, samāse kate niccaṃ niggahītalopo ca. “Saṅghassa dātabbaṃ, saṅghassa dātuṃ” iccādīsu samāso na hoti.

Benefit for the Saṅgha is `saṅghattho`; welfare for the world is `lokahito`; what is to be given to the Buddha is `buddhadeyyaṃ`; homage to the Buddha is `buddhappaṇāmo`. Similarly, `buddhathomanā` (praising the Buddha), `buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ` (attending on the Buddha). In accordance with the Sutta is `suttānulomaṃ`. Similarly, `suttānurūpaṃ` (suitable to the Sutta), `suttānukūlaṃ` (agreeable to the Sutta), `suttānuguṇaṃ` (conforming to the Sutta). Worthy of a place is `ṭhānārahaṃ`; worthy of a king is `rājārahaṃ`. Similarly, `rājagghaṃ` (royal price), `rājadeyyaṃ` (a king's gift). One who desires to do is `kattukāmo`. Similarly, `gantukāmo` (desiring to go), `kathetukāmo` (desiring to speak), `daṭṭhukāmo` (desiring to see), `sotukāmo` (desiring to hear). Here, because the `tum`-suffix is an indeclinable, according to the rule ‘asaṅkhyehi sabbāsaṃ’, the elision of its dative case ending is constant; and when a compound is formed, the elision of the niggahīta is also constant. In phrases like ‘‘Saṅghassa dātabbaṃ’’ (to be given to the Saṅgha) and ‘‘Saṅghassa dātuṃ’’ (to give to the Saṅgha), a compound does not occur.

Iti catutthītappuriso.

Thus concludes the Fourth Tappurisa Compound.

Pañcamītappurisa

Fifth Tappurisa Compound

Pañcamītappuriso apagamana, bhaya, virati, mocanādiatthesu paresu hoti.

The Fifth Tappurisa Compound occurs with subsequent words signifying departure, fear, abstinence, liberation, and so forth.

Methunā apetoti methunāpeto, palāsato apagatoti palāsāpagato, nagaramhā niggatoti nagaraniggato, piṇḍapātato paṭikkantoti piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto. Evaṃ gāmanikkhanto, rukkhapatito, sāsanamhā cutoti sāsanacuto, āpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ, udakato uggato udakuggato, bhavato nissaṭo bhavanissaṭo, khandhasaṅgahato nissaṭanti khandhasaṅgahanissaṭaṃ, coramhā bhītoti corabhīto, pāpato bhāyati sīlenāti pāpabhīruko, pāpato jigucchati sīlenāti pāpajigucchī, vaṭṭato nibbindatīti vaṭṭanibbinno, kāyaduccaritato virati kāyaduccaritavirati. Evaṃ vacīduccaritavirati, bandhanā mutto bandhanamutto. Evaṃ bandhanamokkho, kammato samuṭṭhitaṃ kammasamuṭṭhitaṃ[M 0.0228]. Evaṃ kammajātaṃ, kammasambhūtaṃ, kammanibbattaṃ, lokato aggo lokaggo. Evaṃ lokajeṭṭho, lokuttamo, sabbehi jeṭṭho sabbajeṭṭho, sabbehi kaniṭṭho sabbakaniṭṭho. Evaṃ sabbahīno, sabbapacchimo, ukkaṭṭhato ukkaṭṭhoti ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho, omakato omakoti omakomako.

One who is separated from sexual intercourse is `methunāpeto`. One who has departed from a leaf is `palāsāpagato`. One who has gone out from the city is `nagaraniggato`. One who has turned back from almsfood is `piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto`. Similarly, `gāmanikkhanto` (one who has gone out from the village), `rukkhapatito` (one who has fallen from a tree). One who has fallen away from the Dispensation is `sāsanacuto`. Rising up from an offense is `āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ`. One who has emerged from the water is `udakuggato`. One who is released from existence is `bhavanissaṭo`. What is released from the collection of aggregates is `khandhasaṅgahanissaṭaṃ`. One who is afraid of a thief is `corabhīto`. One who, through virtue, fears evil is `pāpabhīruko`. One who, through virtue, is disgusted with evil is `pāpajigucchī`. One who is disenchanted with the round of rebirths is `vaṭṭanibbinno`. Abstinence from bodily misconduct is `kāyaduccaritavirati`. Similarly, `vacīduccaritavirati` (abstinence from verbal misconduct). One who is freed from a bond is `bandhanamutto`. Similarly, `bandhanamokkho` (release from a bond). What arises from kamma is `kammasamuṭṭhitaṃ`. Similarly, `kammajātaṃ` (what is born of kamma), `kammasambhūtaṃ` (what originates from kamma), `kammanibbattaṃ` (what is produced by kamma). The highest in the world is `lokaggo`. Similarly, `lokajeṭṭho` (the eldest in the world), `lokuttamo` (the supreme in the world). The eldest of all is `sabbajeṭṭho`. The youngest of all is `sabbakaniṭṭho`. Similarly, `sabbahīno` (the most inferior of all), `sabbapacchimo` (the last of all). The most excellent of the excellent is `ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho`. The lowest of the low is `omakomako`.

Kvaci niccasamāso hoti, mātito jāto mātujo. Evaṃ pitujo, kammajaṃ, cittajaṃ, utujaṃ iccādi.

Sometimes there is an obligatory compound (`niccasamāso`), as in `mātito jāto` (born of a mother) becoming `mātujo`. Similarly, `pitujo` (born of a father), `kammajaṃ` (born of kamma), `cittajaṃ` (born of mind), `utujaṃ` (born of season), and so forth.

Iti pañcamītappuriso.

Thus concludes the Fifth Tappurisa Compound.

Chaṭṭhītappurisa

Sixth Tappurisa Compound

Rañño putto rājaputto. Evaṃ rājapuriso, buddhasāvako, samuddaghoso, dhaññānaṃ rāsi dhaññarāsi, mattikāya pattoti mattikāpatto, vikārasambandhe chaṭṭhī, mattikāmayapattoti attho. Evaṃ suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ, suvaṇṇabhājanaṃ, pānīyassa thālakaṃ pānīyathālakaṃ.

The king's son is `rājaputto`. Similarly, `rājapuriso` (king's man), `buddhasāvako` (disciple of the Buddha), `samuddaghoso` (ocean's sound). A heap of grain is `dhaññarāsi`. A bowl of clay is `mattikāpatto`; the sixth case expresses the relation of modification, meaning a bowl made of clay. Similarly, `suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ` (golden pot), `suvaṇṇabhājanaṃ` (golden vessel). A dish for drinking water is `pānīyathālakaṃ`.

Samāsamajjhe ī, ūnaṃ bahulaṃ rassattaṃ, daṇḍino kulaṃ daṇḍikulaṃ, hatthipadaṃ, itthirūpaṃ, nadikūlaṃ, naditīraṃ, bhikkhunīnaṃ saṅgho bhikkhunisaṅgho, jambuyā sākhā jambusākhā iccādi.

In the middle of a compound, long `ī` and `ū` are frequently shortened. The family of the staff-bearer is `daṇḍikulaṃ`. `hatthipadaṃ` (an elephant's footprint), `itthirūpaṃ` (a woman's form), `nadikūlaṃ` (a river bank), `naditīraṃ` (a river shore). A community of nuns is `bhikkhunisaṅgho`. The branch of a rose-apple tree is `jambusākhā`, and so forth.

Anta, māna, niddhāraṇiya, pūraṇa, bhāva, suhitatthehi samāso na hoti, mamaṃ anukubbanto, mamaṃ anukurumāno, gunnaṃ kaṇhā sampannakhīratamā. Vibhattāvadhichaṭṭhiyā pana hotiyeva, narānaṃ uttamo naruttamo, naraseṭṭho, naravaro, gaṇānaṃ uttamo gaṇuttamo, dvipadānaṃ uttamo dvipaduttamo iccādi. Sissānaṃ pañcamo sisso, kappassa tatiyo bhāgo, pakkhassa aṭṭhamī, paṭassa sukkatā, rūpassa lahutā, rūpassa [M 0.0229] mudutā, rūpassa kammaññatā. Kvaci hoti, kāyalahutā, cittalahutā, buddhasubuddhatā. Dhammasudhammatā, phalānaṃ suhito, phalānaṃ titto, phalānaṃ asito, karaṇatthe chaṭṭhī.

A compound is not formed with present participles ending in `-anta` and `-māna`; with a genitive of specification (`niddhāraṇiya`); with ordinal numbers (`pūraṇa`); with abstract nouns (`bhāva`); or with words meaning 'sated' (`suhita`). For example: `mamaṃ anukubbanto` (imitating me), `mamaṃ anukurumāno` (imitating me); `gunnaṃ kaṇhā sampannakhīratamā` (the black one among cows, being most abundant in milk). However, with the sixth case specifying the best of a class (`vibhattāvadhichaṭṭhiyā`), it certainly does occur: `narānaṃ uttamo` becomes `naruttamo` (the best of men), `naraseṭṭho` (the chief of men), `naravaro` (the excellent among men); `gaṇānaṃ uttamo` becomes `gaṇuttamo` (the best of groups); `dvipadānaṃ uttamo` becomes `dvipaduttamo` (the best of bipeds), and so forth. [Further examples of non-compounding:] `Sissānaṃ pañcamo sisso` (the fifth of the students), `kappassa tatiyo bhāgo` (the third part of an aeon), `pakkhassa aṭṭhamī` (the eighth day of the fortnight); `paṭassa sukkatā` (the whiteness of the cloth), `rūpassa lahutā` (the lightness of form), `rūpassa mudutā` (the softness of form), `rūpassa kammaññatā` (the workableness of form). Sometimes, however, it does occur: `kāyalahutā` (lightness of body), `cittalahutā` (lightness of mind), `buddhasubuddhatā` (the excellent awakenedness of the Buddha), `dhammasudhammatā` (the excellent nature of the Dhamma). `Phalānaṃ suhito` (sated with fruits), `phalānaṃ titto` (satisfied with fruits), `phalānaṃ asito` (not satisfied with fruits)—here the sixth case has an instrumental sense.

“Bhaṭo rañño putto devadattassā”ti ettha ‘rājaputto’ti na hoti aññamaññānapekkhattā. “Devadattassa kaṇhā dantā”ti ettha ‘devadattakaṇhadantā’ti na hoti aññasāpekkhattā nī. 690. Aññasāpekkhattepi niccaṃ sambandhīpekkhasaddānaṃ samāso hoti vākye viya samāsepi sambandhassa viditattā. Vuttañca “satipi sāpekkhatte gamakattā samāso hotī”ti ka. 328; rū. 352; nī. 691, devadattagurukulaṃ, rājadāsīputto, devadāsīputto iccādi. Tattha devadattassa guru devadattaguru, tassa kulaṃ devadattagurukulanti viggaho. Guruno kulaṃ gurukulaṃ, devadattassa gurukulaṃ devadattagurukulantipi vadanti. “Rañño māgadhassa bimbisārassa putto”ti etthapi aññasāpekkhattā ‘bimbisāraputto’ti na hoti, rañño go ca asso ca puriso cāti atthe ‘rājagavassapurisā’ti hoti dvandato pubbapadassa dvandapadehipi paccekaṃ sambandhassa viditattā. Tathā dvandato parapadassapi, narānañca devānañca sārathi naradevasārathi.

In ‘‘Bhaṭo rañño putto devadattassā’’ (The servant of the king, the son of Devadatta), the compound ‘rājaputto’ (king's son) does not occur due to mutual non-expectancy. In ‘‘Devadattassa kaṇhā dantā’’ (Devadatta's black teeth), the compound ‘devadattakaṇhadantā’ does not occur due to expectancy of another. However, even with expectancy of another, a compound is always formed with words that imply a relationship, because the relationship is understood even in the compound, just as in a sentence. And it is said, ‘‘Satipi sāpekkhatte gamakattā samāso hotī’’ (Even with expectancy, a compound is formed because it conveys the meaning). For example, `devadattagurukulaṃ` (Devadatta's teacher's family), `rājadāsīputto` (the king's slave woman's son), `devadāsīputto` (a god's slave woman's son), and so forth. Here, the analysis is: Devadatta's teacher is `devadattaguru`, his family is `devadattagurukulaṃ`. Some also say that the teacher's family is `gurukulaṃ`, and Devadatta's teacher's family is `devadattagurukulaṃ`. In ‘‘Rañño māgadhassa bimbisārassa putto’’ (The son of King Bimbisāra of Magadha), here too, due to expectancy of another, ‘bimbisāraputto’ does not occur. In the sense of ‘the king's cow and horse and man’, the compound ‘rājagavassapurisā’ is formed, because the connection of the preceding word with each of the words in the dvandva is understood. Similarly, for a word following a dvandva compound: `narānañca devānañca sārathi` becomes `naradevasārathi` (the charioteer of men and gods).

Iti chaṭṭhītappuriso.

Thus concludes the Sixth Tappurisa Compound.

Sattamītappurisa

Seventh Tappurisa Compound

Sattamītappurise rūpe saññā rūpasaññā. Ettha ca kārakānaṃ kriyāsādhanalakkhaṇattā kriyāpadeheva sambandho hoti, tasmā akriyavācakena parapadena saddhiṃ samāse jāte majjhe anurūpaṃ kriyāpadaṃ viññāyati, yathā [M 0.0230] ‘assena yutto ratho assaratho’ iti ‘rūpe saññā’ti rūpe uppannā saññāti attho. Cakkhusmiṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, dhamme rato dhammarato. Evaṃ dhammaruci, dhammagāravo, dāne ajjhāsayo dānajjhāsayo. Evaṃ dānādhimutti, vaṭṭe bhayaṃ vaṭṭabhayaṃ, vaṭṭadukkhaṃ, gāme sūkaro gāmasūkaro, vanamahiṃso, samuddamaccho, itthīsu dhutto itthidhutto, itthisoṇḍo.

In the Seventh Tatpurisa, 'perception in form' is rūpasaññā. Here, since the characteristic of kārakas is the accomplishment of action, the connection is only with verbs. Therefore, when a compound is formed with a non-verbal latter member, an appropriate verb is understood in the middle, as in 'a chariot yoked with a horse is assaratho (horse-chariot).' Thus, 'perception in form' means 'perception arisen in form.' 'Consciousness in the eye' is cakkhuviññāṇa. 'One who delights in the Dhamma' is dhammarato. Similarly, dhammaruci (delight in Dhamma), dhammagāravo (reverence for Dhamma), 'inclination toward giving' is dānajjhāsayo. Likewise, dānādhimutti (resolve for giving), 'fear of the round of existence' is vaṭṭabhaya, 'suffering of the round of existence' is vaṭṭadukkha, 'a pig in the village' is gāmasūkaro, 'a buffalo in the forest' is vanamahiṃso, 'a fish in the ocean' is samuddamaccho, 'a lecher among women' is itthidhutto, 'one fond of women' is itthisoṇḍo.

Upapadakitantesu niccasamāso nī. 682, vane caratīti vanacaro, kāmāvacaro, kucchimhi sayatīti kucchissayo, gabbhe setīti gabbhaseyyo, thale tiṭṭhatīti thalaṭṭho, jalaṭṭho, pabbataṭṭho, paṅke jātaṃ paṅkajaṃ. Evaṃ atrajo, khetrajo iccādi. Idha na hoti nī. 681, bhojane mattaññutā, indriyesu guttadvāro, āsane nisinno, āsane nisīditabbaṃ.

Among those ending in upapada-kṛt suffixes, the compound is obligatory. 'One who wanders in the forest' is vanacaro (forest-dweller); 'one who frequents the realm of desire' is kāmāvacaro; 'one who lies in the belly' is kucchissayo; 'one who sleeps in the womb' is gabbhaseyyo; 'one who stands on land' is thalaṭṭho (land-dweller); jalaṭṭho (water-dweller); pabbataṭṭho (mountain-dweller); 'what is born in mud' is paṅkajaṃ (lotus). Thus, atrajo (born of oneself), khetrajo (born of a field), and so on. Here, this is not the case: bhojane mattaññutā (moderation in food), indriyesu guttadvāro (one whose sense doors are guarded), āsane nisinno (seated on a seat), āsane nisīditabbaṃ (one should sit on a seat).

Iti sattamītappuriso.

Thus ends the Seventh Tatpurisa.

Luttatappurisa

Lutta Tatpurisa

Tappurisapadānaṃ mahāvuttisuttena kvaci vipallāso.

Sometimes there is a transposition of the members of a Tatpurisa compound, according to the Mahāvutti.

Uparigaṅgā, heṭṭhānadī, antovihāro, antosamāpatti, haṃsānaṃ rājā rājahaṃso haṃsarājā vā, māsassa aḍḍhaṃ aḍḍhamāsaṃ, kahāpaṇassa aḍḍhaṃ aḍḍhakahāpaṇaṃ, aḍḍhamāsaṃ, rattiyā aḍḍhaṃ aḍḍharattaṃ. Evaṃ pubbarattaṃ, pararattaṃ, issa attaṃ. Kāyassa pubbabhāgo pubbakāyo, parakāyo, ahassa pubbo pubbaṇho, majjhaṇho, sāyanho, pubbediṭṭho diṭṭhapubbo, tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbo thero, tathāgato diṭṭhapubbo therena iccādi.

Uparigaṅgā (the upper Ganges), heṭṭhānadī (the lower river), antovihāro (the inner monastery), antosamāpatti (the inner attainment). 'The king of swans' (haṃsānaṃ rājā) is rājahaṃso or haṃsarājā. 'Half of the month' (māsassa aḍḍhaṃ) is aḍḍhamāsaṃ. 'Half of a kahāpaṇa' (kahāpaṇassa aḍḍhaṃ) is aḍḍhakahāpaṇaṃ. 'Half of the night' (rattiyā aḍḍhaṃ) is aḍḍharattaṃ. Similarly, pubbarattaṃ (the first part of the night), pararattaṃ (the latter part of the night). 'The front part of the body' (kāyassa pubbabhāgo) is pubbakāyo; parakāyo (the hind part of the body). 'The forepart of the day' (ahassa pubbo) is pubbaṇho (forenoon); majjhaṇho (midday); sāyanho (afternoon). 'Seen before' (pubbe diṭṭho) is diṭṭhapubbo. 'The elder who had seen the Tathāgata before' is tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbo thero. 'The Tathāgata who was seen before by the elder' is tathāgato diṭṭhapubbo therena, and so on.

Iti luttatappuriso.

Thus ends the Lutta Tatpurisa.

Aluttatappurisa

Alutta Tatpurisa

Idāni [M 0.0231] aluttatappurisā vuccante.

Now, the Alutta Tatpurisa compounds are explained.

Dīpaṅkaro, pabhaṅkaro, amatandado, purindado, vessantaro, attantapo, parantapo, raṇañjaho, jutindharo, vijjandharo, dassanenapahātabbadhammo, kutojo, tatojo, itojo, bhayato upaṭṭhānaṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānaṃ, kaṭattākammaṃ, kaṭattārūpaṃ, parassapadaṃ, attanopadaṃ, devānamindo, devānaṃpiyatisso, gavampatitthero, pubbenivāso, majjhekalyāṇaṃ, dūrerūpaṃ, santikerūpaṃ, dūrenidānaṃ, santikenidānaṃ, antevāsiko, janesuto, kāmesumicchācāro iccādi ka. 327; rū. 351; nī. 686.

Dīpaṅkaro, pabhaṅkaro, amatandado (giver of the deathless), purindado (giver of cities), vessantaro, attantapo (one who torments oneself), parantapo (one who torments others), raṇañjaho (abandoner of conflict), jutindharo (bearer of radiance), vijjandharo (bearer of knowledge), dassanenapahātabbadhammo (a state to be abandoned by seeing), kutojo (born from where), tatojo (born from there), itojo (born from here). 'Arising from fear' (bhayato upaṭṭhānaṃ) is bhayatupaṭṭhānaṃ. Kaṭattākammaṃ (deed that has been done), kaṭattārūpaṃ (form that has been produced). Parassapadaṃ (active voice), attanopadaṃ (middle voice). Devānamindo (lord of gods), devānaṃpiyatisso (Tissa, beloved of the gods), gavampatitthero (the elder Gavampati). Pubbenivāso (previous existence), majjhekalyāṇaṃ (beautiful in the middle), dūrerūpaṃ (distant form), santikerūpaṃ (near form), dūrenidānaṃ (distant cause), santikenidānaṃ (near cause). Antevāsiko (a resident pupil), janesuto (heard of among people). Kāmesumicchācāro (misconduct in sensual pleasures), and so on.

Iti aluttatappuriso.

Thus ends the Alutta Tatpurisa.

Sabbo cāyaṃ amāditappuriso abhidheyyavacano parapadaliṅgo ca.

And all these Amādi Tatpurisa compounds are expressive of the meaning of their constituents and take the gender of the latter member.

Amāditappuriso niṭṭhito.

The Amādi Tatpurisa is concluded.

Kammadhārayasamāsa

Kammadhāraya Compound

Atha kammadhārayasaññito paṭhamātappuriso vuccate.

Now, the First Tatpurisa, called Kammadhāraya, is explained.

Kammamiva dvayaṃ dhāretīti kammadhārayo. Yathā kammaṃ kriyañca payojanañca dvayaṃ dhāreti kamme sati tassa dvayassa sambhavato, tathā ayaṃ samāso ekassa atthassa dve nāmāni dhāreti imasmiṃ samāse sati ekatthajotakassa nāmadvayassa sambhavatoti ka. 324; rū. 339; nī. 702.

It is called kammadhāraya because it holds two things like an action (kamma). Just as an action holds two things—the act and the purpose—since the two are possible when there is an action, so too this compound holds two names for one meaning; for when this compound exists, the possibility of two names signifying a single meaning arises.

Api ca kattabbanti kammaṃ, dhāretabbanti dhāriyaṃ, kammañca taṃ dhāriyañcāti kammadhāriyaṃ, yaṃkiñci hitakammaṃ, kammadhāriyasaddasadisattā [M 0.0232] sabbo cāyaṃ samāso kammadhārayoti vuccati issa attaṃ katvā. Yathā hi kammadhāriyasaddo ekassa atthassa dve nāmāni dhāreti, tathā ayaṃ samāsopīti. So eva uttarapadatthapadhānatāsaṅkhātena tappurisalakkhaṇena yuttattā ‘tappuriso’ti ca vuccati. Bhinnapavattinimittānaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ visesanavisesitabbabhāvena ekasmiṃ atthe pavatti tulyādhikaraṇatā nāma, tena tulyādhikaraṇalakkhaṇena yuttattā ‘tulyādhikaraṇasamāso’ti ca vuccati. So eva ca visesanapadavasena guṇavisesadīpanattā ‘visesanasamāso’ti ca vuccati. Tasmiṃ visesanasamāse –

Moreover, kamma is what is to be done, dhāriya is what is to be borne. That which is both kamma and dhāriya is kammadhāriya, any beneficial action. Because this entire compound resembles the word kammadhāriya, it is called kammadhāraya, by changing the 'i' to 'a'. Just as the word kammadhāriya holds two names for one meaning, so too does this compound. And because it is endowed with the characteristic of the Tatpurisa, defined as the prominence of the meaning of the latter word, it is also called 'Tatpurisa.' The application of two words with distinct grounds for their usage to a single meaning, through the relationship of qualifier and qualified, is called tulyādhikaraṇatā (co-referentiality). Because it is endowed with this characteristic of co-referentiality, it is also called tulyādhikaraṇasamāsa (co-referential compound). And because it reveals a particular quality by means of the qualifying word, it is also called visesanasamāsa (qualifying compound). In that qualifying compound–

346. Visesanamekatthena ka. 324; rū. 339; nī. 702; caṃ. 2.2.18; pā. 2.1.57.

346. A qualifier with that which has one meaning.

Visesanabhūtaṃ syādyantapadaṃ ekatthena visesyabhūtena syādyantapadena saddhiṃ ekatthaṃ hoti.

A word ending in a case termination, which is a qualifier, is compounded with a word ending in a case termination, which is the qualified, when they refer to the same thing.

Ettha ca visesīyati dabbaṃ visiṭṭhaṃ karīyati etenāti visesanaṃ. Eko attho yassāti ekatthaṃ, ‘eko’ti samāno, ‘attho’ti abhidheyyattho, nemittakattho, soyeva dvinnaṃ pavattinimittānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena ‘adhikaraṇa’nti ca vuccati. Pavattinimittānañca adhiṭṭhānatte sati padānampi adhiṭṭhānatā siddhā hoti. Iti ekatthanti tulyādhikaraṇaṃ, samānādhikaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti, tena ekatthena. ‘Ekatthaṃ hotī’ti ekatthībhūtaṃ hotīti attho.

Here, 'qualifier' (visesana) is that by which a substance is specified, made distinct. 'Having one meaning' (ekatthaṃ) is that which has one meaning. 'One' (eko) means the same; 'meaning' (attho) refers to the expressed meaning, the ground for application. This same thing, as the basis for two grounds for application, is also called 'substratum' (adhikaraṇa). When it is the basis for the grounds for application, it is established that it is also the basis for the words. Thus, 'having one meaning' (ekatthaṃ) means 'co-referential' (tulyādhikaraṇa); it is said to be 'having the same substratum' (samānādhikaraṇa), by that 'having one meaning.' 'It becomes one thing' (ekatthaṃ hoti) means 'it becomes unified' (ekatthībhūtaṃ hoti).

So ca samāso navavidho visesanapubbapado, visesanuttarapado, visesanobhayapado, upamānuttarapado, sambhāvanāpubbapado, avadhāraṇapubbapado, nanipātapubbapado, kunipātapubbapado, pādipubbapado cāti.

And that compound is of nine kinds: with a prior member as qualifier (visesanapubbapado), with a subsequent member as qualifier (visesanuttarapado), with both members as qualifiers (visesanobhayapado), with a subsequent member as simile (upamānuttarapado), with a prior member as supposition (sambhāvanāpubbapado), with a prior member as determination (avadhāraṇapubbapado), with a prior member as the negative particle na (nanipātapubbapado), with a prior member as the particle ku (kunipātapubbapado), and with a prior member as a preposition (pādipubbapado).

Tattha [M 0.0233] visesanapubbapado yathā? Mahāpuriso, mahānadī, mahabbhayaṃ. Ettha ca “sā senā dissate mahā jā. 2.22.771, bārāṇasirajjaṃ nāma mahā”ti jā. aṭṭha. 1.1.mahāsīlavajātakavaṇṇanā pāḷi dissati. Tasmā samāsepi tiliṅge nipātarūpo mahāsaddo yujjati. Mahā ca so puriso cāti mahāpuriso, mahā ca sā nadī cāti mahānadī, mahā ca taṃ bhayañcāti mahabbhayaṃ, dvittaṃ saṃyoge ca rassattaṃ. Mahāsaddavevacanena mahantasaddenapi vākyaṃ dassetuṃ yujjati, mahanto puriso mahāpuriso, mahantī nadī mahānadī, mahantaṃ bhayaṃ mahabbhayanti. Ca, tasaddehi ca saddhiṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā dassetuṃ yujjati, mahanto ca so puriso cāti mahāpuriso, mahantī ca sā nadī cāti mahānadī, mahantañca taṃ bhayañcāti mahabbhayanti. Mahantasaddo vā mahā hoti, ‘ṭa ntantūna’nti suttena uttarapade pare ntassa sabbassa attaṃ, mahāvuttinā dīgho ca.

Among these, what is an example of a compound with a prior member as qualifier? For example, mahāpuriso (great man), mahānadī (great river), mahabbhayaṃ (great fear). And in this context, the Pāli passage is seen: 'That army appears great (mahā),' 'the kingdom of Bārāṇasī is called great (mahā).' Therefore, in compounds too, the word mahā is appropriate, having the form of an indeclinable in all three genders. 'Great (mahā) and he is a man (puriso)' thus mahāpuriso; 'great (mahā) and she is a river (nadī)' thus mahānadī; 'great (mahā) and that is fear (bhayaṃ)' thus mahabbhayaṃ; doubling and shortening occur in conjunction. It is also appropriate to illustrate the sentence with the synonym mahanta (great) instead of mahā: 'a great (mahanto) man (puriso)' is mahāpuriso; 'a great (mahantī) river (nadī)' is mahānadī; 'a great (mahantaṃ) fear (bhayaṃ)' is mahabbhayaṃ. And, it is fitting to present it fully with the words ca (and) and ta (that): 'great (mahanto) and he (so) is a man (puriso)' thus mahāpuriso; 'great (mahantī) and she (sā) is a river (nadī)' thus mahānadī; 'great (mahantaṃ) and that (taṃ) is fear (bhayaṃ)' thus mahabbhayaṃ. Or, the word mahanta becomes mahā by the rule 'ṭa ntantūna,' where, when a subsequent word follows, the entire 'nta' becomes 'a', and by the Mahāvutti, there is lengthening.

Ettha ca dvīhi casaddehi dvinnaṃ padānaṃ sakatthanānāttaṃ dīpeti. Taṃsaddena sakatthanānāttepi sakatthānaṃ adhikaraṇabhūtassa dabbatthassa ekattaṃ dīpeti. Imasmiṃ byākaraṇe visuṃ rūpavidhānakiccaṃ nāma natthi, taṃtaṃsuttavidhānañca tadanurūpaṃ dassitaviggahavākyañca disvā tassa tassa siddhapadassa atthabyañjanavinicchaye ñāte rūpavidhānakiccaṃ siddhaṃ hoti, santo ca so puriso cāti sappuriso, setahatthī, nīluppalaṃ, lohitacandanaṃ.

Here, the two particles 'ca' indicate the distinctness of the individual meanings of the two words. By the word 'taṃ', even with distinct individual meanings, the unity of the substance, which is the substratum of those meanings, is indicated. In this grammar, there is no separate function called 'word formation'; having seen the rule from each sutta and the corresponding analytical sentence shown, the function of 'word formation' is accomplished when the determination of the meaning and expression of each established word is known. 'A good person (santo) and he (so) is a man (puriso)' thus sappuriso (a good man); setahatthī (a white elephant); nīluppalaṃ (a blue lotus); lohitacandanaṃ (red sandalwood).

Visadisaliṅga, vacanāpi saddā ekatthā honti, vinayo ca so pariyatti cāti vinayapariyatti, vinayo ca so piṭakañcāti vinayapiṭakaṃ, avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo, avijjā ca sā nīvaraṇañcāti avijjānīvaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ itthiratanaṃ, sīlañca taṃ guṇo cāti sīlaguṇo, sīlañca taṃ patiṭṭhā cāti sīlapatiṭṭhā iccādi.

Even words of different gender and number become unified in meaning. 'The discipline (vinayo), and it (so) is the teaching (pariyatti),' thus vinayapariyatti (the discipline-teaching); 'the discipline (vinayo), and it (so) is the basket (piṭakaṃ),' thus vinayapiṭakaṃ (the discipline-basket); 'ignorance (avijjā), and it (sā) is the condition (paccayo),' thus avijjāpaccayo (ignorance-condition); 'ignorance (avijjā), and it (sā) is the hindrance (nīvaraṇaṃ),' thus avijjānīvaraṇaṃ (ignorance-hindrance). Thus, itthiratanaṃ (woman-gem); 'virtue (sīlaṃ), and it (taṃ) is a quality (guṇo),' thus sīlaguṇo (virtue-quality); 'virtue (sīlaṃ), and it (taṃ) is a foundation (patiṭṭhā),' thus sīlapatiṭṭhā (virtue-foundation), and so on.

Tathā [M 0.0234] vīsati ca sā purisā cāti vīsatipurisā, satañca taṃ purisā cāti satapurisā, saṅkhārā ca te paccayo cāti saṅkhārapaccayo, aṅgā ca te janapadañcāti aṅgajanapadaṃ, magadhā ca te raṭṭhañcāti magadharaṭṭhaṃ. Evaṃ kāsiraṭṭhaṃ iccādi.

Similarly, 'twenty (vīsati), and it (sā) is men (purisā),' thus vīsatipurisā (twenty men); 'a hundred (sataṃ), and it (taṃ) is men (purisā),' thus satapurisā (a hundred men); 'formations (saṅkhārā), and they (te) are a condition (paccayo),' thus saṅkhārapaccayo (formation-condition); 'the Aṅgas (aṅgā), and they (te) are a country (janapadaṃ),' thus aṅgajanapadaṃ (the country of Aṅga); 'the Magadhas (magadhā), and they (te) are a kingdom (raṭṭhaṃ),' thus magadharaṭṭhaṃ (the kingdom of Magadha). Thus, kāsiraṭṭhaṃ (the kingdom of Kāsi), and so on.

Idha na hoti rū. 341; nī. 681, puṇṇo mantānīputto, citto gahapati, sakko devarājā, brahmā sahampati iccādi.

This is not the case here: Puṇṇo Mantānīputto (Puṇṇa, son of Mantānī); Citto Gahapati (Citta the householder); Sakko Devarājā (Sakka, king of gods); Brahmā Sahampati (Brahmā Sahampati), and so on.

Kvaci niccasamāso, kaṇhasappo, lohitamālaṃ iccādi.

Sometimes there is an obligatory compound (niccasamāso), for example, kaṇhasappo (black snake), lohitamālaṃ (red garland), and so on.

Visesanuttarapado yathā? Sāriputtatthero, buddhaghosācariyo, ācariyaguttilo vā, mahosadhapaṇḍito, purisuttamo, purisavaro, purisaviseso iccādi.

How is a compound with a subsequent member as qualifier formed? Sāriputtatthero (the Elder Sāriputta), Buddhaghosācariyo (the Teacher Buddhaghosa), or Ācariyaguttilo (the Teacher Guttila), Mahosadhapaṇḍito (Mahosadha the wise), purisuttamo (the supreme person), purisavaro (the excellent person), purisaviseso (the distinguished person), and so on.

Visesanobhayapado yathā? Chinnañca taṃ parūḷhañcāti chinnaparūḷhaṃ, sītañca taṃ uṇhañcāti sītuṇhaṃ, khañjo ca so khujjo cāti khañjakhujjo. Evaṃ andhabadhiro, katañca taṃ akatañcāti katākataṃ, chiddāvachiddaṃ, chinnabhinnaṃ, sittañca taṃ sammaṭṭhañcāti sittasammaṭṭhaṃ, santassa bhāvo saccaṃ, akhemaṭṭhena dukkhañca taṃ aviparītaṭṭhena saccañcāti dukkhasaccaṃ iccādi.

How is a compound with both members as modifiers formed? 'That which is cut and grown over' is chinnaparūḷhaṃ; 'that which is cold and hot' is sītuṇhaṃ; 'he who is lame and hunchbacked' is khañjakhujjo. Similarly, andhabadhiro (blind and deaf); 'that which is done and undone' is katākataṃ; chiddāvachiddaṃ (pierced and unpierced); chinnabhinnaṃ (cut and broken); 'that which is sprinkled and swept' is sittasammaṭṭhaṃ. The state of the peaceful is truth. 'That which is suffering in the sense of being unsafe and truth in the sense of being unalterable' is dukkhasaccaṃ, and so on.

Upamānuttarapado yathā? Sīho viyāti sīho, muni ca so sīho cāti munisīho. Evaṃ munipuṅgavo, buddhanāgo, buddhādicco, raṃsi viyāti raṃsi, saddhammo ca so raṃsi cāti saddhammaraṃsi. Evaṃ vinayasāgaro, samaṇapadumo, samaṇapuṇḍarīko iccādi.

How is a compound with the simile as the latter term formed? 'Like a lion' (sīho viya) is 'a lion' (sīho); 'a sage, and he is a lion,' thus munisīho (sage-lion). Similarly, munipuṅgavo (sage-bull), buddhanāgo (Buddha-elephant), buddhādicco (Buddha-sun). 'Like a ray' (raṃsi viya) is 'a ray' (raṃsi); 'the good Dhamma, and it is a ray,' thus saddhammaraṃsi (good Dhamma-ray). Similarly, vinayasāgaro (Vinaya-ocean), samaṇapadumo (ascetic-lotus), samaṇapuṇḍarīko (ascetic-white-lotus), and so on.

Sambhāvanāpubbapado yathā? Hetu hutvā paccayo hetupaccayo. Evaṃ ārammaṇapaccayo, manussabhūto, devabhūto, dhammo iti saṅkhāto dhammasaṅkhāto, dhammasammato, dhammasaññito[M 0.0235], dhammalakkhito, eva iti saṅkhāto saddo evasaddo. Evaṃ casaddo, vāsaddo, ariyabhūto saṅgho ariyasaṅgho. Evaṃ buddhamuni, paccekamuni iccādi. Ettha ca sambhāvanā nāma sāmaññabhūtassa uttarapadatthassa daḷhaṃ katvā thomanā sarūpavisesadīpanā, na guṇamattadīpanāti adhippāyo. Garū pana “dhammo iti buddhi dhammabuddhi. Evaṃ dhammasaññā, aniccasaññā, dhātusaññā, mātusaññā, pāṇasaññitā, attadiṭṭhi” iccādīnipi ettha āharanti, imāni pana “saraṇaṃ iti gato upagato saraṇaṅgato”ti padaṃ viya itiluttāni paṭhamātappurisapadāni nāma yujjantīti rū. 343; nī. 702.

How is a compound with a conceptual prior term (sambhāvanā) formed? 'A cause, having become, is a condition,' thus hetupaccayo (causal condition). Similarly, ārammaṇapaccayo (object-condition), manussabhūto (one who has become human), devabhūto (one who has become a deva). 'That which is designated as “Dhamma”' is dhammasaṅkhāto; dhammasammato (that which is deemed Dhamma); dhammasaññito (that which is perceived as Dhamma); dhammalakkhito (that which is characterized as Dhamma). The sound designated as 'eva' is evasaddo. Similarly, casaddo (the sound 'ca'), vāsaddo (the sound 'vā'). 'The Sangha, having become noble,' is ariyasaṅgho (Noble Sangha). Similarly, buddhamuni (Buddha-sage), paccekamuni (Paccekabuddha-sage), and so on. Here, sambhāvanā means firmly establishing and praising the general meaning of the latter term, clarifying its specific nature, not merely indicating qualities—this is the intention. However, the teachers also cite here examples such as 'the thought “Dhamma”' is dhammabuddhi (Dhamma-intellect). Similarly, dhammasaññā (perception of Dhamma), aniccasaññā (perception of impermanence), dhātusaññā (perception of elements), mātusaññā (perception of mother), pāṇasaññitā (perception of beings), attadiṭṭhi (view of self), and so on. But these, like the word saraṇaṅgato (one who has gone to refuge), which is formed from 'saraṇaṃ iti gato' (gone as 'refuge'), are appropriately called nominative tatpurisa compounds with an elided 'iti'.

Avadhāraṇapubbapado yathā? Guṇo eva dhanaṃ na maṇisuvaṇṇādīti guṇadhanaṃ. Evaṃ saddhādhanaṃ, sīladhanaṃ, cakkhu eva dvāraṃ na gāmadvārādīti cakkhudvāraṃ. Evaṃ cakkhuvatthu, cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhāyatanaṃ, cakkhudhātu, khandhā eva bhārā khandhabhārā. Ettha ca yadi bharitabbaṭṭhena bhārā nāma siyuṃ, pañcakkhandhā eva bhārā nāma siyuṃ, na sīsabhāra, aṃsabhārādayo. Khandhā hi niccabhārā honti, itare tāvakālikā, khandhamūlikā cāti. Evaṃ atisayatthasambhāvanatthaṃ khandhā eva bhārāti avadhāraṇavākyaṃ payujjati, na sīsabhārādīnaṃ sabbaso bhārabhāvapaṭikkhipanatthanti. Evaṃ sabbattha, avijjā eva malaṃ na kaṃsamalādikanti avijjāmalaṃ, avijjā eva āsavo na madhvāsavādikoti avijjāsavo. Evaṃ taṇhāsallaṃ, paññāsatthaṃ, paññāloko, paññāpajjoto, rāgaggi, dosaggi, mohaggi iccādi. Garū pana “dhanaṃ viyāti dhanaṃ, saddhā eva ariyānaṃ dhanaṃ saddhādhanaṃ, satthaṃ viyāti satthaṃ, paññā eva satthaṃ paññāsattha”nti yojenti, evaṃ sati atisayasambhāvanattho na sijjhati rū. 343; nī. 702.

How is a compound with an emphatic prior term formed? 'Virtue itself is wealth, not gems, gold, and so on,' thus guṇadhanaṃ (virtue-wealth). Similarly, saddhādhanaṃ (faith-wealth), sīladhanaṃ (moral-wealth). 'The eye itself is a door, not a village gate and so on,' thus cakkhudvāraṃ (eye-door). Likewise, cakkhuvatthu (eye-base), cakkhundriyaṃ (eye-faculty), cakkhāyatanaṃ (eye-sphere), cakkhudhātu (eye-element). 'The aggregates themselves are burdens,' thus khandhabhārā (aggregate-burdens). Here, if 'burdens' were so named by reason of being borne, then only the five aggregates would be called burdens, not head-burdens, shoulder-burdens, and the like. For the aggregates are constant burdens, while others are temporary and rooted in the aggregates. Thus, to emphasize the extreme nature and possibility, the emphatic statement 'the aggregates themselves are burdens' is used, not to entirely deny the burden-nature of head-burdens and the like. Similarly in all cases: 'ignorance itself is a stain, not a bronze stain and so on,' thus avijjāmalaṃ (ignorance-stain); 'ignorance itself is a taint, not a liquor taint and so on,' thus avijjāsavo (ignorance-taint). Likewise, taṇhāsallaṃ (craving-dart), paññāsatthaṃ (wisdom-sword), paññāloko (wisdom-light), paññāpajjoto (wisdom-lamp), rāgaggi (lust-fire), dosaggi (hatred-fire), mohaggi (delusion-fire), and so on. However, the teachers explain: '“Wealth” (dhanaṃ) is like wealth (dhanaṃ viya); faith itself is the noble ones’ wealth, thus saddhādhanaṃ (faith-wealth). “Sword” (satthaṃ) is like a sword (satthaṃ viya); wisdom itself is the sword, thus paññāsatthaṃ (wisdom-sword).' If this is the case, the sense of extreme possibility is not established.

347. Nanipātapubbapade nau ka. 326; rū. 341; nī. 707.

347. Regarding a compound with the particle 'na' as the prior term: nau.

Ñānubandho [M 0.0236] paṭisedhamhā aññanakāra nivattanattho, nauiccetaṃ syādyantaṃ aññena syādyantena saha ekatthaṃ hoti. Iminā nañe katthasaññaṃ katvā –

The indicatory `ñ` [in `nañ`] has the purpose of preventing the non-occurrence of meanings other than simple negation. This particle `nau` (i.e., `na`) forms a single meaning with another word ending in a case suffix. By means of this `nañ`, having established a designation of place—

348. Ṭa naussa ka. 333; rū. 344; nī. 717; caṃ. 2.2.20; pā. 2.2.6; “nau” (bahūsu).

348. `A` for `nau`.

Uttarapade pare nauiccetassa ṭānubandho a hotīti nassa attaṃ.

When a latter term follows, `nau`, which has the indicatory letter `ṭ`, becomes `a`; thus, `na` becomes `a`.

Na brāhmaṇo abrāhmaṇo. Ettha siyā – kiṃ vijjamānassa vāyaṃ nisedho, udāhu avijjamānassa vāti, kiñcettha – yadi vijjamānassa nisedho, evaṃ sati loke vijjamānā sabbe brāhmaṇā abrāhmaṇā nāma bhaveyyuṃ. Tasmā “idha jano na brāhmaṇo, tattha jano na brāhmaṇo”tiādinā desādiniyamaṃ vinā loke vijjamānassa brāhmaṇassa nisedho na yujjati, atha loke avijjamānassa nisedho, evañca sati kiṃ avijjamānassa nisedhena nisedhanīyasseva avijjamānattāti? Vuccate – taṃsadisādiatthesu tabbohārassevāyaṃ nisedho. Tathā hi brāhmaṇasadise abrāhmaṇe kesañci brāhmaṇasaññā saṇṭhāti, saññānurūpañca brāhmaṇavohāro tasmiṃ pavattati, evaṃ pavattassa abrāhmaṇe brāhmaṇavohārassa ayaṃ paṭisedho hoti. Yathā taṃ? Lokasmiṃ bālajanānaṃ micchāsaññāvasena micchāvohāro pavattatiyeva “rūpaṃ attā, vedanā attā” iccādi, tesaṃ tassa micchābhāvakhyāpanatthaṃ paṭisedho yojiyati “rūpaṃ anattā, vedanā anattā” mahāva. 20 iccādi. Ettāvatā suddhabrāhmaṇasaddassapi micchāvasena taṃsadise atthe pavattisambhavo siddho hoti, nakārassa [M 0.0237] ca tadatthajotakamattatā siddhā hoti, evañca sati uttarapadatthapadhānatāsaṅkhātaṃ tappurisalakkhaṇampi idha na virujjhati, tasmā abrāhmaṇoti brāhmaṇasadisoti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo tadañña, tabbiruddha, tadabhāvatthādīsu.

'Not a brahmin' is abrāhmaṇo. Here it might be asked: Is this a negation of what exists, or of what does not exist? And what is the point here? If it is a negation of what exists, then all existing brahmins in the world would be called abrāhmaṇā (non-brahmins). Therefore, a negation of an existing brahmin in the world, without a specific designation of place and so on, such as 'Here, a person is not a brahmin; there a person is not a brahmin,' is not appropriate. But if it is a negation of what does not exist in the world, then what is the point of negating what does not exist, since what is to be negated does not exist anyway? It is said: This negation applies to the usage of that term in meanings such as 'similar to that'. For instance, in the case of a non-brahmin resembling a brahmin, some people form the perception of 'brahmin,' and the usage of 'brahmin' occurs in accordance with that perception; this is a negation of such usage of 'brahmin' when applied to a non-brahmin. How so? In the world, foolish people, due to wrong perception, engage in wrong usage, such as saying, 'Form is self, feeling is self,' and so on. To declare the wrongness of that, a negation is applied, saying, 'Form is not-self, feeling is not-self,' and so on. To that extent, the possibility is established that even the term for a true brahmin can be misused and applied to something similar. The particle 'na' is also established as merely indicating that meaning. Thus, the characteristic of a tatpurisa compound, known as the prominence of the meaning of the latter word, is not violated here. Therefore, abrāhmaṇa is said to mean 'similar to a brahmin.' The same principle applies to cases of 'other than that,' 'opposed to that,' 'absence of that,' and so on.

Tattha tadaññatthe –

There, in the sense of 'other than that'—

Saṅkhatā dhammā asaṅkhatā dhammā dha. sa. dukamātikā 8. Ettha ca na saṅkhatā asaṅkhatā, saṅkhatadhammehi aññe dhammāti attho.

Conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena. Here, asaṅkhatā means not 'not conditioned,' but 'phenomena other than conditioned phenomena'.

Tabbiruddhe –

In the sense of 'opposed to that'—

Akusalo, kusalapaṭipakkho dhammoti attho.

Akusalo (unwholesome): the meaning is 'a phenomenon opposed to the wholesome'.

Tadabhāve –

In the sense of 'absence of that'—

Na katvā akatvā, karaṇena sabbaso vināti attho.

'Not having done' is akatvā; the meaning is 'entirely without doing'.

Duvidho paṭisedho pasajjapaṭisedho, payirudāsapaṭisedho cāti.

Negation is of two kinds: direct negation (pasajjapaṭisedho) and implicative negation (payirudāsapaṭisedho).

Tattha attanā yuttapadatthaṃ pasajja laggetvā paṭisedhetīti pasajjapaṭisedho, tadabhāvamattajotako nakāro, kriyāmattanisedhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Akatvā, akātuṃ, akaronto, na karoti, na kātabbaṃ iccādi.

Herein, a pasajjapaṭisedha is a negation made by directly applying it to the meaning of the word with which it is connected. The particle na merely indicates the absence of that, and it is said to be a negation of mere action. For example: akatvā (not having done), akātuṃ (not to do), akaronto (not doing), na karoti (does not do), na kātabbaṃ (should not be done), and so on.

Pasajjamatte aṭṭhatvā taṃsadisādike paritobhāge uggayha nisedhetabbaṃ atthaṃ asati khipati chaḍḍetīti payirudāso, taṃsadisādijotako, dabbanisedhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Abrāhmaṇo iccādi. Evaṃ asamaṇo, asakyaputtiyo, amitto, mittadhammavidhuroti attho.

Not being limited to a mere direct negation, but having grasped the surrounding parts, such as 'similar to that,' it discards or throws away the meaning to be negated when it is absent—this is a payirudāsa. It indicates 'similar to that' and so on, and is said to be a negation of substance. For example: abrāhmaṇo (non-brahmin), and so on. Similarly, asamaṇo (non-ascetic), asakyaputtiyo (non-Sakyan son), amitto (non-friend); the meaning is 'one devoid of the qualities of a friend'.

349. Ana sare ka. 334; rū. 345; nī. 718; caṃ. 5.2.119; pā. 6.3.105.

349. The particle 'an' [occurs] before a vowel.

Sare pare nauiccetassa ana hoti.

When a vowel follows, the particle na becomes ana.

Na [M 0.0238] ariyo anariyo, ariyadhammavimukhoti attho. Na āvāso anāvāso, na issaro anissaro. Na īti anīti, ‘ītī’ti upaddavo, na yutto upāyo anupāyo, na ūmi anūmi, na yuttā esanā anesanā, na yutto okāso anokāso, na atikkamma anatikkamma, anādāya, anoloketvā iccādi.

'Not noble' is anariyo; the meaning is 'turned away from the noble Dhamma'. 'Not a dwelling' is anāvāso. 'Not a lord' is anissaro. 'Not calamity' is anīti; 'īti' means 'disaster'. 'Not a proper means' is anupāyo. 'Not a wave' is anūmi. 'Not proper seeking' is anesanā. 'Not a proper opportunity' is anokāso. 'Not transgressing' is anatikkamma; anādāya (without taking); anoloketvā (without regarding), and so on.

Bahulādhikārā ayuttatthānampi samāso hoti ka. 336; rū. 347; nī. 689, puna na gāyitabbāti apunageyyā, gāthā, candaṃ na ullokentīti acandamullokikāni, mukhāni, sūriyaṃ na passantīti asūriyapassā, rājakaññā, saddhaṃ na bhuñjati sīlenāti asaddhabhojī. Evaṃ alavaṇabhojī, atthaṃ na kāmentīti anatthakāmā. Evaṃ ahitakāmā, okāsaṃ na kāresīti anokāsaṃkāretvā. Evaṃ animittaṃkatvā, mūlamūlaṃ na gacchatīti amūlamūlaṃgantvā iccādi.

By the authority of 'frequent usage,' compounds are formed even in inappropriate contexts. 'That which should not be sung again' is apunageyyā (a verse). 'Faces that do not look up at the moon' are acandamullokikāni (faces). 'Royal maidens who do not see the sun' are asūriyapassā (royal maidens). 'One who does not partake of faith with virtue' is asaddhabhojī. Similarly, alavaṇabhojī (one who does not eat salt). 'Those who do not desire benefit' are anatthakāmā. Similarly, ahitakāmā (those who do not desire welfare). 'Without having made an opportunity' is anokāsaṃkāretvā. Similarly, animittaṃkatvā (without having made a sign). 'Without having gone to the very root' is amūlamūlaṃgantvā, and so on.

“Puna gāyitabbāti punageyyā, na punageyyā apunageyyā. Atthaṃ kāmentīti atthakāmā, na atthakāmā anatthakāmā. Atha vā na attho anattho, anatthaṃ kāmentīti anatthakāmā” iccādinā vākye yojite pana yuttasamāsā honti. Garū pana “atthaṃ na kāmenti anatthameva kāmentīti anatthakāmā, hitaṃ na kāmenti ahitameva kāmentīti ahitakāmā, phāsuṃ na kāmenti aphāsumeva kāmentīti aphāsukāmā”ti yojesuṃ, dvādhippāyapadaṃ nāmetaṃ.

“‘That which should be sung again’ is punageyyā; ‘not punageyyā’ is apunageyyā. ‘Those who desire benefit’ are atthakāmā; ‘not atthakāmā’ are anatthakāmā. Or, ‘not benefit’ is anattho; ‘those who desire anattha’ are anatthakāmā.” When connected in a sentence in this way, however, they become suitable compounds. But the teachers explained: “Those who do not desire benefit but desire only detriment are anatthakāmā. Those who do not desire well-being but desire only harm are ahitakāmā. Those who do not desire ease but desire only discomfort are aphāsukāmā.” This is called a word with two interpretations.

Kunipātapubbapade niccasamāsattā aññapadena viggaho, khuddakā nadī kunnadī, khuddako sombho kusombho, khuddakaṃ vanaṃ kubbanaṃ.

In a compound with the particle ku as the first member, due to its being a permanent compound, the analysis is with another word. 'A small river' is kunnadī. 'A small pool' is kusombho. 'A small forest' is kubbanaṃ.

350. Sare kada kussuttaratthe ka. 335; rū. 346; nī. 719.

350. Before a vowel, ku becomes kad when it has the sense of the latter term.

Sarādike [M 0.0239] uttarapade pare uttarapadatthe vattamānassa kunipātassa kadi hoti.

When a latter term beginning with a vowel follows, the particle ku, when it has the sense of the latter term, becomes kad.

Kucchitaṃ annaṃ kadannaṃ, kucchitaṃ asanaṃ kadasanaṃ, kucchito ariyo kadariyo, maccharī.

'Contemptible food' is kadannaṃ. 'Contemptible eating' is kadasanaṃ. 'A contemptible noble one' is kadariyo, meaning a miser.

Sareti kiṃ? Kuputtā, kudārā, kudāsā.

Why [is it specified] 'before a vowel'? [To exclude cases such as:] kuputtā (a bad son), kudārā (a bad wife), kudāsā (a bad servant).

Uttarattheti kiṃ? Kucchito oṭṭho yassāti kuoṭṭho.

Why [is it specified] 'in the sense of the latter term'? [To exclude cases such as:] 'one whose lip is contemptible' is kuoṭṭho.

351. Kāppatthe ka. 336; rū. 347; nī. 720.

351. In the sense of 'little'.

Uttarapade pare uttarapadatthe ṭhitassa appatthe vattamānassa kunipātassa kā hoti vā.

When a latter term follows, the particle ku, which has the sense of the latter term and means 'little', optionally becomes kā.

Appakaṃ lavaṇaṃ kālavaṇaṃ. Evaṃ kāpupphaṃ.

'A little salt' is kālavaṇaṃ. Similarly, kāpupphaṃ.

Pādipubbapado ca niccasamāsova, pakaṭṭhaṃ vacanaṃ pāvacanaṃ, dīghattaṃ, pakaṭṭhaṃ hutvā nītaṃ paṇītaṃ, pamukhaṃ hutvā dhānaṃ padhānaṃ. Evaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ, vividhā mati vimati, adhiko devo adhidevo, atireko viseso vā dhammo abhidhammo, sundaro gandho sugandho, kucchito gandho duggandho. Sobhaṇaṃ kataṃ sukataṃ, kucchitaṃ kataṃ dukkaṭaṃ, viparīto patho uppatho. Evaṃ ummaggo, uddhammo, ubbinayoiccādi.

A compound with pā and other prefixes as its first member is also a permanent compound. For example: pakaṭṭhaṃ vacanaṃ (excellent speech) is pāvacanaṃ, with lengthening of the vowel. Pakaṭṭhaṃ hutvā nītaṃ (brought to excellence) is paṇītaṃ. Pamukhaṃ hutvā dhānaṃ (being foremost, a support) is padhānaṃ. Similarly: paṭṭhānaṃ (foundation). Vividhā mati (diverse thought) is vimati (doubt). Adhiko devo (superior deity) is adhidevo. Atireko viseso vā dhammo (a surpassing or special doctrine) is abhidhammo. Sundaro gandho (a beautiful scent) is sugandho. Kucchito gandho (a foul scent) is duggandho. Sobhaṇaṃ kataṃ (well done) is sukataṃ. Kucchitaṃ kataṃ (badly done) is dukkaṭaṃ. Viparīto patho (a wrong path) is uppatho. Similarly: ummaggo (wrong path; tunnel), uddhammo (false Dhamma), ubbinayo (wrong Vinaya), and so on.

Ayampi kammadhārayasamāso abhidheyyavacano parapadaliṅgo ca.

This Appositional Compound also has its meaning determined by its members and takes the gender of the final word.

Kammadhārayasamāso niṭṭhito.

The Appositional Compound is concluded.

Digusamāsa

The Numerical Compound

Atha [M 0.0240] digusaṅkhāto paṭhamātappuriso vuccate.

Now, the first Tappurisa compound, known as the Digu or Numerical Compound, is explained.

Dve gāvo digu, saṅkhyāpubbattena napuṃsakekattena ca digusaddasadisattā sabbo cāyaṃ samāso digūti vuccati.

'Two cows' is digu. Because this type of compound is preceded by a numeral, is singular and neuter, and thus resembles the word digu, this entire class of compound is called digu.

352. Saṅkhyādi ka. 321; rū. 349; nī. 699.

352. Beginning with a numeral.

Samāhārekatthe saṅkhyāpubbakaṃ ekatthaṃ napuṃsakaṃ hoti, samāhāravacaneneva ekattañca siddhaṃ.

In the sense of a collective unity, a compound preceded by a numeral becomes a single neuter noun; and the singularity is established by the very term 'collection'.

Dve gāvo digu, ‘gossū’ti suttena ossa uttaṃ, tayo lokā tilokaṃ, tayo lokā ñāṇasmiṃ samāhaṭā sampiṇḍitāti tilokaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ lokānaṃ samāhāroti tilokaṃ, tayo ca te lokā cāti tilokaṃ. Evaṃ tibhavaṃ, tipurisaṃ, tīṇi malāni timalaṃ, tiratanaṃ, tisso saññāyotisaññaṃ, ‘syādīsu rasso’ti rassattaṃ. Cattāro pathā catuppathaṃ, cattāri saccāni catusaccaṃ, catasso disā catuddisaṃ. Evaṃ pañcasikkhāpadaṃ, saḷāyatanaṃ, sattāhaṃ, aṭṭhapadaṃ, navalokuttaraṃ, dasasikkhāpadaṃ, satayojanaṃ, sahassayojanaṃ iccādi.

'Two cows' is digu; by the rule gossu, the o of go becomes u. 'Three worlds' is tilokaṃ. 'The three worlds gathered and condensed in knowledge' is tilokaṃ. 'The collection of the three worlds' is tilokaṃ. 'And those three are worlds' is tilokaṃ. Similarly: tibhavaṃ (the three existences), tipurisaṃ (three persons), 'tīṇi malāni' (three defilements) is timalaṃ, tiratanaṃ (the three jewels), 'tisso saññāyo' (three perceptions) is tisaññaṃ; by the rule syādīsu rasso, there is shortening. 'Four paths' is catuppathaṃ. 'Four truths' is catusaccaṃ. 'Four directions' is catuddisaṃ. Similarly: pañcasikkhāpadaṃ (the five precepts), saḷāyatanaṃ (the six sense bases), sattāhaṃ (a week), aṭṭhapadaṃ (the eight-fold path), navalokuttaraṃ (the nine supramundane states), dasasikkhāpadaṃ (the ten precepts), satayojanaṃ (a hundred yojanas), sahassayojanaṃ (a thousand yojanas), and so on.

Imasmiṃ samāhāradigumhi sabbaṃ napuṃsakameva rassantameva ekavacanantameva cāti.

In this collective Numerical Compound, every instance is neuter, ends in a short vowel, and is in the singular number.

Asamāhāradigu rū. 350 nī. 703 yathā? Eko puggalo ekapuggalo, tayo bhavā tibhavā, catasso disā catuddisā iccādi.

How is a non-collective Numerical Compound formed? For example: eko puggalo (one person) is ekapuggalo; tayo bhavā (the three existences) are tibhavā; catasso disā (the four directions) are catuddisā, and so on.

Saṅkhyāṭhāne pana ka. 392; rū. 418; nī. 831 dve satāni dvisataṃ. Evaṃ tisataṃ, catusataṃ, pañcasataṃ, chasataṃ, sattasataṃ, aṭṭhasataṃ, navasataṃ, dasasataṃ, dvisahassaṃ, tisahassaṃ, catusahassaṃ, pañcasahassaṃ, dasasahassaṃ.

However, in the case of numerals as the final member: dve satāni (two hundred) is dvisataṃ. Similarly: tisataṃ (three hundred), catusataṃ (four hundred), pañcasataṃ (five hundred), chasataṃ (six hundred), sattasataṃ (seven hundred), aṭṭhasataṃ (eight hundred), navasataṃ (nine hundred), dasasataṃ (ten hundred), dvisahassaṃ (two thousand), tisahassaṃ (three thousand), catusahassaṃ (four thousand), pañcasahassaṃ (five thousand), dasasahassaṃ (ten thousand).

Dve [M 0.0241] satasahassāni dvisatasahassaṃ. Evaṃ “tisatasahassaṃ, catusatasahassaṃ, pañcasatasahassa”nti vā “dvisatāni, dve satāni, tisatāni, tīṇi satāni, catusatāni, cattāri satāni, dvisahassāni, dve sahassāni, tisahassāni, tīṇi sahassāni, dvisatasahassāni, dve satasahassānī”ti vā evaṃ vacanadvayañca vākyañca veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ satasahassepīti.

Dve satasahassāni (two hundred thousand) is dvisatasahassaṃ. Similarly, tisatasahassaṃ (three hundred thousand), catusatasahassaṃ (four hundred thousand), pañcasatasahassaṃ (five hundred thousand). Or, dvisatāni or dve satāni (two hundred); tisatāni or tīṇi satāni (three hundred); catusatāni or cattāri satāni (four hundred); dvisahassāni or dve sahassāni (two thousand); tisahassāni or tīṇi sahassāni (three thousand); dvisatasahassāni or dve satasahassāni (two hundred thousand)—in this way, both the dual expressions and the phrasal constructions should be understood. This applies similarly in the case of a hundred thousand.

Ettha siyā – digu nāma saṅkhyāpubbameva siyā, imesu ca sabbaṃ saṅkhyāpadameva hotīti? Digumhi pubbaṃ saṅkhyāpadameva siyā, parapadaṃ pana saṅkhyāpadampi aññampi yujjatīti.

Here a question might arise: 'Is a Digu compound by definition one that must have a numeral as its first member, and in these examples, is every member a numeral?' The answer is: In a Digu compound, the first member must indeed be a numeral, but the final member may suitably be either a numeral or another word.

Digusamāso niṭṭhito.

The Numerical Compound is concluded.

Bahubbīhisamāsa

The Possessive Compound

Atha bahubbīhisamāso vuccate.

Now the Possessive Compound (Bahubbīhi) is explained.

Bahavo vīhayo yasmiṃ dese soyaṃ bahubbīhi, tādiso gāmo vā deso vā janapado vā, bahubbīhisaddasadisattā sabbo cāyaṃ samāso bahubbīhīti vuccati. Yathā hi bahubbīhisaddo samāsapadatthe atikkamma gāma, desa, janapadaiccādīnaṃ aññesaṃ padānaṃ atthesu tiṭṭhati, tathā ayaṃ samāsopi. Aññapadatthapadhāno hi bahubbīhisamāso.

Much rice is in that place; it is 'bahubbīhi' (having much rice). Such a village, region, or country, because of its similarity to the word 'bahubbīhi', this entire compound is called 'bahubbīhi'. For just as the word 'bahubbīhi' transcends the meaning of its constituent words and stands for the meaning of other words such as village, region, country, and so on, so too does this compound. Indeed, the Bahubbīhi compound has the meaning of another word as its principal element.

So saṅkhepena duvidho tagguṇasaṃviññāṇo, atagguṇasaṃviññāṇo cāti.

Briefly, it is of two kinds: that which implies its own qualities (tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa), and that which does not imply its own qualities (atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa).

Tattha ‘guṇo’ti appadhānabhūto samāsapadānaṃ attho, so aññapadatthassa visesanabhūtattā tassa aññapadatthassa guṇoti [M 0.0242] atthena tagguṇoti vuccati, viññātabboti viññāṇo, aññapadattho, tagguṇaṃ amuñcitvā tagguṇena saheva viññāṇo aññapadattho yasminti tagguṇasaṃviññāṇo, na tagguṇasaṃviññāṇo atagguṇasaṃviññāṇo, yattha samāsapadattho avayavabhāvena vā sahavidheyyabhāvena vā aññapadatthe antogadho hoti, so tagguṇasaṃviññāṇo. Yathā? Chinnahattho puriso, buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa bhattaṃ deti, saputtadāro āgato, pādayo upasaggā nāmāti.

Herein, 'guṇa' means the non-principal meaning of the compound's constituent words. Since it serves as a qualifier to the meaning of another word, it is called 'tagguṇa' in the sense that it is a quality of that other word. 'Viññāṇa' means 'that which is to be understood', which is the meaning of the other word. That compound wherein the meaning of the other word is understood together with its quality, without abandoning it, is 'tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa'. That which is not 'tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa' is 'atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa'. Where the meaning of the compound's constituent words is included in the meaning of another word, either as a component part or as something predicated together, that is 'tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa'. For example: 'chinnahattho puriso' (a man with a severed hand); 'buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa bhattaṃ deti' (he gives food to the community of monks headed by the Buddha); 'saputtadāro āgato' (he has come with his son and wife); 'pādayo upasaggā nāmā' (the prefixes beginning with pa- are called upasaggas).

Ettha ca ‘buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa bhattaṃ detī’ti bhikkhusaṅghassa ca bhattaṃ deti, pamukhabhūtassa buddhassa ca bhattaṃ detīti attho. ‘Saputtadāro āgato’ti puttadārā ca āgatā, puriso ca āgatoti attho. ‘Pādayo upasaggā nāmā’ti pa-kāro ca upasaggo nāma, parādayo ca upasaggā nāmāti attho. Evaṃ yojanārahatā aññapadatthena saha samāsapadatthassa vidheyyatā nāmāti.

Herein, the phrase 'buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa bhattaṃ deti' means that food is given to the community of monks and also food is given to the Buddha, who is foremost. The phrase 'saputtadāro āgato' means that the son and wife came, and the man also came. The phrase 'pādayo upasaggā nāmā' means that the prefix pa- is called an upasagga, and the prefixes beginning with parā are also called upasaggas. Thus, the predicability of the meaning of the compound's constituent words together with the meaning of the other word, being suitable for such an analysis, is so called.

Atagguṇasaṃviññāṇo yathā? Dinnasuṅko rājā dānaṃ deti, pabbatādīni khettāni kassati iccādi. Imesu pana samāsapadattho avidheyyo, aññapadattho eva vidheyyo.

An example of atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa is as follows: 'dinnasuṅko rājā dānaṃ deti' (a king to whom taxes have been given gives a gift); 'pabbatādīni khettāni kassati' (he cultivates fields on mountains, etc.).
