In these, however, the meaning of the compound's constituent words is not the predicate; only the meaning of the other word is the predicate.

Paṭhamābahubbīhi

The First Bahubbīhi Compound

Paṭhamābahubbīhi, dutiyābahubbīhi, tatiyābahubbīhi, catutthībahubbīhi, pañcamībahubbīhi, chaṭṭhībahubbīhi, sattamībahubbīhi cāti sattavidho.

First Bahubbīhi, Second Bahubbīhi, Third Bahubbīhi, Fourth Bahubbīhi, Fifth Bahubbīhi, Sixth Bahubbīhi, and Seventh Bahubbīhi—thus it is sevenfold.

Tattha paṭhamābahubbīhi sahapubbapada, upamānapubbapada, saṅkhyobhayapada, disantarāḷattha, byatihāralakkhaṇavasena pañcavidho.

Therein, the First Bahubbīhi compound is fivefold, by way of: having 'saha' as the prior member, having a simile as the prior member, having both members as numbers, having the sense of the space between directions, and being characterized by reciprocity.

Tattha –

Therein:

353. Vānekamaññatthe ka. 328; rū. 352; nī. 708.

353. Optionally, many in the sense of another.

Anekaṃ [M 0.0243] syādyantapadaṃ aññapadassa atthe vikappena ekatthaṃ hoti.

Many words with case endings optionally become one in meaning in the sense of another word.

Saha vitakkenāti savitakko, vitakkena saha yo vattatīti vā savitakko, samādhi.

‘Saha vitakkena’ becomes ‘savitakko’; or, that which occurs together with initial application is ‘savitakko,’ for example, concentration.

Ettha ca ‘saha vitakkenā’ti ettha paṭhamāvibhattiyā atthabhūto aññapadattho vākyasāmatthiyena sijjhati. Na hi kriyākārakarahitaṃ vākyaṃ nāma sambhavati, iminā suttena sahapada, vitakkapadānaṃ samādhisaṅkhātena aññapadatthena ekatthībhāvo hoti, ekatthībhāve ca honte vākye ṭhitānaṃ aññapadānaṃ vibhattīnañca sabbe atthā ekatthabhūtena samāsena vuttā nāma honti, aññapadāni ca vibhattiyo ca vuttatthā nāma, vuttatthānañca attharahitattā payogakiccaṃ natthi, tasmā ‘ekatthatāya’nti suttena vibhattīnaṃ lopo, evaṃ sabbasamāsesu vākyedissamānānaṃ ya, ta, eta, ima, iti, eva, iva, viya, ca, vāiccādīnaṃ aññapadānaṃ mahāvuttisuttena lopo, vibhattīnañca lope sati sarantānaṃ byañjanantānañca samāsapadānaṃ sayameva pakatibhāvo, idha pana ‘sahassa soññatthe’ti suttena sahasaddassa sattaṃ, tato syādyuppatti, savitakko samādhi, savitakkā samādhayo, savitakkā paññā, savitakkā paññāyo, savitakkaṃ jhānaṃ, savitakkāni jhānāni iccādinā sabbaliṅga, vibhatti, vacanehi yojetvā payogasiddhi veditabbā.

Herein, in ‘saha vitakkena,’ the meaning of another word, which is the meaning of the nominative case, is established by the capacity of the sentence. For a sentence devoid of action and agent cannot exist. By this rule, the words ‘saha’ and ‘vitakka’ are unified in meaning with another word denoted by ‘samādhi’. When this unification of meaning occurs, all the meanings of the other words and case endings present in the sentence are considered to be expressed by the compound, which has a single meaning. The other words and the case endings are deemed to have their meanings expressed; and since their meanings are expressed, they have no function in the usage. Therefore, by the rule ‘ekatthatāya,’ there is elision of the case endings. Similarly, in all compounds, other words seen in the analytic phrase, such as ya, ta, eta, ima, iti, eva, iva, viya, ca, vā, etc., are elided by a rule in the Mahāvutti. With the elision of the case endings, the constituent words of the compound, whether ending in vowels or consonants, naturally revert to their base form. Here, however, by the rule ‘sahassa soññatthe,’ the word ‘saha’ becomes ‘sa’. Then, the case endings are applied. The correctness of the usage should be understood by applying it with all genders, cases, and numbers, as in: ‘savitakko samādhi,’ ‘savitakkā samādhayo,’ ‘savitakkā paññā,’ ‘savitakkā paññāyo,’ ‘savitakkaṃ jhānaṃ,’ ‘savitakkāni jhānāni,’ etc.

Upamānapubbapado yathā? Kāyabyāmānaṃ samapamāṇattā nigrodho iva parimaṇḍalo nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo, nigrodho iva vā parimaṇḍalo yo hotīti so nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo, rājakumāro, saṅkho iva paṇḍaro saṅkhapaṇḍaro, kāko [M 0.0244] iva sūro kākasūro, sattānaṃ paññācakkhupaṭilābhakaraṇena tesaṃ cakkhu viya bhūtoti cakkhubhūto, lokuttaradhammapaṭilābhakaraṇena tesaṃ dhammo viya bhūtoti dhammabhūto, niccasommahadayatāya brahmā viya bhūtoti brahmabhūto, andho viya bhūto ayanti andhabhūto iccādi.

An example of a compound with a simile as the prior member is as follows: Due to the equal measure of his height and fathom, he is ‘round like a banyan tree’ (nigrodho iva parimaṇḍalo), which becomes ‘nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo’. Or, one who is round like a banyan tree is ‘nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo,’ for example, a royal prince. ‘White like a conch’ (saṅkho iva paṇḍaro) becomes ‘saṅkhapaṇḍaro’. ‘Brave like a crow’ (kāko iva sūro) becomes ‘kākasūro’. Because of causing beings to obtain the eye of wisdom, he has become like an eye for them—thus, ‘cakkhubhūto’. Because of causing them to obtain the supramundane Dhamma, he has become like the Dhamma for them—thus, ‘dhammabhūto’. Because of his constantly gentle heart, he has become like Brahmā—thus, ‘brahmabhūto’. This one has become like a blind person—thus, ‘andhabhūto’, and so on.

Saṅkhyobhayapado yathā? Dve vā tayo vā pattā dvittippattā, idha vāsaddāyeva aññapadāni nāma, aniyamabhūto tesaṃ attho aññapadattho nāma. Dvīhaṃ vā tīhaṃ vā dvīhatīhaṃ, cha vā pañca vā vācā chappañcavācā. Evaṃ sattaṭṭhamāsā, ekayojanadviyojanāni iccādi.

An example of a compound with both members as numbers is as follows: ‘Two or three bowls’ (dve vā tayo vā pattā) becomes ‘dvittippattā.’ Here, the words ‘vā’ themselves are the ‘other words,’ and their indeterminate meaning is the ‘meaning of the other word’. ‘Two or three days’ (dvīhaṃ vā tīhaṃ vā) becomes ‘dvīhatīhaṃ.’ ‘Six or five speeches’ (cha vā pañca vā vācā) becomes ‘chappañcavācā.’ Similarly, ‘sattaṭṭhamāsā’ (seven or eight months), ‘ekayojanadviyojanāni’ (one or two yojanas), and so on.

Disantarāḷattho yathā? Dakkhiṇassā ca pubbassā ca yadantarāḷaṃ hoti sā dakkhiṇapubbā. Evaṃ pubbuttarā, pacchimuttarā, aparadakkhiṇā, mahāvuttinā pubbapade rassattaṃ. Dakkhiṇā ca sā pubbā cāti dakkhiṇapubbā iccādinā kammadhārayopi yujjati.

An example of a compound in the sense of the space between directions is as follows: The intermediate space between the southern and the eastern direction is ‘dakkhiṇapubbā’ (southeast). Similarly, ‘pubbuttarā’ (northeast), ‘pacchimuttarā’ (northwest), ‘aparadakkhiṇā’ (southwest). According to the Mahāvutti, the prior member is shortened. By analyzing it as ‘Dakkhiṇā ca sā pubbā ca,’ ‘dakkhiṇapubbā’ etc. is also suitable as a Kammadhāraya compound.

Byatihāralakkhaṇe ka. 328; rū. 352; nī. 708 –

In the characteristic of reciprocity:

354. Tattha gahetvā tena paharitvā yuddhe sarūpaṃ.

354. Therein, having seized, with that having struck, in battle, its own form.

Sattamyantaṃ tatiyantañca samānarūpaṃ syādyantapadaṃ tattha gahetvā tena paharitvā yuddhe aññapadatthe ekatthaṃ hoti vā.

A word with a case ending, having the same form, which represents a word ending in the seventh case and a word ending in the third case, optionally becomes one in meaning in the sense of another word, when ‘seizing therein’ and ‘striking with that’ in battle is understood.

355. Ṅi vītihāre ka. 404; rū. 370.

355. The suffix Ṅi in the sense of reciprocal action.

Aññapadatthavisaye kriyābyatihāre gamyamāne padante ṅānubandho ipaccayo hoti, ettha ikāro rasso eva.

When reciprocal action is understood in the domain of the meaning of another word, the suffix ‘i’ with the anubandha ‘ṅa’ occurs at the end of the word. Here, the vowel ‘i’ is indeed short.

356. Ṅi smiṃca ka. 403; rū. 354.

356. When Ṅi or smiṃ follows.

Vipaccayante [M 0.0245] uttarapade pare pubbapadantassa āttaṃ hoti.

When a subsequent word ending in the 'i' suffix follows, the final vowel of the prior word becomes long 'ā'.

Kesesu ca kesesu ca gahetvā idaṃ yuddhaṃ pavattatīti kesākesi, daṇḍehi ca daṇḍehi ca paharitvā idaṃ yuddhaṃ pavattatīti daṇḍādaṇḍi. Evaṃ muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi, musalāmusali.

‘Having seized hair by hair, this battle proceeds’—thus ‘kesākesi.’ ‘Having struck with stick against stick, this battle proceeds’—thus ‘daṇḍādaṇḍi.’ Similarly, ‘muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi,’ ‘musalāmusali.’

Iti paṭhamābahubbīhi.

Thus ends the First Bahubbīhi.

Dutiyābahubbīhi

The Second Bahubbīhi

Āgatā samaṇā imaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ soyaṃ āgatasamaṇo, saṅghārāmo. Ettha ca samāsapadassa attho duvidho vāccattho, abhidheyyattho cāti.

‘Monks have come to this monastery’ (āgatā samaṇā imaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ)—that monastery is ‘āgatasamaṇo’. Herein, the meaning of a compound word is twofold: the expressed meaning (vāccattho) and the designated meaning (abhidheyyattho).

Tattha saṅghārāmassa samaṇehi pattabbabhāvasaṅkhātā kammasatti vāccattho nāma, sattimantabhūto saṅghārāmo abhidheyyattho nāma.

There, the objective capacity, designated as the monastery's state of being attainable by monks, is called the expressed meaning (vāccattho); while the monastery itself, as the possessor of that capacity, is called the referential meaning (abhidheyyattho).

Tattha āgatasamaṇasaddo vāccatthameva ujuṃ vadati, na abhidheyyatthaṃ, āgatasamaṇoti sutvā samaṇehi pattabbabhāvamattaṃ jānāti, saṅghārāmadabbaṃ na jānātīti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā tassaṃ abhidheyyattho aññena saṅghārāmasaddena ācikkhiyati, vāccatthassa pana tena ujuṃ vuttattā puna vattabbābhāvato dutiyāvibhattiyā ācikkhanakiccaṃ natthi, tasmā saṅghārāmapade dutiyāvibhattisambhavo natthi, liṅgatthamattavisayā paṭhamāvibhatti eva pavattati, puna padantarasambandhe sati “saṅghārāmaṃ passati āgatasamaṇaṃ, saṅghārāmena gāmo sobhati āgatasamaṇena, saṅghārāmassa pūjeti āgatasamaṇassā”tiādinā tato sabbā vibhattiyo [M 0.0246] pavattanti. Esa nayo sabbesu vācakapadesu netabboti.

There, the word ‘āgatasamaṇa’ directly conveys only the expressed meaning, not the referential meaning. It is said that upon hearing ‘āgatasamaṇa,’ one understands merely the state of being attainable by monks; one does not understand that it is the substance of a monastery. Therefore, its referential meaning is indicated by another word, ‘saṅghārāma.’ Since the expressed meaning is directly stated by it, there is no need for further statement, and thus the second case ending has no function of indicating. Hence, the second case ending does not occur with the word ‘saṅghārāma.’ Only the first case ending, whose scope is merely the meaning of the gender, is employed. However, when there is a connection with other words, all case endings are then applied, such as: ‘saṅghārāmaṃ passati āgatasamaṇaṃ’ (one sees the monastery to which monks have come); ‘saṅghārāmena gāmo sobhati āgatasamaṇena’ (the village is beautified by the monastery to which monks have come); ‘saṅghārāmassa pūjeti āgatasamaṇassā’ (one honors the monastery to which monks have come), and so on. This principle should be applied to all such indicative words.

Āgatasamaṇā sāvatthi, āgatasamaṇaṃ jetavanaṃ, āgacchanti samaṇā imanti vā āgatasamaṇo, vihāro. Ārūḷhā vānarā imaṃ rukkhanti ārūḷhavānaro, rukkho. Sampattā gāmikā yaṃ gāmanti sampattagāmiko. Evaṃ paviṭṭhagāmiko iccādi.

Sāvatthī, to which monks have come, is ‘āgatasamaṇā Sāvatthi’; Jetavana, to which monks have come, is ‘āgatasamaṇaṃ Jetavanaṃ’. Or, from ‘monks come to this’ (āgacchanti samaṇā imaṃ) is derived ‘āgatasamaṇo,’ a monastery. From ‘monkeys have climbed this tree’ (ārūḷhā vānarā imaṃ rukkhaṃ) is derived ‘ārūḷhavānaro,’ a tree. From ‘villagers have arrived at which village’ (sampattā gāmikā yaṃ gāmaṃ) is derived ‘sampattagāmiko,’ a village. Similarly, ‘paviṭṭhagāmiko,’ and so forth.

Iti dutiyābahubbīhi.

Thus the Accusative Bahubbīhi.

Tatiyābahubbīhi

The Instrumental Bahubbīhi

Jitāni indriyāni yenāti jitindriyo, samaṇo. Diṭṭho catusaccadhammo yenāti diṭṭhadhammo. Evaṃ pattadhammo, viditadhammo, pariyogāḷhadhammo, katāni catumaggakiccāni yenāti katakicco, bahuvacane sati katāni kiccāni yehi te katakiccā, arahanto. Dhammena adhigatā bhogā yenāti dhammādhigatabhogo, puriso. Evaṃ adhammādhigatabhogo. Evaṃ kattari. Karaṇe pana chinno rukkho yenāti chinnarukkho, pharasu iccādi.

‘Jitāni indriyāni yena’ (the faculties have been conquered by whom), thus ‘jitindriyo’ (one with conquered faculties), a recluse. ‘Diṭṭho catusaccadhammo yena’ (the Dhamma of the four truths has been seen by whom), thus ‘diṭṭhadhammo’ (one who has seen the Dhamma). Similarly, ‘pattadhammo’ (one who has attained the Dhamma), ‘viditadhammo’ (one who has known the Dhamma), ‘pariyogāḷhadhammo’ (one who has penetrated the Dhamma). ‘Katāni catumaggakiccāni yena’ (the duties of the four paths have been done by whom), thus ‘katakicco’ (one whose duty is done). In the plural, ‘katāni kiccāni yehi te’ (those by whom the duties have been done) are ‘katakiccā’ (those whose duties are done), i.e., Arahants. ‘Dhammena adhigatā bhogā yena’ (wealth has been acquired through Dhamma by whom), thus ‘dhammādhigatabhogo’ (one whose wealth is acquired through Dhamma), a person. Similarly, ‘adhammādhigatabhogo’ (one whose wealth is acquired through unrighteousness). This is in the agentive sense. In the instrumental sense, however: ‘chinno rukkho yena’ (a tree is cut by what), thus ‘chinnarukkho’ (that by which a tree is cut), an axe, and so forth.

Iti tatiyābahubbīhi.

Thus the Instrumental Bahubbīhi.

Catutthībahubbīhi

The Dative Bahubbīhi

Dinno suṅko yassa rañño soyaṃ dinnasuṅko, upanītaṃ bhojanaṃ yassāti upanītabhojano, natthi tulo etassāti atulo, ‘ṭa nañssā’ti na-kārassa ṭattaṃ, natthi paṭipuggalo yassāti appaṭipuggalo, natthi sīlaṃ assāti dussīlo, natthi paṭisandhipaññā assāti duppañño, ‘ghapassantassāppadhānassā’ti suttena ghasaññassa āssa [M 0.0247] rassattaṃ. Natthi sīlaṃ assāti nissīlo, nippañño, apañño, virūpaṃ mukhaṃ assāti dummukho. Evaṃ dummano, dubbaṇṇo, natthi attano uttaro adhiko yassāti anuttaro, ‘ana sare’ti suttena nassa ana.

‘Dinno suṅko yassa rañño’ (a toll has been given to which king), he is ‘dinnasuṅko’ (one to whom a toll is given). ‘Upanītaṃ bhojanaṃ yassa’ (food has been brought to whom), thus ‘upanītabhojano’ (one to whom food is brought). ‘Natthi tulo etassa’ (there is no equal to this one), thus ‘atulo’ (unequaled). ‘Natthi paṭipuggalo yassa’ (there is no counterpart to whom), thus ‘appaṭipuggalo’ (without counterpart). ‘Natthi sīlaṃ assa’ (he has no virtue), thus ‘dussīlo’ (unvirtuous). ‘Natthi paṭisandhipaññā assa’ (he has no relinking-wisdom), thus ‘duppañño’ (unwise); by the rule ‘ghapassantassāppadhānassā,’ the final vowel of a word termed ‘gha’ is shortened. ‘Natthi sīlaṃ assa’ (he has no virtue), thus ‘nissīlo’ (without virtue), ‘nippañño’ (without wisdom), ‘apañño’ (without wisdom). ‘Virūpaṃ mukhaṃ assa’ (he has an ugly face), thus ‘dummukho’ (ugly-faced). Similarly, ‘dummano’ (bad-minded), ‘dubbaṇṇo’ (of bad complexion). ‘Natthi attano uttaro adhiko yassa’ (there is no one higher or superior to him), thus ‘anuttaro’ (unsurpassed); by the rule ‘ana sare,’ ‘na’ becomes ‘ana’ before a vowel.

Idha bāhiratthabahubbīhi nāma vuccati, sattāhaṃ parinibbutassa assāti sattāhaparinibbuto, aciraṃ parinibbutassa assāti aciraparinibbuto, māso jātassa assāti māsajāto, dvemāsajāto, eko māso abhisittassa assa raññoti ekamāsābhisitto, ekāhaṃ matassa assāti ekāhamataṃ. Evaṃ dvīhamataṃ, tīhamataṃ, ekāhaṃ paṭicchannāya assāti ekāhappaṭicchannā. Evaṃ dvīhappaṭicchannā, āpatti. Yojanaṃ gatassa assāti yojanagato, dviyojanagato iccādi.

Here, this is called a Bahubbīhi of external meaning. ‘Sattāhaṃ parinibbutassa assa’ (one for whom seven days have passed since his final Nibbāna), thus ‘sattāhaparinibbuto’. ‘Aciraṃ parinibbutassa assa’ (one for whom not long has passed since his final Nibbāna), thus ‘aciraparinibbuto’. ‘Māso jātassa assa’ (one for whom a month has passed since birth), thus ‘māsajāto’ (one month old). ‘Dvemāsajāto’ (two months old). ‘Eko māso abhisittassa assa rañño’ (a king for whom one month has passed since his anointing), thus ‘ekamāsābhisitto’. ‘Ekāhaṃ matassa assa’ (one for whom one day has passed since death), thus ‘ekāhamataṃ’ (one day dead). Similarly, ‘dvīhamataṃ’ (two days dead), ‘tīhamataṃ’ (three days dead). ‘Ekāhaṃ paṭicchannāya assa’ (an offense for which one day has passed since its concealment), thus ‘ekāhappaṭicchannā’. Similarly, ‘dvīhappaṭicchannā’. This refers to an offense (āpatti). ‘Yojanaṃ gatassa assa’ (one by whom a yojana has been traversed), thus ‘yojanagato’ (one who has gone a yojana). ‘Dviyojanagato’ (one who has gone two yojanas), and so forth.

Iti catutthībahubbīhi.

Thus the Dative Bahubbīhi.

Pañcamībahubbīhi

The Ablative Bahubbīhi

Niggatā janā asmā gāmāti niggatajano, apagataṃ kāḷakaṃ itoti apagatakāḷako, paṭo. Apagatakāḷakaṃ, vatthaṃ. Apetaṃ viññāṇaṃ yamhāti apetaviññāṇaṃ, matasarīraṃ iccādi.

‘Niggatā janā asmā gāmā’ (people have gone forth from this village), thus ‘niggatajano,’ a village from which the people have gone forth. ‘Apagataṃ kāḷakaṃ ito’ (the black color has departed from this), thus ‘apagatakāḷako,’ a cloth from which the black color has departed. ‘Apagatakāḷakaṃ,’ a garment. ‘Apetaṃ viññāṇaṃ yamhā’ (consciousness has departed from which), thus ‘apetaviññāṇaṃ,’ that from which consciousness has departed, i.e., a dead body, and so forth.

Iti pañcamībahubbīhi.

Thus the Ablative Bahubbīhi.

Chaṭṭhībahubbīhi

The Genitive Bahubbīhi

Chinno hattho yassa soti chinnahattho, hatthacchinno, jāto chando yassāti jātachando, chandajāto, sañjātaṃ pītisomanassaṃ yassāti sañjātapītisomanasso, pītisomanassasañjāto, visuddhaṃ sīlaṃ yassāti visuddhasīlo[M 0.0248], sīlavisuddho, mahanto kāyo yassāti mahākāyo.

‘Chinno hattho yassa so’ (he whose hand is cut off), thus ‘chinnahattho’ (one with a cut-off hand), or ‘hatthacchinno’. ‘Jāto chando yassa’ (in whom desire has arisen), thus ‘jātachando’ (one in whom desire has arisen), or ‘chandajāto’. ‘Sañjātaṃ pītisomanassaṃ yassa’ (in whom joy and gladness have arisen), thus ‘sañjātapītisomanasso’ (one in whom joy and gladness have arisen), or ‘pītisomanassasañjāto’. ‘Visuddhaṃ sīlaṃ yassa’ (whose virtue is pure), thus ‘visuddhasīlo’ (one of pure virtue), or ‘sīlavisuddho’. ‘Mahanto kāyo yassa’ (whose body is great), thus ‘mahākāyo’ (one with a great body).

Idha upamānapubbapado nāma vuccati, suvaṇṇassa viya vaṇṇo yassāti suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, brahmuno viya saro yassāti brahmassaro, nāgassa viya gati assāti nāgagati. Evaṃ sīhagati, nāgavikkamo, sīhavikkamo, sīhassa viya hanu assāti sīhahanu, eṇissa viya jaṅghā yassāti eṇijaṅgho, usabhassa viya assa khandhoti usabhakkhandho iccādi.

Here, this is called a compound with a preceding simile (upamānapubbapada). ‘Suvaṇṇassa viya vaṇṇo yassa’ (one whose color is like gold), thus ‘suvaṇṇavaṇṇo’. ‘Brahmuno viya saro yassa’ (one whose voice is like Brahmā’s), thus ‘brahmassaro’. ‘Nāgassa viya gati assa’ (one whose gait is like an elephant’s), thus ‘nāgagati’. Similarly, ‘sīhagati’ (one whose gait is like a lion’s), ‘nāgavikkamo’ (one whose stride is like an elephant’s), ‘sīhavikkamo’ (one whose stride is like a lion’s). ‘Sīhassa viya hanu assa’ (one whose jaw is like a lion’s), thus ‘sīhahanu’. ‘Eṇissa viya jaṅghā yassa’ (one whose shanks are like a deer’s), thus ‘eṇijaṅgho’. ‘Usabhassa viya assa khandho’ (one whose shoulders are like a bull’s), thus ‘usabhakkhandho,’ and so forth.

Rūpaṃ vuccati sabhāvo, yādisaṃ rūpaṃ assāti yathārūpaṃ. Evaṃ tathārūpaṃ, evaṃ rūpaṃ assāti evarūpaṃ, bindulopo. Evaṃ ādi assāti evamādi. Tathā iccādi, iccevamādi, īdisaṃ nāmaṃ yassāti itthannāmo, evaṃnāmo, kīdisaṃ nāmaṃ yassāti kinnāmo, ‘konāmo’ti ettha mahāvuttinā kiṃsaddassa kottaṃ.

‘Rūpa’ is here called ‘nature’ (sabhāvo). ‘Yādisaṃ rūpaṃ assa’ (one that has whatever kind of nature), thus ‘yathārūpaṃ’. Similarly, ‘tathārūpaṃ’ (one that has such a nature). ‘Evaṃ rūpaṃ assa’ (one that has such a nature), thus ‘evarūpaṃ’; there is elision of the bindu. ‘Evaṃ ādi assa’ (one that has such a beginning), thus ‘evamādi’. Similarly, ‘tathā iccādi,’ ‘iccevamādi.’ ‘Īdisaṃ nāmaṃ yassa’ (one whose name is such-and-such), thus ‘itthannāmo’ or ‘evaṃnāmo’. ‘Kīdisaṃ nāmaṃ yassa’ (one whose name is of what kind), thus ‘kinnāmo’. Here, in ‘konāmo,’ the word ‘kiṃ’ becomes ‘ko’ according to the Mahāvutti.

Ko samudayo yassa dhammassāti kiṃsamudayo, kā jāti yassāti kiṃjātiko, kiṃnidānaṃ yassāti kiṃnidāno, kati vassāni yassāti kativasso, ko attho assāti kimatthaṃ, vacanaṃ. ‘Kvattho’ti mahāvuttinā kiṃsaddassa kottaṃ, yādiso attho assāti yadattho, tādiso attho assāti tadattho, ediso attho yassa vinayassāti etadattho, vinayo. Etadatthā, vinayakathā. Etadatthaṃ, sotāvadhānaṃ iccādi.

‘Ko samudayo yassa dhammassa’ (a Dhamma whose origin is what?), thus ‘kiṃsamudayo’. ‘Kā jāti yassa’ (one whose birth is what?), thus ‘kiṃjātiko’. ‘Kiṃnidānaṃ yassa’ (one whose cause is what?), thus ‘kiṃnidāno’. ‘Kati vassāni yassa’ (one whose years are how many?), thus ‘kativasso’. ‘Ko attho assa’ (that which has what purpose?), thus ‘kimatthaṃ,’ a statement. In ‘kvattho,’ the word ‘kiṃ’ becomes ‘ko’ according to the Mahāvutti. ‘Yādiso attho assa’ (that which has whatever purpose), thus ‘yadattho’. ‘Tādiso attho assa’ (that which has such a purpose), thus ‘tadattho’. ‘Ediso attho yassa vinayassa’ (the Vinaya whose purpose is this), thus ‘etadattho,’ the Vinaya. ‘Etadatthā,’ a talk on the Vinaya. ‘Etadatthaṃ,’ giving ear, and so forth.

Iti chaṭṭhībahubbīhi.

Thus the Genitive Bahubbīhi.

Sattamībahubbīhi

The Locative Bahubbīhi

Sampannāni sassāni yasmiṃ janapade soyaṃ sampannasasso, sulabhā bhikkhā yasmiṃ janapade soyaṃ subhikkho[M 0.0249], dullabhā bhikkhā yasminti dubbhikkho, bahavo gāmā asmiṃ janapadeti bahugāmo. Evaṃ bahujano, gāmo. Natthi gāmakhettaṃ yasmiṃ araññe tayidaṃ agāmakaṃ, samāsante ko. Saṃvijjanti manussā yasmiṃ gāme samanusso, na vijjanti manussā yasmiṃ gāme amanusso iccādi.

‘Sampannāni sassāni yasmiṃ janapade so’ (a country in which crops are abundant), thus ‘sampannasasso’. ‘Sulabhā bhikkhā yasmiṃ janapade so’ (a country in which alms are easy to obtain), thus ‘subhikkho’. ‘Dullabhā bhikkhā yasmiṃ’ (in which alms are hard to obtain), thus ‘dubbhikkho’. ‘Bahavo gāmā asmiṃ janapade’ (in this country are many villages), thus ‘bahugāmo’. Similarly, ‘bahujano,’ a village with many people. ‘Natthi gāmakhettaṃ yasmiṃ araññe tad idaṃ’ (that forest in which there is no village or field) is ‘agāmakaṃ’; the suffix ‘ka’ is added at the end of the compound. ‘Saṃvijjanti manussā yasmiṃ gāme’ (a village in which people are present), thus ‘samanusso’. ‘Na vijjanti manussā yasmiṃ gāme’ (a village in which people are not present), thus ‘amanusso,’ and so forth.

Iti sattamībahubbīhi.

Thus the Locative Bahubbīhi.

Bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi

The Bahubbīhi of Different Case-relations

Bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi nāma vuccati, ekarattiṃ vāso assāti ekarattivāso, samānena janena saddhiṃ vāso assāti samānavāso, ubhato kammato uppannaṃ byañjanadvayaṃ assāti ubhatobyañjano, aluttasamāso. Evaṃ kaṇṭhasmiṃ kāḷo assāti kaṇṭhekāḷo, urasmiṃ lomāni assāti urasilomo, yassa hatthe patto atthīti pattahattho. Evaṃ asihattho, daṇḍahattho, chattaṃ pāṇimhi assāti chattapāṇi. Evaṃ satthapāṇi, daṇḍapāṇi, vajirapāṇi, dāne ajjhāsayo assāti dānajjhāsayo, dānādhimuttiko, buddhesu bhatti assāti buddhabhattiko, buddhe gāravo assāti buddhagāravo, dhammagāravo iccādi.

The Bahubbīhi of different case-relations is so called. ‘Ekarattiṃ vāso assa’ (one whose stay is for one night), thus ‘ekarattivāso’. ‘Samānena janena saddhiṃ vāso assa’ (one whose stay is with the same people), thus ‘samānavāso’. ‘Ubhato kammato uppannaṃ byañjanadvayaṃ assa’ (one who has two characteristics arisen from both actions), thus ‘ubhatobyañjano’; this is an unelided compound. Similarly: ‘kaṇṭhasmiṃ kāḷo assa’ (one who has black on the throat), thus ‘kaṇṭhekāḷo’. ‘Urasmiṃ lomāni assa’ (one who has hair on the chest), thus ‘urasilomo’. ‘Yassa hatthe patto atthi’ (one in whose hand there is a bowl), thus ‘pattahattho’. Similarly, ‘asihattho’ (sword-in-hand), ‘daṇḍahattho’ (staff-in-hand). ‘Chattaṃ pāṇimhi assa’ (one in whose hand there is an umbrella), thus ‘chattapāṇi’. Similarly, ‘satthapāṇi’ (weapon-in-hand), ‘daṇḍapāṇi’ (rod-in-hand), ‘vajirapāṇi’ (thunderbolt-in-hand). ‘Dāne ajjhāsayo assa’ (one whose inclination is towards giving), thus ‘dānajjhāsayo’ or ‘dānādhimuttiko’. ‘Buddhesu bhatti assa’ (one whose devotion is in the Buddhas), thus ‘buddhabhattiko’. ‘Buddhe gāravo assa’ (one whose reverence is for the Buddha), thus ‘buddhagāravo,’ ‘dhammagāravo,’ and so forth.

Tipadabahubbīhi

The Three-Term Bahubbīhi

Tipadabahubbīhi nāma vuccati, parakkamena adhigatā sampadā yehi te parakkamādhigatasampadā, dhammena adhigatā bhogā yehi te dhammādhigatabhogā, oṇīto pattamhā pāṇi yena so oṇītapattapāṇi, sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ viya kāyo assāti sīhapubbaddhakāyo, mattā bahavo mātaṅgā yasmiṃ vaneti mattabahumātaṅgaṃ iccādi.

The three-term Bahubbīhi is explained as follows: 'those by whom wealth is acquired through effort' are 'parakkamādhigatasampadā' (those who have wealth acquired through effort); 'those by whom possessions are acquired through righteousness' are 'dhammādhigatabhogā' (those who have possessions acquired through righteousness); 'he by whom the hand is withdrawn from the bowl' is 'oṇītapattapāṇi' (one who has the hand withdrawn from the bowl); 'he whose body is like the forepart of a lion' is 'sīhapubbaddhakāyo' (one who has a body like the forepart of a lion); 'that forest in which there are many intoxicated elephants' is 'mattabahumātaṅgaṃ', and so on.

Bahubbīhisamāso niṭṭhito.

The Bahubbīhi compound is concluded.

Dvandasamāsa

The Dvandva Compound

Atha [M 0.0250] dvandasamāso dīpiyate.

Now the Dvandva compound is explained.

Dve ca dve ca padāni dvandā, dve ca dve ca atthā vā dvandā, mahāvuttinā dvinnaṃ dvisaddānaṃ dvandādeso. Dvandasaddasadisattā sabbo cāyaṃ samāso dvandoti vuccati.

'Two and two words' are 'dvandā'; or 'two and two meanings' are 'dvandā'. By extensive usage, there is the substitution of 'dvanda' for two instances of the word 'dvi' (two). And because this entire compound resembles the word 'dvanda', it is called 'dvanda'.

Atha vā dve avayavā andiyanti bandhiyanti etthāti dvando, yugaḷassetaṃ nāmaṃ “pādadvandaṃ munindassa, vandāmi sirasāmaha”nti ettha viya, idha pana padayugaḷaṃ atthayugaḷañca gayhati. Ubhayapadatthapadhāno hi dvando.

Alternatively, because two components are joined and bound together herein, it is called 'dvanda'. This is a name for a pair, as in 'I bow my head to the pair of feet of the Lord of Sages'. Here, however, a pair of words and a pair of meanings are to be understood. For the 'dvanda' is indeed that in which the meaning of both terms is principal.

Ettha siyā – yadi ubhayapadatthappadhāno dvando, evañca sati dvande kathaṃ ekatthībhāvalakkhaṇaṃ siyāti? Vuccate – abhinnavidheyyatthattā. Vacanapathañhi patvā kattubhāvakammabhāvādiko vidheyyattho eva padānaṃ accantappadhānattho hoti vacanavākyasampattiyā padhānaṅgattā, so ca vidheyyattho dvandepi abhinno eva hoti. Tathā hi “sāriputtamoggallānā gacchanti, sāriputtamoggallāne passati” iccādīsu dve atthā ekavibhattiyā visayā hutvā ekakattu, ekakammādibhāvena ekattaṃ gacchanti, evaṃ dvandepi dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bahunnaṃ vā padānaṃ ekatthībhāvalakkhaṇaṃ labbhatiyevāti.

Here it might be asked: If a 'dvanda' has the meaning of both terms as principal, then how can the characteristic of having a single meaning apply to a 'dvanda'? It is said: because the meaning to be predicated is of an identical nature. For when words reach the path of expression, the meaning to be predicated—such as agency, objectivity, and so on—becomes the most principal meaning of the words, due to being a principal part for the completion of the sentence; and that meaning to be predicated is indeed identical even in a 'dvanda'. Thus, in instances such as 'Sāriputta and Moggallāna go,' 'He sees Sāriputta and Moggallāna,' the two meanings, having become the domain of a single case-ending, attain unity by way of being a single agent, a single object, and so on. Thus, even in a 'dvanda', the characteristic of having a single meaning can indeed be obtained for two, three, or many words.

357. Catthe ka. 329; rū. 357; nī. 709.

357. In the sense of 'ca'.

Anekaṃ syādyantapadaṃ casaddassa atthe ekatthaṃ hoti vā.

Many words ending in case inflections, in the sense of the word 'ca' (and), optionally become a single meaning.

Ettha ca samuccayo, anvācayo, itarītarayogo, samāhāroti cattāro casaddatthā honti.

Here, there are four meanings of the word 'ca': 'samuccaya' (conjunction), 'anvācaya' (subsequent collection), 'itarītarayoga' (mutual connection), and 'samāhāra' (aggregation).

Tattha samuccayo yathā? Cīvarañca piṇḍapātañca senāsanañca detīti. Anvācayo yathā? Dānañca deti, sīlañca rakkhatīti. Ime [M 0.0251] dve casaddatthā vākyadvande eva labbhanti, na samāsadvande padānaṃ aññamaññaṃ nirapekkhattāti vadanti. Taṃ anvācaye yujjati nānākriyāpekkhattā, samuccaye pana “cīvarañca piṇḍapātañca senāsanañca detī”ti vā “cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanāni detī”ti vā evaṃ dvidhāpi yojetuṃ yujjatiyeva “lābhī hoti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna”nti ma. ni. 1.65 pāḷidassanato. Anvācayopi vā samāsadvande no na labbhati “mālāgandhavilepanadhāraṇamaṇḍanavibhūsanaṭṭhānā”ti dī. ni. 1.10 pāḷidassanato. Evaṃ pana yujjeyya – casaddattho ekakriya, nānākriyāpekkhanabhedena duvidho hoti samuccayo, anvācayo cāti, tesu ca ekeko avayavappadhāna, samudāyappadhānabhedena duvidho hoti itarītarayogo, samāhāro cāti. Tattha itarītarayoge avayavappadhānattā sabbavibhattīsu bahuvacanameva yujjati.

Among these, how is 'samuccaya' (conjunction) exemplified? 'He gives robes, and alms-food, and lodging.' How is 'anvācaya' (subsequent collection) exemplified? 'He gives alms and maintains virtue.' These two meanings of 'ca' are found only in sentence-dvandvas, not in compound-dvandvas, because the words are mutually independent, so they say. This applies to 'anvācaya' because it involves dependence on different actions, but in 'samuccaya', it is indeed correct to phrase it in two ways: 'He gives robes, and alms-food, and lodging,' or 'He gives robes, alms-food, and lodgings.' This is justified by the Pāli passage: 'he is a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites'. 'Anvācaya' is also found in compound-dvandvas, as seen in the Pāli passage: 'from the occasion of wearing, adorning, and beautifying with garlands, perfumes, and ointments'. However, it might be argued thus: the meaning of 'ca' is twofold, 'samuccaya' (conjunction) and 'anvācaya' (subsequent collection), distinguished by whether it expects a single action or multiple actions. And each of these is twofold, distinguished by emphasizing individual components ('avayavappadhāna') or emphasizing the collective ('samudāyappadhāna'), resulting in 'itarītarayoga' (mutual connection) and 'samāhāra' (aggregation). In 'itarītarayoga', because the emphasis is on individual components, only the plural form is appropriate in all grammatical cases.

Dvande paṇītataraṃ pubbe nipatati. Sāriputto ca moggallāno ca sāriputtamoggallānā, sāriputtamoggallāne, sāriputtamoggallānehi iccādi. Evaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇā, brāhmaṇagahapatikā, khattiyabrāhmaṇā, devamanussā, candimasūriyā.

In a 'dvanda', the more excellent term is placed first. 'Sāriputta and Moggallāna' become 'sāriputtamoggallānā', 'sāriputtamoggallāne', 'sāriputtamoggallānehi', and so on. Thus: 'samaṇabrāhmaṇā' (ascetics and brahmins), 'brāhmaṇagahapatikā' (brahmins and householders), 'khattiyabrāhmaṇā' (nobles and brahmins), 'devamanussā' (gods and humans), 'candimasūriyā' (the moon and the sun).

Appakkhara, bahvakkharesu appakkharaṃ kvaci pubbaṃ hoti, gāmanigamā, gāmajanapadā iccādi.

Among terms with fewer syllables and many syllables, sometimes the one with fewer syllables comes first, as in 'gāmanigamā' (village and town), 'gāmajanapadā' (village and district), and so on.

Kvaci ivaṇṇu’vaṇṇantā pubbe honti, aggi ca dhūmo ca aggidhūmā, rattidivā, dhātuliṅgāni.

Sometimes terms ending in 'i' or 'u' come first. 'Aggi ca dhūmo ca' (fire and smoke) become 'aggidhūmā'; 'rattidivā' (night and day); 'dhātuliṅgāni' (elements and genders).

Avaṇṇantesu sarādipadaṃ pubbaṃ hoti, attho ca dhammo ca atthadhammā, dhammatthā vā iccādi.

Among those ending in 'a', the term beginning with a vowel comes first, such as 'attho ca dhammo ca' (meaning and Dhamma) becoming 'atthadhammā', or 'dhammatthā', and so on.

Ayañca [M 0.0252] niyamo dvipadadvandesu yebhuyyena labbhati, bahupadadvandesu na labbhati.

And this rule is mostly found in two-term 'dvanda' compounds, but not in multi-term 'dvanda' compounds.

Samāhāradvande –

In the 'Samāhāra Dvanda' (Aggregative Compound) –

358. Samāhāre napuṃsakaṃ ka. 322; rū. 359; nī. 700.

358. In a 'samāhāra' (aggregative compound), it is neuter.

Catthe samāhāre ekatthapadaṃ napuṃsakaṃ hoti, ekavacanantattaṃ pana samāhāravacaneneva siddhaṃ, ayañca samāhāro pāṇyaṅgādīnaṃ dvandesu niccaṃ labbhati, rukkhatiṇādīnaṃ dvandesu vikappena labbhati.

In the sense of 'ca', in an aggregative compound, the single term is neuter. Its singular ending, however, is already established by the word 'samāhāra' (aggregation) itself. And this 'samāhāra' is invariably found in 'dvanda' compounds of body parts and the like, and optionally found in 'dvanda' compounds of trees, grass, and the like.

Tattha niccaladdhesu tāva pāṇyaṅgadvande –

Among those invariably found, first, in 'dvanda' compounds of body parts –

Cakkhu ca sotañca cakkhusotaṃ, mukhañca nāsikā ca mukhanāsikaṃ, ‘syādīsu rasso’ti rassattaṃ. Hanu ca gīvā ca hanugīvaṃ. Evaṃ kaṇṇanāsaṃ, chavi ca maṃsañca lohitañca chavimaṃsalohitaṃ, nāmañca rūpañca nāmarūpaṃ, jarā ca maraṇañca jarāmaraṇaṃ. Bahulādhikārā kvaci vikapparūpampi dissati, hatthā ca pādā ca hatthapādaṃ, hatthapādā vā iccādi.

'Cakkhu ca sotañca' (eye and ear) become 'cakkhusotaṃ'. 'Mukhañca nāsikā ca' (mouth and nose) become 'mukhanāsikaṃ', with shortening due to the rule 'syādīsu rasso' (shortening in syādi etc.). 'Hanu ca gīvā ca' (jaw and neck) become 'hanugīvaṃ'. Thus: 'kaṇṇanāsaṃ' (ear and nose); 'chavi ca maṃsañca lohitañca' (skin, flesh, and blood) become 'chavimaṃsalohitaṃ'; 'nāmañca rūpañca' (name and form) become 'nāmarūpaṃ'; 'jarā ca maraṇañca' (aging and death) become 'jarāmaraṇaṃ'. Due to the governing rule of 'bahula' (variously applicable), sometimes a variant form is also seen, such as 'hatthā ca pādā ca' (hands and feet) becoming 'hatthapādaṃ', or 'hatthapādā', and so on.

Tūriyaṅgadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of musical instrument parts –

Naccañca gītañca vāditañca naccagītavāditaṃ. Evaṃ sammatāḷaṃ, ‘samma’nti kaṃsatāḷaṃ, ‘tāḷa’nti hatthatāḷaṃ, saṅkho ca paṇavo ca ḍiṇḍimo ca saṅkhapaṇavaḍiṇḍimaṃ iccādi.

'Naccañca gītañca vāditañca' (dancing, singing, and instrumental music) become 'naccagītavāditaṃ'. Thus: 'sammatāḷaṃ', where 'samma' means bronze cymbals and 'tāḷa' means hand-clapping; 'saṅkho ca paṇavo ca ḍiṇḍimo ca' (conch, kettledrum, and tambourine) become 'saṅkhapaṇavaḍiṇḍimaṃ', and so on.

Yoggaṅgadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of yoke components –

Phālo ca pācanañca phālapācanaṃ, yugañca naṅgalañca yuganaṅgalaṃ iccādi.

'Phālo ca pācanañca' (plowshare and goad) become 'phālapācanaṃ'. 'Yugañca naṅgalañca' (yoke and plow) become 'yuganaṅgalaṃ', and so on.

Senaṅgadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of army components –

Hatthino [M 0.0253] ca assā ca hatthiassaṃ. Evaṃ rathapattikaṃ, asi ca cammañca asicammaṃ. ‘Camma’nti saraparittāṇaphalakaṃ, dhanu ca kalāpo ca dhanukalāpaṃ iccādi.

'Hatthino ca assā ca' (elephants and horses) become 'hatthiassaṃ'. Thus: 'rathapattikaṃ' (chariots and foot soldiers). 'Asi ca cammañca' (sword and shield) become 'asicammaṃ'. 'Camma' means a board for protection from arrows. 'Dhanu ca kalāpo ca' (bow and quiver) become 'dhanukalāpaṃ', and so on.

Khuddakapāṇadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of small creatures –

Ḍaṃsā ca makasā ca ḍaṃsamakasaṃ. Evaṃ kunthakipillikaṃ su. ni. 607, kīṭapaṭaṅgaṃ iccādi.

'Ḍaṃsā ca makasā ca' (gadflies and mosquitoes) become 'ḍaṃsamakasaṃ'. Thus: 'kunthakipillikaṃ' (small insects and ants), 'kīṭapaṭaṅgaṃ' (insects and moths), and so on.

Niccaveridvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of perpetual enemies –

Ahi ca nakulo ca ahinakulaṃ, biḷāro ca mūsikā ca biḷāramūsikaṃ, rassattaṃ. Kākolūkaṃ, sappamaṇḍūkaṃ, nāgasupaṇṇaṃ iccādi.

'Ahi ca nakulo ca' (snake and mongoose) become 'ahinakulaṃ'. 'Biḷāro ca mūsikā ca' (cat and rat) become 'biḷāramūsikaṃ', with shortening. 'Kākolūkaṃ' (crow and owl), 'sappamaṇḍūkaṃ' (snake and frog), 'nāgasupaṇṇaṃ' (nāga and supaṇṇa/garuḍa), and so on.

Sabhāgadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of similar categories –

Sīlañca paññāṇañca sīlapaññāṇaṃ, samatho ca vipassanā ca samathavipassanaṃ, vijjā ca caraṇañca vijjācaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ satisampajaññaṃ, hiriottappaṃ, uddhaccakukkuccaṃ, thinamiddhaṃ iccādi.

'Sīlañca paññāṇañca' (virtue and wisdom) become 'sīlapaññāṇaṃ'. 'Samatho ca vipassanā ca' (tranquility and insight) become 'samathavipassanaṃ'. 'Vijjā ca caraṇañca' (knowledge and conduct) become 'vijjācaraṇaṃ'. Thus: 'satisampajaññaṃ' (mindfulness and clear comprehension), 'hiriottappaṃ' (moral shame and moral dread), 'uddhaccakukkuccaṃ' (restlessness and remorse), 'thinamiddhaṃ' (sloth and torpor), and so on.

Vividhaviruddhadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of various opposites –

Kusalākusalaṃ, sāvajjānavajjaṃ, kaṇhasukkaṃ, hīnapaṇītaṃ, chekabālaṃ iccādi.

'Kusalākusalaṃ' (wholesome and unwholesome), 'sāvajjānavajjaṃ' (blameworthy and blameless), 'kaṇhasukkaṃ' (dark and bright), 'hīnapaṇītaṃ' (inferior and excellent), 'chekabālaṃ' (clever and foolish), and so on.

Ekasaṅgītidvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of single collections –

Dīgho ca majjhimo ca dīghamajjhimaṃ, aṅguttarasaṃyuttakaṃ, khandhakavibhaṅgaṃ iccādi.

'Dīgho ca majjhimo ca' (Dīgha and Majjhima) become 'dīghamajjhimaṃ'. 'Aṅguttarasaṃyuttakaṃ' (Aṅguttara and Saṃyutta), 'khandhakavibhaṅgaṃ' (Khandhaka and Vibhaṅga), and so on.

Saṅkhyāparimāṇadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of numbers and measures –

Ekakadukaṃ, dukatikaṃ, tikacatukkaṃ, catukkapañcakaṃ iccādi.

'Ekakadukaṃ' (one and two), 'dukatikaṃ' (two and three), 'tikacatukkaṃ' (three and four), 'catukkapañcakaṃ' (four and five), and so on.

Pacanacaṇḍāladvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of cooks and outcastes –

Orabbhikā [M 0.0254] ca sūkarikā ca orabbhikasūkarikaṃ. Evaṃ sākuṇikamāgavikaṃ, sapākacaṇḍālaṃ, venarathakāraṃ, pukkusachavaḍāhakaṃ iccādi.

'Orabbhikā ca sūkarikā ca' (sheep-butchers and pig-butchers) become 'orabbhikasūkarikaṃ'. Thus: 'sākuṇikamāgavikaṃ' (fowlers and deer-hunters), 'sapākacaṇḍālaṃ' (dog-cookers and outcastes), 'venarathakāraṃ' (bamboo-workers and cart-makers), 'pukkusachavaḍāhakaṃ' (scavengers and corpse-burners), and so on.

Liṅgavisabhāgadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of dissimilar genders –

Itthipumaṃ, dāsidāsaṃ iccādi.

'Itthipumaṃ' (women and men), 'dāsidāsaṃ' (female slaves and male slaves), and so on.

Disādvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of directions –

Pubbā ca aparā ca pubbāparaṃ. Evaṃ dakkhiṇuttaraṃ, pubbadakkhiṇaṃ, pubbuttaraṃ, aparadakkhiṇaṃ, aparuttaraṃ.

'Pubbā ca aparā ca' (east and west) become 'pubbāparaṃ'. Thus: 'dakkhiṇuttaraṃ' (south and north), 'pubbadakkhiṇaṃ' (east and south), 'pubbuttaraṃ' (east and north), 'aparadakkhiṇaṃ' (west and south), 'aparuttaraṃ' (west and north).

Nadīdvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of rivers –

Gaṅgāyamunaṃ, mahisarabhu, sabbattha napuṃsakattā ante dīghānaṃ rassattaṃ sattasu vibhattīsu ekavacanantañca.

'Gaṅgāyamunaṃ' (Ganges and Yamuna), 'mahisarabhu' (Mahī and Sarabhū). Everywhere, due to being neuter, the long vowels at the end become short, and the singular ending is used in all seven cases.

Iti niccasamāhārarāsi.

Thus, the collection of invariable collective compounds.

Vikappaladdhesu ka. 323; rū. 360; nī. 701 tiṇavisesadvande –

Among those optionally obtained, in 'dvanda' compounds of specific grasses –

Usīrāni ca bīraṇāni ca usīrabīraṇaṃ, usīrabīraṇā. Evaṃ muñjapabbajaṃ, muñjapabbajā, kāsakusaṃ, kāsakusā.

'Usīrāni ca bīraṇāni ca' (usīra grass and bīraṇa grass) become 'usīrabīraṇaṃ' or 'usīrabīraṇā'. Thus: 'muñja' and 'pabbaja' become 'muñjapabbajaṃ' or 'muñjapabbajā'; 'kāsa' and 'kusa' become 'kāsakusaṃ' or 'kāsakusā'.

Rukkhavisesadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of specific trees –

Khadiro ca palāso ca khadirapalāsaṃ, khadirapalāsā, dhavo ca assakaṇṇo ca dhavassakaṇṇaṃ, dhavassakaṇṇā, pilakkhanigrodhaṃ, pilakkhanigrodhā, assatthakapītanaṃ kapitthanaṃ (katthaci), assatthakapītanā, sākasālaṃ, sākasālā.

Khadira and palāsa become khadirapalāsaṃ, khadirapalāsā; dhava and assakaṇṇa become dhavassakaṇṇaṃ, dhavassakaṇṇā; pilakkha and nigrodha become pilakkhanigrodhaṃ, pilakkhanigrodhā; assattha and kapītana become assatthakapītanaṃ, assatthakapītanā; sāka and sāla become sākasālaṃ, sākasālā.

Pasuvisesadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of specific animals –

Gajā [M 0.0255] ca gavajā ca gajagavajaṃ, gajagavajā, gomahisaṃ, gomahisā, eṇeyyavarāhaṃ, eṇeyyavarāhā, ajeḷakaṃ, ajeḷakā, kukkuṭasūkaraṃ, kukkuṭasūkarā, hatthigavassavaḷavaṃ, hatthigavassavaḷavā.

Gaja and gavaja become gajagavajaṃ, gajagavajā; go and mahisa become gomahisaṃ, gomahisā; eṇeyya and varāha become eṇeyyavarāhaṃ, eṇeyyavarāhā; aja and eḷaka become ajeḷakaṃ, ajeḷakā; kukkuṭa and sūkara become kukkuṭasūkaraṃ, kukkuṭasūkarā; hatthi, gava, assa, and vaḷava become hatthigavassavaḷavaṃ, hatthigavassavaḷavā.

Sakuṇavisesadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of specific birds –

Haṃsabilavaṃ, haṃsabilavā, kāraṇḍavacakkavākaṃ, kāraṇḍavacakkavākā, bakabalākaṃ, bakabalākā.

Haṃsa and bilava become haṃsabilavaṃ, haṃsabilavā; kāraṇḍava and cakkavāka become kāraṇḍavacakkavākaṃ, kāraṇḍavacakkavākā; baka and balāka become bakabalākaṃ, bakabalākā.

Dhanadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of wealth –

Hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ, hiraññasuvaṇṇā, maṇi ca saṅkho ca muttā ca veḷuriyañca maṇisaṅkhamuttaveḷuriyaṃ, maṇisaṅkhamuttaveḷuriyā, jātarūparajataṃ, jātarūparajatā.

Hirañña and suvaṇṇa become hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ, hiraññasuvaṇṇā; 'maṇi ca saṅkho ca muttā ca veḷuriyañca' (jewel, conch, pearl, and beryl) become maṇisaṅkhamuttaveḷuriyaṃ, maṇisaṅkhamuttaveḷuriyā; jātarūpa and rajata become jātarūparajataṃ, jātarūparajatā.

Dhaññadvande –

In 'dvanda' compounds of grains –

Sāliyavaṃ, sāliyavā, tilamuggamāsaṃ, tilamuggamāsā, nipphāvakulatthaṃ, nipphāvakulatthā.

Sāli and yava become sāliyavaṃ, sāliyavā; tila, mugga, and māsa become tilamuggamāsaṃ, tilamuggamāsā; nipphāva and kulattha become nipphāvakulatthaṃ, nipphāvakulatthā.

Byañjanānaṃ dvande –

In the dvanda compound of condiments –

Macchamaṃsaṃ, macchamaṃsā, sākasūpaṃ, sākasūpā, gabyamāhisaṃ, gabyamāhisā, eṇeyyavārāhaṃ, eṇeyyavārāhā, migamāyūraṃ, migamāyūrā.

Fish and meat: `macchamaṃsaṃ`, `macchamaṃsā`; vegetables and soup: `sākasūpaṃ`, `sākasūpā`; cattle and buffalo: `gabyamāhisaṃ`, `gabyamāhisā`; deer and boar: `eṇeyyavārāhaṃ`, `eṇeyyavārāhā`; deer and peacock: `migamāyūraṃ`, `migamāyūrā`.

Janapadadvande –

In the dvanda compound of countries –

Kāsikosalaṃ, kāsikosalā, vajjimallaṃ, vajjimallā, cetavaṃsaṃ, cetavaṃsā, majjhañca sūrasenañca majjhasūrasenaṃ, majjhasūrasenā, kurupañcālaṃ, kurupañcālā.

Kāsī and Kosala: `Kāsikosalaṃ`, `Kāsikosalā`; Vajji and Malla: `Vajjimallaṃ`, `Vajjimallā`; Ceta and Vaṃsa: `Cetavaṃsaṃ`, `Cetavaṃsā`; Majjha and Sūrasena: `Majjhasūrasenaṃ`, `Majjhasūrasenā`; Kuru and Pañcāla: `Kurupañcālaṃ`, `Kurupañcālā`.

Iti vikappasamāhārarāsi.

Thus, the collection of alternative and collective compounds.

Dvandasamāso niṭṭhito.

The dvanda compound is concluded.

Visesavidhāna

Special Rules

Idāni [M 0.0256] pubbe vuttāni avuttāni ca chasu samāsesu visesavidhānāni vuccante.

Now, the special rules—both previously mentioned and unmentioned—for the six compounds are explained.

Napuṃsakekattaṃ, samāsantarasso, pumbhāvātideso, samāsante ka, samāsante a, nānādeso, abyayo, saṅkhyā.

Neuter singular, shortening within a compound, gender substitution to masculine, ka at the end of a compound, a at the end of a compound, diverse substitutions, indeclinables, and numerals.

Napuṃsakekattarāsi

Collection of Neuter Singulars

Tattha sabbo abyayībhāvo napuṃsakaliṅgo eva, samāhārabhūtā digu, dvandā napuṃsakā ca ekattasaṅkhyā ca.

Here, all abyayībhāva compounds are indeed neuter in gender. Collective digu and dvanda compounds are neuter and singular in number.

359. Kvacekattañca chaṭṭhiyā ka. 327; rū. 351; nī. 704; caṃ. 2.2.69-73; pā. 2.4.22-25.

359. And sometimes singular for the sixth-case compound.

Chaṭṭhīsamāse kvaci napuṃsakattaṃ ekattañca hoti.

In the sixth-case compound, it is sometimes neuter and singular.

Chāyā, sabhāsvevāyaṃ vidhi, salabhānaṃ chāyā salabhacchāyaṃ …sabhacchāyaṃ (mūlapāṭhe). Evaṃ sakaṭacchāyaṃ, gharacchāyaṃ. Idha na hoti, rukkhacchāyā, pabbatacchāyā. Sabhāsadde amanussasabhāsvevāyaṃ vidhi, brahmūnaṃ sabhā brahmasabhaṃ. Evaṃ devasabhaṃ, indasabhaṃ, yakkhasabhaṃ, rakkhasasataṃ. Manussasabhāsu natthi, khattiyasabhā, rājasabhā iccādi.

This rule applies only to `chāyā` and `sabhā`. The shadow of the grasshoppers is `salabhacchāyaṃ`. Similarly, `sakaṭacchāyaṃ` (shadow of the cart), `gharacchāyaṃ` (shadow of the house). Here it does not occur: `rukkhacchāyā` (shadow of the tree), `pabbatacchāyā` (shadow of the mountain). Regarding the word `sabhā`, this rule applies only to non-human assemblies. The assembly of the Brahmās is `brahmasabhaṃ`. Similarly, `devasabhaṃ` (assembly of the devas), `indasabhaṃ` (assembly of Indra), `yakkhasabhaṃ` (assembly of the yakkhas), `rakkhasasataṃ` (a hundred rākṣasas). It does not occur in human assemblies, such as `khattiyasabhā` (assembly of the khattiyas), `rājasabhā` (royal assembly), and so on.

Kvacīti kiṃ? Rājaparisā.

Why 'sometimes'? `Rājaparisā` (royal assembly).

Iti napuṃsakekattarāsi.

Thus, the collection of neuter singulars.

Samāsantarassarāsi

Collection of Shortening within Compounds

‘Syādīsu rasso’ti suttena abyayībhāva, samāhāradigu, dvandānaṃ kassaci tappurisassa ca syādīsu rasso.

By the rule ‘Syādīsu rasso’ (shortening before case endings), shortening occurs in abyayībhāva, samāhāradigu, and dvanda compounds, and for some tappurisa compounds, before case endings.

Abyayībhāve –

In the Abyayībhāva compound –

Upamaṇikaṃ [M 0.0257] adhitthi, upavadhu.

`Upamaṇikaṃ`, `adhitthi`, `upavadhu`.

Samāhāradigumhi –

In the samāhāradigu compound –

Catuddisaṃ, dasitthi, dasavadhu.

`Catuddisaṃ`: in the four quarters; `dasitthi`: ten women; `dasavadhu`: ten brides.

Samāhāradvande –

In the samāhāradvanda compound –

Mukhanāsikaṃ, hanugīvaṃ.

`Mukhanāsikaṃ`: mouth and nose; `hanugīvaṃ`: jaw and neck.

Tappurise –

In the Tappurisa compound –

Salabhacchāyaṃ, brahmasabhaṃ.

`Salabhacchāyaṃ`: the shadow of grasshoppers; `brahmasabhaṃ`: the assembly of Brahmās.

360. Ghapassantassāppadhānassa ka. 403; rū. 354; nī. 858; caṃ. 2.2.86; pā. 1.2.48.

360. For `gha` (feminine suffixes) at the end and not principal.

Syādīsu antabhūtassa appadhānabhūtassa ca ghapassa rasso hoti.

Before case endings, the vowel of a feminine suffix (`gha`) that is at the end and not the principal part is shortened.

Bahubbīhimhi –

In the Bahubbīhi compound –

Bahukañño, poso, bahuitthi, kulaṃ, bahuvadhu, kulaṃ.

`Bahukañño`: having many daughters; `poso`: a man. `Bahuitthi`: having many wives; `kulaṃ`: a family. `Bahuvadhu`: having many daughters-in-law; `kulaṃ`: a family.

Abyayībhāve –

In the Abyayībhāva compound –

Upamaṇikaṃ, adhitthi, upavadhu.

Upamaṇikaṃ, adhitthi, upavadhu.

Antassāti kiṃ? Saddhādhano, puriso.

What is meant by 'at the end'? Saddhādhano puriso (a person whose wealth is faith).

Appadhānassāti kiṃ? Rājakaññā, rājakumārī, brahmabandhū.

What is meant by 'not principal'? Rājakaññā (royal maiden), rājakumārī (royal princess), brahmabandhū (kinswoman of Brahmā).

361. Gossu ka. 342; rū. 337; nī. 722; caṃ. 2.2.85; pā. 1.2.48.

361. For go, u is substituted.

Syādīsu antabhūtassa appadhānabhūtassa ca gossa u hoti.

Before case endings, u is substituted for go when it is at the end and is not the principal element.

Tiṭṭhagu [M 0.0258] cittagu.

Tiṭṭhagu (one who has standing cows), cittagu (one who has variegated cows).

Appadhānassāti kiṃ? Rājagavo.

What is meant by 'not principal'? Rājagavo (royal cow).

Antassāti kiṃ? Gokulaṃ.

What is meant by 'at the end'? Gokulaṃ (herd of cows).

Iti samāsantarassarāsi.

Thus, the section on the shortening of final vowels in compounds.

Pumbhāvātidesarāsi

The Section on Masculine Substitution

362. Itthiyaṃ bhāsitapumitthī pumāvekatthe ka. 331; rū. 353; nī. 714; caṃ. 5.2.29; pā. 6.3.34.

362. A feminine word that is also spoken as masculine becomes like a masculine word when followed by a feminine word in apposition.

‘Ekatthe’ti tulyādhikaraṇe, itthiyaṃ vattamāne ekatthe uttarapade pare kadāci bhāsitapumo itthiliṅgasaddo pumā iva hoti. Caturaṅgamidaṃ vidhānaṃ, pubbapadaṃ itthiliṅgañca bhāsitapumañca siyā, parapadaṃ niyatitthiliṅgañca pubbapadena ekatthañca siyāti.

'Ekatthe' means in apposition. When followed by a subsequent word that is feminine and in apposition, a feminine word that is also spoken as masculine sometimes becomes like a masculine word. This is a four-limbed rule: the prior word must be feminine and also spoken as masculine, and the subsequent word must be of a fixed feminine gender and in apposition with the prior word.

Dīghā jaṅghā yassa so dīghajaṅgho, puriso, dīghajaṅghā, itthī, dīghajaṅghaṃ, kulaṃ.

Dīghā jaṅghā yassa so dīghajaṅgho, a man; dīghajaṅghā, a woman; dīghajaṅghaṃ, a family.

Ettha ca ye saddā katthaci pulliṅgarūpā honti, katthaci itthipaccayayuttā itthiliṅgarūpā, te bhāsitapumā nāma. Dīgho maggo, dīghā ratti, gato puriso, gatā itthī, kumāro, kumārī, brāhmaṇo, brāhmaṇī iccādi.

Here, those words which are sometimes masculine in form and sometimes feminine in form with feminine suffixes, are called 'spoken as masculine.' For example, dīgho maggo—a long road, dīghā ratti—a long night, gato puriso—a man gone, gatā itthī—a woman gone, kumāro—a boy, kumārī—a girl, brāhmaṇo—a brahmin, brāhmaṇī—a brahmin woman, and so on.

Ye pana itthipaccayayuttā niccaṃ itthiliṅgarūpā honti, te bhāsitapumā nāma na honti, kaññā, paññā, saddhā, nadī, itthī, pathavī iccādi. Tathā sabhāvaitthiliṅgāpi niyatapunnapuṃsakaliṅgāpi bhāsitapumā na honti, devatā, ratti, dhenu, vadhū, sakko, devo, brahmā, ratanaṃ, saraṇaṃ iccādi.

Those which always have feminine forms with feminine suffixes are not called 'spoken as masculine'—such as kaññā (maiden), paññā (wisdom), saddhā (faith), nadī (river), itthī (woman), pathavī (earth), and so on. Similarly, those with naturally feminine genders or fixed masculine or neuter genders are not called 'spoken as masculine'—such as devatā (deity), ratti (night), dhenu (cow), vadhū (bride), sakko (Sakka), devo (god), brahmā (Brahmā), ratanaṃ (jewel), saraṇaṃ (refuge), and so on.

Idha pana dīghasaddo “dīgho bālāna saṃsāro”ti dha. pa. 60 ādīsu bhāsitapumo, so visesyaliṅgānugatavasena idha itthipaccayayutto [M 0.0259] itthiliṅgasaddo nāma. Iminā suttena pumbhāvātidese kate tattha āpaccayo antaradhāyati, ‘ghapassantassāppadhānassā’ti suttena samāsantassa ākārassa rassattaṃ, kumārī bhariyā yassa so kumārabhariyo, īpaccayanivatti. Yuvati jāyā yassa so yuvajāyo, tipaccayanivatti. Brahmabandhū bhariyā yassa so brahmabandhubhariyo, ūpaccayanivatti.

Here, however, the word dīgha (long), as in phrases like ‘dīgho bālāna saṃsāro’ (long is the cycle for fools), is a ‘spoken as masculine’ word. Due to its conformity with the gender of the qualified word, here it is a feminine word with a feminine suffix. By this rule, when masculine substitution is made, the ā suffix disappears; according to the rule ‘ghapassantassāppadhānassā,’ the long ā at the end of the prior member of the compound becomes short. Kumārī bhariyā yassa so kumārabhariyo (he whose wife is a maiden is called kumārabhariyo)—here the suffix ī is removed. Yuvati jāyā yassa so yuvajāyo (he whose wife is a young woman is called yuvajāyo)—here the suffix ti is removed. Brahmabandhū bhariyā yassa so brahmabandhubhariyo (he whose wife is a kinswoman of Brahmā is called brahmabandhubhariyo)—here the suffix ū is removed.

Itthiyanti kiṃ? Kumārī ratanaṃ yassa so kumārīratano, puriso, idha parapadaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ na hoti, tasmā pumbhāvātideso na kātabbo, yadi kareyya, kumāro ratanaṃ yassa kumāraratanoti evaṃ aniṭṭhattho bhaveyya.

What is meant by 'in the feminine'? Kumārī ratanaṃ yassa so kumārīratano (he whose jewel is a maiden is a kumārīratano), a man. Here, the subsequent word is not feminine in gender, therefore masculine substitution should not be applied. If it were applied, it would result in an undesirable meaning such as kumāro ratanaṃ yassa kumāraratano (he whose jewel is a boy is a kumāraratano).

Ekattheti kiṃ? Kumārīsu bhatti yassa so kumārībhattiko. Evaṃ samaṇībhattiko, brāhmaṇībhattiko, samāsante ko, idha parapadaṃ pubbapadena ekatthaṃ na hoti, tasmā pumbhāvātideso na kātabbo, yadi kareyya, kumāresu bhatti yassa so kumārabhattikoti evaṃ aniṭṭhattho bhaveyya.

What is meant by 'in the same meaning'? Kumārīsu bhatti yassa so kumārībhattiko (he whose devotion is to maidens is a kumārībhattiko). Similarly, samaṇībhattiko (he whose devotion is to female ascetics), brāhmaṇībhattiko (he whose devotion is to Brahmin women); ka is at the end of the compound. Here, the subsequent word does not refer to the same meaning as the prior word, therefore masculine substitution should not be applied. If it were applied, it would result in an undesirable meaning like kumāresu bhatti yassa so kumārabhattiko (he whose devotion is to boys is a kumārabhattiko).

Itthīti kiṃ? Daṭṭhabbaṭṭhena diṭṭhi, gāmaṇikulaṃ diṭṭhi yena so gāmaṇidiṭṭhi, idha gāmaṇisaddo bhāsitapumo hoti, idha pana kulavācakattā napuṃsakaliṅge tiṭṭhati, itthipaccayo natthi, tasmā pumbhāvātidesakiccaṃ natthi.

What is meant by 'feminine'? Diṭṭhi in the sense of that which is to be seen. Gāmaṇikulaṃ diṭṭhi yena so gāmaṇidiṭṭhi (he by whom the headman's family is seen is a gāmaṇidiṭṭhi). Here, the word gāmaṇi is spoken as masculine, but here, because it denotes a family, it remains in the neuter gender. There is no feminine suffix, so there is no function for masculine substitution.

Bhāsitapumoti kiṃ? Saddhā pakati yassa so saddhāpakatiko. Evaṃ paññāpakatiko, idha pubbapadaṃ niyatitthiliṅgattā bhāsitapumaṃ na hotīti. Saddhādhano, paññādhano, saddhādhuro paññādhuro iccatra duvaṅgavekallaṃ hoti.

What is meant by 'spoken as masculine'? Saddhā pakati yassa so saddhāpakatiko (he whose nature is faith is a saddhāpakatiko). Similarly, paññāpakatiko (he whose nature is wisdom). Here, because the prior word has a fixed feminine gender, it is not spoken as masculine. In saddhādhano (one whose wealth is faith), paññādhano (one whose wealth is wisdom), saddhādhuro (one whose burden is faith), paññādhuro (one whose burden is wisdom), there is a deficiency of two factors.

Kammadhārayamhi ka. 332; rū. 343; nī. 716 pana ‘ekatthe’ti padaṃ visuṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ na hoti anekatthassa idha asambhavato. Dīghā ca sā jaṅghā cāti [M 0.0260] dīghajaṅghā, kumārī ca sā bhariyā cāti kumārabhariyā. Evaṃ khattiyakaññā, brāhmaṇakaññā, yuvati ca sā bhariyā cāti yuvabhariyā, brahmabandhū ca sā bhariyā cāti brahmabandhubhariyā.

In the case of a Kammadhāraya compound, however, the word ‘ekatthe’ is not a separate element because a different referent is not possible here. Dīghā ca sā jaṅghā cāti dīghajaṅghā (long and that is a leg, thus dīghajaṅghā [a long leg]), kumārī ca sā bhariyā cāti kumārabhariyā (a maiden and that is a wife, thus kumārabhariyā [a maiden-wife]). Similarly, khattiyakaññā (Khattiya maiden), brāhmaṇakaññā (Brahmin maiden), yuvati ca sā bhariyā cāti yuvabhariyā (young and that is a wife, thus yuvabhariyā [a young wife]), brahmabandhū ca sā bhariyā cāti brahmabandhubhariyā (a kinswoman of Brahmā and that is a wife, thus brahmabandhubhariyā [a kinswoman-of-Brahmā-wife]).

Itthiyanti kiṃ? Kumārī ca sā ratanañcāti kumārīratanaṃ. Evaṃ samaṇīpadumaṃ.

What is meant by 'in the feminine'? Kumārī ca sā ratanañcāti kumārīratanaṃ (a maiden and that is a jewel, thus kumārīratanaṃ [a maiden-jewel]). Similarly, samaṇīpadumaṃ (a nun-lotus).

Itthīti kiṃ? Gāmaṇikulañca taṃ diṭṭhi cāti gāmaṇidiṭṭhi.

What is meant by 'feminine'? Gāmaṇikulañca taṃ diṭṭhi cāti gāmaṇidiṭṭhi (a headman's family and that is a view, thus gāmaṇidiṭṭhi [a headman's family-view]).

Bhāsitapumoti kiṃ? Saddhāpakati, gaṅgānadī, taṇhānadī, pathavīdhātu.

What is meant by 'spoken as masculine'? Saddhāpakati (nature of faith), gaṅgānadī (Ganges river), taṇhānadī (river of craving), pathavīdhātu (earth element).

Saññāsaddesu pana caturaṅgayuttepi vidhānaṃ na hoti, nandādevī, nandāpokkharaṇī, kāyagatāsati, paṭhamāvibhatti, dutiyāvibhatti, pañcamīvibhatti, chaṭṭhīvibhatti iccādi.

In the case of proper nouns, however, this rule does not apply even when the four factors are present—Nandādevī, Nandāpokkharaṇī, kāyagatāsati (mindfulness directed to the body), paṭhamāvibhatti (the first case ending), dutiyāvibhatti (the second case ending), pañcamīvibhatti (the fifth case ending), chaṭṭhīvibhatti (the sixth case ending), and so on.

363. Kvaci paccaye ka. 332; rū. 343; nī. 716; caṃ. 5.2.31; pā. 6.3.35.

363. Sometimes, before a suffix.

Paccaye pare kadāci bhāsitapumo itthiliṅgasaddo kvaci pumāva hoti.

When a suffix follows, a feminine word that is also spoken as masculine sometimes becomes like a masculine word.

Byattatarā, byattatamā, ettha ca byattānaṃ itthīnaṃ atisayena byattāti byattatarā, byattatamāti attho. Evaṃ paṇḍitatarā, paṇḍitatamā iccādi.

Byattatarā (more skilled), byattatamā (most skilled)—here, among skilled women, the one exceedingly skilled is called 'more skilled' or 'most skilled.' Similarly, paṇḍitatarā (more learned), paṇḍitatamā (most learned), and so on.

364. Sabbādayo vuttimatte ka. 331; rū. 353; nī. 714; caṃ. 5.2.41; pā. 6.3.35.

364. Words like sabba in a compound expression.

Vuttimatte ṭhāne sabbādināmakā sabbanāmasaddā pumāva honti.

In the context of a mere derivative expression, pronominal words, such as `sabba` and others, become masculine.

Sā pamukhā yassa so tappamukho. Evaṃ tappadhāno, tāya tāhi vā sampayutto taṃsampayutto. Sā eva pamukhā tappamukhā. Evaṃ tappadhānā, tassā mukhaṃ tammukhaṃ, tassaṃ gāthāyaṃ [M 0.0261] tāsu gāthāsu vā tatra, tāya gāthato tāhi vā gāthāhi tato, tassaṃ velāyaṃ tadā iccādi.

She is foremost; he of whom she is foremost is `tappamukho`. Similarly, `tappadhāno`. Associated with her or with them is `taṃsampayutto`. She herself is foremost, `tappamukhā`. Similarly, `tappadhānā`. Her face is `tammukhaṃ`. 'In that verse' or 'in those verses' becomes `tatra`; 'from that verse' or 'from those verses' becomes `tato`; 'at that time' becomes `tadā`, and so on.

Ettha ca vutti nāma samāsa, taddhitā’ yādidhātupaccayanta, vibhattipaccayantānaṃ nāmaṃ.

And here, 'vutti' is the name for a compound, a taddhita derivative, a nominal ending in a suffix from a verbal root such as -ya, or a nominal ending in a case suffix.

Iti pumbhāvātidesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on the extension of the masculine gender.

Samāsantakapaccayarāsi

The Section on the Compound-Final Suffix -ka

365. Ltitthiyūhi ko ka. 338; rū. 356; nī. 725; caṃ. 4.4.140; pā. 5.4.152.

365. The suffix -ka is added after feminine stems ending in -ī or -ū.

Aññapadatthavisaye kattuiccādīhi ltupaccayantehi itthiyaṃ ī, ūkārantehi ca bahulaṃ kapaccayo hoti.

In the context of a bahubbīhi compound, the suffix -ka is frequently added after feminine stems ending in -ī or -ū, and after stems ending in the suffix -tu, such as `kattu`.

Bahavo kattāro yasmiṃ dese so bahukattuko. Evaṃ bahuvattuko, bahukā nadiyo yasmiṃ dese so bahunadiko. Evaṃ bahuitthiko, gāmo, bahuitthikā, sabhā, bahuitthikaṃ, kulaṃ. Evaṃ bahukumārikaṃ, bahubrahmabandhuko.

A country in which there are many agents is `bahukattuko`. Similarly, `bahuvattuko` (having many speakers). A country in which there are many rivers is `bahunadiko`. Similarly, a village with many women is `bahuitthiko gāmo`; an assembly with many women is `bahuitthikā sabhā`; a family with many women is `bahuitthikaṃ kulaṃ`. Similarly, `bahukumārikaṃ` (having many maidens), `bahubrahmabandhuko` (having many kinsmen who are brahmins).

Ettha ca ‘brahmabandhū’ti rassapadaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadati, dīghapadaṃ brāhmaṇiṃ vadati, kapaccaye pare dīghānaṃ mahāvuttinā rassattaṃ icchanti.

Here, the form with a short vowel, `brahmabandhu`, denotes a brahmin male, while the form with a long vowel, `brahmabandhū`, denotes a brahmin female. When the suffix -ka follows, the shortening of the long vowel is desired according to general grammatical rule.

Bahulanti kiṃ? Bahukattā, gāmo.

Why is the word `bahulaṃ` (frequently) used? For cases such as `bahukattā gāmo` (a village with many agents).

366. Vāññato ka. 338; rū. 356; nī. 725; caṃ. 6.2.72; pā. 5.4.152.

366. Optionally, after other stems.

Aññapadatthavisaye ltitthiyūhi aññato avaṇṇivaṇṇuvaṇṇantehi bahulaṃ kapaccayo hoti vā.

In the context of a bahubbīhi compound, the suffix -ka is frequently and optionally added after stems ending in -a, -i, and -u.

Avaṇṇantamhā [M 0.0262] tāva –

First, from stems ending in -a:

Agāmakaṃ, araññaṃ, bahugāmako, janapado, sasotako, asotako, salomako, sapakkhako, bahumālako, bahumālo, bahumāyako, bahumāyo.

`Agāmakaṃ araññaṃ` (a forest without a village); `bahugāmako janapado` (a country with many villages); `sasotako` (having streams); `asotako` (without streams); `salomako` (having hair); `sapakkhako` (having wings); `bahumālako` or `bahumālo` (having many garlands); `bahumāyako` or `bahumāyo` (having many illusions).

Ivaṇṇantamhā –

From stems ending in -i:

Sundarā diṭṭhi yassa so sammādiṭṭhiko, sammādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhiko, micchādiṭṭhi, matapatikā, itthī, saddhāpakatiko, paññāpakatiko, bahuhatthiko, bahudaṇḍiko.

He whose view is good is `sammādiṭṭhiko` or `sammādiṭṭhi` (one with right view); `micchādiṭṭhiko` or `micchādiṭṭhi` (one with wrong view); `matapatikā itthī` (a woman whose husband is dead); `saddhāpakatiko` (one whose nature is faith); `paññāpakatiko` (one whose nature is wisdom); `bahuhatthiko` (having many hands); `bahudaṇḍiko` (having many staffs).

Uvaṇṇantamhā –

From stems ending in -u:

Sahetuko, ahetuko, sacakkhuko, acakkhuko, sabhikkhuko, abhikkhuko, dīghāyuko, appāyuko, bahudhenuko, vajo, bahurattaññuko, bhikkhusaṅgho.

`Sahetuko` (having a cause), `ahetuko` (without a cause); `sacakkhuko` (having eyes), `acakkhuko` (without eyes); `sabhikkhuko` (having monks), `abhikkhuko` (without monks); `dīghāyuko` (long-lived), `appāyuko` (short-lived); `bahudhenuko vajo` (a cow-pen with many cows); `bahurattaññuko bhikkhusaṅgho` (a community of monks with many long-ordained members).

Itthiliṅge kamhi pare akārassa mahāvuttinā vā ‘adhātussa ke…’ti suttena vā bahulaṃ ikārattaṃ hoti, bahuputtikā, itthī, bahuputtakā vā, ekaputtikā, ekaputtakā iccādi.

In the feminine gender, when the suffix -ka follows, the final vowel -a frequently becomes -i, either by general grammatical rule or by the sutta `adhātussa ke…`. For example: `bahuputtikā itthī` (a woman with many sons), or `bahuputtakā`; `ekaputtikā` (a woman with one son), or `ekaputtakā`, and so on.

Iti samāsantakapaccayarāsi.

Thus ends the section on the compound-final suffix -ka.

Samāsantaapaccayarāsi

The Section on the Compound-Final Suffix -a

367. Samāsanta ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.52; pā. 5.4.68; ‘tva’ (bahūsu).

367. At the end of a compound.

‘Samāsanto+a’ iti dvipadamidaṃ, samāsanto hutvā apaccayo hotīti attho. Adhikārasuttamidaṃ.

This is a two-word rule: `samāsanto` and `a`. The meaning is that the suffix -a occurs at the end of a compound. This is a governing rule.

368. Pāpādīhi bhūmiyā ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.72; …pe… 5.4.75; ‘godāvarīnaṃ’ (bahūsu).

368. After `pāpa` and other such words, with `bhūmi`.

Pāpādīhi [M 0.0263] parāya bhūmiyā samāsanto ahoti, ‘bhūmisaddassā’ti vattabbe niyatitthiliṅgadassanatthaṃ ‘bhūmiyā’ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ aññatthapi.

The compound-final suffix -a is added to `bhūmi` when it follows `pāpa` and other such words. Although `bhūmisaddassa` (of the word `bhūmi`) should have been stated, `bhūmiyā` is used to indicate its fixed feminine gender. This is also the case elsewhere.

Pāpānaṃ bhūmi pāpabhūmaṃ, pāpānaṃ uppattibhūmityattho, jātiyā bhūmi jātibhūmaṃ, satthujātaraṭṭhaṃ. Evaṃ pacchābhūmaṃ, majjhimadese pacchābhāgaraṭṭhaṃ.

`Pāpānaṃ bhūmi` becomes `pāpabhūmaṃ`, meaning the ground for the arising of evils. `Jātiyā bhūmi` becomes `jātibhūmaṃ`, the land where the Teacher was born. Similarly, `pacchābhūmaṃ`, the country in the western part of the Middle Country.

369. Saṅkhyāhi ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.73; pā. 5.4.75.

369. After numerals.

Saṅkhyāhi parāya bhūmiyā samāsanto a hoti.

The compound-final suffix -a is added to `bhūmi` when it follows a numeral.

Dve bhūmiyo etthāti dvibhūmo, dvibhūmako, pāsādo, dvibhūmiko vā, tisso bhūmiyo etesanti vā tīsu bhūmisu pariyāpannāti vā tebhūmakā, dhammā, catubhūmakā, dhammā, tebhūmikā, catubhūmikā vā. Digumhi-dve bhūmiyo dvibhūmaṃ, tisso bhūmiyo tibhūmaṃ, catasso bhūmiyo catubhūmaṃ iccādi.

That in which there are two floors is `dvibhūmo` or `dvibhūmako pāsādo` (a two-storied palace), or optionally `dvibhūmiko`. Those phenomena in which there are three planes, or which are comprised within three planes, are `tebhūmakā dhammā` (phenomena of the three planes) or `catubhūmakā dhammā` (phenomena of the four planes); optionally `tebhūmikā` or `catubhūmikā`. In a Digu compound: `dve bhūmiyo` becomes `dvibhūmaṃ`; `tisso bhūmiyo` becomes `tibhūmaṃ`; `catasso bhūmiyo` becomes `catubhūmaṃ`, and so on.

370. Nadīgodhāvarīnaṃ ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.73; pā. 5.4.75.

370. Of `nadī` and `godhāvarī`.

Saṅkhyāhi parāsaṃ nadī, godhāvarīnaṃ samāsanto a hoti.

After numerals, from 'nadī' and 'godhāvarī', the compound-final suffix 'a' occurs.

Pañca nadiyo pañcanadaṃ, pañca vā nadiyo yasmiṃ padese so pañcanado, satta godhāvariyo sattagodhāvaraṃ.

Five rivers are 'pañcanadaṃ'; or, a region in which there are five rivers is 'pañcanado'. Seven Godhāvarī rivers are 'sattagodhāvaraṃ'.

371. Asaṅkhyehi caṅgulyānaññāsaṅkhyatthesu ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.74; pā. 5.4.86.

371. And after non-numerals, from 'aṅguli', in senses other than those of 'other' and 'innumerable'.

Aññattho ca asaṅkhyattho ca aññāsaṅkhyatthā. Tattha ‘aññattho’ti aññapadattho bahubbīhisamāso, ‘asaṅkhyattho’ti asaṅkhyatthasamāso [M 0.0264] abyayībhāvasamāsoti vuttaṃ hoti, na aññāsaṅkhyatthā anaññāsaṅkhyatthā, aññāsaṅkhyatthavajjitesu samāsesu asaṅkhyehi upasaggehi ca saṅkhyāhi ca parāya aṅguliyā samāsanto a hoti. Casaddena “sugataṅgulena, pamāṇaṅgulena” iccādīni sijjhanti.

The sense of 'other' and the sense of 'innumerable' are 'aññāsaṅkhyatthā'. Here, 'aññattho' is said to be a Bahubbīhi compound having the sense of another word; 'asaṅkhyattho' is said to be an Avyayībhāva compound having the sense of 'innumerable'. 'Anaññāsaṅkhyatthā' are senses other than 'aññāsaṅkhyatthā'. In compounds excluding the senses of 'other' and 'innumerable', after non-numerals (prefixes) and numerals, from 'aṅguli' which follows, the compound-final suffix 'a' occurs. By the word 'ca', forms such as 'sugataṅgulena' and 'pamāṇaṅgulena' are established.

Aṅgulīhi niggataṃ niraṅgulaṃ, aṅguliyo atikkantaṃ accaṅgulaṃ, ime dve amādisamāsā, dve aṅguliyo samāhaṭāti dvaṅgulaṃ.

That which has gone out from the fingers is 'niraṅgulaṃ'; that which has surpassed the fingers is 'accaṅgulaṃ'—these two are Avyayībhāva compounds. Two fingers collected together is 'dvaṅgulaṃ'.

Anaññāsaṅkhyatthesūti kiṃ? Pañca aṅguliyo asminti pañcaṅguli, hattho. Aṅguliyā samīpaṃ upaṅguli. “Caturaṅgulaṃ kaṇṇaṃ osāretvā mahāva. 66, aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ, dvaṅgulaparamaṃ, caturaṅgulaparamaṃ, aṭṭhaṅgulaparama”ntiādīsu ‘aṅgula’nti akārantaṃ pamāṇavācīsaddantaraṃ.

Why 'in senses other than 'other' and 'innumerable''? For 'pañca aṅguliyo asmin'ti pañcaṅguli, hattho' (a hand in which there are five fingers). 'Aṅguliyā samīpaṃ upaṅguli' (near the finger). In phrases such as 'caturaṅgulaṃ kaṇṇaṃ osāretvā', 'aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ', 'dvaṅgulaparamaṃ', 'caturaṅgulaparamaṃ', and 'aṭṭhaṅgulaparamaṃ', 'aṅgula' is another 'a'-ending word that denotes a measure.

372. Dārumhaṅgulyā ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.97; pā. 5.4.114; ‘dārumyaṅgulyā’ (bahūsu).

372. From 'aṅguli' after 'dāru'.

Dārusaṅkhāte aññapadatthe pavattāya aṅguliyā samāsanto ahoti.

From 'aṅguli', when it occurs in the sense of another word designated as 'dāru', the compound-final suffix 'a' occurs.

Pañca aṅguliyo assāti pañcaṅgulaṃ, dāru. Ettha ca aṅgulipamāṇāvayavo dhaññādīnaṃ mānaviseso ‘dārū’ti vuccati.

That which has five fingers is 'pañcaṅgulaṃ', a piece of wood. And here, a specific measure for grains and so on, a component having the measure of a finger, is called 'dāru'.

373. Dīghāhovassekadesehi ca ratyā ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.75; pā. 5.4.87.

373. After 'dīgha', 'aho', 'vassa', and 'ekadesa', and from 'ratti'.

Dīgho ca aho ca vasso ca ekadeso cāti dvando, ekadeso nāma pubba, parādi, anaññāsaṅkhyatthesu dīghādīhi ca asaṅkhyehi ca saṅkhyāhi ca parāya rattiyā samāsanto a hoti. Casaddena “ciraratta”nti sijjhati.

'Dīgha', 'aho', 'vassa', and 'ekadesa' form a Dvanda compound. 'Ekadesa' refers to 'pubba', 'para', and so on. In senses other than 'other' and 'innumerable', from 'ratti' which follows 'dīgha' and others, and non-numerals and numerals, the compound-final suffix 'a' occurs. By the word 'ca', 'ciraratta' is established.

Dīghā [M 0.0265] rattiyo dīgharattaṃ, dīghā rattidivaparaṃparātyattho. Aho ca ratti ca ahorattaṃ, vassena temitā ratti vassarattaṃ, rattiyā pubbaṃ pubbarattaṃ, rattiyā paraṃ pararattaṃ, rattiyā aḍḍhaṃ aḍḍharattaṃ, rattiṃ atikkanto atiratto, dve rattiyo dvirattaṃ. Evaṃ tirattaṃ, caturattaṃ, pañcarattaṃ, chārattaṃ, vādhikārattā “ekarattaṃ, ekarattī”ti sijjhati.

Long nights are 'dīgharattaṃ', meaning a long succession of nights and days. Day and night are 'ahorattaṃ'. A night moistened by rain is 'vassarattaṃ'. The former part of the night is 'pubbarattaṃ'; the latter part of the night is 'pararattaṃ'; half of the night is 'aḍḍharattaṃ'. One who has surpassed the night is 'atiratto'. Two nights are 'dvirattaṃ'. Similarly, 'tirattaṃ', 'caturattaṃ', 'pañcarattaṃ', 'chārattaṃ'. Due to the governing rule of optionality, 'ekarattaṃ' and 'ekarattī' are established.

Anaññāsaṅkhyatthesūti kiṃ? Dīghā ratti etthāti dīgharatti, hemanto. Rattiyā samīpaṃ uparatti.

Why 'in senses other than 'other' and 'innumerable''? For 'dīghā ratti etthā'ti dīgharatti, hemanto' (winter, in which there is a long night). 'Rattiyā samīpaṃ uparatti' (near the night).

374. Go tvacatthe cālope ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.77; pā. 5.4.92.

374. From 'go', however, in a sense other than 'skin', and when there is no elision.

Acatthe ca anaññā’saṅkhyatthesu ca pavattā gosaddamhā alopaṭṭhāne samāsanto a hoti.

From the word 'go', when it occurs in a sense other than 'skin' and in senses other than 'other' and 'innumerable', the compound-final suffix 'a' occurs in a situation of non-elision.

Rañño go rājagavo, attano go sagavo, paresaṃ go paragavo, pañcagavo, pañcagavaṃ. Evaṃ dasagavaṃ.

The king's cow is 'rājagavo'; one's own cow is 'sagavo'; the cow of others is 'paragavo'; 'pañcagavo', 'pañcagavaṃ'. Similarly, 'dasagavaṃ'.

Alopeti kiṃ? Pañcahi gohi kīto pañcagu. Ettha ca tena kītoti etasmiṃ atthe taddhitapaccayassa lopo, tena ayaṃ apaccayo na hoti, ‘gossū’ti ossuttaṃ.

Why 'without elision'? For 'pañcahi gohi kīto pañcagu' (bought with five cows). Here, in the sense of 'bought with that', there is elision of a taddhita suffix; therefore this 'a' suffix does not occur. By the rule 'gossu', the 'o' becomes 'u'.

Acattheti kiṃ? Gavajā ca gāvo ca gavajagavo, yomhi gossa gavattaṃ.

Why 'in a sense other than skin'? For 'gavajā ca gāvo ca gavajagavo', in which 'go' has the meaning of 'cow'.

Anaññāsaṅkhyatthesūti kiṃ? Cittagu, upagu.

Why 'in senses other than 'other' and 'innumerable''? 'Cittagu', 'upagu'.

375. Rattidiva dāragava caturassā ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.62; pā. 5.4.77.

375. 'Rattidiva', 'dāragava', 'caturassa'.

Ete tayo saddā aantā nipaccante.

These three words are irregularly formed as ending in 'a'.

Ratti ca divā ca rattidivaṃ, dārā ca gāvo ca dāragavaṃ, catasso assiyo yassa so caturasso, apaccayo, assissa issa attaṃ.

Night and day are 'rattidivaṃ'. Wives and cows are 'dāragavaṃ'. He who has four mares is 'caturasso'; the 'a' suffix is added, and the 'i' of 'assi' becomes 'a'.

376. Āyāmenugavaṃ ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.69; pā. 5.4.83.

376. In the sense of length, 'anugavaṃ'.

Āyāme [M 0.0266] gamyamāne anugavanti nipaccate.

When length is implied, 'anugavaṃ' is irregularly formed.

Gohi anuṭṭhitaṃ sakaṭaṃ anugavaṃ.

A cart yoked along with the oxen is 'anugavaṃ'.

Āyāmeti kiṃ? Gunnaṃ pacchā anugu.

Why 'in the sense of length'? 'Gunnaṃ pacchā anugu' (behind the cows).

377. Akkhismāññatthe ka. 337; rū. 350; nī. 722; caṃ. 4.4.96; pā. 5.4.113.

377. From 'akkhi', in the sense of another.

Aññapadatthe pavattā akkhimhā samāsanto a hoti.

From 'akkhi', when it occurs in the sense of another word, the compound-final suffix 'a' occurs.

Visālāni akkhīni yassa so visālakkho, virūpāni akkhīni yassa so virūpakkho, anekasahassāni akkhīni yassa so sahassakkho, lohitāni akkhīni yassa so lohitakkho. Evaṃ nīlakkho, nīlakkhi vā. Bahulādhikārā anaññatthepi, akkhīnaṃ paṭimukhaṃ paccakkhaṃ, akkhīnaṃ parabhāgo parokkhaṃ, akkhīnaṃ tirobhāgo tirokkhaṃ. Akkhisaddena cettha pañcindriyāni gayhanti.

He whose eyes are large is 'visālakkho'; he whose eyes are deformed is 'virūpakkho'; he who has a thousand eyes is 'sahassakkho'; he whose eyes are red is 'lohitakkho'. Similarly, 'nīlakkho', or optionally 'nīlakkhi'. Due to the governing rule of 'bahula', even in senses other than 'other', what is before the eyes is 'paccakkhaṃ'; what is beyond the eyes is 'parokkhaṃ'; what is hidden from the eyes is 'tirokkhaṃ'. And here, by the word 'akkhi', the five sense faculties are understood.

Mahāvuttinā kvaci samāsanto a, ā, ipaccayā honti.

According to the Mahāvutti, the compound-final suffixes 'a', 'ā', and 'i' sometimes occur.

Tattha apaccaye –

Therein, regarding the suffix 'a':

Vāyuno sakhā vāyusakho, vāyusaṅkhāto sakhā assāti vā vāyusakho, aggi, sabbesaṃ piyā’piyamajjhattānaṃ sakhāti sabbasakho, sabbe vā sakhāyo assāti sabbasakho, mettāvihārī. “Sabbamitto sabbasakho”ti theragā. 648 pāḷi. Pāpānaṃ sakhāti pāpasakho, pāpā sakhāro yassāti vā pāpasakho. “Pāpamitto pāpasakho”ti dī. ni. 3.253 pāḷi. Pahito pesito attā yenāti pahitatto, majjhimo attā sabhāvo yassāti majjhatto, chātaṃ ajjhattasantānaṃ saṇṭhānaṃ (mūlapāṭhe) yassāti chātajjhatto, suhito attā yassāti suhitatto[M 0.0267], yato saṃyato attā yassāti yatatto, ṭhito attā assāti ṭhitattoiccādi.

The friend of the wind is 'vāyusakho'; or, he whose friend is designated as wind is 'vāyusakho', that is, fire. The friend of all—the beloved, the unloved, and the neutral—is 'sabbasakho'; or, he who has all as friends is 'sabbasakho', that is, one dwelling in loving-kindness. The Pāli text states: 'sabbamitto sabbasakho' (a friend to all, a companion to all). The friend of evils is 'pāpasakho'; or, he whose companions are evil is 'pāpasakho'. The Pāli text states: 'pāpamitto pāpasakho' (an evil friend, an evil companion). He by whom the self is sent forth or dispatched is 'pahitatto'; he whose self or nature is in the middle is 'majjhatto'; he whose inner continuity is hungry is 'chātajjhatto'; he whose self is well-fed is 'suhitatto'; he whose self is restrained is 'yatatto'; he whose self is established is 'ṭhitatto', and so on.

Āpaccaye –

Regarding the suffix 'ā':

Paccakkho dhammo yassāti paccakkhadhammā, chādetīti chado, moho, vivaṭo chado yasminti vivaṭacchadā, sammāsambuddho.

He whose Dhamma is directly perceptible is 'paccakkhadhammā'. That which covers is 'chado', that is, delusion. He from whom the covering is removed is 'vivaṭacchadā', the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Ipaccaye –

Regarding the suffix 'i':

Sundaro gandho yassāti sugandhi, kucchito gandho yassāti duggandhi, pūtino gandho yassāti pūtigandhi, surabhino gandho surabhigandhi. “Sarīrassa sugandhino, guṇagandhiyutto aha”nti pāḷi.

He whose fragrance is beautiful is 'sugandhi'; he whose fragrance is foul is 'duggandhi'; he whose fragrance is putrid is 'pūtigandhi'; he whose fragrance is delightful is 'surabhigandhi'. The Pāli text states: 'Of a fragrant body, I am endowed with the fragrance of virtue.'

Iti samāsantaapaccayarāsi.

Thus ends the section on suffixes at the end of compounds.

Nānādesarāsi

Section on Various Substitutions

378. Uttarapade ka. 333-334; rū. 344-345; nī. 717-718.

378. When a subsequent word follows.

Uttarapade pare pubbapade vidhi hotīti attho. Adhikārasuttamidaṃ.

When the subsequent word follows, a rule applies to the preceding word; this is the meaning. This is a governing rule.

“Abrāhmaṇo, anariyo, abhikkhuko, ananto”iccādīsu samāse uttarapade pare na-kārassa a, ana honti.

In compounds such as 'abrāhmaṇo', 'anariyo', 'abhikkhuko', 'ananto', and so on, when the subsequent word follows, the particle 'na' becomes 'a' or 'ana'.

379. Nakhādayo ka. 328; rū. 352; nī. 708; caṃ. 5.2.95; pā. 6.3.75.

379. Nakha and so forth.

Nakhādayo saddā napakatikā sijjhanti.

Words such as 'nakha' and so forth are formed irregularly.

Nā’ssa khamatthīti nakho, ‘kha’nti sukhaṃ, dukkhañca, nā’ssa kulamatthīti nakulo, evaṃnāmako brāhmaṇo, pumassa sakaṃ puṃsakaṃ [M 0.0268] natthi puṃsakaṃ etasminti napuṃsako, khañjanaṃ vekallagamanaṃ khattaṃ, natthi khattaṃ etassāti nakkhattaṃ, kaṃ vuccati sukhaṃ, tabbiruddhattā akaṃ vuccati dukkhaṃ, natthi akaṃ etasminti nāko, saggo, na muñcatīti namuci, māro. Na galati na cavatīti nagaraṃ, gehe vattabbe ‘agāra’nti sijjhati.

He has no 'kha', hence 'nakho' (nail). 'Kha' means pleasure and also pain. He has no family, hence 'nakulo' (mongoose), or a brahmin of that name. That in which there is no masculinity is 'napuṃsako' (neuter). The movement of a wagtail is crooked, which is 'khattaṃ'; that which has no crookedness is 'nakkhattaṃ' (star). 'Kaṃ' is said to be pleasure; because it is the opposite, 'akaṃ' is said to be pain. That in which there is no pain is 'nāko', heaven. He does not release, hence 'Namuci', that is, Māra. It does not perish nor pass away, hence 'nagaraṃ' (city). When a house is to be spoken of, 'agāra' is formed.

380. Nago vā pāṇini ka. 333-334; rū. 344-345; nī. 717-718; caṃ. 5.2.96; pā. 6.3.77; ‘nago vāppāṇini’ (bahūsu).

380. Or 'nago' according to Pāṇini.

Apāṇimhi nagoti sijjhati vā.

Alternatively, 'nago' is formed when the meaning is not a living creature.

Na gacchantīti nagā, rukkhā. Nagā, pabbatā. Agā, rukkhā, agā, pabbatā.

They do not go, hence 'nagā', that is, trees. 'Nagā' also means mountains. 'Agā' means trees, and 'agā' also means mountains.

Apāṇinīti kiṃ? Ago vasalo kiṃ tena. Ettha ‘ago’ti duggatajano, ‘vasalo’ti lāmako, ‘kiṃ tenā’ti nindāvacanaṃ, “sītenā”tipi pāṭho. Evaṃ neke, aneke, nekāni, anekāni iccādi.

Why the specification 'apāṇini'? 'An outcaste who cannot move, what of him?' Here, 'ago' means a destitute person; 'vasalo' means a base person; 'kiṃ tena' is a term of censure. There is also the reading 'sītena'. Similarly, 'neke', 'aneke', 'nekāni', 'anekāni', and so on.

Iti na-rāsi.

Thus ends the section on 'na'.

381. Sahassa soññatthe ka. 404; rū. 370; nī. 859; caṃ. 5.2.97; pā. 6.3.82.

381. Of 'saha', 'so' in the sense of another word.

Aññapadatthe samāse uttarapade pare sahassa so hoti vā.

In a compound that refers to another word, when a subsequent word follows, 'saha' optionally becomes 'so'.

Puttena saha yo vattatīti saputto, sahaputto.

He who exists together with his son is 'saputto' or 'sahaputto'.

Aññattheti kiṃ? Saha katvā, saha yujjhitvā.

Why the specification 'in the sense of another word'? For example: 'saha katvā' (having done together), 'saha yujjhitvā' (having fought together).

382. Saññāyaṃ ka. 404; rū. 370; nī. 859; caṃ. 5.2.98; pā. 6.3.78.

382. In a name.
