525. Mātito ca bhaginiyaṃ cho ka. 352; rū. 376; nī. 765.

525. Mātito ca bhaginiyaṃ cho .

Mātito pitito ca bhaginiyaṃ cho hoti.

Mātito pitito ca bhaginiyaṃ cho hoti.

Mātu bhaginī mātucchā udā. 22, pitu bhaginī pitucchā saṃ. ni. 2.243.

Mātu bhaginī mātucchā , pitu bhaginī pitucchā .

526. Mātāpitūsvāmaho ka. 352; rū. 376; nī. 765; caṃ. 3.1.60; pā. 4.2.36.

526. Mātāpitūsvāmaho .

Mātāpitūhi tesaṃ mātāpitūsu āmaho hoti.

Mātāpitūhi tesaṃ mātāpitūsu āmaho hoti.

Mātu mātā mātāmahī, mātu pitā mātāmaho ma. ni. 2.411, pitu mātā pitāmahī, pitu pitā pitāmaho.

Mātu mātā mātāmahī, mātu pitā mātāmaho , pitu mātā pitāmahī, pitu pitā pitāmaho.

Iti kularāsi.

Iti kularāsi.

Hita, sādhu, araharāsi

Hita, sādhu, araharāsi

527. Hite [M 0.0329] reyyaṇa ka. 352; rū. 376; nī. 765.

527. Hite reyyaṇa .

Mātāpitūhi tesaṃ hite reyyaṇa hoti.

Mātāpitūhi tesaṃ hite reyyaṇa hoti.

Mātu hito metteyyo, pitu hito petteyyo. Mātāpitūsu suppaṭipanno.

Mātu hito metteyyo, pitu hito petteyyo. Mātāpitūsu suppaṭipanno.

528. Iyo hite ka. 356; rū. 381; nī. 773.

528. Iyo hite .

Tassa hitanti atthe iyo hoti.

Tassa hitanti atthe iyo hoti.

Upādānānaṃ hitaṃ upādāniyaṃ. Evaṃ oghaniyaṃ, yoganiyaṃ, ganthaniyaṃ, nīvaraṇiyaṃ, suttavibhattiyā aññatthesupi iyo, samānodare sayito sodariyo.

Upādānānaṃ hitaṃ upādāniyaṃ. Evaṃ oghaniyaṃ, yoganiyaṃ, ganthaniyaṃ, nīvaraṇiyaṃ, suttavibhattiyā aññatthesupi iyo, samānodare sayito sodariyo.

529. Cakkhvādito sso ka. 353; rū. 378; nī. 767.

529. Cakkhvādito sso .

Tassa hitanti atthe cakkhvādīhi sso hoti.

Tassa hitanti atthe cakkhvādīhi sso hoti.

Cakkhussa hitaṃ cakkhussaṃ a. ni. 5.208, subharūpaṃ cakkhubhesajjañca. Āyuno hitaṃ āyussaṃ a. ni. 5.231, āyuvaḍḍhanavidhi.

Cakkhussa hitaṃ cakkhussaṃ , subharūpaṃ cakkhubhesajjañca. Āyuno hitaṃ āyussaṃ , āyuvaḍḍhanavidhi.

530. Ṇyo tattha sādhu ka. 353; rū. 378; nī. 767; caṃ. 3.4.100, 103; pā. 4.4.98, 103, 105.

530. Ṇyo tattha sādhu .

Tasmiṃ sādhūti atthe ṇyo hoti.

The suffix 'ṇya' occurs in the sense of 'good in that'.

Sabhāyaṃ sādhu sabbho, ‘sādhū’ti kusalo yogyo hito vā. Mittānaṃ hitaṃ mettaṃ. Suttavibhāgā aññatrapi ṇyo, rathaṃ vahatīti racchā, rathavīthi.

Good in an assembly is 'sabbho'. 'Sādhu' means skilled, suitable, or beneficial. Beneficial to friends is 'mettaṃ'. From the Suttavibhāga and also elsewhere, the suffix 'ṇya' is seen; for example, 'rathaṃ vahatīti racchā' (that which carries a chariot is a street), meaning a chariot path.

531. Kammāniyaññā ka. 353; rū. 378; nī. 767.

531. The suffixes 'niya' and 'ñña' from 'kamma'.

Tasmiṃ [M 0.0330] sādhūti atthe kammamhā niya, ññā honti.

In the sense of 'good in that', the suffixes 'niya' and 'ñña' occur after 'kamma'.

Kamme sādhu kammaniyaṃ, kammaññaṃ.

Good in action is 'kammaniyaṃ' or 'kammaññaṃ'.

532. Kathāditiko ka. 353; rū. 378; nī. 767; caṃ. 3.4.104; pā. 4.4.102.

532. The suffix 'ika' from 'kathā' and so on.

Tattha sādhūti atthe kathādīhi iko hoti.

In the sense of 'good therein', the suffix 'ika' occurs after 'kathā' and so on.

Kathāyaṃ sādhu kathiko, dhammakathāyaṃ sādhu dhammakathiko, saṅgāme sādhu saṅgāmiko, gāmavāse sādhu gāmavāsiko, upavāse sādhu upavāsiko.

Good in discourse is a 'kathiko' (speaker); good in Dhamma-discourse is a 'dhammakathiko' (Dhamma-speaker); good in battle is a 'saṅgāmiko' (warrior); good in village-dwelling is a 'gāmavāsiko' (villager); good in fasting is an 'upavāsiko' (one who fasts).

533. Pathādīhi ṇeyyo ka. 352; rū. 376; nī. 765; caṃ. 3.4.105; pā. 4.4.104.

533. The suffix 'ṇeyya' from 'patha' and so on.

Tattha sādhūti atthe pathādīhi ṇeyyo hoti.

In the sense of 'good therein', the suffix 'ṇeyya' occurs after 'patha' and so on.

Pathe sādhu pātheyyaṃ, saṃ vuccati dhanaṃ, tassa pati sapati, sapatimhi sādhu sāpateyyaṃ.

Good on the path is 'pātheyyaṃ' (provisions). 'Saṃ' is called wealth; its master is 'sapati'. Good in a master is 'sāpateyyaṃ' (property).

534. Dakkhiṇāyārahe ka. 352; rū. 376; nī. 765; caṃ. 4.1.80; pā. 5.1.69.

534. From 'dakkhiṇā' in the sense of 'worthy'.

Dakkhiṇāsaddamhā arahatthe ṇeyyo hoti.

From the word 'dakkhiṇā', the suffix 'ṇeyya' occurs in the sense of 'worthy'.

Dakkhiṇaṃ arahatīti dakkhiṇeyyo.

One who is worthy of an offering is a 'dakkhiṇeyyo'.

535. Āyo tumantā ka. 352; rū. 376; nī. 765; ‘rāyo tumantā’ (bahūsu).

535. The suffix 'āya' after words ending in '-tuṃ'.

Tumantamhā arahatthe āyo hoti.

After a word ending in '-tuṃ', the suffix 'āya' occurs in the sense of 'worthy'.

Ghātetuṃ [M 0.0331] arahatīti ghātetāyo, jāpetuṃ arahatīti jāpetāyo, ‘jāpetu’nti hāpetuṃ, pabbājetuṃ arahatīti pabbājetāyo, mahāvuttinā āyamhi sabinduno ussa lopo.

One worthy of being killed is 'ghātetāyo'; one worthy of being ruined is 'jāpetāyo'—'jāpetuṃ' means 'hāpetuṃ' (to cause to be deprived); one worthy of being banished is 'pabbājetāyo'. According to the Mahāvutti, when 'āya' follows, the 'u' with the bindu is elided.

Iti hita, sādhu, araharāsi.

Thus ends the section on 'beneficial', 'good', and 'worthy'.

Vikatirāsi

The Section on Modifications

536. Tassa vikārāvayavesu ṇa ṇika ṇeyyamayā ka. 352, 351, 372; rū. 376, 374, 385; nī. 765, 764, 798; caṃ. 3.3.103; pā. 4.3.134.

536. In the sense of its modifications and parts, the suffixes 'ṇa', 'ṇika', 'ṇeyya', and 'maya'.

Tassa vikāro, tassa avayavoti atthesu ṇādayo honti, pakatiyā uttari avatthantarāpatti vikāro.

In the senses 'its modification' and 'its part', the suffixes beginning with 'ṇa' occur. A modification is the attainment of another state beyond the original nature.

Udumbarassa vikati odumbaraṃ, bhasmā, udumbarassa avayavo odumbaraṃ, paṇṇādi. Kapotāvayavo kāpotaṃ, maṃsalohitapattādi.

The modification of the udumbara tree is 'odumbaraṃ', such as ashes. A part of the udumbara tree is 'odumbaraṃ', such as its leaves and so forth. A part of a pigeon is 'kāpotaṃ', such as its flesh, blood, feathers, and so forth.

Ṇikamhi-kappāsassa vikati kappāsikaṃ, suttaṃ vatthañca.

Regarding the suffix 'ṇika': the modification of cotton is 'kappāsikaṃ', meaning thread and cloth.

Ṇeyyamhi-eṇissa avayavo eṇeyyaṃ, maṃsaṃ. Kosakimīnaṃ vikati koseyyaṃ, suttaṃ vatthañca.

Regarding the suffix 'ṇeyya': a part of a deer is 'eṇeyyaṃ', meaning its flesh. The modification of silkworms is 'koseyyaṃ', meaning silk thread and cloth.

Mayamhi-tiṇānaṃ vikati tiṇamayaṃ. Evaṃ dārumayaṃ, naḷamayaṃ, mattikāmayaṃ, gunnaṃ vikati gomayaṃ, karīsaṃ.

Regarding the suffix 'maya': the modification of grass is 'tiṇamayaṃ'. Similarly, 'dārumayaṃ' (wooden), 'naḷamayaṃ' (made of reeds), 'mattikāmayaṃ' (earthen). The modification of cattle is 'gomayaṃ', meaning manure.

537. Jatuto mayaṇa vā ka. 372; rū. 385; nī. 798; caṃ. 3.3.108; pā. 4.3.138; jatuto saṇa vā (bahūsu).

537. From 'jatu', 'maya' and 'ṇa' optionally.

Tassa vikārāvayavesu jatuto mayaṇa hoti vā.

In the sense of its modifications and parts, the suffixes 'maya' and 'ṇa' occur optionally after 'jatu'.

Jatuno vikāro jatumayaṃ.

The modification of lac is 'jatumayaṃ'.

Iti vikatirāsi.

Thus ends the section on modifications.

Visesarāsi

The Section on Special Senses

538. Taratamissikiyiṭṭhātisaye ka. 363; rū. 390; nī. 786; caṃ. 4.3.45; pā. 5.3.55, 57.

538. The suffixes 'tara', 'tama', 'issika', 'iya', and 'iṭṭha' are used in the sense of superiority.

Atisayatthe [M 0.0332] ete paccayā bhavanti.

These suffixes occur in the sense of superiority.

Pāpānaṃ atisayena pāpoti pāpataro, pāpatamo, pāpissiko, pāpiyo, pāpiṭṭho, itthiyaṃ pāpatarā, atisayatopi atisayapaccayo hoti, atisayena pāpiṭṭho pāpiṭṭhataro.

From 'pāpa' (evil), in the sense of superiority: 'pāpatara' (more evil), 'pāpatama' (most evil), 'pāpissika' (exceedingly evil), 'pāpiyo' (more evil), 'pāpiṭṭha' (most evil). In the feminine, 'pāpatarā'. A suffix of superiority may be added even to a superlative form: one who is exceedingly the most evil is 'pāpiṭṭhataro'.

539. Vacchādīhi tanutte taro ka. 363; rū. 390; nī. 786; caṃ. 4.3.74; pā. 5.3.91.

539. From 'vaccha' and so forth, the suffix 'tara' occurs in the sense of youth or smallness.

Vacchādīhi sabbatanubhāve taro hoti.

From 'vaccha' and so forth, the suffix 'tara' occurs in the sense of complete youth or smallness.

Atitaruṇo vaccho vacchataro, itthiyaṃ vacchatarī. Yobbanassa tanutte yobbanapattānaṃ susuttassa tanutte atitaruṇo usabho ukkhataro, assabhāvassa tanutte taruṇaasso assataro, itthiyaṃ assatarī. Sāmatthiyassa tanutte taruṇausabho usabhataro.

A very young calf is 'vacchataro'; in the feminine, 'vacchatarī'. In the sense of the tenderness of youth, for those who have attained youth, in the sense of the tenderness of a very young one, a very young bull is 'ukkhataro'. In the sense of the youthfulness of a horse's nature, a young horse is 'assataro'; in the feminine, 'assatarī'. In the sense of the tenderness of strength, a young bull is 'usabhataro'.

540. Kiṃmhā niddhāraṇe taratamā ka. 363; rū. 390; nī. 786; caṃ. 4.3.77; pā. 5.3.92, 93; ‘…ratara ratamā’ (bahūsu).

540. From 'kiṃ', the suffixes 'tara' and 'tama' occur in the sense of selection.

Kiṃsaddā niddhāraṇe gamyamāne tara, tamā honti.

From the word 'kiṃ', when selection is implied, the suffixes 'tara' and 'tama' occur.

Kataro bhavataṃ devadatto, kataro bhavataṃ yaññadatto, katamo bhavataṃ devadatto, katamo bhavataṃ yaññadatto, ‘kissa ko’ti suttena tara, tamesu kissa kattaṃ.

Which of you is Devadatta? Which of you is Yaññadatta? Which of you is Devadatta? Which of you is Yaññadatta? By the rule 'kissa ko', 'kiṃ' becomes 'ka' before 'tara' and 'tama'.

Iti visesarāsi.

Thus ends the Section on Distinction.

Samūharāsi

The Section on Collections

541. Samūhe [M 0.0333] kaṇaṇaṇikā ka. 354; rū. 379; nī. 771; caṃ. 3.1.43-47; pā. 4.2.37-42.

541. The suffixes 'ka', 'ṇa', and 'ṇikā' are used in the sense of collection.

Tassa samūhoti atthe kaṇa, ṇa, ṇikā honti.

In the sense 'its collection', the suffixes 'ka', 'ṇa', and 'ṇikā' occur.

Gottapaccayantehi tāva – rājaññānaṃ samūho rājaññakaṃ, mānussakaṃ.

First, from words ending in lineage suffixes: the collection of nobles is 'rājaññakaṃ'; the collection of humans is 'mānussakaṃ'.

Ukkhādīhi-ukkhānaṃ usabhānaṃ samūho okkhakaṃ, oṭṭhānaṃ samūho oṭṭhakaṃ, urabbhānaṃ samūho orabbhakaṃ. Evaṃ rājakaṃ, rājaputtakaṃ, hatthikaṃ, dhenukaṃ, sasaṃ adenti bhakkhantīti sasādakā, tesaṃ samūho sasādakakaṃ. Ikkhaṇikaṃ.

From 'ukkha' and so forth: the collection of bulls is 'okkhakaṃ'; the collection of camels is 'oṭṭhakaṃ'; the collection of rams is 'orabbhakaṃ'. Similarly, 'rājakaṃ' (collection of kings), 'rājaputtakaṃ' (collection of princes), 'hatthikaṃ' (collection of elephants), 'dhenukaṃ' (collection of cows). Those who give and eat hares are called 'sasādakā'; their collection is 'sasādakakaṃ'. A collection of astrologers is 'ikkhaṇikaṃ'.

Ṇamhi-amittānaṃ samūho amittaṃ.

With the suffix 'ṇa': the collection of enemies is 'amittaṃ'.

Ṇikamhi-apūpānaṃ samūho āpūpikaṃ, sakuṇānaṃ samūho sākuṇiko saṃkulānaṃ samūho saṃkulikaṃ?.

With the suffix 'ṇika': the collection of cakes is 'āpūpikaṃ'; the collection of birds is 'sākuṇiko'.

542. Janādīhi tā ka. 355; rū. 380; nī. 771; caṃ. 3.1.69; pā. 4.2.43.

542. From 'jana' and so forth, the suffix 'tā'.

Tassa samūhoti atthe tā hoti.

In the sense 'its collection', the suffix 'tā' occurs.

Janatā, rājatā, bandhutā, gāmatā, sahāyatā, nagaravāsīnaṃ samūho nāgaratā iccādi.

'Janatā' (a group of people), 'rājatā' (a group of kings), 'bandhutā' (a group of relatives), 'gāmatā' (a village community), 'sahāyatā' (a group of friends); the collection of city-dwellers is 'nāgaratā', and so on.

543. Ayūbhadvitīhaṃse ka. 354; rū. 379; nī. 771; caṃ. 4.2.47, 48; pā. 5.2.43, 44.

543. The suffix 'aya' is used with 'ubha', 'dvi', and 'ti' in the sense of 'part'.

Ubha, dvi, tīhi tassa aṃsatthe ayo hoti.

From 'ubha', 'dvi', and 'ti', in the sense of 'its part', the suffix 'aya' occurs.

Ubho aṃsā bhāgā assāti ubhayaṃ, dve aṃsā assāti dvayaṃ, tayo aṃsā assāti tayaṃ, vatthuttayaṃ, ratanattayaṃ, dve vā tayo vā aṃsā assāti dvattayaṃ.

That which has both parts ('aṃsā') or portions ('bhāgā') is 'ubhayaṃ'; that which has two parts is 'dvayaṃ'; that which has three parts is 'tayaṃ', e.g., 'vatthuttayaṃ' (the threefold subject), 'ratanattayaṃ' (the Triple Gem); that which has two or three parts is 'dvattayaṃ'.

Iti samūharāsi.

Thus ends the section on collections.

Datta, nibbattarāsi

The Section on 'Given' and 'Produced'

544. Tena [M 0.0334] datte liyā ka. 358, 356; rū. 383, 381; nī. 778, 773.

544. The suffixes 'la' and 'iya' are used in the sense of 'given by that'.

Tena dattoti atthe la, iyā honti. Mahāvuttinā dinnasaddassa dattattaṃ.

In the sense 'given by that', the suffixes 'la' and 'iyā' occur. According to the Mahāvutti, 'dinna' is equivalent to 'datta'.

Devena dattoti devalo jā. 1.8.65. ‘Devilo’tipi devīlo? pāḷi. Deviyo, devadatto vā.

Given by a god is 'devalo'. 'Devilo' is also a Pāḷi reading. Or 'deviyo', or 'devadatto'.

Evaṃ brahmalo, brahmiyo, brahmadatto, sivena bissanudevarājena datto sīvalo, sīviyo, itthiyaṃ sīvali, sīviyi, sissa dīgho.

Similarly, 'brahmalo', 'brahmiyo', 'brahmadatto'. Given by Siva, the divine king Viṣṇu, is 'sīvalo' or 'sīviyo'; in the feminine, 'sīvali', 'sīviyi'; the 'i' in 'siva' is lengthened.

545. Tena nibbatte ka. 353; rū. 378; nī. 767; ‘tena nibbatte imo’?.

545. In the sense of 'produced by that'.

Tena nibbatte imo hoti.

In the sense of 'produced by that', the suffix 'ima' occurs.

Pākena nibbattaṃ pākimaṃ, pheṇena nibbattaṃ pheṇimaṃ, veṭhanena nibbattaṃ veṭhimaṃ. Evaṃ vedhimaṃ, gopphanena nibbattaṃ gopphimaṃ pārā. aṭṭha. 2.431, pupphadāmaṃ, karaṇena nibbattaṃ kittimaṃ, kuttimaṃ vā, mahāvuttinā karaṇassa kittaṃ kuttañca. Suttavibhattena saṃhārimaṃ, āhārimaṃ iccādīni sijjhanti.

Produced by cooking is 'pākimaṃ'; produced by foam is 'pheṇimaṃ'; produced by wrapping is 'veṭhimaṃ'. Similarly, 'vedhimaṃ'; produced by plaiting is 'gopphimaṃ', a flower garland. Produced by making is 'kittimaṃ' or 'kuttimaṃ'. According to the Mahāvutti, for 'karaṇa' there are 'kitta' and 'kutta'. By the Suttavibhatta, 'saṃhārimaṃ', 'āhārimaṃ', and so on, are formed.

Iti datta, nibbattarāsi.

Thus, the section on 'given' and 'produced'.

La, ita, karāsi

The section on 'la', 'ita', and 'ka'.

546. Tannissite lo ka. 358; rū. 383; nī. 778; ‘llo’ (bahūsu).

546. In the sense of 'dependent on that', the suffix 'la' occurs.

Tannissitatthe lo hoti.

In the sense of 'dependent on that', the suffix 'la' occurs.

Vedaṃ ñāṇaṃ nissitaṃ vedallaṃ, lassa dvittaṃ, duṭṭhu nissitaṃ duṭṭhullaṃ. “Madanīyaṃ, bandhanīyaṃ, mucchanīyaṃ, rajanīyaṃ, gamanīyaṃ, dassanīyaṃ” [M 0.0335] iccādīni karaṇe vā adhikaraṇe vā anīyapaccayena sijjhanti.

Knowledge dependent on the Veda is 'vedallaṃ'; there is doubling of 'la'. That which is evilly based is 'duṭṭhullaṃ'. 'Madanīyaṃ', 'bandhanīyaṃ', 'mucchanīyaṃ', 'rajanīyaṃ', 'gamanīyaṃ', 'dassanīyaṃ', and so on, are formed by the suffix 'anīya' in the sense of instrument or locus.

‘Dhūmāyitatta’ntiādīsu dhūmo viya attānaṃ ācaratīti dhūmāyitaṃ, gaganaṃ, dhūmāyitaṃ eva dhūmāyitattaṃ, sakatthe tta. Evaṃ timirāyitattaṃ, nāmadhātuto saṃ. ni. 3.87 āyapaccayena siddhaṃ.

In 'dhūmāyitatta' and so on: that which behaves like smoke is 'dhūmāyitaṃ', for example, the sky. The very state of being 'dhūmāyita' is 'dhūmāyitattaṃ', with 'tta' in its own sense. Similarly, 'timirāyitattaṃ', formed from a nominal root with the suffix 'āya'.

547. Sañjātā tārakādvitvito ka. 555; rū. 612; nī. 1142; caṃ. 4.2.37 …pe… 5.2.36; ‘sañjātaṃ…’ (bahūsu).

547. After 'tārakā' and so on, the suffix 'ita' occurs in the sense of 'arisen'.

Tārakādīhi te assa sañjātāti atthe ito hoti.

After 'tārakā' and so on, in the sense of 'they have arisen for him', the suffix 'ita' occurs.

Tārakā sañjātā assāti tārakitaṃ, gaganaṃ. Pupphāni sañjātāni assāti pupphito. Evaṃ phalito, rukkho. Pallavāni sañjātāni assāti pallavitā, latā. Dukkhaṃ sañjātaṃ assāti dukkhito, sukhaṃ sañjātaṃ assāti sukhito.

Stars have arisen for it, thus the sky is 'tārakitaṃ' (starry). Flowers have arisen for it, thus it is 'pupphito' (flowery). Similarly, the tree is 'phalito' (fruit-bearing). Sprouts have arisen for it, thus the creeper is 'pallavitā' (leafy). Suffering has arisen for him, thus he is 'dukkhito' (sorrowful). Happiness has arisen for him, thus he is 'sukhito' (joyful).

Paṇḍā vuccati paññā, paṇḍā sañjātā assāti paṇḍito, daṇḍo sañjāto assāti daṇḍito. Mahāvuttinā tassa natte malaṃ sañjātaṃ assāti malinaṃ. Tathā pipāsā sañjātā assāti pipāsito, jighacchā sañjātā assāti jighacchito, bubhukkhā sañjātā assāti bubhukkhito, mucchā sañjātā assāti mucchito, visaññā sañjātā assāti visaññito, nindā sañjātā assāti nindito.

'Paṇḍā' is called wisdom; one for whom wisdom has arisen is 'paṇḍito'. A staff has arisen for him, thus he is 'daṇḍito'. According to the Mahāvutti, when dirt has arisen for him, the form is 'malinaṃ'. Similarly, one for whom thirst has arisen is 'pipāsito'; one for whom hunger has arisen is 'jighacchito'; one for whom ravenous hunger has arisen is 'bubhukkhito'; one for whom delusion has arisen is 'mucchito'; one for whom loss of consciousness has arisen is 'visaññito'; one for whom blame has arisen is 'nindito'.

Evaṃ gabba-thambhe gabbito. Dabba-pāṭave dabbito. Antaraṃ sañjātaṃ assāti antarito, vaccaṃ sañjātaṃ assāti vaccito.

Similarly, 'gabbito' is formed in the sense of pride and arrogance. 'Dabbito' is formed in the sense of skill and cleverness. One for whom an interval has arisen is 'antarito'. One for whom excrement has arisen is 'vaccito'.

548. Nindāññātappapaṭibhāgarassadayāsaññāsu ko ka. 391; rū. 423; nī. 835; caṃ. 4.3.62, 63, 64; pā. 5.3.73-79, 96, 97.

548. The suffix 'ka' occurs in the senses of blame, unknown, small amount, resemblance, shortness, compassion, and designation.

Nindādīsu [M 0.0336] jotaniyesu nāmasmā ko hoti.

From a noun, the suffix 'ka' occurs when indicating blame and so on.

Nindāyaṃ – kucchito samaṇo samaṇako. Evaṃ muṇḍako, assako, uddhumātakaṃ, vinīlakaṃ, vipubbakaṃ, aṭṭhikaṃ iccādi.

In the sense of blame: a despicable ascetic is 'samaṇako'. Similarly: 'muṇḍako' (a mere shaven one), 'assako' (a mere horse), 'uddhumātakaṃ' (a bloated corpse), 'vinīlakaṃ' (a discolored corpse), 'vipubbakaṃ' (a festering corpse), 'aṭṭhikaṃ' (a mere skeleton), and so on.

Aññāte – aññāto asso assako, kassa ayaṃ assoti vā assako iccādi.

In the sense of 'unknown': an unknown horse is 'assako'. Or, 'whose horse is this?' is expressed as 'assako', and so on.

Appatthe – appakaṃ telaṃ telakaṃ. Evaṃ ghatakaṃ, khuddakaṃ dhanu dhanukaṃ, rathakaṃ, gāmakaṃ iccādi.

In the sense of 'small amount': a little oil is 'telakaṃ'. Similarly, 'ghatakaṃ' (a little ghee), a small bow is 'dhanukaṃ', 'rathakaṃ' (a small chariot), 'gāmakaṃ' (a small village), and so on.

Paṭibhāgatthe – hatthirūpakaṃ hatthikaṃ. Evaṃ assakaṃ, balībaddako iccādi.

In the sense of resemblance: an elephant image is 'hatthikaṃ'. Similarly, 'assakaṃ' (a horse image), 'balībaddako' (an ox image), and so on.

Rasse-rasso manusso manussako. Evaṃ rukkhako, pilakkhako iccādi.

In the sense of shortness: a short man is 'manussako'. Similarly, 'rukkhako' (a short tree), 'pilakkhako' (a short fig tree), and so on.

Dayāyaṃ-anukampito putto puttako. Evaṃ vacchako, itthikā, ambakā, kumārikā iccādi.

In the sense of compassion: a pitied son is 'puttako'. Similarly, 'vacchako' (a dear calf), 'itthikā' (a dear woman), 'ambakā' (a dear mother), 'kumārikā' (a dear girl), and so on.

Saññāyaṃ-nāmamattena moro viya morako iccādi.

In the sense of designation: that which is a peacock in name only is 'morako', and so on.

Iti la, ita, ka rāsi.

Thus, the section on 'la', 'ita', and 'ka'.

Abhūtatabbhāvarāsi

The Section on the State of Becoming What It Was Not Before

549. Abhūtatabbhāve karāsabhūyoge vikārācī ka. 391; rū. 423; nī. 835; caṃ. 4.4.35; pā. 5.4.50.

549. When indicating the state of becoming what it was not before, and when in conjunction with the roots 'kar', 'as', and 'bhū', the suffix 'ī' occurs after a noun denoting modification.

Pubbe tassa abhūtassa vatthuno kadāci tathā bhavanaṃ abhūtatabbhāvo, tasmiṃ abhūtatabbhāve jotaniye sati karā’sa, bhūdhātūnaṃ yoge vikāravācimhā nāmasmā cānubandho īpaccayo hoti.

The state of becoming what it was not before is the becoming thus, at some time, of a thing that was not so previously. When that state is to be indicated, and when in conjunction with the roots 'kar', 'as', and 'bhū', the suffix 'ī' with the indicatory letter 'c' occurs after a noun denoting modification.

Adhavalaṃ [M 0.0337] dhavalaṃ karoti dhavalīkaroti, adhavalo dhavalo siyā dhavalīsiyā, adhavalo dhavalo bhavati dhavalībhavati. Evaṃ dhavalīkāro, dhavalībhūto.

One makes the non-white white, thus 'dhavalīkaroti'; the non-white may become white, thus 'dhavalīsiyā'; the non-white becomes white, thus 'dhavalībhavati'. Similarly, 'dhavalīkāro' (the act of whitening), 'dhavalībhūto' (having become white).

Abhūtatabbhāveti kiṃ? Ghaṭaṃ karoti, ghaṭo atthi, ghaṭo bhavati.

Why is the condition 'in the sense of becoming what it was not before' stated? So that the rule does not apply in cases like: one makes a pot; a pot exists; a pot comes into being.

Karāsabhūyogeti kiṃ? Adhavalo dhavalo jāyate.

Why is the condition 'in conjunction with kar, as, and bhū' stated? So that the rule does not apply in cases like: the non-white becomes white (using the verb 'jāyate').

Vikārāti kiṃ? Pakatiyā mā hotu, suvaṇṇaṃ kuṇḍalaṃ karoti, suvaṇṇassa kuṇḍalakaraṇaṃ nāma loke pakatirūpanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ kuṇḍalaṃ siyā, suvaṇṇaṃ kuṇḍalaṃ bhavatīti.

Why is the condition 'from a noun denoting modification' stated? So that the rule may not apply to a noun denoting a natural substance. For example: one makes gold into an earring. The making of an earring from gold is said in the world to be a natural form. Similarly, the rule does not apply in: gold may become an earring; gold becomes an earring.

Iti abhūtatabbhāvarāsi.

Thus ends the section on 'abhūtatabbhāva'.

Sakattharāsi

The Section on 'Sakattha' (Its Own Meaning)

550. Sakatthe ka. 178, 360, 372; rū. 224, 387, 385, 378; nī. 364, 780, 798, 767.

550. In its own meaning.

Sakatthepi paccayā dissanti. ‘Sakattho’ti sakapadattho, pakatiliṅgapadatthoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Suffixes are also seen in their own meaning. 'Sakattha' means the meaning of its own word; that is, the meaning of a word in its natural gender.

Hīno eva hīnako, poto eva potako, devo eva devatā, yathābhūtameva yathābhuccaṃ, karuṇā eva kāruññaṃ, pattakālameva pattakallaṃ, ākāsānantameva ākāsānañcaṃ, pāguññameva pāguññatā, kammaññameva kammaññatā, dānaṃ eva dānamayaṃ, sīlaṃ eva sīlamayaṃ. Evaṃ bhāvanāmayaṃ iccādi.

A low one is simply a low one; a young animal is simply a young animal; a god is simply a deity; as it truly is, is simply truthfulness; compassion is simply compassionateness; the right time is simply the proper time; the infinity of space is simply the infinity of space; skill is simply skillfulness; suitability is simply fitness; giving is simply that which is made of giving; virtue is simply that which is made of virtue. Likewise, that which is made of development, and so on.

Yathā ca amaccaputtā eva ‘amaccaputtiyā’ti vuccanti, evaṃ “sakyaputto eva sakyaputtiyo, asamaṇo hoti asakyaputtiyo [M 0.0338] pārā. 55, evaṃ nāṭaputtiyo, dāsaputtiyo”tipi yujjati.

Just as the sons of ministers are called 'amaccaputtiyā,' so too it is fitting thus: 'a Sakyan son is simply a Sakyan son; a non-ascetic is a non-Sakyan son; likewise, a son of an actor, a son of a slave.'

‘Bhayadassivā, atthadassimā’ti vantu, mantupaccayāsakatthepi yujjanti. ‘Brahmavaṇṇī, devavaṇṇī’ti ettha brahmuno vaṇṇo brahmavaṇṇo, brahmavaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo assa atthīti atthe sati īpaccayo paccayattho eva hoti, na sakattho. Brahmavaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo yassa soyaṃ brahmavaṇṇīti atthe sati sakatthoyeva. Api ca ekasmiṃ aññapadatthe dve samāsa, taddhitā vattantītipi yujjati, tathā ‘paguṇassa bhāvo pāguññatā’tiādīsu dve taddhitapaccayā bhāvattheti.

In 'bhayadassivā' and 'atthadassimā,' the suffixes 'vantu' and 'mantu' are also used in the sense of 'sakattha' (its own meaning). In 'brahmavaṇṇī' and 'devavaṇṇī,' 'brahmavaṇṇa' is the color of Brahmā. When the meaning is 'having a color like Brahmā's color,' the suffix 'ī' expresses only the meaning of the suffix, not the 'sakattha' meaning. When the meaning is 'one whose color is like Brahmā's color,' then it is 'sakattha' itself. Moreover, it is fitting that two compounds or derivatives can apply to a single external referent, as in 'the state of being proficient is proficiency' and so on, where two derivative suffixes convey the meaning of an abstract quality.

Iti sakattharāsi.

Thus ends the section on 'Sakattha' (Its Own Meaning).

Niddiṭṭhapaccayarāsi

The Section on Specified Suffixes

551. Aññasmiṃ ka. 352; rū. 376; nī. 765.

551. In another meaning.

Pubbe niddiṭṭhā ṇādayo paccayā niddiṭṭhatthato aññesupi atthesu dissanti.

The previously mentioned suffixes, such as 'ṇa' and so on, are also seen in meanings other than those already specified.

Magadhesu jāto māgadho, magadhesu saṃvaḍḍhito māgadho, magadhesu nivuttho māgadho, magadhānaṃ magadhesu vā issaro māgadho iccādi, ṇo.

Born in Magadha, he is a 'māgadho'; raised in Magadha, he is a 'māgadho'; dwelling in Magadha, he is a 'māgadho'; the lord of the Magadhans or in Magadha, he is a 'māgadho', and so on, with the suffix 'ṇa'.

Kāsiṃ agghatīti kāsiyo cūḷava. 376, ‘kāsī’ti sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā vuccati, iyo.

'Kāsiṃ agghatīti kāsiyo' (that which is worth a kāsi is a kāsiyo); 'kāsī' is said to be a hundred or a thousand. This is formed with the suffix 'iyo'.

Evamaññepi paccayā yathānurūpaṃ veditabbā.

Similarly, other suffixes should be understood as appropriate.

552. Dissantaññepi paccayā ka. 351, 352; rū. 374, 376; nī. 764, 765.

552. Other Suffixes are Also Seen

Pubbe [M 0.0339] niddiṭṭhapaccayehi aññepi paccayā niddiṭṭhesu aniddiṭṭhesu ca atthesu dissanti.

Other suffixes, apart from those previously mentioned, are seen in both mentioned and unmentioned meanings.

Visadisā vividhā (moga.) mātaro vimātaro, tāsaṃ puttā vemātikā netti 95, ikaṇa.

Dissimilar mothers are 'vimātaro'; their sons are 'vemātikā'. This is formed with the suffix 'ikaṇa'.

Pathe gacchantīti pathāvino ma. ni. 2.347, aghaṃ dukkhaṃ pāpaṃ vā gacchatīti aghāvī, āvī.

Those who go on the path are 'pathāvino'; one who goes to 'aghaṃ'—suffering or evil—is 'aghāvī'. This is formed with the suffix 'āvī'.

Issā assa atthīti issukī jā. 1.6.43, ukī.

One who has envy is 'issukī'. This is formed with the suffix 'ukī'.

Dhuraṃ vahantīti dhorayhā a. ni. 3.58, yhaṇa.

Those who bear a burden are 'dhorayhā'. This is formed with the suffix 'yhaṇa'.

Lobhassa hitā lobhaneyyā. Evaṃ dosaneyyā, mohaneyyā, aneyyo.

Beneficial to greed are 'lobhaneyyā'. Likewise, 'dosaneyyā' (beneficial to hatred) and 'mohaneyyā' (beneficial to delusion). This is formed with the suffix 'aneyya'.

Dassanaṃ arahatīti dassaneyyo. Evaṃ vandaneyyo, pūjaneyyo, namassaneyyo, eyyo.

Worthy of being seen is 'dassaneyyo'. Likewise, 'vandaneyyo' (worthy of veneration), 'pūjaneyyo' (worthy of worship), and 'namassaneyyo' (worthy of homage). This is formed with the suffix 'eyya'.

Oghānaṃ hitā oghaniyā, yoganiyā, ganthaniyā, kammaniyaṃ, attaniyaṃ, dassaniyaṃ, pūjaniyo, namassaniyo iccādi, aniyo.

Beneficial to floods are 'oghaniyā'; also 'yoganiyā' (beneficial to yokes), 'ganthaniyā' (beneficial to bonds), 'kammaniyaṃ' (related to kamma), 'attaniyaṃ' (related to self), 'dassaniyaṃ' (to be seen), 'pūjaniyo' (to be honored), 'namassaniyo' (to be revered), and so on. This is formed with the suffix 'aniya'.

Yaṃ parimāṇaṃ assāti yāvaṃ, yāvantassa bhāvo yāvatvaṃ. Evaṃ tāvatvaṃ, tva.

That which has a certain measure is 'yāvaṃ'; the state of being 'yāvant' is 'yāvatvaṃ'. Likewise, 'tāvatvaṃ'. This is formed with the suffix 'tva'.

Paramānaṃ uttamapurisānaṃ bhāvo kammaṃ vā pāramī, samaggānaṃ bhāvo kammaṃ vā sāmaggī, ṇī.

The state or action of supreme beings is 'pāramī' (perfection); the state or action of the harmonious is 'sāmaggī' (harmony). This is formed with the suffix 'ṇī'.

“Nāgavatā, sīhavatā, ājaññavatā” iccādīsu bhāve vantupaccayaṃ icchanti.

In 'nāgavatā' (having the qualities of an elephant), 'sīhavatā' (having the qualities of a lion), 'ājaññavatā' (having the qualities of a thoroughbred horse), and so on, they desire the suffix 'vantu' to indicate a state.

Mātu bhātā mātulo, ulo.

A mother's brother is 'mātulo' (maternal uncle). This is formed with the suffix 'ulo'.

Iti niddiṭṭhapaccayarāsi.

Thus ends the section on Specified Suffixes.

Vuddhirāsi

The Section on Vowel Augmentation (Vuddhi)

‘Padānamādissāyuvaṇṇassāeo [M 0.0340] ṇānubandhe’ti padādibhūtānaṃ akāra, ivaṇṇu’vaṇṇānaṃ ā, e, ovuddhi.

By the rule 'Padānamādissāyuvaṇṇassāeo ṇānubandhe,' the vuddhi of the initial a-vowel, i-vowel, and u-vowel of a word is ā, e, and o.

Ādicco, vāsiṭṭho, venateyyo, meniko, pettikaṃ, odumbaraṃ, oḷumpiko, odagyaṃ, dobhaggaṃ, sobhaggaṃ iccādi.

Ādicco, vāsiṭṭho, venateyyo, meniko, pettikaṃ, odumbaraṃ, oḷumpiko, odagyaṃ, dobhaggaṃ, sobhaggaṃ, and so on.

Ṇānubandheti kiṃ? Nāmako, padako, purātano.

Why the specification 'with the anubandha ṇa'? The examples are nāmako, padako, purātano, where vuddhi does not occur.

‘Majjhe’ti suttena padamajjhepi vuddhi, vāseṭṭho, aḍḍhateyyo iccādi.

By the rule 'Majjhe', vuddhi occurs even in the middle of a word, as in vāseṭṭho, aḍḍhateyyo, and so on.

553. Saṃyogepi kvaci ka. 405; rū. 365; nī. 864; ‘pi’ (bahūsu natthi).

553. Even in a conjunct, sometimes.

Ṇānubandhe paccaye pare saṃyogepi kvaci vuddhi hoti.

When a suffix with ṇa as an anubandha follows, vuddhi sometimes occurs even in a conjunct.

Petteyyo, pettikaṃ, decco, pamukhe sādhu pāmokkhaṃ, pamuditassa bhāvo pāmojjaṃ, vattabbanti vākyaṃ, bhajitabbanti bhāgyaṃ, bhoggaṃ, yoggaṃ iccādi.

Petteyyo, pettikaṃ, decco; pāmokkhaṃ ('good in the foremost'); pāmojjaṃ ('the state of being delighted'); vākyaṃ ('that which is to be said'); bhāgyaṃ ('that which is to be partaken of'); bhoggaṃ, yoggaṃ, and so on.

Iti vuddhirāsi.

Thus, the section on Vuddhi.

Loparāsi

The Section on Elision.

‘Lopovaṇṇivaṇṇāna’nti suttena ṇyamhi pare avaṇṇi’vaṇṇānaṃ lopo.

By the rule 'Lopovaṇṇivaṇṇānaṃ', when the suffix ṇya follows, there is elision of the a-vowel and the i-vowel.

Tattha avaṇṇe-paṇḍiccaṃ, tacchaṃ, dāyajjaṃ, dvidhā bhāvo dvejjhaṃ, karuṇāyeva kāruññaṃ iccādi.

Therein, regarding the a-vowel: paṇḍiccaṃ, tacchaṃ, dāyajjaṃ; dvejjhaṃ, which is a twofold state; kāruññaṃ, which is compassion itself; and so on.

Ivaṇṇe-adhipatissa bhāvo ādhipaccaṃ. Evaṃ ādicco, koṇḍañño iccādi.

Regarding the i-vowel: ādhipaccaṃ is the state of being a lord. Similarly, ādicco, koṇḍañño, and so on.

‘Uvaṇṇassāvaṅa [M 0.0341] sare’ti sare pare uvaṇṇassa avaṅa hoti.

By the rule 'Uvaṇṇassāvaṅa sare', when a vowel follows, the u-vowel becomes avaṅa.

Ṇamhi-lahuno bhāvo lāghavaṃ, rāghavaṃ, jamburukkhe bhavaṃ jambavaṃ. Tathā kapilavatthumhi bhavaṃ kāpilavatthavaṃ, vanaṃ. Bhātuno apaccaṃ bhātabyo, gabyaṃ, dabyaṃ.

When ṇa follows: lāghavaṃ is the state of being light; rāghavaṃ; jambavaṃ is that which arises in the Jambu tree. Similarly, kāpilavatthavaṃ is that which arises in Kapilavatthu; vanaṃ. Bhātabyo is the offspring of a brother; gabyaṃ; dabyaṃ.

‘Ṭe satissā…’ti ṭamhi paccaye vīsati, tīsatīnaṃ tilopo.

By the rule 'Ṭe satissā...', when the suffix ṭa follows, there is elision of 'ti' from vīsati (twenty) and tīsati (thirty).

Vīsatiyā pūraṇo vīso, ekūnavīso. Evaṃ tīso, ekūnatīso.

Vīso (the twentieth) is that which completes twenty; ekūnavīso (the nineteenth). Similarly, tīso (the thirtieth); ekūnatīso (the twenty-ninth).

‘Rānubandhentasarādissā’ti rānubandhe paccaye padantasarādīnaṃ lopo.

By the rule 'Rānubandhentasarādissā', when a suffix with 'ra' as an anubandha follows, there is elision of the final vowel of a word and of initial parts.

Metteyyo, petteyyo, kivaṃ, kittakaṃ, īdī, īdikkho, īdiso, āhacca, upahacca, sakkacca, adhikicca, kiriyā, vedagū, pāragū iccādi.

Metteyyo, petteyyo, kivaṃ (how much?), kittakaṃ (how many?), īdī (suchlike), īdikkho (of this sort), īdiso (of this kind), āhacca (having struck), upahacca (having struck down), sakkacca (respectfully), adhikicca (with reference to), kiriyā (action), vedagū (one who has mastered the Veda), pāragū (one who has gone beyond), and so on.

554. Paccayānaṃ lopo ka. 391; rū. 423; nī. 830; moggallāne ‘lopo’ tveva dissati.

554. Elision of Suffixes.

Paccayānaṃ kvaci lopo hoti.

Sometimes there is elision of suffixes.

Buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ, cakkhu suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā saṃ. ni. 4.85. Ettha ca ratanassa bhāvo ratanaṃ, attano bhāvo attā, attano sakassa bhāvo attaniyanti evaṃ bhāvapaccayalopo.

The sublime jewel is in the Buddha; the eye is empty of self or of what pertains to self. Here, 'ratanaṃ' is 'the state of being a jewel'; 'attā' is 'the state of being self'; 'attaniyaṃ' is 'the state of being one's own'—thus, there is elision of the suffix denoting state.

“Buddhānussati dhammānussati”ādīsu “buddhassa bhāvo buddho, buddhassa ayaṃ guṇo buddho”tiādinā nayena paccayalopo veditabbo.

In such cases as 'recollection of the Buddha' and 'recollection of the Dhamma', the elision of the suffix is to be understood by the method of 'the state of a Buddha is a Buddha', 'this quality of a Buddha is a Buddha', and so on.

555. Lopo vīmantuvantūnaṃ ka. 268; rū. 397; nī. 518.

555. Elision of vī, mantu, and vantu.

Iyi’ṭṭhesu [M 0.0342] paresu vī, mantu, vantūnaṃ lopo hoti.

When the suffixes iya and iṭṭha follow, there is elision of vī, mantu, and vantu.

Medhāvīnaṃ atisayena medhāvīti medhiyo, medhiṭṭho, satimantānaṃ atisayena satimāti satiyo, satiṭṭho, guṇavantānaṃ atisayena guṇavāti guṇiyo, guṇiṭṭho.

Among the wise, one who is exceedingly wise is medhiyo or medhiṭṭho; among the mindful, one who is exceedingly mindful is satiyo or satiṭṭho; among the virtuous, one who is exceedingly virtuous is guṇiyo or guṇiṭṭho.

Iti loparāsi.

Thus, the section on Elision.

Khuddakarāsi niṭṭhito.

The Minor Section is completed.

Nānāttarāsi

The Section on Various Matters.

556. Jo vuddhassiyiṭṭhesu ka. 262; rū. 391; nī. 513; caṃ. 4.3.50; pā. 5.3.61, 62.

556. 'Jo' for 'vuddha' when 'iya' and 'iṭṭha' follow.

Iyi’ṭṭhapaccayesu paresu vuddhasaddassa jo hoti.

When the suffixes iya and iṭṭha follow, the word 'vuddha' becomes 'jo'.

Vuddhānaṃ atisayena vuddhoti jeyyo, jeṭṭho.

Among the old, one who is exceedingly old is jeyyo (senior) or jeṭṭho (eldest).

557. Bāḷhantikapasatthānaṃ sādhanedasajā ka. 263, 264, 265; rū. 392, 393, 394; nī. 512, 514, 515; caṃ. 4.3.49, 51; pā. 5.3.60, 63; ‘… dasā’ (bahūsu).

557. `Sādha`, `neda`, `sa`, and `ja` [are the substitutes] for `bāḷha`, `antika`, and `pasattha`.

Iya, iṭṭhapaccayesu paresu bāḷha, antika, pasatthasaddānaṃ sādha, neda, sa, jādesā honti.

When the suffixes `iya` and `iṭṭha` follow, the words `bāḷha`, `antika`, and `pasattha` are replaced by `sādha`, `neda`, `sa`, and `ja` respectively.

Bāḷhānaṃ atisayena bāḷhoti sādhiyo, sādhiṭṭho, antikānaṃ atisayena antikoti nediyo, nediṭṭho, pasatthānaṃ atisayena pasatthoti seyyo, seṭṭho, jeyyo, jeṭṭho.

One who is exceedingly strong among the strong is `sādhiyo`, `sādhiṭṭho`; one who is exceedingly near among the near is `nediyo`, `nediṭṭho`; one who is exceedingly praised among the praised is `seyyo` (better), `seṭṭho` (best), `jeyyo` (superior), `jeṭṭho` (chief).

558. Kaṇakana appayuvānaṃ ka. 266, 267; rū. 395, 396; nī. 516, 517; caṃ. 4.3.53; pā. 5.3.64.

558. `Kaṇa` and `kana` [are the substitutes] for `appa` and `yuva`.

Iya[M 0.0343], iṭṭhapaccayesu paresu appa, yuvasaddānaṃ kaṇa, kanaādesā honti.

When the suffixes `iya` and `iṭṭha` follow, the words `appa` and `yuva` are replaced by `kaṇa` and `kana` respectively.

Appānaṃ navānaṃ atisayena appo navoti kaṇiyo, kaṇiṭṭho, yuvānaṃ taruṇānaṃ atisayena yuvā taruṇoti kaniyo, kaniṭṭho, kaniye vaye bhavā kaññā.

One who is exceedingly young among the young is `kaṇiyo`, `kaṇiṭṭho`; one who is exceedingly youthful among the youthful is `kaniyo`, `kaniṭṭho`; one who exists in a young age is `kaññā` (maiden).

559. Kosajjājjava pārisajja suhajja maddavārisyāsa bhājaññatheyyabāhusaccā ka. 360, 361; rū. 387, 388; nī. 780, 781; ‘…rissā…” (bahūsu).

559. `Kosajja` (sloth), `ājjava` (uprightness), `pārisajja` (belonging to an assembly), `suhajja` (good-heartedness), `maddava` (gentleness), `ārisya` (enmity), `āsabha` (eminence), `ājañña` (nobility), `theyya` (theft), and `bāhusacca` (erudition).

Bhāva, kammesu ṇānubandhe paccaye pare ete saddā nipaccante. Tattha ajjava, maddavā’sabhasaddā ṇamhi sijjhanti, sesā ṇyamhi.

These words are irregularly formed when a suffix with `ṇa` as an anubandha follows, in the sense of state or action. Among them, the words `ajjava`, `maddava`, and `āsabha` are formed with the suffix `ṇa`, while the rest are formed with `ṇya`.

Tattha ujuno bhāvo ajjavaṃ, iminā suttena ṇamhi ussa attaṃ, ‘uvaṇṇassāvaṅa…’ iti ussa avattaṃ. Evaṃ muduno bhāvo maddavaṃ, usabhassa bhāvo āsabhaṃ, ussa āttaṃ. Kusitassa kusītassa? bhāvo kosajjaṃ, iminā ilopo, tyassa jjattaṃ, parisāsu uppanno pārisajjo dī. ni. 2.215, dāgamo, suhadayova suhado, yalopo, suhadassa bhāvo sohajjaṃ jā. 1.5.23, isino idaṃ ārisyaṃ, issa ārittaṃ, ājāniyassa ājānīyassātipi dissati bhāvo ājaññaṃ, yalopo, puna ‘lopovaṇṇivaṇṇāna’nti ilopo, tato paraṃ sandhirūpaṃ, ājāniyo eva vā ājañño jā. 1.1.24, sakatthe ṇyo, thenassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vā theyyaṃ, nassa yattaṃ, bahusutassa bhāvo bāhusaccaṃ, ussa attaṃ, puna sandhirūpaṃ.

Herein, the state of being straight is `ajjavaṃ` (uprightness); by this rule, with `ṇa` following, `u` becomes `a`; by the rule `uvaṇṇassāvaṅa…`, `u` becomes `ava`. Similarly, the state of being soft is `maddavaṃ` (gentleness). The state of a bull is `āsabhaṃ` (eminence), where `u` becomes `ā`. The state of being lazy is `kosajjaṃ` (sloth); by this rule, `i` is elided, and `tya` becomes `jja`. One who arises in assemblies is `pārisajjo`; `da` is inserted. One who is good-hearted is `suhado`; `ya` is elided; the state of being good-hearted is `sohajjaṃ`. This belonging to a seer is `ārisyaṃ` (enmity), where `i` becomes `āri`. The state of a thoroughbred is `ājaññaṃ` (nobility); `ya` is elided; again, by `lopovaṇṇivaṇṇāna`, `i` is elided; thereafter, it is a sandhi form. Alternatively, `ājañño` is simply a thoroughbred, with the suffix `ṇya` in its own sense. The state or act of a thief is `theyyaṃ` (theft), where `na` becomes `ya`. The state of being learned is `bāhusaccaṃ` (erudition), where `u` becomes `a`; again, it is a sandhi form.

560. Adhātussa ke pāṇiniye, cande ca ‘kāka’iti pañcamyantaṃ dissate syādito ghessi ka. 404; rū. 370; nī. 859.

560. Of the `a` of a non-root, `i` [is substituted] before `ka`, when a `gha` suffix follows after `sya`, etc.

‘Ghessī’ti [M 0.0344] ghe+assa+i, chapadamidaṃ suttaṃ.

`Ghessī` is `ghe` + `assa` + `i`; this is a six-word rule.

Adhātussa avayavabhūte kakāre pare pubbassa akārassa bahulaṃ i hoti kanissite ghe asyādito pare sati.

When the letter `ka`, being a component of a non-root, follows, the preceding `a`-sound frequently becomes `i`, when a `gha` suffix, not associated with the desiderative, follows after a `sya` etc. [case ending].

Bālikā, ekikā, hatthipotikā, mahallikā, kumbhakārikā, kammakārikā, annadāyikā, upāsikā, sāvikā, dhammavācikā.

Examples are: `Bālikā` (a young girl), `ekikā` (a solitary woman), `hatthipotikā` (a female keeper of young elephants), `mahallikā` (an old woman), `kumbhakārikā` (a female potter), `kammakārikā` (a female worker), `annadāyikā` (a female giver of food), `upāsikā` (a female lay follower), `sāvikā` (a female disciple), `dhammavācikā` (a female reciter of the Dhamma).

Adhātussāti kiṃ? Kulupakā- bhikkhunī, dhenupakā, khīrupakā-vacchī, idha dhātvādesopi kakāro dhātusaññaṃ labhatiyeva.

Why `adhātussa` (of a non-root)? [For example,] a nun who is `kulupakā` (frequenting families), `dhenupakā` (living by a cow); a calf that is `khīrupakā` (living on milk). Here, the letter `ka`, even though a substitute for a root, indeed obtains the designation of 'root'.

Keti kiṃ? Vedanā, cetanā.

Why `ke` (before `ka`)? [For example,] `vedanā` (feeling), `cetanā` (volition).

Asyāditoti kiṃ? Bahuparibbājakā-rājadhānī.

Why `asyādito` (after `sya`, etc.)? [For example,] `Bahuparibbājakā-rājadhānī` (a capital city with many wanderers).

Assāti kiṃ? Bahukattukā-sālā.

Why `assa` (of the `a`)? [For example,] `Bahukattukā-sālā` (a hall with many agents).

Ettha ca bahavo paribbājakā yassā sā bahuparibbājakāti viggaho. Paribbājakasaddo pakatisyādisaddo hoti, tasmā kanissitassa ghasaññassa ākārassa syādito parattā pubbassa assa ittaṃ na bhavati. Yadi bhaveyya, bahukā paribbājikāyo yassanti atthappasaṅgo siyāti.

Here, the analysis of `bahuparibbājakā` is: 'she to whom many wanderers belong'. The word `paribbājaka` is by nature a nominal stem (`syādi` word); therefore, because the `ā`-sound (designated `gha` and related to the `ka`) follows a `syādi` [stem], the preceding `a` does not become `i`. If it were to become so, the unintended meaning 'she to whom many female wanderers (`paribbājikā`) belong' would arise.

Iti nānāttarāsi niṭṭhito.

Thus ends the collection of miscellaneous rules.

Iti niruttidīpaniyā nāma moggallānabyākaraṇa-

Thus in the Niruttidīpanī, a commentary on the Moggallāna Grammar—

Dīpaniyā taddhitakaṇḍo pañcamo.

The fifth chapter of the Dīpanī: the Taddhita section.

6. Ākhyātakaṇḍa

6. The Chapter on Verbal Inflections

Suddhakatturūpa

The Form of the Pure Agent

Atha [M 0.0345] dhātupaccayasaṃsiddhaṃ kāla, kāraka, purisa, saṅkhyābhedadīpakaṃ liṅgabhedarahitaṃ kriyāpadhānavācakaṃ tyādyantanāmakaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ dīpiyate.

Now, the verbal form (`ākhyātapada`) is explained. It is formed from roots and suffixes; it indicates distinctions of time, agent, person, and number; it is devoid of gender distinction; its primary meaning is action; and it is named by its endings, `ti` and so forth.

Tattha kriyaṃ dhāretīti dhātu. Sā pakatidhātu, vikatidhātu, nāmadhātuvasena tividhā.

Therein, a root (`dhātu`) is that which bears action. It is threefold: primary root, derived root, and denominative root.

Tattha bhū, hū, gamu, paca iccādi pakatidhātu nāma sabhāvena siddhattā.

Therein, `bhū`, `hū`, `gamu`, `paca`, etc., are called primary roots, because they are established by their own nature.

Titikkha, tikiccha, bubhukkha, jighacchaiccādi vikatidhātu nāma saṅkhatavasena siddhattā.

`Titikkha`, `tikiccha`, `bubhukkha`, `jighaccha`, etc., are called derived roots, because they are established by way of formation.

Puttīya, pabbatāya iccādi nāmadhātu nāma nāmabhūtassa sato kriyavācīpaccayayogena dhātuṭṭhāne ṭhitattā.

`Puttīya`, `pabbatāya`, etc., are called denominative roots because, although being nouns, they stand in the place of a root through connection with a suffix that denotes action.

Pakatidhātu ca sakammikā’kammikavasena duvidhā.

Primary roots, moreover, are twofold: transitive and intransitive.

Tatthayā dhātu kammāpekkhaṃ kriyaṃ vadati, sā sakammikā nāma. Gāmaṃ gacchati, odanaṃ pacati iccādi.

Therein, a root that expresses an action requiring an object is called transitive. For example: `gāmaṃ gacchati` (he goes to the village), `odanaṃ pacati` (he cooks rice), and so on.

Yā kammanirapekkhaṃ kriyaṃ vadati, sā akammikā nāma. Bhavati, hoti, tiṭṭhati, seti iccādi.

That which expresses an action independent of an object is called intransitive. For example: 'He exists', 'he is', 'he stands', 'he lies', and so on.

Sakammikā ca ekakammika, dvikammikavasena duvidhā.

And transitive verbs are twofold, by way of having one object and having two objects.

Tattha yā ekakammāpekkhaṃ kriyaṃ vadati, sā ekakammikā nāma. Gāmaṃ gacchati, odanaṃ pacati iccādi.

Therein, that which expresses an action requiring a single object is called monotransitive. For example: 'He goes to the village', 'he cooks rice', and so on.

Yā padhānā’padhānavasena kammadvayāpekkhaṃ kriyaṃ vadati, sā dvikammikā nāma.

That which expresses an action requiring two objects, by way of principal and subordinate, is called ditransitive.

Sā ca nyādi, duhādivasena duvidhā.

And that ditransitive verb is twofold, by way of the 'nyādi' class and the 'duhādi' class.

Tattha [M 0.0346] yā dhātu pāpanatthā hoti, sā nyādi nāma. Ajaṃ gāmaṃ neti, bhāraṃ gāmaṃ vahati, sākhaṃ gāmaṃ ākaḍḍhati.

Therein, that root which has the meaning of causing to reach or attain is called 'nyādi'. For example: 'He leads the goat to the village', 'he carries the load to the village', 'he drags the branch to the village'.

Sesā dvikammikā duhādi nāma. Gāviṃ khīraṃ duhati, brāhmaṇaṃ kambalaṃ yācati, dāyakaṃ bhikkhaṃ bhikkhati, goṇaṃ vajaṃ rundhati, bhagavantaṃ pañhaṃ pucchati, sissaṃ dhammaṃ anusāsati, bhagavā bhikkhū etaṃ [vacanaṃ] avoca, rājā amaccaṃ vacanaṃ bravīti iccādi.

The remaining ditransitive verbs are called 'duhādi'. For example: 'He milks milk from a cow', 'he asks a brahmin for a blanket', 'he begs a donor for alms', 'he confines an ox in a pen', 'he asks the Blessed One a question', 'he instructs a disciple in the Dhamma', 'the Blessed One spoke this word to the monks', 'the king speaks a word to a minister', and so on.

Tattha yadā kammasmiṃ rūpaṃ sijjhati, tadā vibhatti, paccayā nyādimhi padhānakammaṃ vadanti, duhādimhi apadhānakammaṃ, sabbadhātūsu kāritayoge kāritakammanti, sabbañcetaṃ dhātūnaṃ pakatiatthavasena vuttaṃ, anekatthattā pana dhātūnaṃ atthantaravacane vā nānupasaggayoge vā akammikāpi sakammikā honti, sakammikāpi akammikā honti.

Therein, when a form is accomplished in the sense of the object, then the inflections and suffixes express the principal object in the 'nyādi' class, the subordinate object in the 'duhādi' class, and the causative object in the causative construction of all roots. All this is stated according to the inherent meaning of the roots. However, due to the multiple meanings of roots, or in the expression of a different meaning, or in combination with various prefixes, intransitive verbs can become transitive, and transitive verbs can become intransitive.

Atthantaravacane tāva –

First, in the expression of a different meaning:

Vida – sattāyaṃ, dhammo vijjati, saṃvijjati.

The root 'vid' – in the sense of existence: 'dhammo vijjati' (the Dhamma exists), 'saṃvijjati' (it is found).

Vida – ñāṇe, dhammaṃ vidati.

The root 'vid' – in the sense of knowledge: 'dhammaṃ vidati' (he knows the Dhamma).

Vida – lābhe, dhanaṃ vindati.

The root 'vid' – in the sense of gain: 'dhanaṃ vindati' (he finds wealth).

Vida – anubhavane, sukhaṃ vedeti, vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti ma. ni. 3.303.

The root 'vid' – in the sense of experiencing: 'sukhaṃ vedeti' (he feels pleasure), 'vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti' (he experiences the result).

Vida – ārocane, vedayāmahaṃ bhante vedayatīti maṃ dhāretu cūḷava. aṭṭha. 102, kāraṇaṃ nivedeti, dhammaṃ paṭivedeti iccādi.

The root 'vid' – in the sense of announcing: 'vedayāmahaṃ' (we announce), 'bhante vedayatīti maṃ dhāretu' (Venerable sir, may he consider me as one who announces); 'kāraṇaṃ nivedeti' (he reports the reason), 'dhammaṃ paṭivedeti' (he comprehends the Dhamma), and so on.

Nānupasaggayoge –

In combination with various prefixes:

Pada-gatiyaṃ, maggaṃ pajjati, paṭipajjati, maggo uppajjati, nipajjati, sampajjati, bhogo bhavati, sambhavati, bhogaṃ anubhavati, taṇhaṃ [M 0.0347] abhibhavati, paribhavati, adhibhavati, araññaṃ abhisambhavati, ajjhogāhatīti attho. Gacchantaṃ magge abhisambhavati, sampāpuṇātīti attho iccādi.

The root 'pad' – in the sense of going: 'maggaṃ pajjati' (he goes on the path), 'paṭipajjati' (he proceeds), 'maggo uppajjati' (the path arises), 'nipajjati' (he lies down), 'sampajjati' (he attains), 'bhogo bhavati' (enjoyment comes into being), 'sambhavati' (it comes into being), 'bhogaṃ anubhavati' (he experiences enjoyment), 'taṇhaṃ abhibhavati' (he overcomes craving), 'paribhavati' (he despises), 'adhibhavati' (he dominates), 'araññaṃ abhisambhavati' (he penetrates the forest – meaning he plunges into it); 'gacchantaṃ magge abhisambhavati' (he overtakes the one walking on the path – meaning he reaches him), and so on.

Padānaṃ byañjanasampattiyā vā atthasampattiyā vā upakārakā vibhatti, paccayā paccayā nāma.

Inflections and suffixes, which are instrumental for the perfection of words either in their form or in their meaning, are called suffixes.

Tattha vibhattiyo tyādi, tvādiiccādinā aṭṭhavidhā bhavanti, sarūpato channavutividhā.

Therein, inflections are eightfold by way of 'ti' etc., 'tu' etc., and so on; and ninety-sixfold in terms of their forms.

Tattha pubbachakkabhūtāni aṭṭhacattālīsarūpāni parassapadāni nāma. Parachakkabhūtāni aṭṭhacattālīsarūpāni attanopadāni nāma.

Therein, the forty-eight forms that constitute the first group are called 'parassapada'. The forty-eight forms that constitute the second group are called 'attanopada'.

Tattha parahitapaṭisaṃyuttesu ṭhānesu pavattibahulāni padāni parassapadāni nāma. Attahitapaṭisaṃyuttesu pavattibahulāni attanopadāni nāmāti eke.

Therein, words that frequently occur in contexts connected with the welfare of others are called 'parassapada'. Words that frequently occur in contexts connected with one's own welfare are called 'attanopada', so say some.

Paro vuccati kattā sabbakriyāsādhāraṇattā, attā vuccati kammaṃ sakasakakriyāsādhāraṇattā, parassa abhidhāyakāni padāni parassapadāni, attano abhidhāyakāni padāni attanopadānīti aññe.

'Para' is called the agent because it is common to all actions; 'atta' is called the object because it is common to its respective actions. Words denoting 'para' are called 'parassapada'; words denoting 'atta' are called 'attanopada', so say others.

Attā vuccati padatthānaṃ sarīrabhūtā kriyā, kattunā pana sādhyaṭṭhena kriyarūpāni bhāva, kammānipi attāti vuccanti. Sādhakaṭṭhena tehi parabhūto kattā paro nāmāti apare.

'Atta' is called the action that is the essence of the word's meaning. But actions in the sense of being accomplished by the agent, and forms of action such as states and objects, are also called 'atta'. The agent, being distinct from them in the sense of being the accomplisher, is called 'para', so say others.

Attā vuccati amhattho, paro vuccati tumha, nāmattho, pubbachakkāni parabahulattā parassapadāni nāma, parachakkāni pana rūḷhīvasena attanopadāni nāmātipi vadanti. Idaṃ na yujjati parachakkesu tabbahulamattassāpi asiddhattā. Pāḷibhāsaṃ pana patvā dvinnaṃ chakkānaṃ attahita, parahitesu vā tīsu kārakesu vā pavattinānāttaṃ na dissatiyeva, tasmā imasmiṃ ganthe taṃ nāmadvayaṃ na gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Atta' is called the meaning of 'amha' (I/we); 'para' is called the meaning of 'tumha' (you) and nominals. The first group of endings are called 'parassapada' due to the prevalence of 'para'. But the second group, they say, are also called 'attanopada' by convention. This is not appropriate, because the mere prevalence of 'atta' is not established in the second group. However, in the Pali language, no difference in application is seen between the two groups, whether in relation to one's own welfare, the welfare of others, or the three syntactic roles. Therefore, it should be understood that in this text that pair of names is not adopted.

Paccayā [M 0.0348] pana catubbidhā vikaraṇa, kicca, kārita, dhātupaccayavasena.

Suffixes, however, are fourfold: by way of vikaraṇa, kicca, kārita, and dhātu suffixes.

Tattha ye dhātusiddhāni tyādipadāni tabbādipadāni ca gaṇavibhāgavasena aññamaññaṃ visadisarūpāni karonti, te vikaraṇapaccayā nāma, la, ya, ṇoiccādayo.

Therein, those suffixes which make the verb forms derived from roots, such as those ending in 'ti' etc. and 'tabba' etc., dissimilar to one another according to the division of groups, are called vikaraṇa suffixes—such as 'la', 'ya', 'ṇo', and so on.

Bhāva, kammavisayo kyo kiccapaccayo nāma.

The suffix 'kya', which pertains to the state (bhāva) and the object (kamma), is called the kicca suffix.

Paresaṃ āṇāpanasaṅkhāte payojakabyāpāre pavattā ṇi, ṇāpipaccayā kāritapaccayā nāma.

The suffixes 'ṇi' and 'ṇāpi', which operate in the causative function, described as commissioning others, are called kārita suffixes.

Visuṃ taṃtaṃkriyavācībhāvena dhāturūpā kha, cha, saiccādikā paccayā dhātupaccayā nāma.

The suffixes such as 'kha', 'cha', and 'sa', which are of the nature of a root by individually expressing various actions, are called 'dhātu-paccayas' (root-suffixes).

“Kāla, kāraka, purisa, saṅkhyābhedadīpaka”nti ettha atīta, paccuppannā’nāgata, kālavimuttavasena kālabhedo catubbidho.

In the phrase 'indicators of distinctions of time, syntactic role, person, and number,' the distinction of time is fourfold, based on past, present, future, and freedom from time.

Tattha hiyyattanī, ajjattanī ajjatanī (bahūsu), parokkhāti imā tisso vibhattiyo atīte kāle vattanti.

Among these, the three inflections—hiyattanī, ajjattanī, and parokkhā—occur in past time.

Vattamānā, pañcamīti dve paccuppanne.

The present (vattamānā) and the imperative (pañcamī)—these two occur in the present.

Ekā bhavissantī anāgate.

One, the future (bhavissantī), occurs in the future.

Sattamī, kālātipattīti dve kālavimutte vattanti, ayaṃ kira porāṇiko vibhattīnaṃ kamo, so ca pāḷiyā sametiyeva.

The optative (sattamī) and the conditional (kālātīpattī)—these two occur in the timeless. This, it is said, is the ancient order of inflections, and it agrees with the Pāli.

“Sabbe saddhammagaruno, vihaṃsu viharanti ca.

“All who revere the True Dhamma have dwelt and dwell.

Athopi viharissanti, esā buddhāna dhammatā”ti a. ni. 4.21 ca –

And they will dwell; such is the nature of the Buddhas.”

“Abbhatītā ca ye buddhā, vattamānā anāgatā”ti ca apa. thera 1.1.588 pāḷī. Imasmiṃ kame pañcamī, sattamīti nāmadvayampi anvatthavasena siddhaṃ [M 0.0349] bhavati. Pacchā pana garuno vatticchāvasena vibhattīnaṃ nānākamaṃ karonti.

And the Pāli phrase is: “The Buddhas who have passed, are present, and are future.” In this sequence, the two names—pañcamī (imperative) and sattamī (optative)—are also established based on their inherent meaning. Later, however, teachers make various sequences of the inflections according to their desired usage.

Kattu, kamma, bhāvā pana kārakabhedo nāma. Tattha bhāvo duvidho sādhya, sādhanavasena visesana, visesyavasena ca. Tattha dhātvatthakriyā sādhyabhāvo nāma. Paccayatthakriyā sādhanabhāvo nāma.

The agent (kattu), object (kamma), and state (bhāva), however, are called the distinction of kāraka. Among these, the state (bhāva) is twofold: by way of the state to be accomplished (sādhya) and the instrumental state (sādhana), and by way of qualifier and qualified. Here, the action that is the meaning of the verbal root is called the state to be accomplished. The action that is the meaning of the affix is called the instrumental state.

Tesu sādhyabhāvo nānādhātūnaṃ vasena nānāvidho hoti. Sādhanabhāvo nānādhātvatthānaṃ pavattākārasaṅkhātena ekaṭṭhena ekova hoti. So pana yathā jāti nāma anuppannapakkhe ṭhite saṅkhatadhamme uppādentī viya khāyati, tathā vohāravisayamatte ṭhite sabbadhātvatthe pātubhonte karonto viya khāyati, tasmā so sādhananti ca kārakanti ca vuccati. Yathā ca jātivasena uppannā saṅkhatadhammā “cintanaṃ jātaṃ, phusanaṃ jāta” miccādinā ekantameva jātiṃ visesenti, tathā paccayatthavasena pātubhontā nānādhātvatthāpi “bhuyyate, gamyate, paccate, bhavanaṃ, gamanaṃ, pacana” miccādinā ekantameva paccayatthaṃ visesenti. Vatticchāvasena pana bhāvasādhanapadesu dhātvattha, paccayatthānaṃ abhedopi vattuṃ yujjatiyeva. Idha pana dvīsu bhāvesu sādhanabhāvo adhippetoti.

Among these, the state to be accomplished (sādhyabhāva) is of various kinds according to different verbal roots. The instrumental state (sādhanabhāva), however, is singular, being characterized by the manner of occurrence in a single sense of various verbal root meanings. Yet, just as birth, while abiding in the unarisen aspect, appears to produce conditioned phenomena, so too does it appear to manifest all verbal root meanings, making them appear within the sphere of conventional usage. Therefore, it is called both 'instrumental' (sādhana) and 'kāraka' (agentive relation). And just as conditioned phenomena arisen by way of birth exclusively specify birth, such as 'thinking has arisen, touching has arisen,' so too do various verbal root meanings, when manifested by way of the affix-meaning, exclusively specify the affix-meaning, such as 'is being, is being gone, is being cooked, being, going, cooking.' However, according to the desire for expression, it is indeed appropriate to speak of the non-distinction between the verbal root meaning and the affix-meaning in expressions of the instrumental state. Here, however, the instrumental state is intended among the two states.

Paṭhama, majjhimu’ttamapurisā purisabhedo. ‘Puriso’ti ca “yaṃkiñcāyaṃ purisapuggalo paṭisaṃvedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā”ti ma. ni. 3.1 ettha attā eva vuccati, so ca attā “so karoti, so paṭisaṃvedetī”ti a. ni. 6.43; visuddhi. 2.580 ettha kārakoti vuccati. Iti ‘puriso’ti kārako eva.

The first, middle, and supreme persons are the distinction of person. And the term 'person' (purisa) here refers to the self (attā) in the phrase 'whatever this person (purisapuggala) experiences, be it pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure.' And that self is called the kāraka (agentive relation) where it says, 'He does, he experiences.' Thus, 'person' is indeed a kāraka.

So ca tividho nāmattho, tumhattho, amhattho cāti. Tattha attano ajjhattasantānabhūtattā amhattho uttamapuriso [M 0.0350] nāma, sesā pana kamena paṭhamapuriso, majjhimapurisoti vuccanti. Vibhattiyo pana taddīpakattā paṭhamapurisādināmaṃ labhanti. Idañca nāmaṃ kārakabhede antogadhamevāti katvā imasmiṃ ganthe na gahitanti.

And this (person) is threefold: the meaning of a noun (nāmattha), the meaning of 'you' (tumhattha), and the meaning of 'I' (amhattha). Among these, the 'I'-meaning is called the supreme person (uttamapurisa) because it pertains to one's own internal continuity. The rest, however, are called the first person (paṭhamapurisa) and the middle person (majjhimapurisa) in order. The inflections, however, acquire the names 'first person,' etc., because they illuminate these. And this name is considered as included within the distinction of kāraka and is thus not taken up in this text.

Saṅkhyābhedo duvidho ekatta, bahuttavasena.

The distinction of number is twofold: by way of singularity and plurality.

‘Liṅgabhedarahita’nti “puriso gacchati, itthī gacchati, kulaṃ gacchati” iccādīsu ‘puriso’iccādīnaṃ abhidheyyapadānaṃ liṅgānugato rūpabhedo ākhyātapade natthi.

As for 'devoid of gender distinction,' it means that in phrases like 'a man goes, a woman goes, a family goes,' there is no difference in the form of the finite verb (ākhyātapada) corresponding to the gender of the subject words (abhidheyyapada) like 'man,' etc.

‘Kriyāpadhānavācaka’nti ettha kriyaṃ eva padhānato abhidhāti, na nāmapadaṃ viya dabbaṃ padhānato abhidhātīti adhippāyo.

As for 'primarily expressing action,' here the meaning is that it primarily expresses action (kriyā), not primarily a substance (dabba) like a noun (nāmapada).

Tattha kriyā nāma dhātvatthabhāvo vuccati, sā ca kālavasena atītakriyā, paccuppannakriyā, anāgatakriyā, kālavimuttakriyāti catubbidhā hoti.

Here, action (kriyā) is said to be the state of the verbal root meaning, and it is fourfold according to time: past action, present action, future action, and timeless action.

Āṇattikriyā, āsiṭṭhakriyā, anumatikriyā, parikappakriyā, araha, sakka, vidhi, nimantanā’mantanādikriyāti bahuvidho kriyābhedoti.

The distinction of action is of many kinds, such as imperative action, optative action, permissive action, hypothetical action, action of fitness, action of capability, injunctive action, and actions like invitation and summoning.

Bhū-sattāyaṃ, santassa bhāvo sattā, tassaṃ sattāyaṃ, bhūdhātu sattāyamatthe vattate, sabbapadatthānaṃ sadda, buddhivisayabhāvena vijjamānabhāve vattatetyattho.

As for 'bhū' in the sense of 'being' (sattāyaṃ): 'being' (sattā) is the state of the existent (santa). In that 'being,' the verbal root 'bhū' functions in the sense of 'being.' The meaning is that it functions in the sense of the existence of all word-meanings by way of being sound and objects of cognition.

561. Kriyatthā ka. 432, 455; rū. 362, 530; nī. 905, 936; pā. 3.1.91.

561. For the purpose of action.

Adhikārasuttamidaṃ, kriyatthā paraṃ vibhatti, paccayā bhavantīti attho. Kriyā attho yassāti kriyattho. Pakatidhātu, vikatidhātu, nāmadhātuvasena tividho dhātu, kāritapaccayantarūpampi vikatidhātumhi saṅgayhati.

This is an adhikāra-sutta (governing rule). The meaning is that after that which is for the purpose of action (kriyatthā), inflections (vibhatti) and suffixes (paccaya) occur. That which has action as its purpose is a 'kriyattha'. The verbal root (dhātu) is threefold: natural root, modified root, and nominal root. Even the form with a causative suffix is included under the modified root.

562. Vattamāneti [M 0.0351] anti si tha mi ma te ante se vhe e mhe ka. 414; rū. 428; nī. 872; caṃ. 1.2.82; pā. 3.2.123.

562. In the present tense: ti, anti, si, tha, mi, ma; te, ante, se, vhe, e, mhe.

Ārabhitvā niṭṭhaṃ anupagato bhāvo vattamāno nāma, taṃsambandhīkālopi tadūpacārena vattamānoti vuccati. Vattamāne kāle kriyatthā paraṃ tyādivibhattiyo bhavanti. Ayañca vibhatti tyādīti ca vattamānakālavisayattā vattamānāti ca sijjhati.

That state (bhāva) which has begun but not yet reached conclusion is called the present (vattamāna). The time connected with it is also figuratively called the present. In the present time, inflections like ti, etc., occur after that which is for the purpose of action (kriyatthā). And this inflection is established as 'ti, etc.' and also as 'vattamānā' because it pertains to the present time.

563. Pubbāparachakkānamekānekesu tumhamhasesesu dve dve majjhimuttamapaṭhamā ka. 408; rū. 431; nī. 867.

563. Of the former and latter sets of six, in the singular and plural, with regard to 'you' (tumha), 'I' (amha), and the rest (sesa), there are two each for the middle, supreme, and first persons.

Tumhanāmaṃ, amhanāmaṃ, tadubhayato sesanāmanti tīsu nāmesu payujjamānesu vā gamyamānesu vā ekasmiṃ vā anekesu vā atthesu pubbachakka, parachakkānaṃ dve dve majjhima, uttama, paṭhamā vibhattiyo bhavanti. “Uttamanti uttaraṃ antima”nti cūḷamoggallāne vuttaṃ.

When the three nominal stems—the 'you' stem (tumha-nāma), the 'I' stem (amha-nāma), and the remaining nominal stems (sesa-nāma) other than these two—are used or understood, whether in a singular or plural sense, two inflections each for the middle, supreme, and first persons from the former set of six and the latter set of six occur. In the Cūḷamoggallāna, it is stated: 'Uttama means the ultimate, the last.'

Ettha ca vibhattividhānamukhena taṃtaṃsaññāvidhānampi siddhaṃ hoti.

And here, by means of the exposition of the inflections, the assigning of their respective designations is also established.

Kathaṃ?Ti, anti, si, tha, mi, ma iti pubbachakkaṃ nāma.

How so? Ti, anti, si, tha, mi, ma—this is called the former set of six.

Te, ante, se, vhe, e, mhe iti parachakkaṃ nāma.

Te, ante, se, vhe, e, mhe—this is called the latter set of six.

Pubbachakke ca-ti, antidvayaṃ paṭhamadukaṃ nāma, si, thadvayaṃ majjhimadukaṃ nāma, mi, madvayaṃ uttamadukaṃ nāma. Evaṃ parachakke.

And in the former set of six: the pair ti, anti is called the first pair; the pair si, tha is called the middle pair; the pair mi, ma is called the supreme pair. Similarly, in the latter set of six.

Tattha tulyādhikaraṇabhūte sesanāme payujjamāne vā gamyamāne vā paṭhamadukaṃ bhavati. Tathā tumhanāme majjhimadukaṃ, amhanāme uttamadukaṃ. Dukesu ca ekasmiṃ atthe vattabbe ekavacanaṃ, bahumhi vattabbe bahuvacanaṃ.

Therein, when the remaining nominal stem (sesa-nāma), being in apposition, is used or understood, the first pair occurs. Likewise, with the 'you' nominal stem (tumha-nāma), the middle pair occurs; and with the 'I' nominal stem (amha-nāma), the supreme pair occurs. And in these pairs, when a single meaning is to be expressed, the singular is used; when many are to be expressed, the plural is used.

Ettha [M 0.0352] ca nāmānaṃ atthanissitā katvattha, kammatthā idha nāmatthāti vuccanti. Kattu, kammasaṅkhāte yasmiṃ nāmatthe tyādivibhattiyo bhavanti, so nāmattho tyādivācakānaṃ eva vāccabhūto vuttattho nāma hoti, na syādivibhattīnaṃ.

And here, the agent-meaning (kattuttha) and object-meaning (kammattha), which are dependent on the sense of the nominal stems, are called the nominal meaning. The nominal meaning, designated as agent or object, in which the verbal inflections like ti, etc., occur—that nominal meaning is indeed the expressed meaning (vuttattha) of the words like ti, etc., and not of the nominal inflections like si, etc.

Vuttakattu, kammādhiṭṭhānassa ca liṅgatthassa vācakaṃ nāmapadaṃ abhidheyyapadaṃ nāma, etadeva tulyādhikaraṇapadanti ca vuccati.

The nominal word (nāmapada) that expresses the meaning of the nominal stem (liṅgattha) which is the basis for the expressed agent or object is called the subject word (abhidheyyapada), and this same is also called the appositional word (tulyādhikaraṇapada).

Amādayo ca atthavācakavibhattiyo etasmiṃ okāsaṃ na labhanti, liṅgatthamattajotikā paṭhamāvibhatti eva okāsaṃ labhati. Evarūpāni tulyādhikaraṇabhūtāni abhidheyyapadāni sandhāya sutte ‘tumhamhasesesū’ti vuttaṃ.

And the inflections expressing meaning, such as aṃ, etc., do not find a place here; only the first inflection (paṭhamā-vibhatti), which merely illuminates the meaning of the nominal stem, finds a place. Referring to such subject words which are in apposition, the phrase 'tumhamhasesesu' is stated in the sutta.

Idañca suttaṃ suddhehi tumha’mha, sesanāmehi yuttavākye ca missakehi yuttavākye cāti dvīsu dvīsu vākyesu veditabbaṃ.

And this rule should be understood in two kinds of sentences: sentences connected with pure nominal stems—the 'tumha' (you) and 'amha' (I) stems, and the remaining nominal stems—and sentences connected with mixed ones.

Tattha suddhehi yutte paccekaṃ dukāni vattanti. Yathā? So gacchati, te gacchanti, tvaṃ gacchasi, tumhe gacchatha, ahaṃ gacchāmi, mayaṃ gacchāmāti.

Among these, in sentences connected with pure nominal stems, individual pairs occur. For example: 'He goes,' 'they go,' 'you (sg.) go,' 'you (pl.) go,' 'I go,' 'we go.'

Tathā suddhadvandepi. Yathā? So ca so ca gacchati, gacchanti vā. Te ca te ca gacchanti, so ca te ca gacchanti, tvañca tvañca gacchasi, gacchatha vā. Tumhe ca tumhe ca gacchatha, tvañca tumhe ca gacchathāti.

Similarly, also in pure dvanda constructions. For example: 'He and he goes,' or 'they go.' 'They and they go,' 'he and they go,' 'you (sg.) and you (sg.) go,' or 'you (pl.) go.' 'You (pl.) and you (pl.) go,' 'you (sg.) and you (pl.) go.'

Missakehi yutte dvandavākye pana ‘vippaṭisedhe’ti saṅketattā paradukāni eva okāsaṃ labhanti, tesu ca bahuvacanāni eva. Yathā? So ca tvañca gacchatha, so ca ahañca gacchāma, tvañca ahañca gacchāma, so ca tvañca ahañca gacchāma. Ekavacanacatukkaṃ.

However, in dvanda sentences connected with mixed nominal stems, because of the convention of 'vippaṭisedha' (conflict), only the latter persons find application, and among those, only the plural forms. For example: 'He and you go,' 'he and I go,' 'you and I go,' 'he and you and I go.' This is the tetrad of singulars.

Te ca tumhe ca gacchatha, te ca mayañca gacchāma, tumhe ca mayañca gacchāma, te ca tumhe ca mayañca gacchāma. Bahuvacanacatukkaṃ.

'They and you (pl.) go,' 'they and we go,' 'you (pl.) and we go,' 'they and you (pl.) and we go.' This is the tetrad of plurals.

So [M 0.0353] ca tumhe ca gacchatha, so ca mayañca gacchāma, tvañca mayañca gacchāma, so ca tvañca mayañca gacchāma. Ekavacanamūlacatukkaṃ.

'He and you (pl.) go,' 'he and we go,' 'you (sg.) and we go,' 'he and you (sg.) and we go.' This is the tetrad with a singular base.

Te ca tvañca gacchatha, te ca ahañca gacchāma, tumhe ca ahañca gacchāma, te ca tumhe ca ahañca gacchāma. Bahuvacanamūlacatukkaṃ.

'They and you (sg.) go,' 'they and I go,' 'you (pl.) and I go,' 'they and you (pl.) and I go.' This is the tetrad with a plural base.

Api ca tvañca so ca gacchatha, ahañca so ca gacchāma, tvañca ahañca so ca gacchāma, tumhe ca so ca gacchatha, mayañca so ca gacchāma, tvañca te ca gacchatha, ahañca te ca gacchāmaiccādīnipi catukkāni veditabbāni.

Furthermore, 'you (sg.) and he go,' 'I and he go,' 'you (sg.) and I and he go,' 'you (pl.) and he go,' 'we and he go,' 'you (sg.) and they go,' 'I and they go,' and so on—these tetrads should also be understood.

Atrimā pāḷī – tuvañca putto suṇisā ca nattā, sammodamānā gharamāvasetha jā. 1.8.7. Ahañca putto suṇisā ca nattā, sammodamānā gharamāvasema jā. 1.8.7.

Here is a Pāḷi passage: 'You, son, daughter-in-law, and grandchild, rejoicing together, may you dwell in the house.' 'I, son, daughter-in-law, and grandchild, rejoicing together, may we dwell in the house.'

Ahañca dāni āyasmā ca sāriputto bhikkhusaṅghaṃ pariharissāma ma. ni. 2.160.

Now I and the Venerable Sāriputta will look after the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Ahañca ime ca bhikkhū samādhinā nisīdimhā.

I and these bhikkhus sat in concentration.

Ahañca bhariyā ca dānapatī ahumhā jā. 2.22.1593.

I and my wife were donors.

Ahañca sāmiko ca dānapatī ahumhā jā. 2.22.1617 iccādi.

I and my husband were donors, and so on.

Yaṃ pana “so ca gacchati, tvañca gacchasī”ti vattabbe “tumhe gacchathā”ti vā “so ca gacchati, ahañca gacchāmī”ti vattabbe “mayaṃ gacchāmā”ti vā vacanaṃ, taṃ pakatibahuvacanameva, na paropurisabahuvacanaṃ.

However, the utterance 'you (pl.) go' when one should say 'he goes, and you (sg.) go,' or the utterance 'we go' when one should say 'he goes, and I go'—that is simply the natural plural, not the plural of the other person.

Yañca kaccāyane – “sabbesamekābhidhāne paro puriso”ti nī. 216 piṭṭhe suttaṃ, tatthapi sabbesaṃ dvinnaṃ vā tiṇṇaṃ vā missakabhūtānaṃ [M 0.0354] nāma, tumha’mhānaṃ ekato abhidhāne missakadvandavākye paro puriso yojetabboti attho na na sambhavatīti.

And as for the rule in the Kaccāyana grammar—'When all are designated as one, the latter person is used'—there too, when the nominal stems of all, whether two or three, being mixed, along with the 'tumha' and 'amha' stems, are designated together, the meaning that the latter person should be employed in a mixed dvanda sentence is by no means impossible.

564. Kattari lo ka. 455; rū. 433; nī. 925.

564. `La` [is affixed] in the agentive sense.

Aparokkhesu māna, nta, tyādīsu paresu kriyatthā paraṃ kattari lānubandho apaccayo hoti. Lānubandho ‘ūlasse’ti sutte visesanattho.

When non-proximate suffixes such as `māna`, `nta`, `ti`, etc., follow, the suffix `a` with the anubandha `l` occurs after a root in the agentive sense. The anubandha `l` in the rule 'ūlasse' serves the purpose of specification.

Etena yattha māna, nta, tyādayo kattari vattanti, tattha ayaṃ lapaccayoti lapaccayena tesaṃ kattuvācakabhāvaṃ ñāpeti, esa nayo “kyo bhāvakammesu…” iccādīsupi.

By this, it is indicated that wherever `māna`, `nta`, `ti`, and the like occur in the agentive sense, this `la`-suffix is employed, and through this `la`-suffix, their nature as expressing the agent is made known. This principle also applies in instances such as '`kya` in the sense of state and action,' and so on.

Ettha ca vikaraṇapaccayā nāma byañjanapūraṇā eva honti, na atthapūraṇā, tasmā yasmiṃ payoge tehi vinā padarūpaṃ na sijjhati, tattheva te vattanti. Yattha sijjhati, tattha na vattanti, ayampi lapaccayo dhātuto paraṃ vibhattisare vā āgamasare vā asante vattati, sante pana “pacāmi, pacāma, pacāhi, gameti, gamenti, vajjeti, vajjenti”-iccādīsu kāriyantaratthāya vattati. Yattha ca paccayānaṃ lopo vihito, tattha gaṇantara, rūpantarappasaṅgapaṭisiddhāya vattati, aññattha na vattati.

Here, the suffixes called 'vikaraṇa' are merely consonant-fillers, not meaning-fillers. Therefore, they occur only in a usage where the form of the word cannot be accomplished without them. Where it can be accomplished, they do not occur. This `la`-suffix also occurs after a root in the absence of a personal ending vowel or an augment vowel. But when one is present, it occurs for the purpose of another function, as in 'pacāmi, pacāma, pacāhi, gameti, gamenti, vajjeti, vajjenti,' and so on. And where the elision of suffixes is prescribed, it occurs in order to prevent the contingency of another class or another form, but not elsewhere.

565. Yuvaṇṇānameo paccaye ka. 485; rū. 434; nī. 975; caṃ. 1.1.82; pā. 3.1.60.

565. Of the vowels `i` and `u`, `e` and `o` are the respective substitutes when a suffix follows.

Vibhatti, paccayā paccayo nāma. I, kī, khi, ci, ji iccādayo ivaṇṇā nāma. Cu, ju, bhū, hū iccādayo uvaṇṇā nāma. Paccaye pare ekakkharadhātvantānaṃ ivaṇṇu’vaṇṇānaṃ kamena e, ovuddhiyo honti. ‘Paro kvacī’ti parasaralopo.

Personal endings and suffixes are called `paccaya`. Roots ending in `i`, such as `i`, `kī`, `khi`, `ci`, `ji`, are called `ivaṇṇā` (i-vowel roots). Roots ending in `u`, such as `cu`, `ju`, `bhū`, `hū`, are called `uvaṇṇā` (u-vowel roots). When a suffix follows, the final `i` and `u` vowels of monosyllabic roots are strengthened to `e` and `o` respectively. By the rule 'paro kvaci', the following vowel is elided.

Saṃpubbo-sambhoti[M 0.0355], sambhonti, sambhosi, sambhotha, sambhomi, sambhoma.

Preceded by `saṃ`: sambhoti, sambhonti, sambhosi, sambhotha, sambhomi, sambhoma.

Anupubbo-anubhavane, so bhogaṃ anubhoti, te bhogaṃ anubhonti, tvaṃ bhogaṃ anubhosi, tumhe bhogaṃ anubhotha, ahaṃ bhogaṃ anubhomi, mayaṃ bhogaṃ anubhoma.

Preceded by `anu`, in the sense of experiencing: He experiences enjoyment, they experience enjoyment, you (sg.) experience enjoyment, you (pl.) experience enjoyment, I experience enjoyment, we experience enjoyment.

Tattha yathā “nīlo paṭo”ti ettha nīlasaddassa attho duvidho vāccattho, abhidheyyatthoti.

Therein, just as in the phrase 'a blue cloth,' the meaning of the word 'blue' is twofold: the expressed meaning and the designatable meaning.

Tattha guṇasaṅkhāto sakattho vāccattho nāma.

Therein, its own meaning, which is designated as a quality, is called the expressed meaning.

Guṇanissayo dabbattho abhidheyyattho nāma.

The meaning of substance, which is the substratum of the quality, is called the designatable meaning.

Nīlasaddo pana vaccātthameva ujuṃ vadati, nīlasaddamattaṃ suṇanto nīlaguṇameva ujuṃ jānāti, tasmā “paṭo” iti padantarena nīlasaddassa abhidheyyattho ācikkhīyati.

The word 'blue,' however, directly expresses only the expressed meaning; one who hears merely the word 'blue' directly understands only the quality of blue. Therefore, the designatable meaning of the word 'blue' is indicated by another word, that is, 'cloth'.

Tathā “anubhotī”ti ettha tisaddassa attho duvidho vāccattho, abhidheyyatthoti.

Similarly, in 'anubhoti,' the meaning of the suffix 'ti' is twofold: the expressed meaning and the designatable meaning.

Tattha kattusattisaṅkhāto sakattho vāccattho nāma.

Therein, its own meaning, which is designated as the agentive power, is called the expressed meaning.

Sattinissayo liṅgattho abhidheyyattho nāma.

The meaning of the substantive agent, which is the substratum of that power, is called the designatable meaning.

Tisaddo pana vāccatthameva ujuṃ vadati, na abhidheyyatthaṃ. “Anubhotī”ti suṇantosādhyakriyāsahitaṃ kattārameva ujuṃ jānāti, na kiñci dabbanti attho. Tasmā “so” iti padantarena tisaddassa abhidheyyattho ācikkhīyati, vāccatthassa pana tisaddeneva ujuṃ vuttattā tatiyāvibhattiyā puna ācikkhitabbakiccaṃ natthi, liṅgatthajotanatthaṃ abhidheyyapade paṭhamāvibhatti eva pavattatīti. Esa nayo sabbattha.

However, the suffix 'ti' directly states only the expressed meaning, not the denoted meaning. When hearing 'anubhoti,' one directly understands only the agent associated with the action to be accomplished, not any substance; that is the meaning. Therefore, the denoted meaning of the suffix 'ti' is indicated by another word, such as 'so' (he); but since the expressed meaning is already directly stated by the suffix 'ti' itself, there is no further task for the third case ending to indicate again. Only the first case ending occurs in the word denoting the meaning, for the purpose of clarifying the gender. This principle applies everywhere.

566. Eonamayavā sare ka. 513, 514; rū. 435, 491; nī. 1027, 1028.

566. When a vowel follows, 'e' and 'o' become 'aya' and 'ava' respectively.

Sare [M 0.0356] pare e, onaṃ kamena aya, avā honti. Ya, vesu a-kāro uccāraṇattho.

When a vowel follows, 'e' and 'o' become 'aya' and 'ava' respectively. In 'ya' and 'va', the letter 'a' is for the purpose of pronunciation.

Bhavati, bhavanti, bhavasi, bhavatha.

He is, they are, you are (singular), you are (plural).

567. Himimesvassa ka. 478; rū. 438; nī. 959.

567. The 'a' is lengthened before 'hi', 'mi', and 'me'.

Hi, mi, mesu paresu a-kārassa dīgho hoti.

When 'hi', 'mi', and 'me' follow, the letter 'a' becomes long.

Bhavāmi, bhavāma.

I am, we are.

Parachakke – bhavate, bhavante, bhavase, bhavavhe, bhave, bhavamhe.

In the other set of six: bhavate, bhavante, bhavase, bhavavhe, bhave, bhavamhe.

Papubbo bhū-pavattiyaṃ, nadī pabhavati.

The root 'bhū' with the prefix 'pa' is used in the sense of arising: The river originates.

Adhyā’bhi, paripubbo hiṃsāyaṃ, adhibhavati, abhibhavati, paribhavati.

The root 'bhū' with the prefixes 'adhi', 'abhi', and 'pari' is used in the sense of harming or overcoming: adhibhavati, abhibhavati, paribhavati.

Vipubbo vināse, pākaṭe, sobhaṇe ca, vibhavati.

With the prefix 'vi', it is used in the sense of destruction, manifestation, and beauty: vibhavati.

Parāpubbo parājaye, parābhavati.

With the prefix 'parā', it is used in the sense of defeat: parābhavati.

Abhi, saṃpubbo pattiyaṃ, ajjhogāhe ca, abhisambhavati, tathā pātubbhavati, āvibhavati iccādi.

With the prefixes 'abhi' and 'saṃ', it is used in the sense of attainment and plunging into: abhisambhavati. Similarly, pātubbhavati, āvibhavati, and so on.

Iti suddhakatturūpaṃ.

Thus, the forms of the root 'bhū'.

Suddhabhāvakammarūpa

Pure Bhāva and Kamma Forms

568. Kyo [M 0.0357] bhāvakammesvaparokkhesu māna nta tyādīsu ka. 440; rū. 445; nī. 920; caṃ. 1.1.80; pā. 3.1.67.

568. The suffix 'kya' is used in bhāva and kamma constructions in the non-perfect tenses, and before 'māna', 'nta', 'ti', and other such suffixes.

Parokkhāvajjitesu māna, ntapaccayesu tyādīsu ca paresu kriyatthā bhāvasmiṃ kammani ca kānubandho yapaccayo hoti, bahulādhikārā kvaci kattari ca.

When the suffixes 'māna', 'nta', 'ti', and so on follow—excluding the perfect tense—the suffix 'ya' with the anubandha 'k' occurs in the bhāva and kamma constructions, which have the meaning of action. Due to the governing rule of 'variously', it sometimes also occurs in the agent construction.

Rūpaṃ vibhuyyati, so pahīyissati saṃ. ni. 1.249, bhattaṃ paccati, gimhe udakaṃ chijjati, kusūlo bhijjati.

Form is experienced, it will be abandoned, food is cooked, in summer water is cut off, the granary is broken.

569. Na te kānubandhanāgamesu.

569. Those vowel changes do not occur when caused by a suffix with anubandha 'k' or by an augment.

Kānubandhe nāgame ca ivaṇṇu’vaṇṇānaṃ assa ca te e, o,-ā na hontīti kyamhi vuddhi natthi.

When a suffix with anubandha 'k' or an augment follows, the vuddhi substitutions—'e' for 'i'/'ī', 'o' for 'u'/'ū', and 'ā' for 'a'—do not occur. Therefore, there is no vuddhi before the 'kya' suffix.

Kamme-tena purisena bhogo anubhūyati, tena bhogā anubhūyanti, tena tvaṃ anubhūyasi, tena tumhe anubhūyatha, tena ahaṃ anubhūyāmi, tena mayaṃ anubhūyāma. Yassa dvittaṃ rassattañca, anubhuyyati, anubhuyyanti.
