Mara-pāṇacāge, maritthāti mato, kālaṅkato.

The root `Mara` is in the sense of abandoning life. 'He died' (`marittha`) becomes `mato` (dead), which means `kālaṅkato` (he has passed away).

Ramu-kīḷāyaṃ, ramitthāti rato, abhirato.

The root `Ramu` is in the sense of playing. 'He delighted' (`ramittha`) becomes `rato` (delighted), `abhirato` (greatly delighted).

Ramu-uparame[M 0.0482], virato, paṭivirato, uparato.

The root `Ramu` is in the sense of ceasing. Hence `virato` (abstained), `paṭivirato` (refrained), `uparato` (ceased).

Sara-gati, cintāsu, bahulādhikārā kālattayepi tapaccayo, sarati, asari, sarissatīti sato, anussato, patissato.

The root `Sara` is in the sense of moving and thinking. Due to its wide application, the suffix `-ta` is used in all three tenses. Thus from `sarati` (he remembers), `asari` (he remembered), and `sarissati` (he will remember) come the forms `sato` (mindful), `anussato` (recollected), and `patissato` (mindful).

Hara-haraṇe, harīyitthāti hato, āhato, nihato.

The root `Hara` is in the sense of taking. 'It was taken' (`harīyittha`) becomes `hato` (taken), `āhato` (struck), `nihato` (struck down).

Tassa ṭatte-āhaṭo, nihaṭo, udāhaṭo, samudāhaṭo, avahaṭo.

When its `ra` becomes `ṭa`: `āhaṭo` (brought), `nihaṭo` (put down), `udāhaṭo` (cited), `samudāhaṭo` (expounded), `avahaṭo` (taken away).

Hana-hiṃsāyaṃ, haññitthāti hato, vihato, samūhato avippavāso mahāva. 145, samūhatā sīmā mahāva. 146.

The root `Hana` is in the sense of harming. 'He was struck' (`haññittha`) becomes `hato` (struck), `vihato` (destroyed), `samūhato` (abolished). The form `samūhato`, as in `samūhatā sīmā` (the boundary is abolished), implies `avippavāso` (non-separation).

Tipaccayamhi bahulādhikārā akānubandhepi antalopo. Paṭhamaṃ karīyatīti pakati, ākāro ākati, vikāro vikati, gāyanaṃ gīti, uggīti, saṅgīti, anugāyanaṃ anugīti, gamanaṃ gati, gantabbāti vā gati, gacchanti etthāti vā gati, āgamanaṃ āgati, sugati, duggati, samāgamanaṃ saṅgati, jananaṃ jāti, jāyanti etāya, etthāti vā jāti, ṭhānaṃ ṭhiti, saṇṭhiti, avaṭṭhiti, punappunaṃ tananaṃ santati, dhārenti etāyāti dhīti, mahāvuttinā īttaṃ.

With the suffix `-ti`, due to wide application, there is elision of the final vowel of the root even when it is not an `a`-root. `Pakati` (nature) is so called because 'it is done first' (`paṭhamaṃ karīyati`). From `ākāra` (appearance) comes `ākati` (figure). From `vikāra` (alteration) comes `vikati` (change). From `gāyana` (singing) comes `gīti` (song); also `uggīti` (chanting), `saṅgīti` (communal chanting). From `anugāyana` (singing after) comes `anugīti`. From `gamana` (going) comes `gati` (destination); or 'what should be gone to' (`gantabbā`); or 'where they go' (`gacchanti ettha`). From `āgamana` (coming) comes `āgati` (arrival). Also `sugati` (good destination), `duggati` (bad destination). From `samāgamana` (coming together) comes `saṅgati` (association). From `janana` (birth) comes `jāti` (birth); or 'by which they are born' (`jāyanti etāya`), or 'wherein they are born' (`ettha`). From `ṭhāna` (standing) comes `ṭhiti` (stability); also `saṇṭhiti` (firm standing), `avaṭṭhiti` (persistence). From 'repeated stretching' (`punappunaṃ tananaṃ`) comes `santati` (continuity). `Dhīti` (wisdom) is so called because 'they hold with this' (`dhārenti etāya`); the long `ī` is by the Mahāvutti.

Namanaṃ nati, unnati, samunnati, onati, avanati, bharitabbāti bhati, manati jānāti etāyāti mati, vividhā mati vimati, ramaṇaṃ rati, āramaṇaṃ ārati, viramaṇaṃ virati, abhiramaṇaṃ abhirati, paṭiviramaṇaṃ pativirati, saraṇaṃ sati, saranti etāyāti vā sati, anussati, paṭissati, upahananaṃ upahati.

From `namana` (bending) comes `nati` (inclination); also `unnati` (progress), `samunnati` (great progress), `onati` (condescension), `avanati` (humility). `Bhati` (wages) is so called because 'it is to be borne' (`bharitabbā`). `Mati` (thought) is so called because 'one thinks or knows with it' (`manati jānāti etāya`). 'Varied thought' (`vividhā mati`) is `vimati` (doubt). From `ramaṇa` (delight) comes `rati` (delight). From `āramaṇa` (resorting to) comes `ārati` (abstinence). From `viramaṇa` (abstaining) comes `virati` (abstinence). From `abhiramaṇa` (great delight) comes `abhirati` (fondness). From `paṭiviramaṇa` (refraining) comes `pativirati` (refraining). From `saraṇa` (remembering) comes `sati` (mindfulness); or it is `sati` because 'they remember with it' (`saranti etāya`). Also `anussati` (recollection), `paṭissati` (mindfulness). From `upahanana` (striking) comes `upahati` (enmity).

Tavantupaccayamhi-akāsīti katavā, ahanīti hatavā.

With the suffix `-tavantu`: the aorist `akāsi` (he did) corresponds to `katavā` (one who has done); the aorist `ahani` (he struck) corresponds to `hatavā` (one who has struck).

Tāvīpaccayamhi-katāvī, hatāvī.

With the suffix `-tāvī`: `katāvī` (one who has done), `hatāvī` (one who has struck).

Tvādīsu [M 0.0483] –

With the suffixes `tvā` and so on:

728. Tuṃtunatabbesu vā.

728. Or with `tuṃ`, `tuna`, and `tabba`.

Karadhātussa ra-kārassa ā hoti vā tuṃ, tuna, tabbesu. Tunasaddena tvāna, tvāpi saṅgayhanti.

The `ra` of the root `kara` optionally becomes `ā` before the suffixes `tuṃ`, `tuna`, and `tabba`. The mention of `tuna` also includes `tvāna` and `tvā`.

729. Karassā tave.

729. `Karassā tave`.

Karassa ra-kārassa ā hoti tavepaccayamhi.

The `ra` of the root `kara` becomes `ā` before the suffix `tave`.

Kātuṃ, kātave, kātuna, kātabbaṃ.

`Kātuṃ` (to do), `kātave` (for doing), `kātuna` (having done), `kātabbaṃ` (to be done).

Yathā karassa, tathā mahāvuttinā harassa rūpaṃ sijjhati, hāthuṃ, hātave, hātuna. Tesaṃ tuṇḍena hātūna, muñce pubbakataṃ iṇaṃ jā. 1.14.10.

Just as for the root `kara`, so too for the root `hara` the form is accomplished according to the Mahāvutti: `hāthuṃ` (to take), `hātave` (for taking), `hātuna` (having taken). For example: 'Having taken with their beaks (`tesaṃ tuṇḍena hātūna`), they release the debt previously made (`muñce pubbakataṃ iṇaṃ`).'

Tvāmhi āssa ittaṃ, āhitvā, soṇḍāyudakamāhitvā jā. 1.10.9 (…hatvā).

Before `tvā`, its `ā` becomes `i`. For example, `āhitvā` (having placed), as in `soṇḍāyudakamāhitvā` (having drawn up water with its trunk).

Iti visaṃyogarūparāsi.

Thus ends the section on forms from roots with a single final consonant.

Sadisasaṃyogarūparāsi

The Section on Forms with Identical Conjunct Consonants

Atha sadisasaṃyogarūparāsi vuccate.

Now the section on forms with identical conjunct consonants is spoken.

Tupaccayamhi –

With the suffix `-tu`:

730. Pararūpamayakāre byañjane.

730. Assimilation to the following consonant, excluding the letter 'y'.

Yakāravajjite byañjanapaccaye pare sabbadhātūnaṃ antabyañjano pararūpaṃ āpajjate.

When a consonantal suffix follows, one that is devoid of the letter 'y', the final consonant of any root is assimilated to the following consonant.

Karotīti kattā, kātuṃ arahati, kātuṃ sakkoti, karaṇasīlo, karaṇadhammo, sakkaccaṃ vā karotīti attho. Bharatīti bhattā, haratīti hattā.

Kattā (doer) is so called because 'he does' (karoti). The meaning is 'he is worthy to do' (kātuṃ arahati), 'he is able to do' (kātuṃ sakkoti), 'he is of a disposition to do' (karaṇasīlo), 'he has the nature to do' (karaṇadhammo), or 'he does carefully' (sakkaccaṃ vā karoti). Similarly, bhattā (supporter) is so called because 'he supports' (bharati); hattā (carrier) is so called because 'he carries' (harati).

Tvādīsu [M 0.0484] ra-kārassa āttaṃ, saṃyoge pare rassattañca, katvā, katvāna.

With the suffixes tvā and so on, the 'r' of the root 'kar' becomes 'ā', and this is then shortened before a conjunct consonant. For example: katvā, katvāna.

Pararūpattaṃ, kattuna, kattuṃ, kattabbaṃ, bharaṇaṃ bhattuṃ, bhattave, haraṇaṃ hattuṃ, abhihattuṃ, hattave.

Assimilation to the following consonant occurs in: kattuna (having done), kattuṃ (to do), kattabbaṃ (to be done); from bharaṇa (supporting) come bhattuṃ (to support), bhattave (for supporting); from haraṇa (carrying) come hattuṃ (to carry), abhihattuṃ (to carry towards), hattave (for carrying).

Āpa, ṇāpa, khipa, gupa, caja, ñapa, ñāpa, tapa, dīpa, dhūpa, pada, bhaja, bhuja, mada, mida, yuja, rica, ranja, lipa, lupa, vaca, vatu, vada, vapa, vica, sanja, sica, sambhu, sūca, sūda, supa.

The roots: Āpa (to obtain), ṇāpa (to cause to know), khipa (to throw), gupa (to protect), caja (to abandon), ñapa (to make known), ñāpa (to make known), tapa (to burn), dīpa (to shine), dhūpa (to fumigate), pada (to go), bhaja (to associate), bhuja (to eat, to enjoy), mada (to be intoxicated), mida (to be affectionate), yuja (to yoke), rica (to leave), ranja (to dye), lipa (to smear), lupa (to cut), vaca (to speak), vatu (to be), vada (to speak), vapa (to sow), vica (to separate), sanja (to cling), sica (to sprinkle), sambhu (to trust), sūca (to indicate), sūda (to destroy), supa (to sleep).

Dhātvantabyañjanassa pararūpattaṃ, tapaccayamhi vipubbo āpabyāpane, byāpayati khippaṃ ñāṇabyāpanena byāpituṃ sakkotīti byatto, viyatto.

With the suffix -ta, the final consonant of a root is assimilated to the following consonant. The root āpa, in the sense of pervading, when preceded by the prefix vi-, gives byatto or viyatto (accomplished). This is because 'he quickly pervades' (byāpayati khippaṃ) or 'is able to pervade with knowledge' (ñāṇabyāpanena byāpituṃ sakkoti).

Paripubbo pariyāpuṇane pahutte ca, pariyatto.

The same root, preceded by pari-, is in the sense of mastering and being able, giving the form pariyatto (mastered).

Saṃpubbo paripuṇṇabhāve, samāpayitthāti samatto, parisamatto.

Preceded by saṃ-, the root is in the sense of completion. 'It was completed' (samāpayittha) becomes samatto (completed), parisamatto (fully completed).

Āpubbo ṇāpa-pesane, āṇāpīyitthāti āṇatto.

The root ṇāpa, preceded by ā-, is in the sense of commanding. 'It was commanded' (āṇāpīyittha) becomes āṇatto (commanded).

Khipa-khipane, khipīyitthāti khitto-daṇḍo, khittā-mattikā, khittaṃ-leṭṭu. Evaṃ sabbattha. Pakkhitto, ukkhitto, nikkhitto, vikkhitto, okkhitto, saṃkhitto.

The root khipa is in the sense of throwing. 'It was thrown' (khipīyittha) becomes khitto. For example: khitto daṇḍo (a stick that was thrown), khittā mattikā (clay that was thrown), khittaṃ leṭṭu (a clod that was thrown). Thus it is in all cases. With prefixes: pakkhitto (thrown in), ukkhitto (thrown up), nikkhitto (thrown down), vikkhitto (scattered), okkhitto (thrown down), saṃkhitto (summarized).

Gupa-guttiyaṃ, gopīyitthāti gutto, saṃgutto.

The root gup is in the sense of guarding. 'It was guarded' (gopīyittha) becomes gutto (guarded), and saṃgutto (well-guarded).

Caja-cāge, cajīyitthāti catto.

The root caj is in the sense of giving up. 'It was given up' (cajīyittha) becomes catto (given up).

Upa-paññāpane, paññapīyitthāti paññatto-vinayo, paññattaṃsikkhāpadaṃ, paññattaṃ-āsanaṃ.

The root paññap is in the sense of prescribing. 'It was prescribed' (paññapīyittha) becomes paññatto, as in: paññatto-vinayo, the prescribed discipline; paññattaṃ-sikkhāpadaṃ, the prescribed training rule; and paññattaṃ-āsanaṃ, the prepared seat.

Ñāpa-ñāpane, vikatidhātu nāmesā kāritantattā, paññāpīyitthāti paññatto, saññāpīyitthāti saññatto, viññāpīyitthāti viññatto.

The root ñāp is in the sense of making known. This is a modified root because it is a causative. 'It was made known' (paññāpīyittha) becomes paññatto; 'it was designated' (saññāpīyittha) becomes saññatto; 'it was made to be cognized' (viññāpīyittha) becomes viññatto.

Tapa-santāpe, atappīti tatto, santatto.

The root tap is in the sense of heating. 'It was heated' (atappi) becomes tatto (heated), and santatto (well heated).

Dīpa-dittiyaṃ, adīpitthāti ditto, paditto, āditto.

The root dīp is in the sense of shining. 'It was lit' (adīpittha) becomes ditto (lit), paditto (ablaze), and āditto (burning).

Dhūpa-soṇḍiye[M 0.0485], dhūpati, adhūpi, dhūpissatīti dhutto, surādhutto, akkhadhutto su. ni. 106.

The root dhūp is in the sense of addiction. Because one is addicted (dhūpati), was addicted (adhūpi), or will be addicted (dhūpissati), one is called a dhutto (profligate), such as a surādhutto (drunkard) or an akkhadhutto (gambler).

Pada-gatiyaṃ, apajjīti patto, nipatto, sampatto.

The root pad is in the sense of going. 'It was gone to' (apajji) becomes patto (attained), nipatto (fallen down), and sampatto (arrived).

Bhaja-sambhattiyaṃ, bhajatīti bhatto, sambhatto.

The root bhaj is in the sense of partaking. 'He partakes' (bhajati) becomes bhatto (devoted), and sambhatto (intimate with).

Vipubbo puthakkaraṇe, vibhajitthāti vibhatto.

Preceded by vi-, the same root is in the sense of separating. 'It was divided' (vibhajittha) becomes vibhatto (divided).

Bhuja-pālana, byavaharaṇesu, bhuñjittha, bhuñjīyitthāti vā bhutto, paribhutto.

The root bhuj is in the senses of protecting and enjoying. 'It was enjoyed' (bhuñjittha or bhuñjīyittha) becomes bhutto (enjoyed), and paribhutto (fully enjoyed).

Mada-ummāde, majjitthāti matto, sammatto, pamatto, ummatto.

The root mad is in the sense of intoxication. 'He was intoxicated' (majjittha) becomes matto (intoxicated), sammatto (completely intoxicated), pamatto (negligent), and ummatto (mad).

Mida-sinehane, mijjatīti mitto.

The root mid is in the sense of affection. Because 'he is affectionate' (mijjati), he is called mitto (friend).

Yuja-yoge, yuñjatīti yutto, payutto, uyyutto, niyutto, viyutto, saṃyutto, saññutto.

The root yuj is in the sense of yoking. 'He yokes' (yuñjati) becomes yutto (yoked), payutto (appointed), uyyutto (striving), niyutto (appointed), viyutto (separated), saṃyutto (connected), and saññutto (connected).

Rica-viriñcane, riñcatīti ritto.

The root ric is in the sense of emptying. Because 'he empties' (riñcati), it becomes ritto (empty).

Ranja-rāge, rañjatīti ratto, sāratto, viratto.

The root rañj is in the sense of passion or coloring. 'He delights' (rañjati) becomes ratto (impassioned, colored), sāratto (greatly impassioned), and viratto (dispassionate).

Lipa-limpane, limpīyitthāti litto, ullitto, avalitto.

The root lip is in the sense of smearing. 'It was smeared' (limpīyittha) becomes litto (smeared), ullitto (plastered), and avalitto (smeared on).

Lupa-adassane, luppatīti lutto.

The root lup is in the sense of disappearing or elision. Because 'it disappears' (luppati), it becomes lutto (elided, cut off).

Vaca-viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ.

The root vac is in the sense of distinct speech.

731. Vacādīnaṃ vassuṭa vā ka. 579; rū. 629; nī. 1182.

731. For the roots `vac` and so on, `v` becomes `u` and `c` becomes `ṭ`, optionally.

Vacādīnaṃ vassa uṭa hoti vā kānubandhe ta-kārapaccaye tvādivajjite.

For the roots `vac` and so on, `v` becomes `u` and `c` becomes `ṭ` optionally before the `-ta` suffix which has the anubandha `k`, excluding the suffixes `-tvā` and so on.

Vuccitthāti [M 0.0486] utto-dhammo, uttā-kathā, uttaṃ-vacanaṃ, nirutto, niruttā, niruttaṃ, rāgamo.

Thus, from `vuccittha` (it was said): `utto-dhammo`, the spoken teaching; `uttā-kathā`, the spoken discourse; `uttaṃ-vacanaṃ`, the spoken word; and similarly `nirutto`, `niruttā`, `niruttaṃ`. `rāgamo` is an addition.

732. Assu.

732. `a` becomes `u`.

Vacādīnaṃ assa u hoti kānubandhe ta-kārapaccaye tvādivajjite.

For the roots `vac` and so on, `a` becomes `u` before the `-ta` suffix which has the anubandha `k`, excluding the suffixes `-tvā` and so on.

Vutto-dhammo, vuttā-kathā, vuttaṃ-vacanaṃ.

Examples: `vutto-dhammo`, the spoken teaching; `vuttā-kathā`, the spoken discourse; `vuttaṃ-vacanaṃ`, the spoken word.

Vatu-vattane, vattatīti vatto, pavatto, nivatto.

The root `vat` in the sense of occurring. From `vattati` (it occurs) are formed `vatto`, `pavatto`, `nivatto`.

Vapa-bījanikkhepe, vapīyitthāti vuttaṃ-bījaṃ, ‘assū’ti uttaṃ.

The root `vap` in the sense of sowing seed. From `vapīyittha` (it was sown) is formed `vuttaṃ-bījaṃ` (the sown seed). This is stated by the rule `assa u`.

Vica-vivecane, viviccitthāti vivitto.

The root `vic` in the sense of discerning. From `viviccittha` (it was discerned) is formed `vivitto`.

Sanja-saṅge, sañjatīti satto, āsatto, visatto.

The root `sañj` in the sense of clinging. From `sañjati` (he clings) are formed `satto`, `āsatto`, and `visatto`.

Sica-secane, siñcīyitthāti sitto, āsitto, avasitto, abhisitto.

The root `sic` in the sense of sprinkling. From `siñcīyittha` (it was sprinkled) are formed `sitto`, `āsitto`, `avasitto`, and `abhisitto` (anointed).

Sūca-sūcane, atthaṃ sūcetīti suttaṃ.

The root `sūc` in the sense of indicating. Because it indicates the meaning (`atthaṃ sūceti`), it is a `sutta`.

Sūda-paggharaṇe, atthaṃ sūdatīti suttaṃ.

The root `sūd` in the sense of distilling. Because it distills the meaning (`atthaṃ sūdati`), it is a `sutta`.

Supa-soppane, supatīti sutto iccādi.

The root `sup` in the sense of sleeping. From `supati` (he sleeps) is formed `sutto` (asleep), and so on.

Tipaccayamhi-byāpanaṃ byatti, viyatti, pariyāpuṇanaṃ pariyatti, samāpanaṃ samatti, parisamatti, āṇāpanaṃ āṇatti, gopanaṃ gutti, ñāpanaṃ ñatti, paññāpanaṃ paññatti, saññāpanaṃ saññatti, viññāpanaṃ viññatti.

With the `-ti` suffix: pervasion (`byāpanaṃ`) is `byatti`; distinctness is `viyatti`; learning (`pariyāpuṇanaṃ`) is `pariyatti`; completion (`samāpanaṃ`) is `samatti` and `parisamatti`; command (`āṇāpanaṃ`) is `āṇatti`; guarding (`gopanaṃ`) is `gutti`; announcement (`ñāpanaṃ`) is `ñatti`; prescription (`paññāpanaṃ`) is `paññatti`; designation (`saññāpanaṃ`) is `saññatti`; making cognized (`viññāpanaṃ`) is `viññatti`.

Tapa-tappane, tappanaṃ titti, mahāvuttinā assa ittaṃ. Dīpanaṃ ditti, pajjanaṃ patti, āpatti, uppatti, nippatti, vipatti, sampatti, bhajanaṃ bhatti, sambhatti, bhuñjanaṃ bhutti, yuñjanaṃ yutti, riñcanaṃ ritti, niddhāretvā vuccati attho etāyāti nirutti, vuccati suttassa attho [M 0.0487] etāyāti vutti. “Vivarīyati suttassa attho etāyāti vuttī”tipi vadanti. Vattanaṃ vutti, jīvitavutti, tadāyattavutti, ‘assū’ti assa uttaṃ. Vivecanaṃ vivitti, sajjanaṃ satti, āsatti, visatti iccādi.

The root `tap` in the sense of heating. Heating (`tappanaṃ`) is `titti` (satisfaction); by a major rule, its `a` becomes `i`. Illumination (`dīpanaṃ`) is `ditti`. Attaining (`pajjanaṃ`) is `patti`, `āpatti`, `uppatti`, `nippatti`, `vipatti`, `sampatti`. Sharing (`bhajanaṃ`) is `bhatti`, `sambhatti`. Enjoying (`bhuñjanaṃ`) is `bhutti`. Joining (`yuñjanaṃ`) is `yutti`. Emptying (`riñcanaṃ`) is `ritti`. That by which the meaning is determined and spoken (`niddhāretvā vuccati attho etāya`) is `nirutti` (etymology). That by which the meaning of a discourse is spoken (`vuccati suttassa attho etāya`) is `vutti` (commentary). Some also say: 'That by which the meaning of a discourse is explained (`vivarīyati suttassa attho etāya`) is `vutti`.' Occurring (`vattanaṃ`) is `vutti` (conduct), as in `jīvitavutti` (livelihood) and `tadāyattavutti` (dependent conduct); by the rule `assa u`, `a` becomes `u`. Discernment (`vivecanaṃ`) is `vivitti`. Clinging (`sajjanaṃ`) is `satti`, `āsatti`, `visatti`, and so on.

Tupaccayamhi-khipatīti khittā, gopetīti guttā, cajatīti cattā.

With the `-tu` suffix: one who throws (`khipati`) is `khittā`; one who guards (`gopeti`) is `guttā`; one who abandons (`cajati`) is `cattā`.

Idha chida, bhidādayopi vattabbā, chindatīti chettā, bhindatīti bhettā, bhajatīti bhattā, bhuñjatīti bhuttā, bhottā, yuttā, rittā, littā, luttā, vacati vadatīti vā vattā, viviccatīti vivittā, sañjatīti sattā, suppatīti suttā iccādi.

Here, roots such as `chid` and `bhid` should also be mentioned. One who cuts (`chindati`) is `chettā`; one who splits (`bhindati`) is `bhettā`; one who partakes (`bhajati`) is `bhattā`; one who eats (`bhuñjati`) is `bhuttā` or `bhottā`; one who yokes is `yuttā`; one who empties is `rittā`; one who smears is `littā`; one who robs is `luttā`; one who speaks (`vacati` or `vadati`) is `vattā`; one who discerns (`viviccati`) is `vivittā`; one who clings (`sañjati`) is `sattā`; one who sleeps (`suppati`) is `suttā`, and so on.

Tavantupaccayamhi-khipitthāti khittavā, gopitthāti guttavā, cajitthāti cattavā, chinditthāti chettavā.

With the `-tavant` suffix: from `khipittha` (he threw) is formed `khittavā` (one who has thrown); from `gopittha` (he guarded) is formed `guttavā`; from `cajittha` (he abandoned) is formed `cattavā`; from `chindittha` (he cut) is formed `chettavā`.

Bhaja-puthakkaraṇe, bhājitthāti bhattavā, vibhattavā, abhuñjīti bhuttavā, ayuñjīti yuttavā iccādi.

The root `bhaj` in the sense of dividing. From `bhājittha` (he divided) are formed `bhattavā` and `vibhattavā`. From `abhuñji` (he ate) is formed `bhuttavā`. From `ayuñji` (he yoked) is formed `yuttavā`, and so on.

Tāvīpaccayamhi-khittāvī, guttāvī, cattāvī, chettāvī, vibhattāvī, bhettāvī, bhuttāvī, yuttāvī iccādi.

With the `-tāvin` suffix: `khittāvī` (one who throws), `guttāvī` (one who guards), `cattāvī` (one who abandons), `chettāvī` (one who cuts), `vibhattāvī` (one who divides), `bhettāvī` (one who splits), `bhuttāvī` (one who eats), `yuttāvī` (one who yokes), and so on.

Tvādīsu pararūpatte mahāvuttinā tiṇṇaṃ byañjanānaṃ ādibyañjanassa lopo, chetvā, chetvāna, chettuna, vibhatvā, vibhatvāna, vibhattuna, bhutvā, bhutvāna, bhuttuna iccādi.

With the suffixes `-tvā` and so on, when there is assimilation to the following sound, by a major rule, the first consonant of a three-consonant cluster is elided: `chetvā`, `chetvāna`, `chettuna` (having cut); `vibhatvā`, `vibhatvāna`, `vibhattuna` (having divided); `bhutvā`, `bhutvāna`, `bhuttuna` (having eaten), and so on.

Tuṃ, tavesu-chettuṃ, chettave, chetuṃ, chetave vā, ādibyañjanassa lopo. Vibhattuṃ, vibhattave, bhettuṃ, bhettave, bhottuṃ, bhottave, ādivuddhi iccādi.

With the suffixes `-tuṃ` and `-tave`: `chettuṃ`, `chettave`, or optionally `chetuṃ`, `chetave`, where there is elision of the first consonant of the cluster. `vibhattuṃ`, `vibhattave`. In `bhettuṃ`, `bhettave` and `bhottuṃ`, `bhottave`, there is `vuddhi` of the initial vowel, and so on.

Tabbapaccaye-chettabbaṃ, chetabbaṃ vā, bhettabbaṃ, bhottabbaṃ, vuccatīti vattabbaṃ iccādi.

With the `-tabba` suffix: `chettabbaṃ` or optionally `chetabbaṃ`; `bhettabbaṃ`; `bhottabbaṃ`; from `vuccati` (it is said) is formed `vattabbaṃ`; and so on.

Iti sadisasaṃyogarūparāsi.

Thus ends the section on forms with similar conjunct consonants.

Vaggantarūparāsi

The Section on Forms with Class-Final Nasals

Atha vaggantarūparāsi vuccate.

Now the section on forms with class-final nasals is expounded.

Kamu, kilamu, khanu, khamu, gamu, tanu, timu, damu, bhamu, mana, yamu, vamu, samu, hana.

`kamu`, `kilamu`, `khanu`, `khamu`, `gamu`, `tanu`, `timu`, `damu`, `bhamu`, `mana`, `yamu`, `vamu`, `samu`, `hana`.

733. Manānaṃ niggahītaṃ.

733. Final `m` and `n` become `niggahīta`.

Makāra, nakārantānaṃ dhātūnaṃ anto makāro nakāro ca niggahītaṃ hoti yakāravajjite byañjane pare. ‘Vagge vagganto’ti niggahītassa vaggantattaṃ.

For roots ending in the letters `m` and `n`, the final `m` and `n` become `niggahīta` when a consonant other than `y` follows. By the rule `Vagge vagganto`, the `niggahīta` becomes the corresponding class-final nasal.

Kamu-pādagamane, pakkamitthāti pakkanto, pādena akkamitthāti akkanto, ukkanto, vikkanto, nikkhanto, ‘nito kamassā’ti kassa khattaṃ, saṅkanto, okkanto, avakkanto, apakkanto, atikkanto, paṭikkanto, kassa dvittāni.

The root `kamu` is in the sense of 'walking with the feet.' `pakkanto` means 'he has departed'; `akkanto` means 'he has stepped on with the foot'; also `ukkanto`, `vikkanto`, `nikkhanto`. By the rule `nito kamassa`, `k` becomes `kh`. Also `saṅkanto`, `okkanto`, `avakkanto`, `apakkanto`, `atikkanto`, `paṭikkanto`. These show doubling of the `k`.

Kilamu-khede, kilamitthāti kilanto.

The root `kilamu` is in the sense of 'weariness.' `kilanto` means 'he has become weary'.

Timu-addabhāve, temayittāti tinto.

The root `timu` is in the sense of 'being wet.' `tinto` means 'he has become wet'.

Damu-damane, damitthāti danto.

The root `damu` is in the sense of 'taming.' `danto` means 'he has been tamed'.

Bhamu-anavatthāne, bhamitthāti bhanto, vibbhanto.

The root `bhamu` is in the sense of 'unsteadiness.' `bhanto` means 'he has wandered'; also `vibbhanto`.

Mana-ñāṇe, manatīti manto.

The root `mana` is in the sense of 'knowing.' `manto` means 'one who knows/thinks'.

Vamu-uggilane, vamitthāti vanto.

The root `vamu` is in the sense of 'vomiting.' `vanto` means 'he has vomited'.

Samu-santiyaṃ, sammatīti santo, upasanto, vūpasanto.

The root `samu` is in the sense of 'peace.' `santo` means 'he is calm'; also `upasanto`, `vūpasanto`.

Samu-khede, sammati khijjatīti santo iccādi.

The root `samu` is also in the sense of 'weariness.' `santo` means 'he is weary, he is afflicted,' and so on.

Tipaccayamhi-kāmanaṃ kanti, nikāmanaṃ nikanti, pakkamanaṃ pakkanti, khamanaṃ khanti, tananaṃ tanti, damanaṃ danti, bhamanaṃ bhanti, vibbhanti, mananaṃ manti, samanaṃ santi iccādi.

With the `ti` suffix: `kanti` is desiring; `nikanti` is desiring; `pakkanti` is departing; `khanti` is enduring; `tanti` is stretching; `danti` is taming; `bhanti` and `vibbhanti` are wandering; `manti` is thinking; `santi` is calming, and so on.

Tupaccaye-pakkamatīti [M 0.0489] pakkantā, khanatīti khantā, khamatīti khantā, gacchatīti gantā, tanotīti tantā, temayatīti tintā, damayatīti dantā, bhamatīti bhantā, manatīti mantā.

With the `-tu` suffix: `pakkantā` means 'one who departs'; `khantā`, 'one who digs'; `khantā`, 'one who endures'; `gantā`, 'one who goes'; `tantā`, 'one who stretches'; `tintā`, 'one who moistens'; `dantā`, 'one who tames'; `bhantā`, 'one who whirls'; `mantā`, 'one who thinks'.

Nipubbo yamu-niyamane, niyāmetīti niyantā, vamatīti vantā, samatīti santā, hanatīti hantā iccādi.

The root `yamu` with the prefix `ni-` is in the sense of 'restraining': `niyantā` means 'one who restrains.' Also: `vantā` (one who vomits); `santā` (one who is calm); `hantā` (one who strikes), and so on.

Tvādīsu-gantvā, gantvāna, gantuna, mantvā, mantvāna, mantuna, hantvā, hantvāna, hantuna iccādi.

In the case of the absolutive suffixes beginning with `-tvā`: `gantvā`, `gantvāna`, `gantuna` (having gone); `mantvā`, `mantvāna`, `mantuna` (having thought); `hantvā`, `hantvāna`, `hantuna` (having struck), and so on.

Tuṃ, tavesu-pakkantuṃ, pakkantave, khananaṃ khantuṃ, khantave, gamanaṃ gantuṃ, gantave, mananaṃ mantuṃ, mantave, hananaṃ hantuṃ, hantave iccādi.

In the case of the infinitive suffixes `-tuṃ` and `-tave`: `pakkantuṃ`, `pakkantave` (to depart); `khantuṃ`, `khantave` (to dig); `gantuṃ`, `gantave` (to go); `mantuṃ`, `mantave` (to think); `hantuṃ`, `hantave` (to strike), and so on.

Tabbamhi-abhikkantabbaṃ, paṭikkantabbaṃ, khaññateti khantabbaṃ, gacchīyateti gantabbaṃ, maññateti mantabbaṃ, vamīyateti vantabbaṃ, haññateti hantabbaṃ iccādi.

With the `-tabba` suffix: `abhikkantabbaṃ` (what should be approached), `paṭikkantabbaṃ` (what should be returned to); `khantabbaṃ` (what should be dug); `gantabbaṃ` (what should be gone to); `mantabbaṃ` (what should be thought); `vantabbaṃ` (what should be vomited); `hantabbaṃ` (what should be struck), and so on.

Iti vaggantarūparāsi.

Thus ends the section on forms with class-finals.

Dhātvantavikārarāsi niṭṭhito.

The section on changes to root-finals is concluded.

Paccayavikārarāsi

The Section on Changes to Suffixes

Kādesarāsi

The Section on Substitution by `ka`

Atha paccayavikārarāsi vuccate.

Now the section on changes to suffixes is expounded.

734. Pacā ko ka. 583; rū. 617; nī. 1186.

734. From `pac`, `ka`.

Pacamhā ta, tavantūnaṃ tassa ko hoti.

After the root `pac`, `ka` is the substitute for the `t` of the suffixes `ta` and `tavant`.

Paccitthāti pakko, pakkavā.

`pakko` means 'he has cooked'; also `pakkavā`.

Bahulādhikārā [M 0.0490] tapaccayo kālattayepi hoti, asakkhi, sakkhati, sakkhissatīti sakko, mahāvuttinā tapaccayassa ko.

On account of the governing rule of 'variously,' the `-ta` suffix can occur in all three tenses. Thus `sakko` can mean 'he was able,' 'he is able,' or 'he will be able.' By a major rule, `ka` is the substitute for the `-ta` suffix.

Muca-mocane.

The root `muca` is in the sense of 'releasing'.

735. Mucā vā ka. 583; rū. 617; nī. 1186.

735. From `muc`, optionally.

Mucamhā ta, tavantūnaṃ tassa anantarassa ko hoti vā.

After the root `muc`, `ka` is optionally the substitute for the immediately following `t` of the suffixes `ta` and `tavant`.

Omuccitthāti omukko, omukkavā, paṭimukko, paṭimukkavā.

`omukko` means 'he has taken off'; also `omukkavā`, `paṭimukko`, `paṭimukkavā`.

Susa-sosane.

The root `susa` is in the sense of 'drying up'.

736. Susā kho ka. 583; rū. 617; nī. 1186.

736. From `susa`, `kha`.

Susamhā ta, tavantūnaṃ tassa kho hoti.

After `susa`, `kha` is the substitute for the `t` of the suffixes `ta` and `tavantū`.

Sussitthāti sukkho, sukkhavā.

For example: `sukkho` (dried), `sukkhavā` (one who has dried).

737. Go bhanjādīhi ka. 577; rū. 628; nī. 1180.

737. `Go` after `bhanja` and so forth.

Bhanjādīhi ta, tavantūnaṃ tassa go hoti.

After the roots `bhanja` and so forth, `go` is the substitute for the `t` of the suffixes `ta` and `tavantū`.

Abhañjitthāti bhaggo, bhaggavā, obhaggo, sambhaggo, palibhaggo.

For example: `bhaggo` (broken), `bhaggavā` (one who has broken), `obhaggo` (broken off), `sambhaggo` (completely broken), `palibhaggo` (broken around).

Laga-laggane, lagitthāti laggo, laggavā, vilaggo, vilaggavā.

The root `lag` in the sense of adhering: `laggo` (adhered), `laggavā` (one who has adhered), `vilaggo` (stuck), `vilaggavā` (one who is stuck).

Muja-mujjane, mujjitthāti muggo, muggavā, nimmuggo, ummuggo.

The root `muj` in the sense of sinking: `muggo` (sunk), `muggavā` (one who has sunk), `nimmuggo` (immersed), `ummuggo` (emerged).

Vija-bhaya, calanesu, saṃvijitthāti saṃviggo, saṃviggavā, ubbiggo, ubbiggavā.

The root `vij` in the senses of fear and agitation: `saṃviggo` (agitated), `saṃviggavā` (one who is agitated), `ubbiggo` (terrified), `ubbiggavā` (one who is terrified).

Luja-vināse, palujitthāti paluggo, paluggavā, oluggo, oluggavā, viluggo, viluggavā iccādi.

The root `luj` in the sense of destruction: `paluggo` (perished), `paluggavā` (one who has perished), `oluggo` (fallen apart), `oluggavā` (one who has fallen apart), `viluggo` (destroyed), `viluggavā` (one who is destroyed), and so forth.

Iti kādesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on `ka` substitutions.

Ṭhādesarāsi

The section on `ṭha` substitutions.

Isu[M 0.0491], āsa, esa, kasa, kisa, kilisa, kusa, ghusa, jusa, tusa, disa, dusa, daṃsa, nasa, pisa, pusa, puccha, phusa, bhassa, bhajja, maja, masa, musa, vassa, visa, saja, sisa, silisa, hasa, hassa, haṃsa.

`Isu`, `āsa`, `esa`, `kasa`, `kisa`, `kilisa`, `kusa`, `ghusa`, `jusa`, `tusa`, `disa`, `dusa`, `daṃsa`, `nasa`, `pisa`, `pusa`, `puccha`, `phusa`, `bhassa`, `bhajja`, `maja`, `masa`, `musa`, `vassa`, `visa`, `saja`, `sisa`, `silisa`, `hasa`, `hassa`, `haṃsa`.

738. Sānantarassa tassa ṭho ka. 573; rū. 626; nī. 1176 (thokaṃ visadisaṃ).

738. `Ṭha` is the substitute for the `t` of a suffix immediately following an `s`.

Sakārantehi dhātūhi parassa anantarassa paccayatakārassa ṭho hoti, dhātvantassa pararūpattaṃ, ‘catutthadutiyesvesa’nti saṃyogādissa paṭhamattaṃ.

`Ṭha` is the substitute for the `t` of a suffix immediately following a root ending in `s`; the final consonant of the root is assimilated to the following consonant, and by the rule `catutthadutiyesvesa`, the initial consonant of a conjunct becomes the first of its class.

Isu-icchā, kantīsu, icchīyateti iṭṭho, pariyiṭṭho.

The root `is` in the senses of wishing and desiring: `iṭṭho` (wished, desired), `pariyiṭṭho` (sought after).

Āsa-upavesane, viparitato āsati upavīsatīti vipallaṭṭho.

The root `ās` in the sense of sitting: `vipallaṭṭho` (perverted, contrary), from `viparitato āsati` (he sits wrongly).

Kasa-vappane vilekhane ca.

The root `kas` in the senses of ploughing and scratching.

739. Kasassima ca vā ka. 573; rū. 626; nī. 1176 (thokaṃ visadisaṃ).

739. And optionally `ima` in `kasa`.

Kasamhā parassa paccayatakārassa ṭho hoti, kasassa ādisaramhā paraṃ ima ca hoti vā.

For the `t` of the suffix following `kasa`, `ṭha` is the substitute; and after the initial vowel of `kasa`, `ima` is also optionally inserted.

Kassitthāti kiṭṭhaṃ-sassaṃ, kaṭṭhaṃ vā.

For example: `kiṭṭhaṃ` (a crop), or optionally `kaṭṭhaṃ` (ploughed).

Upapubbo āsanne, upakaṭṭho.

When preceded by `upa`, in the sense of nearness: `upakaṭṭho` (nearby).

Vipubbo pavāse, vūpakaṭṭho.

When preceded by `vi`, in the sense of separation: `vūpakaṭṭho` (secluded).

Kisa-hānimhi, paṭikiṭṭho, nihīnoti attho.

The root `kis` in the sense of diminishing: `paṭikiṭṭho`, meaning 'despised, base'.

Kilisa-vibādhane upatāpe ca, kilissatīti kiliṭṭho, saṃkiliṭṭho, upakkiliṭṭho.

The root `kilis` in the senses of affliction and distress: `kiliṭṭho` (stained, impure), `saṃkiliṭṭho` (defiled), `upakkiliṭṭho` (greatly defiled).

Kusa-akkose, akkosīyitthāti akkuṭṭho. Akkuṭṭho jātivādena.

The root `kus` in the sense of reviling: `akkuṭṭho` (reviled). For example: `Akkuṭṭho jātivādena` (reviled with abuse concerning birth).

Ghusa-sadde[M 0.0492], ghosīyitthāti ghuṭṭho, saṅghuṭṭho. Accharāgaṇasaṅghuṭṭhaṃ saṃ. ni. 1.46. Ugghuṭṭho.

The root `ghus` in the sense of sound: `ghuṭṭho` (proclaimed), `saṅghuṭṭho` (resounding). For example: `Accharāgaṇasaṅghuṭṭhaṃ` (resounding with a host of celestial nymphs). Also, `ugghuṭṭho` (proclaimed aloud).

Jusa-sevāyaṃ, jusīyitthāti juṭṭho.

The root `jus` in the sense of frequenting: `juṭṭho` (frequented, enjoyed).

Tusa-pītimhi, tussitthāti tuṭṭho, santuṭṭho.

The root `tus` in the sense of satisfaction: `tuṭṭho` (pleased, satisfied), `santuṭṭho` (contented).

Disa-pekkhane, passīyitthāti diṭṭho, sandiṭṭho.

The root `dis` in the sense of seeing: `diṭṭho` (seen), `sandiṭṭho` (visible).

Disī-kathane, uddisīyitthāti uddiṭṭho, niddisīyitthāti niddiṭṭho, apadisīyitthāti apadiṭṭho.

The root `dis` in the sense of declaring: `uddiṭṭho` (pointed out), `niddiṭṭho` (explained), `apadiṭṭho` (designated).

Dusa-dūsane, dusīyitthāti duṭṭho.

From the root dus in the sense of corrupting: dusīyittha becomes duṭṭho.

Daṃsa-daṃsane, daṃsīyitthāti daṭṭho, niggahītalopo.

From the root daṃs in the sense of biting: daṃsīyittha becomes daṭṭho, with elision of the niggahīta.

Nasa-adassane, nassitthāti naṭṭho, vinaṭṭho.

From the root nas in the sense of disappearing: nassittha becomes naṭṭho, vinaṭṭho.

Pisa-cuṇṇiye, pisīyitthāti piṭṭhaṃ.

From the root pis in the sense of grinding: pisīyittha becomes piṭṭhaṃ.

Pusa-posane, posīyitthāti puṭṭho, parapuṭṭho.

From the root pus in the sense of nourishing: posīyittha becomes puṭṭho, parapuṭṭho.

Phusa-samphasse, phusīyitthāti phuṭṭho, samphuṭṭho.

From the root phus in the sense of touching: phusīyittha becomes phuṭṭho, samphuṭṭho.

Bhassa-kathane cavane ca, bhassitthāti bhaṭṭho, ābhaṭṭho.

From the root bhass in the sense of speaking and falling: bhassittha becomes bhaṭṭho, ābhaṭṭho.

Masa-āmasane vijjhane ca, masīyitthāti maṭṭho, āmaṭṭho, omaṭṭho, ummaṭṭho. Sattiyā viya omaṭṭho saṃ. ni. 1.21.

From the root mas in the sense of touching and piercing: masīyittha becomes maṭṭho, āmaṭṭho, omaṭṭho, ummaṭṭho. For example, sattiyā viya omaṭṭho (as if pierced by a spear).

Musa-nassane, mussitthāti muṭṭho, pamuṭṭho, sammuṭṭho.

From the root mus in the sense of perishing: mussittha becomes muṭṭho, pamuṭṭho, sammuṭṭho.

Vassa-secane, vassitthāti vuṭṭho-devo, ‘assū’ti uttaṃ.

From the root vass in the sense of raining: vassittha becomes vuṭṭho, as in vuṭṭho-devo; the a becomes u.

Visa-pavesane, pavisitthāti paviṭṭho, niviṭṭho, upaviṭṭho.

From the root vis in the sense of entering: pavisittha becomes paviṭṭho; also niviṭṭho, upaviṭṭho.

Sisa-sese, avasesitthāti avasiṭṭho.

From the root sis in the sense of remaining: avasesittha becomes avasiṭṭho.

Vipubbo visesane, visesitthāti visiṭṭho.

With the prefix vi, in the sense of distinguishing: visesittha becomes visiṭṭho.

Silisa-silesane, silissitthāti siliṭṭho.

From the root silis in the sense of adhering: silissittha becomes siliṭṭho.

Hasa-hāse, [M 0.0493] hasitthāti haṭṭho, pahaṭṭho.

From the root has in the sense of being glad: hasittha becomes haṭṭho, pahaṭṭho.

Hassa, haṃsadhātuyo sadisā eva.

The roots has and haṃs are indeed similar.

Puccha-pucchāyaṃ.

From the root pucch in the sense of asking.

740. Pucchādito ka. 571; rū. 626; nī. 1176.

740. From pucch, etc.

Pucchādīhi parassa antarassa paccayatakārassa ṭho hoti.

After the roots pucch, etc., the ta of the immediately following suffix becomes ṭho.

Pucchīyitthāti puṭṭho.

Pucchīyittha becomes puṭṭho.

Bhajja-bhajjane, bhajjitthāti bhaṭṭhaṃ-dhaññaṃ.

From the root bhajj in the sense of roasting: bhajjittha becomes bhaṭṭhaṃ, as in bhaṭṭhaṃ-dhaññaṃ (roasted grain).

Maja-suddhiyaṃ, suṭṭhu majjitthāti sammaṭṭho-bhūmibhāgo.

From the root maj in the sense of cleansing: suṭṭhu majjittha becomes sammaṭṭho, as in sammaṭṭho-bhūmibhāgo (a well-swept area of ground).

Saja-saṃsaggādīsu, saṃsajjitthāti saṃsaṭṭho, visaṭṭho, nisaṭṭho, osaṭṭho.

From the root saj in the senses of clinging, etc.: saṃsajjittha becomes saṃsaṭṭho; also visaṭṭho, nisaṭṭho, osaṭṭho.

Yaja-pūjāyaṃ.

From the root yaj in the sense of worship.

741. Yajassa yassa ṭiyī ka. 610; rū. 627; nī. 1215.

741. Of yaj, the ya becomes ṭi or yī.

Yajassa yakārassa ṭi, yiādesā honti kānubandhe paccayatakāre tvādivajjite.

The ya of the root yaj becomes ṭi or yī before the ta of a suffix having the indicatory letter k, with the exception of tvā, etc.

Yajitthāti iṭṭho, yiṭṭho.

Yajittha becomes iṭṭho or yiṭṭho.

Tipaccayamhi-pariyesanaṃ pariyeṭṭhi.

Before the suffix ti: pariyesanaṃ becomes pariyeṭṭhi.

Esa-gavesane, esanaṃ eṭṭhi, pariyeṭṭhi, tussanaṃ tuṭṭhi, santuṭṭhi, dassanaṃ diṭṭhi, sandiṭṭhi, vassanaṃ vuṭṭhi, ‘assū’ti uttaṃ. Visajjanaṃ visaṭṭhi.

From the root is in the sense of seeking: esanaṃ becomes eṭṭhi, pariyeṭṭhi. tussanaṃ becomes tuṭṭhi, santuṭṭhi. dassanaṃ becomes diṭṭhi, sandiṭṭhi. vassanaṃ becomes vuṭṭhi; the a becomes u. visajjanaṃ becomes visaṭṭhi.

Tvādīsu-disa-pekkhane, ‘disassa passadassadasādadakkhā’ti suttena disassa dasādeso, mahāvuttinā vakāralopo, daṭṭhā, daṭṭhāna, daṭṭhuna.

Before suffixes such as tvā, from the root dis in the sense of seeing: by the rule 'disassa passadassadasādadakkhā', the root dis is replaced by das. According to the Mahāvutti, the v is elided, yielding: daṭṭhā, daṭṭhāna, daṭṭhuna.

‘Tuṃyānā’ti [M 0.0494] tvāpaccayassa tuṃādeso. Nekkhamaṃ daṭṭhu khemato su. ni. 426, gāthāvasena niggahītalopo.

By the rule 'Tuṃyānā,' tuṃ is a substitute for the suffix tvā. In the verse 'nekkhamaṃ daṭṭhu khemato,' the niggahīta is elided for metrical reasons.

Tuṃ, tavesu-daṭṭhuṃ, daṭṭhave, pucchanaṃ puṭṭhuṃ, puṭṭhave.

Before the suffixes tuṃ and tave: daṭṭhuṃ, daṭṭhave; puṭṭhuṃ, puṭṭhave.

Tabbamhi-tussitabbanti tuṭṭhabbaṃ, toṭṭhabbaṃ, passitabbanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, pucchitabbanti puṭṭhabbaṃ, phusitabbanti phoṭṭhabbaṃ.

Before the suffix tabba: tussitabbaṃ becomes tuṭṭhabbaṃ or toṭṭhabbaṃ; passitabbaṃ becomes daṭṭhabbaṃ; pucchitabbaṃ becomes puṭṭhabbaṃ; phusitabbaṃ becomes phoṭṭhabbaṃ.

Iti ṭhādesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on the substitution of ṭha.

Ḍhādesarāsi

The Section on the Substitution of ḍha

742. Dahā ḍho ka. 576; rū. 607; nī. 1179.

742. After dah, ḍho.

Dahamhā parassa anantarassa paccayatakārassa ḍho hoti, pararūpatte saṃyogādissa tatiyattaṃ.

After the root dah, the ta of the immediately following suffix becomes ḍho; upon assimilation to the following sound, the initial consonant of the conjunct becomes the third of its class.

Daha-dayhane, dayhitthāti daḍḍho.

From the root dah in the sense of burning: dayhittha becomes daḍḍho.

743. Bahassuma ca ka. 576; rū. 607; nī. 1179.

743. And of bah, uma.

Bahamhā parassa anantarassa tassa ḍho hoti, bahassa ādisaramhā uma ca hoti.

After the root bah, the immediately following ta becomes ḍho, and the initial vowel of bah becomes uma.

Baha-vuddhiyaṃ, abahīti buḍḍho, bassa vo, vuḍḍho.

From the root bah in the sense of increase: abahī becomes buḍḍho. The b can also become v, yielding vuḍḍho.

Timhi-bahanaṃ vuḍḍhi.

Before the suffix ti: bahanaṃ becomes vuḍḍhi.

744. Lopo vaḍḍhā tissa ‘ttissa’ (bahūsu).

744. Elision of ti after vaḍḍha.

Vaḍḍhamhā parassa tipaccayassa takārassa lopo hoti.

After the root vaḍḍha, the ta of the suffix ti is elided.

Vaḍḍha-vaḍḍhane, vaḍḍhanaṃ vuḍḍhi.

From the root vaḍḍh in the sense of increasing: vaḍḍhanaṃ becomes vuḍḍhi.

Iti ḍhādesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on the substitution of ḍha.

Ṇādesarāsi

The Section on the Substitution of ṇa

Kira [M 0.0495] khī, cara, jara, tara, thara, pūra.

Kir, khī, car, jar, tar, thar, pūr.

745. Kirādīhi ṇo.

745. After kir, etc., ṇo.

Kirādīhi paresaṃ ta, tavantūnaṃ takārassa anantarabhūtassa ṇo hoti, dhātvantassa pararūpattaṃ.

After the roots kir, etc., the immediately following ta of the suffixes ta and tavantū becomes ṇo, and the final of the root assimilates to the following sound.

Kira-ākiraṇe sammissana, khipanesu ca, kiritthāti kiṇṇo, pakiṇṇo, ākiṇṇo, vikkiṇṇo, saṃkiṇṇo, samākiṇṇo.

From the root kir in the senses of scattering, mixing, and throwing: kirittha becomes kiṇṇo; pakiṇṇo, ākiṇṇo, vikkiṇṇo, saṃkiṇṇo, samākiṇṇo.

Pūra-pūraṇe, pūritthāti puṇṇo, sampuṇṇo, paripuṇṇo.

From the root pūr in the sense of filling: pūrittha becomes puṇṇo; sampuṇṇo, paripuṇṇo.

Khī-khaye, khiyitthāti khīṇo.

From the root khī in the sense of destruction: khiyittha becomes khīṇo.

Kiṇṇavā, puṇṇavā, khīṇavā.

Kiṇṇavā, puṇṇavā, khīṇavā.

746. Tarādīhi riṇṇo ka. 581; rū. 616; nī. 1184.

746. After tara, etc., riṇṇo.

Tarādīhi paresaṃ ta, tavantūnaṃ takārassa anantarabhūtassa riṇṇo hoti. ‘Rānubandhentasarādissā’ti dhātvantabyañjanassa ādisarassa ca lopo.

After the roots tara, etc., the immediately following ta of the suffixes ta and tavantū becomes riṇṇo. By the rule 'Rānubandhentasarādissā,' the final consonant of the root and its initial vowel are elided.

Cara-gati, bhakkhanesu, carittha, carīyitthāti vā ciṇṇo, āciṇṇo, samāciṇṇo.

From the root car in the senses of moving and eating: carittha or carīyittha becomes ciṇṇo; āciṇṇo, samāciṇṇo.

Jara-jiraṇe, jiyyitthāti jiṇṇo, anujiṇṇo, parijiṇṇo.

From the root jar in the sense of decaying: jiyyittha becomes jiṇṇo; anujiṇṇo, parijiṇṇo.

Tara-taraṇe, taritthāti tiṇṇo, uttiṇṇo, nittiṇṇo, vitiṇṇo, otiṇṇo, samotiṇṇo.

From the root tar in the sense of crossing over: tarittha becomes tiṇṇo; uttiṇṇo, nittiṇṇo, vitiṇṇo, otiṇṇo, samotiṇṇo.

Thara-vitthāre, vittharitthāti vitthiṇṇo.

From the root thar in the sense of spreading out: vittharittha becomes vitthiṇṇo.

Ciṇṇavā, jiṇṇavā, tiṇṇavā, vitthiṇṇavā.

Ciṇṇavā, jiṇṇavā, tiṇṇavā, vitthiṇṇavā.

Iti ṇādesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on 'ṇa' substitutions.

Thādesarāsi

The Section on 'tha' Substitutions

747. Dhastoostā.

747. Dhasto, utrasto.

Dhasto[M 0.0496], utrastoti ete saddā tapaccayantā sijjhanti.

The words 'dhasto' and 'utrasto' are formed with the 'ta' suffix.

Dhaṃsa-viddhaṃsane, viddhaṃsatīti viddhasto, viddhaṃsito vā.

Dhaṃsa—in destroying: from 'viddhaṃsati' comes 'viddhasto,' or 'viddhaṃsito'.

Tasa-santāse, utrasatīti utrasto, uttasito vā.

Tasa—in fear or terror: from 'utrasati' comes 'utrasto,' or 'uttasito'.

Bhasa-bhasmīkaraṇe, bhasanti bhasmiṃ karonti etenāti bhastā, bhastrā vā, kammāragaggarī, evamādīnipi idha veditabbāni.

Bhasa—in reducing to ashes: that by which 'they reduce to ashes' (`bhasanti`) or 'make into ashes' (`bhasmiṃ karonti`), thus 'bhastā' or 'bhastrā' (the blacksmith's bellows); other similar terms are also to be understood here.

748. Sāsa vasa saṃsa haṃsā tho ‘…saṃsa sasā tho’ (bahūsu).

748. Sāsa, vasa, saṃsa, haṃsa: tho.

Etehi parassa anantarassa paccayatakārassa tho hoti.

After these roots, the 'ta' of the immediately following suffix becomes 'tho'.

Sāsa-anusiṭṭhimhi.

Sāsa—in instruction.

749. Sāsassa sisā ‘sāsassa sisa vā’ (bahūsu).

749. 'Sāsa' becomes 'sisā'.

Sāsassa sisā honti kānubandhe paccayatakāre tvādivajjite, dhātvantassa pararūpattaṃ saṃyogādissa ca paṭhamattaṃ.

'Sāsa' becomes 'sisā' when followed by a suffix with an anubandha 'ka,' excluding 'tvā' and so forth; the final sound of the root is assimilated to the following sound; and the first member of a conjunct consonant is doubled.

Sāsīyatīti sittho, anusāsīyatīti anusiṭṭho. “Anusiṭṭho so mayā”ti mahāva. 126 ettha pana tthakārassa ṭṭhakāroti vuttiyaṃ vutto. Taṃ taṃ atthaṃ sāsati ettha, etenāti vā satthaṃ, saddasatthaṃ, vedasatthaṃ.

'Sāsīyatīti' becomes 'sittho'; 'anusāsīyatīti' becomes 'anusiṭṭho.' However, in the phrase 'Anusiṭṭho so mayā,' it is stated in the commentary that 'ttha' becomes 'ṭṭha.' Because it teaches or instructs (sāsati) a particular meaning (atthaṃ) here, or by means of it, it is 'satthaṃ,' such as 'saddasatthaṃ' or 'vedasatthaṃ'.

Vasa-nivāse, ‘assū’ti uttaṃ, avasīti vuttho, vasīyitthāti vā vuttho, vassaṃ vasitthāti vassaṃvuttho, āvasīyitthāti āvutthaṃ-jetavanaṃ, nivasitthāti nivuttho, ajjhāvasitthāti ajjhāvuttho. Bahulādhikārā “rukkhe adhivatthā [M 0.0497] devatā”ti pāci. 86 ettha uttaṃ natthi. Uposathaṃ upavasitthāti uposathaṃupavuttho, upavasīyitthāti vā upavutthouposatho, parivāsaṃ parivasitthāti parivāsaṃparivuttho, parivasīyitthāti vā parivuttho-parivāso.

Vasa—in dwelling: vocalization to 'u' is stated, as in 'assū'; 'avasī' becomes 'vuttho,' or 'vasīyitthā' becomes 'vuttho'; 'vassaṃ vasitthā' becomes 'vassaṃvuttho' (having dwelt for the rains); 'āvasīyitthā' becomes 'āvutthaṃ-jetavanaṃ' (the Jeta Grove dwelt in); 'nivasitthā' becomes 'nivuttho' (having resided); 'ajjhāvasitthā' becomes 'ajjhāvuttho' (having inhabited). Due to the rule of 'bahulādhikāra' (frequent application), in the phrase 'rukkhe adhivatthā devatā' (the deity dwelling in the tree), vocalization to 'u' is not present. 'Uposathaṃ upavasitthā' becomes 'uposathaṃupavuttho,' or 'upavasīyitthā' becomes 'upavutthouposatho' (the Uposatha observed); 'parivāsaṃ parivasitthā' becomes 'parivāsaṃparivuttho,' or 'parivasīyitthā' becomes 'parivuttho-parivāso' (the probation undergone).

Saṃsa-pasaṃsane, pasaṃsīyitthāti pasattho.

Saṃsa—in praise: 'pasaṃsīyitthā' becomes 'pasattho'.

Haṃsa-pahaṃsane, haṃsīyitthāti hattho, niggahītalopo, pahattho.

Haṃsa—in rejoicing: 'haṃsīyitthā' becomes 'hattho,' with the elision of the niggahīta; also 'pahattho'.

Tipaccayamhi-anusāsanaṃ anusitthi, anusiṭṭhi vā, nivasanaṃ nivutthi.

With the 'ti' suffix: 'anusāsanaṃ' becomes 'anusitthi' or 'anusiṭṭhi'; 'nivasanaṃ' becomes 'nivutthi'.

Tupaccayamhi-sadevakaṃ lokaṃ sāsati anusāsatīti satthā.

With the 'tu' suffix: 'sadevakaṃ lokaṃ sāsati anusāsatīti' (he rules and instructs the world with its deities), thus 'satthā' (Teacher).

Tavantupaccayamhi-nivasitthāti nivutthavā.

With the 'tavantu' suffix: 'nivasitthā' becomes 'nivutthavā'.

Tāvīmhi-nivutthāvī.

With the 'tāvī' suffix: 'nivutthāvī'.

Tuṃ, tavesu-vasanaṃ vatthuṃ, vatthave.

With the 'tuṃ' and 'tave' suffixes: 'vasanaṃ' becomes 'vatthuṃ' and 'vatthave'.

Tabbamhi-dvāramūle vatthabbaṃ, sabhāye vatthabbaṃ.

With the 'tabba' suffix: 'dvāramūle vatthabbaṃ' (one should dwell at the door), 'sabhāye vatthabbaṃ' (one should dwell in the assembly).

Vasa-paridahane, bahulādhikārā uttaṃ natthi, vāsitabbanti vatthaṃ, nivāsīyitthāti nivatthaṃ, vatthabbaṃ, nivatthabbaṃ.

Vasa—in wearing: by the governing rule of 'bahulādhikāra' (wide application), vocalization to 'u' is not present; because it is worn, it is 'vatthaṃ'; 'nivāsīyitthā' becomes 'nivatthaṃ'; also 'vatthabbaṃ,' 'nivatthabbaṃ'.

Iti thādesarāsi.

Thus the section on 'tha' substitutions.

Dhādesarāsi

The section on 'dha' substitutions.

Idha, kudha, gidha, badha, budha, budhi, midha, yudha, rādha, rudha, vidha, sidha, sudha, thabhi, rabha, labha, lubha, sambhū, duha, naha, muha.

Idha (to prosper), kudha (to be angry), gidha (to be greedy), badha (to bind), budha (to know), budhi (to know), midha (to be sluggish), yudha (to fight), rādha (to accomplish), rudha (to obstruct), vidha (to pierce), sidha (to accomplish), sudha (to purify), thabhi (to prop), rabha (to begin), labha (to gain), lubha (to be greedy), sambhū (to arise), duha (to milk), naha (to bind), muha (to be deluded).

750. Dho dhabhahehi ka. 576; rū. 607; nī. 1179; ‘dho dhahabhehi’ (bahūsu).

750. The substitution 'dha' occurs for 'ta' after roots ending in 'dha' and 'bha'.

Etehi parassa anantarassa tassa dho hoti.

After these roots, the 'ta' of the immediately following suffix becomes 'dha'.

Idha-ijjhane[M 0.0498], dhātvantassa pararūpattaṃ saṃyogādissa ca tatiyattaṃ, samijjhitthāti samiddho-mahaddhano.

Idha—in prospering: the final of the root assimilates to the following sound, and the first of the conjunct becomes the third letter of its class; 'samijjitthā' becomes 'samiddho,' as in 'mahaddhano' (one of great wealth).

Kudha-kope, kujjhatīti kuddho, saṃkuddho.

From the root `kudh` in the sense of anger. One is angry, thus `kuddho`, `saṃkuddho`.

Gidha-gedhe, gijjhitthāti giddho, anugiddho, abhigiddho.

From the root `gidh` in the sense of greed. One was greedy, thus `giddho`, `anugiddho`, `abhigiddho`.

Badha-bandhane, bajjhitthāti baddho, pabaddho, ābaddho, nibaddho.

From the root `badh` in the sense of binding. One was bound, thus `baddho`, `pabaddho`, `ābaddho`, `nibaddho`.

Budha-ñāṇe jāgare vikasane ca, bujjhati jānātīti buddho, sambuddho, sammāsambuddho, pabujjhati jāgarotīti vā pabuddho, paṭibuddho.

From the root `budh` in the sense of knowledge, awakening, and blooming. One understands, that is, knows, thus `buddho`, `sambuddho`, `sammāsambuddho`; or one awakens, that is, is awake, thus `pabuddho`, `paṭibuddho`.

Budhi-nivāraṇe, paribundhīyatīti palibuddho. Vātapalibuddho, pittapalibuddho, semhapalibuddho.

From the root `budh` in the sense of obstruction. One is completely obstructed, thus `palibuddho`. For example: obstructed by wind, obstructed by bile, obstructed by phlegm.

Midha-mijjhane, mijjhatīti middhaṃ, middho. Kapimiddho.

From the root `midh` in the sense of torpor. One is sluggish, thus `middhaṃ`, `middho`. For example: `kapimiddho`, a monkey's torpor.

Yudha-sampahāre, yujjhīyateti yuddhaṃ. Mallayuddhaṃ, meṇḍayuddhaṃ, hatthiyuddhaṃ, kukkuṭayuddhaṃ.

From the root `yudh` in the sense of combat. It is fought, thus `yuddhaṃ`. For example: wrestlers' combat, rams' combat, elephants' combat, cocks' combat.

Rādha-ārādhane, ārādhayitthāti āraddho, abhiraddho.

From the root `rādh` in the sense of pleasing. One was pleased, thus `āraddho`, `abhiraddho`.

Vipubbo-virajjhane, viraddho.

With the prefix `vi`, from the root `rādh` in the sense of offending: `viraddho`.

Rudha-āvaraṇe, rundhīyitthāti ruddho, oruddho, avaruddho.

From the root `rudh` in the sense of obstructing. It was obstructed, thus `ruddho`, `oruddho`, `avaruddho`.

Nipubbo-nirodhe, nirujjhitthāti niruddho.

With the prefix `ni`, from the root `rudh` in the sense of cessation. It ceased, thus `niruddho`.

Vipubbo-virodhe, virujjhitthāti viruddho, paṭiviruddho.

With the prefix `vi`, from the root `rudh` in the sense of opposition. It was opposed, thus `viruddho`, `paṭiviruddho`.

Anupubbo-kantiyaṃ, anuruddho.

With the prefix `anu`, from the root `rudh` in the sense of affection: `anuruddho`.

Vidha-vijjhane, vijjhitthāti viddho. Sallaviddho.

From the root `vidh` in the sense of piercing. It was pierced, thus `viddho`. For example: `sallaviddho`, pierced by a dart.

Sidha-nipphattiyaṃ, sijjhitthāti siddho.

From the root `sidh` in the sense of accomplishment. It was accomplished, thus `siddho`.

Papubbo-pākaṭabhāve, pasiddho.

With the prefix `pa`, from the root `sidh` in the sense of being well-known: `pasiddho`.

Ni, paṭipubbo nivāraṇe, nisiddho, paṭisiddho.

With the prefixes `ni` and `paṭi`, from the root `sidh` in the sense of prohibition: `nisiddho`, `paṭisiddho`.

Sudha-sujjhane, sujjhatīti suddho, visuddho, parisuddho.

From the root `sudh` in the sense of purification. One is pure, thus `suddho`, `visuddho`, `parisuddho`.

Thabhi-thambhane[M 0.0499], thambhatīti thaddho, patthaddho, upatthaddho.

From the root `thabh` in the sense of making firm. One is firm, thus `thaddho`, `patthaddho`, `upatthaddho`.

Rabha-ārabhe, ārabhitthāti āraddho, ārabbhitthāti vā āraddho, samāraddho.

From the root `rabh` in the sense of undertaking. It was undertaken (`ārabhittha` or `ārabbhittha`), thus `āraddho`, `samāraddho`.

Labha-lābhe, alabhīti laddho, labbhitthāti vā laddho, paṭiladdho, upaladdho.

From the root `labh` in the sense of gain. One gained (`alabhi`), or it was gained (`labbhittha`), thus `laddho`, `paṭiladdho`, `upaladdho`.

Lubha-giddhiyaṃ, lubbhatīti luddho, paluddho, viluddho.

From the root `lubh` in the sense of greed. One is greedy, thus `luddho`, `paluddho`, `viluddho`.

Sambhū-passaddhiyaṃ, passambhitthāti passaddho.

From the root `sambh` in the sense of calming. It was calmed, thus `passaddho`.

Duha-dohane, duyhitthāti duddhā-gāvī.

From the root `duh` in the sense of milking. She was milked, thus `duddhā gāvī`, a milked cow.

Naha-bandhane, sannayhitthāti sannaddho, onaddho, avanaddho.

From the root `nah` in the sense of binding. One was bound, thus `sannaddho`, `onaddho`, `avanaddho`.

Muha-andhabhāve, muyhatīti muddho-bālo.

From the root `muh` in the sense of delusion. One is deluded, thus `muddho`, a fool.

Tipaccayamhi-ijjhanaṃ iddhi, ijjhanti etāyāti vā iddhi, samijjhanaṃ samiddhi, gijjhanaṃ giddhi, mijjhanaṃ middhi, abhirādhanaṃ abhiraddhi, virujjhanaṃ viruddhi, paṭiviruddhi, sijjhanaṃ siddhi, saṃsiddhi, paṭisiddhi, sujjhanaṃ suddhi, visuddhi, pārisuddhi, labhanaṃ laddhi, upaladdhi, lubbhanaṃ luddhi, passambhanaṃ passaddhi, muyhanaṃ muddhi.

With the suffix `-ti`: `ijjhanaṃ` (thriving) becomes `iddhi` (success), or 'one thrives by this,' thus `iddhi`; `samijjhanaṃ` (accomplishment) becomes `samiddhi` (success); `gijjhanaṃ` (greed) becomes `giddhi` (greed); `mijjhanaṃ` (torpor) becomes `middhi` (torpor); `abhirādhanaṃ` (pleasing) becomes `abhiraddhi` (delight); `virujjhanaṃ` (opposition) becomes `viruddhi` and `paṭiviruddhi` (opposition, counter-opposition); `sijjhanaṃ` (accomplishment) becomes `siddhi`, `saṃsiddhi`, and `paṭisiddhi` (success, complete success, counter-success); `sujjhanaṃ` (purification) becomes `suddhi`, `visuddhi`, and `pārisuddhi` (purity, great purity, complete purity); `labhanaṃ` (getting) becomes `laddhi` and `upaladdhi` (view, perception); `lubbhanaṃ` (greed) becomes `luddhi` (greediness); `passambhanaṃ` (calming) becomes `passaddhi` (tranquility); `muyhanaṃ` (delusion) becomes `muddhi` (delusion).

Tavantu, tāvīsu- “samiddhā, samiddhāvī”tiādinā vattabbaṃ.

With the suffixes `-vant` and `-āvin`: this should be explained with examples such as `samiddhā` and `samiddhāvī`.

Tvādīsu-rabha-ārabhe, āraddhā, āraddhāna.

With the suffixes `-tvā` and so on, from the root `rabh` in the sense of undertaking: `āraddhā`, `āraddhāna`.

Labha-lābhe, laddhā, laddhāna, paṭiladdhā, paṭiladdhāna.

From the root `labh` in the sense of gain: `laddhā`, `laddhāna` (having gained); `paṭiladdhā`, `paṭiladdhāna` (having regained).

Tuṃ, tavesu-budha-ñāṇe, buddhuṃ, buddhave, subuddhuṃ, subuddhave, boddhuṃ, boddhave, laddhuṃ, laddhave, paṭiladdhuṃ, paṭiladdhave.

With the suffixes `-tuṃ` and `-tave`: from the root `budha` in the sense of knowledge: `buddhuṃ`, `buddhave` (to know); `subuddhuṃ`, `subuddhave` (to know well); `boddhuṃ`, `boddhave` (to know). Also: `laddhuṃ`, `laddhave` (to get); `paṭiladdhuṃ`, `paṭiladdhave` (to regain).

Tabbamhi-boddhabbaṃ, laddhabbaṃ, paṭiladdhabbaṃ.

With the suffix `-tabba`: `boddhabbaṃ` (what ought to be known); `laddhabbaṃ` (what ought to be gotten); `paṭiladdhabbaṃ` (what ought to be regained).

751. Vaddhassa vā.

751. Or of `vaddha`.

Vaddhassa u hoti vā kānubandhe paccayatakāre tvādivajjite.

Of the root `vaddh`, the vowel is optionally changed to `u` before the `t` of a suffix with an indicatory `k`, excluding `-tvā` and so on.

Vaddhitthāti [M 0.0500] vuddho, vaddho vā, vaddhanaṃ vuddhi, mahāvuttinā uttaṃ. Tipaccayassa ca tassa lopo.

It grew, thus `vuddho` or `vaddho`. `Vaddhanaṃ` (growing) becomes `vuddhi` (growth), as stated in the Mahāvutti. And there is elision of the `t` of the suffix `-ti`.

Iti dhādesarāsi.

Thus the section on substitutions involving `dh`.

Visaṃyoganādesarāsi

The Section on Non-Substitution for Disjunct Roots.

Hā, i, ci, ji, ṭi, thī, dī,pī, mi, lī, thu, dū, dhū, pū, bhū, lū, vu, su, hu, āsa, katha, kupa, pala, mala, supa, paḷa.

Hā, i, ci, ji, ṭi, thī, dī, pī, mi, lī, thu, dū, dhū, pū, bhū, lū, vu, su, hu, āsa, katha, kupa, pala, mala, supa, paḷa.

752. Bhidādito no kta, ktavantūnaṃ.

752. From `bhid` and so on, `na` replaces `kta` and `ktavantu`.

Bhidādimhā paresaṃ kta, ktavantūnaṃ takārassa anantarabhūtassa no hoti.

After the roots `bhid` and so on, the immediately following `t` of the suffixes `kta` and `ktavantu` becomes `na`.

Hā-cāge, hīyitthāti hīno, pahīno, nihīno, ohīno. Ettha ca noādesaṃ katvā pacchā ‘ūbyañjanassā’ti īāgamo, tassa ca kvaci rasso. Evaṃ parattha.

`Hā` in the sense of abandoning. It was abandoned, thus `hīno`, `pahīno`, `nihīno`, `ohīno`. Here, after making the substitution to `na`, the augment `ī` is inserted by the rule `ūbyañjanassa`, and this is sometimes shortened. Similarly in other cases.

Adhipubbo-i-āyatte, adhicca etīti adhino.

The root `i`, preceded by `adhi`, is used in the sense of dependence. One who approaches intentionally is `adhino` (dependent).

Ci-caye, cayitthāti cino, ācino.

The root `ci` is used in the sense of accumulating. One who accumulates is `cino` (collector), `ācino` (gatherer).

Ji-jaye, pañcamāre jinātīti jino.

The root `ji` is used in the sense of victory. Because he conquers the five Māras, he is a `jino` (conqueror).

Ḍi-gatiyaṃ, ḍetīti ḍino.

The root `ḍī` is used in the sense of movement. One who flies is `ḍino` (one who has flown).

Thī-saṅghāte, thīyatīti thinaṃ.

The root `thī` is used in the sense of contracting. That which contracts is `thinaṃ` (sloth).

Dī-khaye, anukkamena dīyati khiyyatīti dino-divaso.

The root `dī` is used in the sense of waning. That which gradually wanes or wastes away is `dino` or `divaso` (day).

Pī-tappane, pīnitthāti pīno.

The root `pī` is used in the sense of delighting. One who is delighted is `pīno` (plump, full).

Mi-pakkhepe, minātīti mino.

The root `mi` is used in the sense of scattering. One who scatters is `mino` (a fish).

Lī-laye, līyitthāti līno, allīyitthāti allīno. Nilīyitthāti nilīno, paṭilīyitthāti paṭilīno, paṭilīnacaro bhikkhu, paṭisallīyitthāti paṭisallīno.

The root `lī` is used in the sense of clinging. One who clings is `līno` (clinging). One who adheres is `allīno` (adhering). One who hides is `nilīno` (hidden). One who withdraws is `paṭilīno` (withdrawn), as in `paṭilīnacaro bhikkhu` (a monk of withdrawn conduct). One who is secluded is `paṭisallīno` (secluded).

Thu-nitthunane[M 0.0501], nitthunātīti nitthuno.

The root `thu` is used in the sense of lamenting. One who laments is `nitthuno` (lamenter).

Dū-khede, dūyateti dūno.

The root `dū` is used in the sense of affliction. One who is afflicted is `dūno` (afflicted).

Dhū-niddhūnane, ahite dhamme dhunātīti dhuno, dhonopaññavā.

The root `dhū` is used in the sense of shaking off. Because he shakes off unbeneficial states, he is `dhuno` (one who shakes off), as in `dhonopaññavā` (one with cleansed wisdom).

Pū-sodhane, punātīti puno, dantaṃ punanti etenāti dantapoṇo, nassa ṇattaṃ.

The root `pū` is used in the sense of cleansing. One who purifies is `puno` (purifier). They clean the teeth with this, thus it is `dantapoṇo` (tooth-cleaner); the `na` becomes `ṇa`.

Bhū-vuddhiyaṃ, bhavati vaḍḍhatīti bhūno-hitarāsi.

The root `bhū` is used in the sense of growth. That which becomes or grows is `bhūno` (embryo), a mass of benefit.

Lū-chedane, lunātīti luno.

The root `lū` is used in the sense of cutting. One who cuts is `luno` (cutter).

Vu-saṃvaraṇe, āvuṇātīti āvuṇo.

The root `vu` is used in the sense of covering. One who covers is `āvuṇo` (coverer).

Su-savane, suṇātīti suno, soṇo, nassa ṇattaṃ.

The root `su` is used in the sense of hearing. One who hears is `suno` or `soṇo` (a dog); the `na` becomes `ṇa`.

Su-pasavane vā, pasavati vaḍḍhatīti sunaṃ-uddhumātaṃ.

Or the root `su` is used in the sense of swelling. That which swells or increases is `sunaṃ`, meaning `uddhumātaṃ` (swollen, inflated).

Hu-pūjā, dānesu, āhutabbanti āhunaṃ, pāhutabbanti pāhunaṃ-dātabbavatthu.

The root `hu` is used in the sense of offerings and gifts. That which is to be offered is `āhunaṃ` (offering). That which is to be given as a gift is `pāhunaṃ` (a gift for a guest), an object to be given.

Āsa-upavesane, acchatīti āsino, tuṇhī acchatīti tuṇhīmāsino.

The root ās is used in the sense of sitting. One who sits is āsino (seated). One who sits silently is tuṇhīmāsino (one who sits in silence).

Katha-thaddhe theriye ca, kathatīti kathinaṃ.

The root kath is used in the sense of stiffness and firmness. That which is stiff is kathinaṃ (the kathina robe-frame).

Kupa-kope, hirī kuppati etenāti hirīkopinaṃ.

The root kup is used in the sense of being agitated. Shame is agitated by this, thus it is hirīkopinaṃ (that which agitates shame; the private parts).

Pala-gatiyaṃ, paletīti palino.

The root pal is used in the sense of going. One who goes away is palino (grey-haired).

Mala-malinabhāve, malatīti malino, malinaṃ-vatthaṃ.

The root mal is used in the sense of being stained. That which is stained is malino (stained, defiled), as in malinaṃ vatthaṃ (a stained garment).

Supa-soppane, supatīti supino.

The root sup is used in the sense of sleeping. One sleeps, thus it is a supino (dream).

Paḷa-gatiyaṃ, paḷetīti paḷino, paḷinā jambudīpāte pārā. aṭṭha. 1.tatiyasaṃgītikathā.

The root paḷ is used in the sense of going. One who goes is paḷino, as in the phrase paḷinā jambudīpāte.

Iti visaṃyoganādesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on derivations without conjunction.

Sasaṃyoganādesarāsi

The Section on Derivations with Conjunction

Khida[M 0.0502], chida, tuda, dā, nuda, pata, pada, bhida, vida, sada.

The roots are: khid, chid, tud, dā, nud, pat, pad, bhid, vid, sad.

‘Bhidādito no ktaktavantūna’nti tassa no, dhātvantassa pararūpattaṃ, khijjitthāti khinno, chijjitthāti chinno, sañchinno, tuditthāti tunno, patunno, nitunno, vitunno.

By the rule 'From the bhid group onwards, -kta and -ktavantu become -na,' the suffix is -na. The final consonant of the root is assimilated to the following consonant. Thus, from khid comes khinno (distressed); from chid comes chinno (cut off), sañchinno (completely cut off); from tud comes tunno (pricked), patunno (pierced), nitunno (struck down), vitunno (pierced through).

Nuda-khepe, nuditthāti nunno, panunno.

The root nud is used in the sense of pushing away. That which is pushed away is nunno (pushed away), panunno (driven away).

Pata-patane, patatīti panno, pannadhajo, nnassa ṇṇatterukkhapaṇṇaṃ, pattaṃ vā.

The root pat is used in the sense of falling. That which falls is panno (fallen), as in pannadhajo (one with a fallen banner). The nna can become ṇṇa, as in rukkha-paṇṇaṃ (tree leaf) or pattaṃ (leaf).

Pada-gatiyaṃ, pajjitthāti panno, āpanno, uppanno, nipanno, vipanno, sampanno, upapanno, samupapanno, pariyāpanno.

The root pad is used in the sense of going. One who has gone is panno (attained). Other forms include: āpanno (fallen into), uppanno (arisen), nipanno (lain down), vipanno (perished), sampanno (endowed with), upapanno (reborn), samupapanno (fully reborn), pariyāpanno (included in).

Bhida-vidāraṇe, bhijjitthāti bhinno, pabhinno, sambhinno, paribhinno, vibhinno.

The root bhid is used in the sense of splitting. That which is split is bhinno (split). Other forms include: pabhinno (broken), sambhinno (broken up), paribhinno (completely broken), vibhinno (divided).

Vida-tuṭṭhiyaṃ, nibbindatīti nibbinno.

From the root vid in the sense of feeling: one who becomes disenchanted (nibbindati) is nibbinno (disenchanted).

Sada visaraṇa, gatyā’vasānesu, sīditthāti sanno, osanno, pasīditthāti pasanno, abhippasanno, nisīditthāti nisinno, sannisinno, ‘sadajarānamīma’iti īma, saṃyoge rasso ca.

The root sad is used in the senses of sinking, going, and ending. One who sinks (sīdati) is sanno (sunken) or osanno (settled down). One who becomes serene (pasīdati) is pasanno (serene) or abhippasanno (fully serene). One who sits down (nisīdati) is nisinno (seated) or sannisinno (well-seated). By the rule 'sadajarānamīma', the suffix is -īma, and there is shortening in conjunction.

Tavantumhi-khinnavā, chinnavā, sañchinnavā, tunnavā, patunnavā, panunnavā, pannavā, āpannavā, bhinnavā, sambhinnavā, sannavā, pasannavā, nisinnavā.

With the suffix -vantu: khinnavā (one who was distressed), chinnavā (one who has cut), sañchinnavā (one who has completely cut), tunnavā (one who has pricked), patunnavā (one who has pierced), panunnavā (one who has driven away), pannavā (one who has attained), āpannavā (one who has fallen into), bhinnavā (one who has broken), sambhinnavā (one who has broken up), sannavā (one who has sunk), pasannavā (one who has become serene), nisinnavā (one who has sat down).

753. Dātvinno ka. 582; rū. 631; nī. 1185.

753. From the root dā, the suffix is -inna.

Dādhātumhā paresaṃ ta, tavantūnaṃ tassa inno hoti.

After the root dā, the suffixes -ta and -tavantu are replaced by inna.

Dīyitthāti dinno, padinno, ādinno, samādinno, upādinno, pariyādinno, nnassa ṇṇatte upādiṇṇo.

That which is given (dīyati) is dinno (given). Other forms include: padinno (given forth), ādinno (taken up), samādinno (undertaken), upādinno (clung to), pariyādinno (taken possession of). When nna becomes ṇṇa, the form is upādiṇṇo.

Iti sasaṃyoganādesarāsi.

Thus, the section on substitutions with conjunctions.

Hādesarāsi

The section on 'h' substitutions.

Ūha[M 0.0503], gāhu, guha, baha, bāha, buha, muha, ruha, vaha.

Ūha, gāhu, guha, baha, bāha, buha, muha, ruha, vaha.

754. Ruhādīhi ho ḷo ca ka. 589; rū. 621; nī. 1192; ‘…ḷa ca’ (bahūsu).

754. From 'ruha' and so forth, 'ho' and 'ḷo' occur.

Ruhādīhi parassa anantarabhūtassa tapaccayassa takārassa ho hoti, dhātvantassa ḷo hoti.

From 'ruha' and so forth, 'ho' occurs for the 'ta' of the 'ta' affix immediately following, and 'ḷo' occurs at the end of the root.

Ūha-sañcaye, byūhitthāti byūḷho, viyūḷho, paribyūḷho, devāsurasaṅgāmo samupabyūḷho ahosi saṃ. ni. 1.249.

Ūha—in accumulation. (Examples:) 'byūḷho' (from 'byūhittha'), 'viyūḷho', 'paribyūḷho'. The battle between gods and asuras was well-arrayed.

Gāhu-bhusatthe vilolane ca, mā gāḷhaṃ paridevayi. Āgāḷhāya ceteti. Gāhitthāti gāḷho, pagāḷho, āgāḷho, ogāḷho, ajjhogāḷho pārā. aṭṭha. 1.1.

Gāhu—in intensity and agitation. 'Do not lament intensely.' 'One intends with intensity.' (Examples:) 'gāḷho' (from 'gāhittha'), 'pagāḷho', 'āgāḷho', 'ogāḷho', 'ajjhogāḷho'.

Baha-vuddhimhi.

Baha—in growth.

755. Muhabahabuhānañca te kānubandhetve ka. 517; rū. 488; nī. 1105; “muhabahānañca…” (bahūsu).

755. And for 'muha', 'baha', and 'buha', the 'ka' augment (occurs).

Tvādivajjite kānubandhe paccayatakāre pare muha, baha, buhānañca guhassa ca dīgho hoti.

When the 'ta' of an affix with the 'ka' marker, and which is not 'tvā' or the like, follows, the vowel of 'muha', 'baha', 'buha', and 'guha' is lengthened.

‘Ruhādīhiho ḷo cā’ti dhātvantassaḷo, tapaccayassa ho, abahīti bāḷhaṃ.

By the rule 'Ruhādīhi ho ḷo ca', 'ḷo' is substituted for the final of the root, and 'ho' for the 'ta' suffix. (Example:) 'abahi' becomes 'bāḷhaṃ'.

Buha-uddharaṇe, abuhitthāti būḷho, abbūḷho, abūḷhasallo su. ni. 785.

Buha—in lifting up: 'abuhitthā' becomes 'būḷho'; also 'abbūḷho', 'abūḷhasallo'.

Muha-andhabhāve.

Muha—in delusion.

756. Muhā vā.

756. Or after 'muh'.

Muhamhā parassa anantarabhūtassa takārassa ho hoti, dhātvantassa ca ḷo hoti vā.

After 'muha', 'ho' is substituted for the immediately following 'ta', and 'ḷo' is optionally substituted for the final of the root.

Muyhitthāti [M 0.0504] mūḷho, muddho vā.

From 'muyhitthā' comes 'mūḷho', or alternatively 'muddho'.

Ruha-janane, gatiyañca, ruhitthāti rūḷho, parūḷho, ārūḷho, orūḷho, virūḷho, nirūḷho.

Ruha—in generation and in movement: 'ruhitthā' becomes 'rūḷho'; also 'parūḷho', 'ārūḷho', 'orūḷho', 'virūḷho', 'nirūḷho'.

Vaha-pāpane, vahitthāti vūḷho, ‘assū’ti uttaṃ.

Vaha—in conveying: 'vahitthā' becomes 'vūḷho'; the vocalization to 'u' is stated, as in 'assū'.

Tipaccayamhi-ruhanaṃ rūḷhi, niruhanaṃ nirūḷhi, viruhanaṃ virūḷhi.

With the 'ti' suffix: 'ruhanaṃ' becomes 'rūḷhi'; 'niruhanaṃ' becomes 'nirūḷhi'; 'viruhanaṃ' becomes 'virūḷhi'.

Tvādīsu –

In the case of 'tvā' and other suffixes—

757. Pyo vā tvāssa samāse.

757. 'Pya' is optionally substituted for 'tvā' in a compound.

Samāsaṭṭhāne tvāpaccayassa pānubandho yo hoti vā. Pānubandho ‘pye sissā’ti visesanattho. ‘Hassa vipallāso’ti ha, yānaṃ vipariyāyo.

In a compound, 'ya' with the marker 'p' is optionally substituted for the 'tvā' suffix. The marker 'p' serves for specification, as in the rule 'pye sissā'. The phrase 'reversal of h' means that 'h' is the reverse of 'y'.

Byuyha, paribyuyha. Byūhitvā, viyūhitvā vā, vigāyha, vigāhitvā, ogāyha, ogāhitvā, ajjhogāyha, ajjhogāhitvā.

Byuyha, paribyuyha. Byūhitvā, or viyūhitvā. Vigāyha, vigāhitvā. Ogāyha, ogāhitvā. Ajjhogāyha, ajjhogāhitvā.

Bahulādhikārā asamāsepi pyo hoti, guyha, gūhitvā, niguyha, nigūhitvā, oguyha, ogūhitvā.

Due to the rule of abundance, the suffix `ya` occurs even in non-compounds: guyha, gūhitvā; niguyha, nigūhitvā; oguyha, ogūhitvā.

Naha-bandhane, sannayha, sannāhitvā.

From the root `nah` in the sense of binding: sannayha, sannāhitvā.

Bāha-nivāraṇe, dīgho, bāyha, bāhitvā, paṭibāyha, paṭibāhitvā.

From the root `bāh` in the sense of preventing, there is lengthening: bāyha, bāhitvā; paṭibāyha, paṭibāhitvā.

Buha-uddharaṇe papubbo, pabbuyha. Samūlaṃ taṇhaṃ pabbuyha saṃ. ni. 1.159 (taṇhamabbumha).

From the root `buh` in the sense of uprooting, when preceded by `pa`: pabbuyha. For example: 'Samūlaṃ taṇhaṃ pabbuyha' (Having uprooted craving with its root).

Āpubbo-abbuyha, “abbuhe sallamattano”ti ādīsu viya. Pamuyha, pamuyhitvā, vimuyha, vimuyhitvā, sammuyha, sammuyhitvā, āruyha, āruhitvā, ārohitvā, oruyha, orohitvā.

When preceded by `ā`: abbuyha, as in such examples as 'abbuhe sallamattano' (one should draw out one's own dart). Further examples: pamuyha, pamuyhitvā; vimuyha, vimuyhitvā; sammuyha, sammuyhitvā; āruyha, āruhitvā, ārohitvā; oruyha, orohitvā.

Saha-sahane, pasayha, pasahitvā vā.

From the root `sah` in the sense of enduring or overcoming: pasayha (forcibly), or pasahitvā.

Iti hādesarāsi.

Thus ends the section on the substitution of `h`.

Tvādivikārarāsi

The Section on the Modifications of `tvā`, etc.

Atha [M 0.0505] tvā, tvāna, tunānaṃ vikāro vuccate.

Now the modification of `tvā`, `tvāna`, and `tuna` is explained.

I, kara, hana.

I, kara, hana.

758. Ito cco.

758. After `i`, there is `cca`.

Idhātumhā parassa tvāssa cco hoti vā.

After the root `i`, `cca` is optionally substituted for the following `tvā`.

Pecca, samecca, abhisamecca, avecca, anvecca, apecca, upecca, samupecca, adhicca, aticca, paṭicca.

Pecca, having departed; samecca, having met; abhisamecca, having fully understood; avecca, having known; anvecca, having followed; apecca, having gone away; upecca, having approached; samupecca, having approached; adhicca, having understood; aticca, having transgressed; paṭicca, having depended upon.

Vāti kiṃ? Upetvā, samupetvā, adhiyitvā.

Why is `vā` stated? For cases such as: upetvā, samupetvā, adhiyitvā.

759. Sādhikarā raccariccā ka. 598; rū. 643; nī. 1203; ‘sāsādhikarā cacariccā’ (bahūsu).

759. After the root `kara` with the prefixes `sa` and `adhi`, there are `racca` and `ricca`.

Santa, adhiparā karamhā tvāssa racca, riccā honti vā, suttavibhattaṃ idha labbhati.

From `santa`, and from the root `kar` with the prefixes `adhi` and `parā`, `racca` and `ricca` are optionally substituted for `tvā`. The division of the sutta is found here.

Sakkacca, ‘sakkacca’nti bindāgamo, adhikicca.

Sakkacca: in 'sakkacca' there is a nasal augment; adhikicca.

Vāti kiṃ? Sakkatvā, sakkaritvā, adhikaritvā.

Why 'vā'? Having respected, having honored, having put in charge.

Suttavibhatte-attaṃ niraṃkacca piyāni sevati jā. 2.21.461, abhisaṅkhacca bhojanaṃ.

In the Suttavibhaṅga: 'Having disregarded oneself, one enjoys pleasant things'; 'having prepared the food.'

760. Hanā racco ka. 598; rū. 643; nī. 1203. ‘sāsādhikarā cacariccā’ (bahūsu).

760. From `han`, `racco`.

Hanamhā tvāssa racco hoti vā samāse. Suttavibhattena haramhāpi.

From the root `han`, `tvā` optionally becomes `racco` in a compound. According to the Suttavibhaṅga, also from `har`.

Āhacca, uhacca, vihacca, saṃhacca, upahacca.

Having struck; having lifted up; having destroyed; having struck together; having injured.

Vāti kiṃ? Āhanitvā, uhanitvā, vihanitvā, saṃhanitvā.

Why 'vā'? Having struck, having extracted, having damaged, having compressed.

Haramhi-sā [M 0.0506] no āhacca poseti jā. 2.22.2334 (āhatva), tato udakamāhacca.

Regarding `har`: 'She supports us, having brought provisions'; 'then having fetched water.'

Disa-pekkhane.

The root `dis` in the sense of seeing.

761. Disā vānavā sa ca ka. 599; rū. 644; nī. 1204; ‘…sa ca’ (bahūsu).

761. From `dis`, `tvā` becomes `vāna` or `vā`, and `dis` becomes `sa`.

Disamhā tvāssa vāna, vā honti vā, disassa ca sassa sa hoti, pararūpanisedhanamidaṃ.

From the root `dis`, `tvā` optionally becomes `vāna` or `vā`; and of `dis`, the `s` becomes `sa`. This is a prohibition of subsequent phonetic assimilation.

Disvāna, disvā.

Disvāna, having seen; disvā, having seen.

Vāti kiṃ? Passitvā.

Why 'vā'? Passitvā, having seen.

Khā, ñā, dā, dhā, hā, ki, khi, ci, ji, nī, lī, si, bhū.

Khā, ñā, dā, dhā, hā, ki, khi, ci, ji, nī, lī, si, bhū.

‘Pyo vā tvāssa samāse’ti tvāssa yo, mahāvuttinā vikappena kvaci yalopo, saṃpubbo khā-ñāṇe, saṅkhāya, saṅkhā, paṭisaṅkhāya, paṭisaṅkhā, aññāya, aññā, abhiññāya, abhiññā, pariññāya, pariññā.

By the rule '`pya` is an optional replacement for `tvā` in a compound,' `tvā` becomes `ya`. According to the Mahāvutti, by an optional rule, the `y` is sometimes elided. From `khā` preceded by `saṃ` in the sense of 'knowing': `saṅkhāya`, `saṅkhā` (having reckoned); `paṭisaṅkhāya`, `paṭisaṅkhā` (having reflected). From `ñā`: `aññāya`, `aññā` (having understood); `abhiññāya`, `abhiññā` (having directly known); `pariññāya`, `pariññā` (having fully comprehended).

Samāseti kiṃ? Ñatvā.

Why 'in a compound'? Ñatvā.

Vāti kiṃ? Ājānitvā, abhijānitvā, parijānitvā.

Why 'vā'? Ājānitvā (having understood), abhijānitvā (having directly known), parijānitvā (having fully comprehended).

Adhiṭṭhāya, adhiṭṭhā, patiṭṭhāya, patiṭṭhā.

Adhiṭṭhāya, adhiṭṭhā (having determined); patiṭṭhāya, patiṭṭhā (having established).

Samāseti kiṃ? Ṭhatvā.

Why 'in a compound'? Ṭhatvā.

Vāti kiṃ? Adhiṭṭhahitvā, patiṭṭhahitvā. Mahāvuttinā ittaṃ, upaṭṭhitvā.

Why 'vā'? Adhiṭṭhahitvā, patiṭṭhahitvā. According to the Mahāvutti, there is the augment `i`, as in `upaṭṭhitvā` (having attended upon).

Ādāya, upādāya, upādā.

Ādāya (having taken); upādāya, upādā (having clung to).

Samāseti kiṃ? Datvā.

Why 'in a compound'? Datvā.

Vāti kiṃ? Ādiyitvā, samādiyitvā, ‘ū byañjanassā’ti īāgamo, ‘dāssiyaṅa’iti suttena sare pare samāse iyādeso.

Why 'vā'? Ādiyitvā, samādiyitvā. By the rule 'ū byañjanassa,' there is the augment `ī`. By the rule 'dāssiyaṅa,' when a vowel follows in a compound, `iy` is the substitute.

762. Tuṃyānā.

762. Tuṃ and yāna.

Tvāssa [M 0.0507] tuñca yānañca honti kvaci samāse.

`Tuṃ` and `yāna` are sometimes substituted for `tvā` in a compound.

Bahulādhikārā gāthāyaṃ asamāsepi, nekkhamaṃ daṭṭhu khemato su. ni. 426, kimabbhutaṃ daṭṭhu marū pamoditā, bindulopo.

Due to the governing principle of 'variously,' this occurs even outside of a compound in verse: 'seeing renunciation as security'; 'what wonder is it, seeing the gods delighted?' There is elision of the nasal dot (`bindu`).

Abhihattuṃ pavāreyya, “abhihaṭu”ntipi pāṭho, saṃyogādissa lopo tassa ṭattaṃ. “Abhihaṭṭhu”ntipi pāci. 2.243 paṭhanti. Byañjanaṃ na sameti.

'One might invite someone to strike (`abhihattuṃ`).' There is also the reading `abhihaṭuṃ`; this involves the elision of the beginning of the consonant cluster and the change of `t` to `ṭ`. Some also read `abhihaṭṭhuṃ`, but the consonant does not conform.

Ādiyāna, upādiyāna. Vidhāya, nidhāya, sandhāya, odhāya, samodhāya, vidahitvā, nidahitvā, odahitvā, samodahitvā. Pahāya, vihāya, ohāya, hitvā, jahitvā.

Ādiyāna (having taken), upādiyāna (having clung to). Vidhāya (having arranged), nidhāya (having deposited), sandhāya (having connected), odhāya (having enclosed), samodhāya (having put together); and their alternate forms: vidahitvā, nidahitvā, odahitvā, samodahitvā. Pahāya (having abandoned), vihāya (having left), ohāya (having given up); also hitvā, jahitvā.

Ivaṇṇesu pyassa dvittaṃ, vikkiyya, vikkiṇitvā.

In the case of roots ending in `i` or `ī`, the consonant is doubled before `ya`: vikkiyya (having sold), vikkiṇitvā (having sold).

Viceyya dānaṃ dātabbaṃ pe. va. 329, ‘ūlasse’ti issa ettaṃ, vicinitvā, vineyya, vinetvā, vinayitvā, allīya, allīyitvā, paṭisallīya, paṭisallīyitvā, yāgamo.

'Having investigated, a gift should be given.' By the rule 'ūlasse,' `i` becomes `e`. Examples: vicinitvā (having discerned); vineyya, vinetvā, vinayitvā (having trained or removed); allīya, allīyitvā (having clung to); paṭisallīya, paṭisallīyitvā (having retreated). There is the augment `y`.

763. Pye sissā ka. 517; rū. 488; nī. 1105.

763. When `ya` follows, the vowel of `si` becomes `ā`.

Pye pare sissa ā hoti.

When `ya` follows, the vowel of `si` becomes `ā`.

Nissāya, upanissāya, apassāya, apassayitvā, avassāya, avassayitvā.

Having depended on, having closely depended on, having leaned against, having leaned against, having relied on, having relied on.

Vāti kiṃ? Adhisetvā, adhisayitvā.

Why 'vā'? Having lain upon, having lain down.

Bhū-sattāyaṃ, rassattaṃ, sambhuyya, vibhuyya, anubhuyya, adhibhuyya, paribhuyya, abhibhuyya.

From the root `bhū` in the sense of 'being,' there is shortening of the vowel: having associated with, having become powerful, having experienced, having overcome, having encompassed, having mastered.

Samāseti [M 0.0508] kiṃ? Bhutvā, edantesu mahāvuttinā essa āttaṃ, nijjhāya, nijjhāyitvā, upanijjhāya, upanijjhāyitvā, abhijjhāya, abhijjhāyitvā.

Why 'in a compound'? Having been. In the case of roots ending in `e`, according to the Mahāvutti, `e` becomes `ā`: having contemplated, having contemplated; having closely contemplated, having closely contemplated; having coveted, having coveted.

Byañjanantadhātūsu ‘vaggalalehi te’ti suttena cavagga, pavagga, sakārehi yassa pubbarūpattaṃ. Tavagge ‘tavaggavaraṇānaṃ ye cavaggabayañā’ti tavaggassa cavaggo, tato yassa pubbarūpattaṃ, vipacca, paripacca, vimucca, adhimucca.

In the case of roots ending in a consonant, by the rule '`vaggalalehi te`,' `y` is assimilated to a preceding `cavagga`, `pavagga`, or `s`. In the case of the `tavagga`, by the rule '`tavaggavaraṇānaṃ ye cavaggabayañā`,' the `tavagga` becomes `cavagga`, and then `y` is assimilated to it. For example: `vipacca` (having cooked), `paripacca` (having ripened), `vimucca` (having been released), `adhimucca` (having been intent on).

Mahāvuttinā yalopo dīgho ca, āpucchā, anāpucchā, vibhajja, saṃvibhajja, visajja, nisajja, paṭinisajja.

According to the Mahāvutti, there is elision of `y` and lengthening of the vowel: having taken leave, without having taken leave, having divided, having shared, having dismissed, having sat down, having sat down again.

Ujjha-visagge, yalopo, ujjha, ujjhiya, ujjhitvā.

From the root `ujjh` in the sense of 'abandoning,' there is elision of `y`: having abandoned (`ujjha`), having abandoned (`ujjhiya`), having abandoned (`ujjhitvā`).

Kati-chedane, kacca, vikacca, kantitvā, vikantitvā.
