Because it is tormented, it is vihaññaṃ (torment); because it is sown, it is vappaṃ (sowing, a seed-bed); sleeping is soppaṃ (sleep); because it should be obtained, it is labbhaṃ; because it should be gone to, it is gammaṃ; because it is fit to be tamed, it is dammaṃ (tamable); because it should be delighted in, it is rammaṃ or abhirammaṃ; because it is examined, it is nisammaṃ (consideration); because it is made uneven, it is visammaṃ (unevenness); because it is touched, it is phasso (contact); for u, there is the substitution of a.

Sāsitabboti sisso, ‘sāsassa sisā’ti sittaṃ.

One who should be instructed is a sisso (disciple). For sās (instruction), sis is substituted, hence sittaṃ (instilled, taught).

Gaha, guha, garaha, duha, vaha, saha.

The roots gah (to grasp), guh (to hide), garah (to blame), duh (to milk), vah (to carry), and sah (to endure).

781. Guhādīhi yaka ka. 541; rū. 552; nī. 1126.

781. From the root guh and so forth, the suffix yaka is applied.

Etehi bhāva, kammesu bahulaṃ yaka hoti, hassa vipallāso.

From these roots, the suffix yaka frequently occurs in the sense of state or being and action or object, and there is a change of ha.

Gahetabbanti gayhaṃ, guhitabbanti guyhaṃ.

Because it should be grasped, it is gayhaṃ; because it should be hidden, it is guyhaṃ.

Garaha-nindāyaṃ, garahitabbanti gārayhaṃ, duhitabbanti duyhaṃ, vahitabbanti vayhaṃ.

The root garah is in the sense of blaming; because it should be blamed, it is gārayhaṃ; because it should be milked, it is duyhaṃ; because it should be carried, it is vayhaṃ.

Saha-sāhase, sahitabbanti sayhaṃ, pasayhaṃ.

The root sah is in the sense of force or endurance; because it should be endured, it is sayhaṃ or pasayhaṃ.

782. Kicca ghacca bhacca gabba lyā ‘…babbaleyyā’ (bahūsu).

782. kicca (duty), ghacca (to be killed), bhacca (servant), gabba (womb), lya (stain).

Ete saddā yapaccayantā sijjhanti, iminā yapaccayaṃ katvā tena saha karassa kiccaṃ, hanassa ghaccaṃ, bharassa bhaccaṃ, gussa gabbaṃ, lissa lyattaṃ katvā sijjhanti.

These words are formed with the ya suffix. By applying this ya suffix, for the root kar there is kicca; for han, ghacca; for bhar, bhacca; for gu, gabba; and for li, lya; thus they are formed.

Karīyateti [M 0.0535] kiccaṃ, kiccayaṃ vā, haññateti ghaccaṃ, haccaṃ vā, bharīyateti bhaccaṃ.

Because it is done, it is kiccaṃ or kiccayaṃ; because it is struck, it is ghaccaṃ or haccaṃ; because it is maintained, it is bhaccaṃ.

Gu-dabbe, guyate gabbaṃ, paṭisallīyate paṭisalyaṃ.

The root gu is in the sense of substance; because it is concealed, it is gabbaṃ (womb, pride); because one retires into seclusion, it is paṭisalyaṃ (seclusion).

Visesavidhānaṃ –

Special Rule—

Bhara-bharaṇe, bharitabbanti bhāriyaṃ, haritabbanti hāriyaṃ, bhājetabbanti bhājiyaṃ, bhājeyyaṃ, upāsitabbanti upāsiyaṃ, icchitabbanti iccheyyaṃ, adhigantabbanti adhigameyyaṃ iccādi.

The root ‘bhara’ is in the sense of bearing. ‘Should be borne’ is bhāriya. ‘Should be taken’ is hāriya. ‘Should be divided’ is bhājiya or bhājeyya. ‘Should be attended to’ is upāsiya. ‘Should be wished for’ is iccheyya. ‘Should be attained’ is adhigameyya, and so forth.

Rundhitabbanti rundheyyaṃ, chinditabbanti chindeyyaṃ, chejjaṃ iccādi.

‘Should be obstructed’ is rundheyya. ‘Should be cut’ is chindeyya or chejja, and so forth.

Dibbitabbanti dibbeyyaṃ, dibbaṃ, bujjhitabbanti bujjheyyaṃ, bodheyyaṃ, bojjhaṃ iccādi.

‘Should be played’ is dibbeyya or dibba. ‘Should be awakened’ or ‘understood’ is bujjheyya, bodheyya, or bojjha, and so forth.

Sotabbanti suṇeyyaṃ, pāpuṇitabbanti pāpuṇeyyaṃ, sakkuṇitabbanti sakkuṇeyyaṃ, na sakkuṇeyyaṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ iccādi.

‘Should be heard’ is suṇeyya. ‘Should be attained’ is pāpuṇeyya. ‘Is possible’ is sakkuṇeyya. ‘Is not possible’ is asakkuṇeyya, and so forth.

Tanitabbanti tāneyyaṃ, taññaṃ, kātabbanti kāriyaṃ, kayyaṃ.

‘Should be stretched’ is tāneyya or tañña. ‘Should be done’ is kāriya or kayya.

Coretabbanti coreyyaṃ, thenīyate theyyaṃ, nassa pararūpattaṃ, cintetabbanti cinteyyaṃ, na cinteyyaṃ acinteyyaṃ, acintiyaṃ, manteyyaṃ, mantiyaṃ, vediyaṃ, vedeyyaṃ iccādi.

‘Should be stolen’ is coreyya. From `thenīyate` (is stolen) comes `theyya`. For `na`, there is substitution of the following form. ‘Should be thought’ is cinteyya. ‘Should not be thought’ is acinteyya or acintiya. `Manteyya` or `mantiya` (should be consulted). `Vediya` or `vedeyya` (should be known), and so forth.

Titikkheyyaṃ, vīmaṃseyyaṃ iccādi ca yojetabbāni.

Titikkheyya (should be endured), vīmaṃseyya (should be investigated), and so forth, should also be applied.

Iti ṇyādipaccayarāsi.

Thus ends the section on suffixes beginning with ṇya.

Aādipaccayarāsi

The Collection of Suffixes Beginning with ‘a’

Atha a, aṇa, ghaka, ghaṇapaccayantā vuccante.

Now, the suffixes `a`, `aṇa`, `ghaka`, and `ghaṇa` are explained.

783. Bhāvakārakesvaghaṇaghaka ‘bhāvakārakesvaghaṇaghakā’ (bahūsu).

783. The suffixes `a`, `ghaṇa`, and `ghaka` are applied in the sense of an action and in agentive roles.

Bhāve chasu kārakesu ca kriyatthā paraṃ a, ghaṇa, ghakapaccayā honti kammādimhi vā akammādimhi vā.

In the sense of an action (bhāva) and in the six agentive roles (kāraka), the suffixes a, ghaṇa, and ghaka are appended to a verbal root, whether it is transitive or intransitive.

784. Kvacaṇa.

784. Sometimes aṇa.

Kammupapadamhā [M 0.0536] kriyatthā paraṃ kattari eva kvaci aṇa hoti.

After a verbal root that is preceded by its object as a compound member, the suffix aṇa sometimes occurs, only in the sense of the agent.

A, aṇa, ghaka, ghaṇa.

A, aṇa, ghaka, ghaṇa.

Amhi tāva –

Firstly, regarding a:

Aggaṃ jānātīti aggañño, vaṃsaṃ jānātīti vaṃsañño, magge tiṭṭhatīti maggaṭṭho-puriso, maggaṭṭhā-itthī, maggaṭṭhaṃ-ñāṇaṃ. Evaṃ phalaṭṭho, thalaṭṭho, jalaṭṭho, pabbataṭṭho, bhūmaṭṭho.

Aggañña is one who knows the highest (aggaṃ jānāti). Vaṃsañña is one who knows the lineage (vaṃsaṃ jānāti). One who stands on the path (magge tiṭṭhati) is a maggaṭṭha (masculine), a maggaṭṭhā (feminine), or maggaṭṭhaṃ (neuter, e.g., knowledge). Similarly: phalaṭṭha (one who stands in the fruit), thalaṭṭha (one who stands on land), jalaṭṭha (one who stands in water), pabbataṭṭha (one who stands on a mountain), bhūmaṭṭha (one who stands on the earth).

Go vuccati ñāṇaṃ saddo ca, gavaṃ tāyati rakkhatīti gottaṃ, parito bhayaṃ tāyati rakkhatīti parittaṃ, annaṃ detīti annado. Evaṃ vatthado, vaṇṇado, yānado, sukhado, dīpado, cakkhudo, dāyaṃ ādadātīti dāyādo, pāraṃ gantuṃ detīti pārado-raso.

Go is said to be knowledge and sound. Gotta is that which protects cows (gavaṃ tāyati rakkhati). Paritta is that which protects from fear all around (parito bhayaṃ tāyati rakkhati). Annada is one who gives food (annaṃ deti). Similarly: vatthada (giver of cloth), vaṇṇada (giver of appearance), yānada (giver of a vehicle), sukhada (giver of happiness), dīpada (giver of a lamp), cakkhuda (giver of vision). Dāyāda is one who receives an inheritance (dāyaṃ ādadāti). Pārada is that which enables one to go to the far shore (pāraṃ gantuṃ deti), i.e., mercury.

Annaṃ dadātīti annadado, dvittaṃ pubbassa rasso ca.

Annadada is one who gives food (annaṃ dadāti); there is doubling of the consonant and shortening of the preceding vowel.

Purindado, mahāvuttinā purasadde assa ittaṃ bindāgamo ca.

Purindada: according to the Mahāvutti, in the word pura, the vowel a becomes i and a nasal (bindu) is inserted.

Sabbaṃ dadātīti sabbadado, saccaṃ sandhetīti saccasandho, janaṃ sandhetīti janasandho.

Sabbadada is one who gives all (sabbaṃ dadāti). Saccasandha is one who joins with truth (saccaṃ sandheti). Janasandha is one who unites people (janaṃ sandheti).

Kaku vuccati guṇarāsi, kakuṃ sandhetīti kakusandho, gāvopāti rakkhatīti gopo-puriso, gopassa bhariyā gopī.

Kaku is said to be a heap of virtues. Kakusandha is one who possesses this heap of virtues (kakuṃ sandheti). Gopa is a man who protects cows (gāvo pāti rakkhati). The wife of a gopa is a gopī.

Kassaṃ vuccati khettaṃ, kassaṃ pāti rakkhatīti kassapo.

Kassa is said to be a field. Kassapa is one who protects the field (kassaṃ pāti rakkhati).

Bhū vuccati pathavī, bhuṃ pāti rakkhatīti bhūpo. Evaṃ bhūmipo.

Bhū is said to be the earth. Bhūpa is one who protects the earth (bhuṃ pāti rakkhati). Similarly, bhūmipa.

Pādena mūlena pathavīrasaṃ āporasañca pivatīti pādapo, suṭṭhu bhāti dibbatīti subho, na mamāyatīti amamo, dve anatthe lāti gaṇhātīti bālo, bahuṃ lāti gaṇhātīti bahulo, rāhu viya lāti gaṇhātīti rāhulo, ādīnaṃ

Pādapa (a tree) is that which drinks the essence of earth and water with its foot, that is, its root (pādena mūlena ... pivati). Subha is that which shines well (suṭṭhu bhāti) or sports (dibbati). Amama is one who is without possessiveness (na mamāyati). Bāla is one who grasps (lāti gaṇhāti) two harmful things (dve anatthe). Bahula is that which grasps much (bahuṃ lāti gaṇhāti). Rāhula is one who grasps like Rāhu (rāhu viya lāti gaṇhāti).

Dukkhaṃ [M 0.0537] vāti bandhatītiādīnavo, aṇṇaṃ udakarāsiṃ vāti bandhatīti aṇṇavo iccādi.

Ādīnava is that which binds suffering (dukkhaṃ vāti bandhati). Aṇṇava is that which binds a mass of water (aṇṇaṃ udakarāsiṃ vāti bandhati), and so on.

Aṇamhi –

Regarding aṇa:

785. Āssāṇāpimhi yuka.

785. Āssāṇāpimhi yuka.

Ṇāpivajjite ṇānubandhe paccaye pare ādantassa dhātussa ante yuka hoti, yāgamoti attho.

When a suffix with the indicator ṇa follows, with the exception of ṇāpi, the augment y (yuka) is inserted at the end of a root ending in ā. The meaning is 'the insertion of y'.

Ñātabbo bujjhitabboti ñāyo-yutti, ñāyati amataṃ padaṃ etenāti ñāyo-ariyamaggo, paṭicca tiṭṭhatīti patiṭṭhāyo, dātabboti dāyo-āmisadāyo, dhammadāyo, khīraṃ pivatīti khīrapāyo, dhaññaṃ minātīti dhaññamāyo, vāti gacchatīti vāyo iccādi.

Ñāya (method) is that which is to be known or understood (ñātabbo bujjhitabbo); it means propriety (yutti). Or, ñāya (the noble path) is that by which the deathless state is known (ñāyati amataṃ padaṃ etena). Patiṭṭhāya is that which is established in dependence (paṭicca tiṭṭhati). Dāya is that which is to be given (dātabbo), such as a material gift (āmisadāya) or a gift of the Dhamma (dhammadāya). Khīrapāya is one who drinks milk (khīraṃ pivati). Dhaññamāya is one who measures grain (dhaññaṃ mināti). Vāya is that which moves or goes (vāti gacchati), and so on.

Ivaṇṇesu amhi tāva –

Firstly, regarding the suffix a after roots ending in i:

Eti pavattatīti āyo, sametīti samayo, veti vinassatīti vayo-mandādi, vigamanaṃ vinassanaṃ vayo-bhaṅgo, udayanaṃ udayo, samudayanaṃ samudayo, samudeti phalaṃ etenāti vā samudayo, aticca ayanaṃ pavattanaṃ accayo, paṭicca phalaṃ eti etasmāti paccayo, kiṇanaṃ kayo, vikkiṇanaṃ vikkayo, khīyanaṃ khayo, khīyanti etthāti vā khayo, rāgassa khayo rāgakkhayo, cayanaṃ cayo, ācayo, uccayo, samuccayo, upacayo, dhammaṃ vicinanti etenāti dhammavicayo, jayanaṃ jayo, vijayo, parājayo, niyyati etenāti nayo-vidhi, vineti ettha, etenāti vā vinayo, sukhena netabbo ñātabboti sunayo, dukkhena netabbo ñātabboti dunnayo, pātabboti payo-jalaṃ khīrañca.

Going or proceeding (eti pavattatīti) is income (āyo). Coming together (sameti) is conjunction (samayo). Perishing (veti vinassati) is decay (vayo), as in mandādi [slowness, etc.]; departure (vigamanaṃ) or destruction (vinassanaṃ) is the breaking of decay (vayo-bhaṅgo). Rising (udayanaṃ) is rise (udayo). Origination (samudayanaṃ) is origin (samudayo); or, that by which a fruit arises is origin (samudayo). Going beyond or proceeding (aticca ayanaṃ pavattanaṃ) is transgression (accayo). That from which a fruit comes dependently (paṭicca phalaṃ eti etasmā) is a condition (paccayo). Buying (kiṇanaṃ) is purchase (kayo). Selling (vikkiṇanaṃ) is sale (vikkayo). Wasting away (khīyanaṃ) is destruction (khayo); or, that wherein things waste away is destruction. The destruction of lust is rāgakkhayo. Piling up (cayanaṃ) is a heap (cayo); also ācayo, uccayo, samuccayo, upacayo. That by which one investigates phenomena is investigation of phenomena (dhammavicayo). Conquering (jayanaṃ) is victory (jayo); also vijayo (triumph), parājayo (defeat). That by which one is led (niyyati etena) is method (nayo) or policy (vidhi). That wherein or by which one is disciplined is discipline (vinayo). That which is easily led or known is good policy (sunayo). That which is led or known with difficulty is bad policy (dunnayo). That which is to be drunk (pātabbo) is a drink (payo), such as water and milk.

Ri-kampane, niccaṃ rayanti phandanti dukkhappattā sattā etthāti nirayo, allīyanaṃ ālayo, niliyanaṃ nilayo, sayanaṃ sayo, bhuso senti etthāti āsayo, ajjhāsayo, visesena [M 0.0538] senti etthāti visayo, nissāya naṃ seti pavattati etthāti nissayo, upanissayo, anusetīti anusayo iccādi.

From the root ri (to tremble): that wherein beings afflicted by suffering constantly tremble and quiver is hell (nirayo). Clinging (allīyanaṃ) is attachment (ālayo). Hiding (niliyanaṃ) is a lair (nilayo). Lying down (sayanaṃ) is a bed (sayo). That wherein one lies intensely (bhuso senti ettha) is an abode or inclination (āsayo); also ajjhāsayo. That wherein one lies in a special way (visesena senti ettha) is an object (visayo). That depending on which one lies or proceeds is support (nissayo); also upanissayo. That which lies latent (anuseti) is a latent tendency (anusayo), and so on.

Aṇamhi –

Regarding aṇa:

Ayanaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ āyo, āyamhā apeto apāyo, āyena upeto upāyo, samudeti etthāti samudāyo, samaveti etthāti samavāyo, pariyāyo, vipariyāyo, netabboti nāyo ñāyo?, nīyati etenāti vā nāyo, bhūmiyaṃ setīti bhūmisāyo iccādi.

Going (ayanaṃ), meaning increase (vaḍḍhanaṃ), is income (āyo). Devoid of income (āyamhā apeto) is a state of loss (apāyo). Endowed with income (āyena upeto) is a means (upāyo). That wherein things arise together is collection (samudāyo). That wherein things come together is combination (samavāyo). Also: pariyāyo (course), vipariyāyo (reversal). That which is to be led (netabbo) is leadership (nāyo); or, that by which one is led is leadership. One who lies on the ground (bhūmiyaṃ seti) is a ground-dweller (bhūmisāyo), and so on.

Uvaṇṇesu amhi tāva –

Firstly, regarding the suffix a after roots ending in u:

Cavanaṃ cavo, javanaṃ javo, abhitthavanaṃ abhitthavo, bhusaṃ davati hiṃsatīti upaddavo, sandhavanaṃ sandhavo, mittabhāvena sandhavo mittasandhavo, bhavatīti bhāvo, vibhavanaṃ vibhavo, sambhavanaṃ sambhavo, sambhavati etasmāti vā sambhavo, adhibhavanaṃ adhibhavo, abhibhavo, paribhavo, parābhavanaṃ vinassanaṃ parābhavo, ravatīti ravo-saddo, lunanaṃ lavo, pasavatīti passāvo, āsavatīti āsavo, paṭimukhaṃ savanaṃ paṭissavo iccādi.

Falling away (cavanaṃ) is decease (cavo). Running (javanaṃ) is speed (javo). Praising (abhitthavanaṃ) is praise (abhitthavo). That which harms violently (bhusaṃ davati hiṃsati) is a calamity (upaddavo). Running together (sandhavanaṃ) is association (sandhavo); friendly association is mittasandhavo. Becoming (bhavati) is existence (bhāvo). Ceasing to be (vibhavanaṃ) is non-existence (vibhavo). Coming into being (sambhavanaṃ) is origin (sambhava); or, that from which one comes into being is origin. Overpowering (adhibhavanaṃ) is mastery (adhibhavo); also conquest (abhibhavo), contempt (paribhava). Perishing (parābhavanaṃ) or destruction (vinassanaṃ) is decline (parābhavo). Sounding (ravati) is a sound (ravo). Cutting (lunanaṃ) is reaping (lavo). Flowing forth (pasavati) is urine (passāvo). Flowing in (āsavati) is an influx (āsavo). A flow in response (paṭimukhaṃ savanaṃ) is an answer (paṭissavo), and so on.

Aṇamhi –

Regarding aṇa:

Bhavanaṃ bhāvo, bhavanti sadda, buddhiyo etenāti bhāvo, sāliṃ lunātīti sālilāvo, kucchitena savati sandatīti kasāvo iccādi.

Becoming (bhavanaṃ) is state (bhāvo); or, that by which words and ideas come to be is state. One who reaps rice (sāliṃ lunāti) is a rice-reaper (sālilāvo). That which flows or exudes in a bad way (kucchitena savati sandati) is a stain, a defilement (kasāvo), and so on.

Edantesu aṇamhi –

Regarding the suffix aṇa after roots ending in e:

Mahāvuttinā essa āyattaṃ, mantaṃ ajjhetīti mantajjhāyo, vajjāvajjaṃ upecca jhāyatīti upajjhāyo-thero, upajjhāyinītherī.

According to the Mahāvutti, the final e of a root becomes āya. One who recites a mantra (mantaṃ ajjheti) is a mantra-reciter (mantajjhāyo). One who contemplates after considering what is blameable and what is not (vajjāvajjaṃ upecca jhāyati) is a preceptor (upajjhāyo), an elder monk; a female preceptor is an upajjhāyinī, an elder nun.

De-pālane[M 0.0539], attani nilīnaṃ dayati rakkhatīti dāyo, migadāyo, tantaṃ vāyatīti tantavāyo.

From the root de (to protect): that which protects what is hidden within (attani nilīnaṃ dayati rakkhati) is a grove (dāyo), as in a deer park (migadāyo). One who weaves thread (tantaṃ vāyati) is a weaver (tantavāyo).

Vhe-avhāne, vhīyatīti vhayo-nāmaṃ, rassattaṃ, āpubbo avhayo iccādi.

From the root vhe (to call): that which is called (vhīyati) is a name (vhayo); there is shortening. With the prefix ā, it becomes avhayo (designation), and so on.

Anekabyañjanesu amhi tāva –

Firstly, regarding the suffix a after polysyllabic roots:

Kamanaṃ kamo, pakkamo, abhikkamo, paṭikkamo, caṅkamati etthāti caṅkamo, hitaṃ karotīti hitakkaro, dukkhena kātabboti dukkaro-attho, dukkarā-paṭipadā, dukkaraṃ-kammaṃ, sukhena kātabboti sukaro, īsaṃ kātabboti īsakkaro, dīpaṃ karotīti dīpaṅkaro, aluttasamāso.

Stepping (kamanaṃ) is a step (kamo); also pakkamo (exertion), abhikkamo (advance), paṭikkamo (retreat). That wherein one walks is a walkway (caṅkamo). One who does good (hitaṃ karoti) is a benefactor (hitakkaro). That which is to be done with difficulty (dukkhena kātabbo) is difficult (dukkaro), e.g., a difficult task (dukkaraṃ kammaṃ), a difficult practice (dukkarā paṭipadā). That which is to be done with ease is easy (sukaro). That which is to be done slightly is easy to do (īsakkaro). One who makes an island or lamp (dīpaṃ karoti) is Dīpaṅkaro; this is a compound with an unelided case ending.

Āgacchatīti āgamo, āgamanaṃ vā āgamo, saṅgamanaṃ saṅgamo, samāgamo, paggaṇhanaṃ paggaho, saṅgaṇhanaṃ saṅgaho, saṅgayhanti ettha, etenāti vā saṅgaho, anuggaho, paṭiggaho, gāvo caranti etthāti gocaro, kāme avacaratīti kāmāvacaro, uraṃ chādetīti uracchado, jirati etenāti jaro, vessaṃ taratīti vessantaro, aluttasamāso.

That which comes (āgacchati) is a scripture (āgamo); or, coming (āgamanaṃ) is a scripture (āgamo). Coming together (saṅgamanaṃ) is a meeting (saṅgamo); also samāgamo. Upholding (paggaṇhanaṃ) is exertion (paggaho). Collecting (saṅgaṇhanaṃ) is a collection (saṅgaho); or, that wherein or by which one collects is a collection. Also: anuggaho (help), paṭiggaho (acceptance). That wherein cows roam (gāvo caranti ettha) is a pasture (gocaro). One who moves in the sense sphere (kāme avacarati) is a being of the sense sphere (kāmāvacaro). That which covers the chest (uraṃ chādeti) is a breastplate (uracchado). That by which one decays (jirati etena) is old age (jaro). One who crosses over to the merchants (vessaṃ tarati) is Vessantaro; this is a compound with an unelided case ending.

Rathe attharatīti rathattharo, assattharo, ariṃ dametīti arindamo, bhagaṃ darati bhindatīti bhagandaro, yugaṃ ravi’ndudvayaṃ dhāretīti yugandharo, dhammaṃ dhāretīti dhammadharo, pajjateti padaṃ, sikkhā eva padaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ, sukhena bharitabboti subharo, dukkhena bharitabboti dubbharo, na maratīti amaro-devo, niyamanaṃ niyamo, saṃyamanaṃ saṃyamo, sirasmiṃ ruhatīti siroruho, sukhena labbhatīti sulabho, dukkhena labbhatīti dullabho, saṃvaritabboti saṃvaro, vuccatīti vaco, subbaco, dubbaco, vāriṃ vahatīti [M 0.0540] vārivaho, sarati gacchatīti saro, manaṃ haratīti manoharo iccādi.

That which is spread on a chariot (rathe attharati) is a chariot-rug (rathattharo); similarly, assattharo (horse-blanket). One who tames the enemy (ariṃ dameti) is a foe-tamer (arindamo). That which splits the anus (bhagaṃ darati) is a fistula (bhagandaro). That which bears the yoke-pair of the sun and moon (yugaṃ ravi-indudvayaṃ dhāreti) is Yugandharo mountain. One who upholds the Dhamma (dhammaṃ dhāreti) is a Dhamma-upholder (dhammadharo). One goes by it (pajjati), hence it is a foot or word (padaṃ). A training rule (sikkhā) itself is a step (padaṃ), hence sikkhāpadaṃ. Easy to support (sukhena bharitabbo) is subharo. Difficult to support (dukkhena bharitabbo) is dubbharo. One who does not die (na marati) is an immortal, a god (amaro). Restraining (niyamanaṃ) is restraint (niyamo). Controlling (saṃyamanaṃ) is self-control (saṃyamo). That which grows on the head (sirasmiṃ ruhati) is hair (siroruho). Easy to obtain (sukhena labbhati) is sulabho; difficult to obtain is dullabho. That which should be restrained (saṃvaritabbo) is restraint (saṃvaro). That which is spoken (vuccati) is speech (vaco); hence subbaco (easy to admonish) and dubbaco (difficult to admonish). That which carries water (vāriṃ vahati) is a cloud (vārivaho). That which flows (sarati) is a lake or an arrow (saro). That which captivates the mind (manaṃ harati) is delightful (manoharo), and so on.

Aṇamhi –

Regarding aṇa:

Kamu-icchā, kantīsu, kāmetīti kāmo, kāmīyatīti vā kāmo, atthaṃ kāmetīti atthakāmo, karaṇaṃ kāro, pakāro, ākāro, vikāro, upakāro, apakāro, kumbhaṃ karotīti kumbhakāro, rathakāro, mālakāro, saṅkharaṇaṃ saṅkhāro, saṅkharīyatīti vā saṅkhāro, saṅkharotīti vā saṅkhāro, parikkhāro, purakkhāro, gacchanti pavattanti kāmā etthāti gāmo, gaṇhātīti gāho, pattaṃ gaṇhātīti pattagāho, rasmiṃ gaṇhātīti rasmigāho, vicaraṇaṃ vicāro, upecca caratīti upacāro, gāmaṃ upecca caratīti gāmūpacāro, jirati hirī bhijjati etenāti jāro, kicchena taritabboti kantāro, mahāvuttinā kicchassa kattaṃ, bindāgamo, vāḷakantāro, yakkhakantāro, attharaṇaṃ atthāro, kathinassa atthāro kathinatthāro, darati bhindati kulavibhāgaṃ gacchati etena janenāti dāro, kuṃ pathaviṃ dāretīti kudāro, rassa lo, kudālo.

From the root kam (to desire, to love): one desires (kāmeti) or it is desired (kāmīyati), hence sensual pleasure (kāmo). One who desires benefit (atthaṃ kāmeti) is a well-wisher (atthakāmo). Doing (karaṇaṃ) is an act (kāro); also pakāro (manner), ākāro (form), vikāro (change), upakāro (help), apakāro (harm). One who makes pots (kumbhaṃ karoti) is a potter (kumbhakāro); also rathakāro (chariot-maker), mālakāro (garland-maker). Forming (saṅkharaṇaṃ) is a formation (saṅkhāro); or, it is formed (saṅkharīyati), or one forms (saṅkharoti), hence saṅkhāro. Also: parikkhāro (requisite), purakkhāro (honoring). That wherein desires move and proceed is a village (gāmo). Seizing (gaṇhāti) is a grasp (gāho); e.g., pattagāho (bowl-holder), rasmigāho (rein-holder). Moving about (vicaraṇaṃ) is examination (vicāro). Moving near (upecca carati) is vicinity (upacāro); e.g., gāmūpacāro (village vicinity). That by which modesty decays and is broken is a paramour (jāro). That which is crossed with difficulty (kicchena taritabbo) is a wilderness (kantāro). According to the Mahāvutti, kiccha becomes katta with the insertion of a nasal. For example: a wilderness with beasts (vāḷakantāro), a wilderness with yakkhas (yakkhakantāro). Spreading (attharaṇaṃ) is a rug (atthāro); e.g., the spreading of the kathina cloth (kathinatthāro). That person by whom a family is split or divided is a wife (dāro). That which splits the earth (kuṃ pathaviṃ dāreti) is a spade (kudāro). The r becomes l, hence kudālo.

Bhuso kriyaṃ dhāretīti ādhāro, pattādhāro, paṭisandhāraṇaṃ paṭisandhāro, pajjati etenāti pādo, uppajjanaṃ uppādo, paṭicca samuppajjanaṃ paṭiccasamuppādo, bharitabbo vahitabboti bhāro, sambharīyati sannicīyatīti sambhāro, bodhisambhāro, dabbasambhāro, māretīti māro, kilesamāro, khandhamāro, maccumāro, niyāmetīti niyāmo, dhammaniyāmo, kammaniyāmo, ārūhatīti āroho, rukkhaṃ ārūhatīti rukkhāroho, hatthāroho, assāroho, rathāroho, labbhatīti lābho, paṭilābho, nivaraṇaṃ nivāro, parivāretīti parivāro, vahatīti vāho, āvāho, vivāho, sarati addhānaṃ pavattatīti [M 0.0541] sāro, virūpena paṭisaraṇaṃ punappunaṃ cintanaṃ vippaṭisāro, paharaṇaṃ pahāro, āhāro, nīhāro, vihāro, abhihāro, parihāro.

It holds an action firmly, thus it is a support (ādhāro); a bowl-support (pattādhāro). Treating kindly (paṭisandhāraṇaṃ) is kind treatment (paṭisandhāro). One goes by this, thus it is a foot (pādo). Arising (uppajjanaṃ) is arising (uppādo). Dependent arising (paṭicca samuppajjanaṃ) is dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādo). What is to be borne or carried is a burden (bhāro). What is gathered or accumulated is an accumulation (sambhāro)—the accumulation for awakening (bodhisambhāro), the accumulation of requisites (dabbasambhāro). He kills, thus he is Māro—the Māra of defilements (kilesamāro), the Māra of aggregates (khandhamāro), the Māra of death (maccumāro). It regulates, thus it is a principle (niyāmo)—the principle of the Dhamma (dhammaniyāmo), the principle of kamma (kammaniyāmo). He ascends, thus it is an ascent (āroho)—ascending a tree is tree-climbing (rukkhāroho); an elephant-rider (hatthāroho), a horse-rider (assāroho), a chariot-rider (rathāroho). It is obtained, thus it is gain (lābho); acquisition (paṭilābho). Hindering (nivaraṇaṃ) is a hindrance (nivāro). He surrounds, thus it is an entourage (parivāro). He carries, thus it is a carrying (vāho)—bringing a bride (āvāho), taking a bride in marriage (vivāho). It moves along a course, thus it is the essence (sāro). A contrary reflection, thinking again and again, is remorse (vippaṭisāro). Striking (paharaṇaṃ) is a blow (pahāro); food (āhāro), taking out (nīhāro), dwelling (vihāro), offering (abhihāro), protection (parihāro).

786. Hanassa ghāto ṇānubandhe ka. 591; rū. 544; nī. 1195.

786. For the root han, ghāto is the substitute when an affix with the anubandha ṇa follows.

Ṇānubandhe paccaye pare hanassa ghāto hoti.

When an affix with the anubandha ṇa follows, ghāto is the substitute for the root han.

Hananaṃ ghāto, vihaññanaṃ vighāto, upahananaṃ upaghāto, paṭihananaṃ paṭighāto.

Killing (hananaṃ) is striking (ghāto); harassing (vihaññanaṃ) is injury (vighāto); oppressing (upahananaṃ) is affliction (upaghāto); striking against (paṭihananaṃ) is resistance (paṭighāto).

Ghakapaccaye vuddhi natthi, ‘manānaṃ niggahīta’nti dhātvānubandhassapi nassa niggahītaṃ vagganto ca, ‘kagā cajānaṃ ghānubandhe’ti ghānubandhe paccaye pare dhātvantānañca, jānaṃ ka, gā honti, nipaccatīti nipako.

When the affix ghaka follows, there is no vowel strengthening. By the rule 'manānaṃ niggahītaṃ,' the anubandha na of the root becomes a niggahīta and the final consonant of the class. By the rule 'kagā cajānaṃ ghānubandhe,' when an affix with the anubandha gha follows, the final ca and ja of a root become ka and ga respectively. He is clever (nipaccati), thus nipako.

Bhanja-bhijjane vibhāge ca, bhañjanaṃ bhaṅgo, vibhajjanaṃ vibhaṅgo, vibhajīyanti dhammā ettha, etenāti vā vibhaṅgo, khandhavibhaṅgo, dhātuvibhaṅgo.

The root bhañj is in the sense of breaking and dividing. Breaking is a break (bhaṅga). Dividing is an analysis (vibhaṅga). Phenomena are analyzed here, or by this, thus it is 'Analysis'—the Analysis of Aggregates, the Analysis of Elements.

Ranja-rāge, rañjanaṃ raṅgo, rañjanti sattā etthāti raṅgo.

The root rañj is in the sense of coloring or passion. Coloring is color (raṅga). Beings are colored or delighted here, thus it is a stage or arena (raṅga).

Sanja-saṅge, sañjanaṃ saṅgo, pasajjanaṃ lagganaṃ pasaṅgo, āsajjatīti āsaṅgo, uttari āsaṅgo uttarāsaṅgo.

The root sañj is in the sense of attachment. Attachment is a bond (saṅga). Strong attachment or clinging is attachment (pasaṅga). One clings to, thus it is clinging (āsaṅga). A higher attachment is an upper robe (uttarāsaṅga).

Saja-sajjane, atisajjanaṃ sambodhanaṃ atisaggo, gassa dvittaṃ.

The root saj is in the sense of letting go. Extreme letting go, or bestowal, is atisagga. There is doubling of 'g'.

Nissajjanaṃ nissaggo, paṭinissaggo, vissajjanaṃ vissaggo, saṃsajjanaṃ missīkaraṇaṃ saṃsaggo, yujjati etthāti yugaṃ, kaliyugaṃ, sakaṭayugaṃ, pitāmahayugaṃ, nitudanaṃ nitudo, panudanaṃ panudo, uddhaṃ bhijjatīti ubbhido, kovidatīti kovido, pakārena kujjhatīti pakudho, bujjhatīti budho-paṇḍito, muyhatīti momūho, loluppatīti loluppo, ādidvittaṃ ottañca iccādi.

Giving up is relinquishment (nissagga); renunciation (paṭinissagga). Giving away is donation (vissagga). Associating, mixing, is association (saṃsagga). It is yoked here, thus it is a yoke or an age (yuga)—the age of strife, a cart-yoke, a grandfather's generation. Piercing is a goad (nituda). Dispelling is dispelling (panuda). It breaks upwards, thus it is an outburst (ubbhida). One knows well, thus one is skilled (kovida). One is angry in a particular way, thus one is irritable (pakudha). One awakens, thus one is the awakened one—the wise person (budha). One is deluded, thus one is the utterly deluded one (momūha). One is greedy, thus one is the greedy one (loluppa). There is doubling of the initial syllable, and the vowel becomes 'o', and so on.

Ghaṇapaccaye-pacanaṃ [M 0.0542] pāko, paccatīti vā pāko, vipāko, viviccanaṃ viveko, siñcanaṃ seko, abhiseko, socanaṃ soko, cajanaṃ cāgo, bhajanaṃ bhāgo, bhuñjanaṃ bhogo, saha bhogo sambhogo, paribhogo, ābhujanaṃ ābhogo, obhujanaṃ obhogo.

When the affix ghaṇa follows: cooking is ripening (pāka), or it ripens, thus it is ripening; maturation (vipāka). Separation is seclusion (viveka). Sprinkling is sprinkling (seka); consecration (abhiseka). Grieving is sorrow (soka). Abandoning is generosity (cāga). Dividing is a portion (bhāga). Enjoying is enjoyment (bhoga); enjoyment with is communal enjoyment (sambhoga); using (paribhoga). Bending towards is reflection (ābhoga). Bending down is a fold (obhoga).

Yaja-pūjāyaṃ, yajanaṃ yāgo, āmisayāgo, dhammayāgo, yujjanaṃ yogo, payogo, āyogo, viyogo, anuyogo, upayujjitabboti upayogo, lujjatīti loko, mahāvuttinā gassa kattaṃ, kāmaloko, rūpaloko, saṃvijjanaṃ saṃvego iccādi.

The root yaj is in the sense of worship. Sacrificing is a sacrifice (yāga): a material sacrifice, a Dhamma sacrifice. Yoking is application (yoga): effort (payoga), exertion (āyoga), separation (viyoga), inquiry (anuyoga). What is to be applied is application (upayoga). It disintegrates, thus it is the world (loka). By a great rule, 'g' becomes 'k'. The world of sense pleasures, the world of form. Being agitated is spiritual urgency (saṃvega), and so on.

787. Anaghaṇasvāparīhi ḷo ka. 614; rū. 581; nī. 1219.

787. After ā and pari, ḷa replaces dah when the suffixes ana or ghaṇa follow.

Ā, parīhi parassa dahassa ḷo hoti ana, ghaṇapaccayesu.

After the prefixes ā and pari, ḷa is the substitute for the root dah when the affixes ana and ghaṇa follow.

Paridayhanaṃ pariḷāho, ‘dahassa dassa ḍo’ti vikappena ḍādeso, dayhanaṃ ḍāho, dāho vā.

Burning all around is anguish (pariḷāha). By the rule 'dahassa dassa ḍo,' ḍa is optionally the substitute for da. Burning is burning (ḍāha), or burning (dāha).

Iti aādipaccayarāsi.

Thus ends the section on suffixes beginning with a.

Anapaccayarāsi

The Section on the Suffix ana

Atha anapaccayantā vuccante.

Now, words ending in the suffix ana are explained.

788. Ano.

788. The Suffix ana

Bhāve ca chasu kārakesu ca kriyatthā anapaccayo hoti, ādantesu parassaralopo, alope yāgamo.

The suffix ana occurs in the sense of a state and in the six case relations to signify an action. For roots ending in ā, the vowel of the suffix is elided. When there is no elision, the augment y is inserted.

Akkhāyate akkhānaṃ, akkhāyati etenāti vā akkhānaṃ, dhammassa akkhānanti dhammakkhānaṃ, paṭisaṅkhāyati pajānāti etenāti paṭisaṅkhānaṃ[M 0.0543], saha gāyanaṃ saṅgāyanaṃ, saha gāyanti sajjhāyanti etthāti vā saṅgāyanaṃ, ñāyate ñāṇaṃ, jānātīti vā ñāṇaṃ, jānanti etenāti vā ñāṇaṃ, paññāyatīti paññāṇaṃ, vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ, saññāṇaṃ, nassa ṇattaṃ.

It is told, thus it is a telling (akkhāna); or one tells by this, thus it is a telling. The telling of the Dhamma is the Dhamma-telling. One reflects, one understands by this, thus it is reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna). Singing together is communal chanting (saṅgāyana); or, they chant together, they recite together here, thus it is a communal chanting. It is known, thus it is knowledge (ñāṇa); or, one knows, thus it is knowledge; or, one knows by this, thus it is knowledge. It is discerned, thus it is discernment (paññāṇa). One cognizes, thus it is consciousness (viññāṇa); a sign (saññāṇa). The na becomes ṇa.

Kārite-ñāpanaṃ, paññāpanaṃ, viññāpanaṃ, saññāpanaṃ.

In the causative: making known (ñāpana), proclaiming (paññāpana), informing (viññāpana), convincing (saññāpana).

Jānanaṃ, pajānanaṃ, vijānanaṃ, sañjānanaṃ, pubbassaralopo, ṭhīyate ṭhānaṃ, tiṭṭhati etthāti vā ṭhānaṃ.

Knowing (jānana), understanding (pajānana), discerning (vijānana), perceiving (sañjānana). There is elision of the preceding vowel. It is stood upon, thus it is a place (ṭhāna); or, one stands here, thus it is a place.

Kārite-ṭhāpanaṃ, patiṭṭhāpanaṃ.

In the causative: placing (ṭhāpana), establishing (patiṭṭhāpana).

Tāyati rakkhatīti tāṇaṃ, parittāṇaṃ, nassa ṇattaṃ.

It protects, it guards, thus it is protection (tāṇa); protection (parittāṇa). The na becomes ṇa.

Avatthāyati etthāti avatthānaṃ, dīyate dānaṃ, diyyati etenāti vā dānaṃ, sammā padīyati assāti sampadānaṃ, apecca ādadāti etasmāti apādānaṃ.

One stands firm in this, thus it is a basis (avatthāna). It is given, thus it is a gift (dāna); or one gives by this, thus it is a gift. It is well given to him, thus it is the dative case (sampadāna). Having gone away, one takes from this, thus it is the ablative case (apādāna).

Kārite-dāpanaṃ, samādapanaṃ.

In the causative: causing to give (dāpana), causing to undertake (samādapana).

Padahīyate padhānaṃ, padahanti etenāti vā padhānaṃ, ādhānaṃ, vidhānaṃ, nidhānaṃ, sannidhānaṃ.

One strives, thus it is striving (padhāna); or one strives by this, thus it is striving. Placing (ādhāna), arranging (vidhāna), depositing (nidhāna), accumulating (sannidhāna).

Kārite-sannidhāpanaṃ.

In the causative: causing to accumulate (sannidhāpana).

Pānaṃ, paṭibhānaṃ, māṇaṃ, pamāṇaṃ, upamāṇaṃ, parimāṇaṃ, nassa ṇattaṃ.

Drinking (pāna), inspiration (paṭibhāna), measuring (māṇa), measure (pamāṇa), comparison (upamāṇa), limit (parimāṇa). The na becomes ṇa.

Yāyati etenāti yānaṃ, uyyānaṃ, niyyānaṃ, vāyanti bhavābhavaṃ gacchanti etenāti vānaṃ, natthi vānaṃ etthāti nibbānaṃ, nibbāyanti etthāti vā nibbānaṃ.

One goes by this, thus it is a vehicle (yāna); a park (uyyāna); departure (niyyāna). They are woven, they go from existence to existence by this, thus it is craving (vāna). There is no craving here, thus it is Nibbāna. Or, they are extinguished here, thus it is Nibbāna.

Kārite-nibbāpanaṃ.

In the causative: causing to be extinguished (nibbāpana).

Avasānaṃ, osānaṃ, pariyosānaṃ, pahānaṃ, parihānaṃ.

Conclusion (avasāna), ending (osāna), final end (pariyosāna), abandonment (pahāna), decline (parihāna).

Kārite-hāpanaṃ, parihāpanaṃ.

In the causative: causing to abandon (hāpana), causing to decline (parihāpana).

Ivaṇṇesu-ayanaṃ [M 0.0544] vikkayanaṃ, vikkiṇanaṃ, khayanaṃ, khiyanaṃ, khiyyanaṃ, iya, iyyādeso, cayanaṃ, cinanaṃ, ācinanaṃ, vicinanaṃ, jayanaṃ, vijayanaṃ, līyanti etthāti leṇaṃ, nassa ṇattaṃ.

In the case of roots ending in the vowel i: going (ayana), selling (vikkayana), selling (vikkiṇana), destruction (khayana), wasting away (khiyana, khiyyana). There is substitution of iya and iyya. Piling up (cayana), collecting (cinana), accumulating (ācinana), investigating (vicinana). Conquering (jayana), victory (vijayana). They hide here, thus it is a cave (leṇa). The na becomes ṇa.

Paṭisallīyanti etthāti paṭisallānaṃ, issa āttaṃ. Seti etthāti senaṃ, sayanaṃ.

One secludes oneself here, thus it is seclusion (paṭisallānaṃ). The vowel 'i' becomes 'ā'. One lies down here, thus it is a bed (senaṃ); lying down (sayanaṃ).

Kārite-sayāpanaṃ iccādi.

In the causative: causing to lie down (sayāpanaṃ), and so on.

Uvaṇṇesu-cavanaṃ, javanaṃ, abhitthavanaṃ, dhunanaṃ, viddhunanaṃ, niddhunanaṃ, bhavanaṃ, abhibhavanaṃ, lavanaṃ, lunanaṃ, savanaṃ, pasavanaṃ iccādi.

In the case of roots ending in the vowel 'u': falling away (cavanaṃ), impelling (javanaṃ), praising (abhitthavanaṃ), shaking (dhunanaṃ), shaking off (viddhunanaṃ), shaking off (niddhunanaṃ), becoming (bhavanaṃ), overcoming (abhibhavanaṃ), reaping (lavanaṃ), cutting (lunanaṃ), hearing (savanaṃ), bringing forth (pasavanaṃ), and so on.

Edantesu-ajjhenaṃ, ajjhāyanaṃ, apacāyanaṃ, jhāyate jhānaṃ, jhāyati etenāti vā jhānaṃ, paṭhamajjhānaṃ, dutiyajjhānaṃ, ujjhānaṃ, nijjhānaṃ, abhijjhānaṃ, sālilāyanaṃ, cīvaravāyanaṃ, gilāyatīti gilāno iccādi.

In the case of roots ending in the vowel 'e': studying (ajjhenaṃ, ajjhāyanaṃ), honoring (apacāyanaṃ). One meditates, thus it is meditation (jhānaṃ); or one meditates by this, thus it is meditation. The first jhāna (paṭhamajjhānaṃ), the second jhāna (dutiyajjhānaṃ). Complaining (ujjhānaṃ), contemplation (nijjhānaṃ), covetousness (abhijjhānaṃ). Playing in the water (sālilāyanaṃ), weaving of robes (cīvaravāyanaṃ). He is sick, thus he is a sick person (gilāno), and so on.

‘Rā nassa ṇo’ti suttena rakāramhā parassa nassa ṇo, kāraṇaṃ, adhikarīyati etthāti adhikaraṇaṃ, saṅkharaṇaṃ, abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ.

By the rule 'rā nassa ṇo,' the 'na' that follows an 'ra' becomes 'ṇa'. Cause (kāraṇaṃ). It is made the basis here, thus it is the basis or locative case (adhikaraṇaṃ). Preparation (saṅkharaṇaṃ), formation (abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ).

Kārite-kārāpanaṃ.

In the causative: causing to be done (kārāpanaṃ).

Ākiraṇaṃ, vikkiraṇaṃ, caraṇaṃ, jiraṇaṃ, taraṇaṃ, kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ, attharaṇaṃ, āgantvā dahanti ettha matasarīranti āḷahanaṃsusānaṃ, dassa ḷo.

Scattering (ākiraṇaṃ); dispersing (vikkiraṇaṃ); walking (caraṇaṃ); aging (jiraṇaṃ); crossing over (taraṇaṃ); overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ); spreading (attharaṇaṃ). A cremation ground (āḷahanaṃ) is where, having come, they burn dead bodies; also a charnel ground (susānaṃ). The 'd' becomes 'ḷ'.

Passīyate passanaṃ, dassanaṃ, suṭṭhu passatīti sudassanorājā, suṭṭhu passitabbanti sudassanaṃ-devanagaraṃ, sandassanaṃ, nidassanaṃ, dhāraṇaṃ, uddhāraṇaṃ, niddhāraṇaṃ, ādidīgho.

Seeing (passanaṃ), vision (dassanaṃ). ‘He sees well,’ thus King Sudassana. ‘It is well seen,’ thus Sudassana, the city of the devas. Showing (sandassanaṃ); pointing out (nidassanaṃ); holding (dhāraṇaṃ); lifting up (uddhāraṇaṃ); determining (niddhāraṇaṃ). The initial vowel is lengthened.

Pūraṇaṃ, paripūraṇaṃ, pharaṇaṃ, vippharaṇaṃ.

Filling (pūraṇaṃ); fulfilling (paripūraṇaṃ); pervading (pharaṇaṃ); spreading out (vippharaṇaṃ).

Kārite-māraṇaṃ.

In the causative: killing (māraṇaṃ).

Nivāraṇaṃ, saraṇaṃ, nissaraṇaṃ, haraṇaṃ, āharaṇaṃ, nīharaṇaṃ iccādi.

Preventing, a hindrance (nivāraṇaṃ); a refuge (saraṇaṃ); escape (nissaraṇaṃ); taking away (haraṇaṃ); bringing (āharaṇaṃ); taking out (nīharaṇaṃ); and so on.

Sāmaññavidhānattā [M 0.0545] saddattha, kujjhanattha, calanatthadhātūhi ruca, juta, vaḍḍhādidhātūhi ca tassīlādīsu ano hoti, ghosati sīlenāti ghosano, ghosati dhammenāti ghosano, ghosati sādhukārenāti ghosano, kodhano, dūsano, padūsano, kopano, calano, phandano, kampano, maṇḍano, bhūsano, vibhūsano, rocano, virocano, verocano, jotano, ujjotano, vaḍḍhano, karoti sīlenāti karaṇo. Rāgo nimittakaraṇo, doso nimittakaraṇo, moho nimittakaraṇo saṃ. ni. 4.349 iccādi.

By a general rule, the suffix 'ana' is used in the sense of ‘one whose nature is,’ etc., with roots meaning sound, anger, and movement, and with roots such as ruc (to shine), jut, vaḍḍh, etc. For example: one whose nature is to make a sound is ghosano; one who proclaims by the Dhamma is ghosano; one who acclaims with cries of ‘sādhu’ is ghosano. Also: kodhano, dūsano, padūsano, kopano, calano, phandano, kampano, maṇḍano, bhūsano, vibhūsano, rocano, virocano, verocano, jotano, ujjotano, vaḍḍhano. One whose nature is to act is karaṇo. Lust is a maker of signs, hatred is a maker of signs, delusion is a maker of signs, and so on.

789. Karā ṇano.

789. From the root 'kar', the suffix 'ana' with the indicatory letter 'ṇ'.

Karamhā kattari ṇānubandho ano hoti.

After the root 'kar', the suffix 'ana', which has the indicatory letter 'ṇ', occurs in the agent sense.

Karoti attano phalanti kāraṇaṃ.

It produces its own fruit, thus it is a cause (kāraṇaṃ).

790. Hāto vīhikālesu.

790. From the root 'hā' in the senses of paddy and time.

Vīhismiṃ kāle ca vattabbe hādhātumhā kattari ṇānubandho ano hoti.

When paddy or time is to be expressed, the suffix 'ana', which has the indicatory letter 'ṇ', occurs after the root 'hā' in the agent sense.

Hāpetīti hāyano, vīhiviseso vassañca. “Kuñjaraṃ saṭṭhihāyana”nti ettha vassaṃ hāyananti vuccati.

It causes to diminish, thus 'hāyano', which means a particular kind of paddy and also a year. In the phrase ‘an elephant of sixty years’ (kuñjaraṃ saṭṭhihāyanaṃ), a year (vassaṃ) is called 'hāyana'.

Iti anapaccayarāsi.

Thus the section on the suffix 'ana'.

Akapaccayarāsi

The Section on the Suffix 'aka'

Atha akapaccayantā vuccante.

Now the words ending in the suffix 'aka' are explained.

791. Āsīsāyamako ‘āsiṃsāmako’ (bahūsu).

791. The suffix 'aka' in the sense of a blessing.

Āsīsā vuccati patthanā, āsīsāyaṃ gamyamānāyaṃ ako hoti kattari.

A blessing (āsīsā) is called an aspiration (patthanā). When a blessing is being expressed, the suffix 'aka' occurs in the agent sense.

Jīvatūti [M 0.0546] jīvako, nandatūti nandako. “Jinabuddhi, dhanabhūti, bhūto, dhammadinno, vaḍḍhamāno”ti ete saddā aññathā sijjhanti, jino imaṃ bujjhatūti jinabuddhi, dhanaṃ etassa bhavati vaḍḍhatīti dhanabhūti, bhavati vaḍḍhatīti bhūto, dhammena dinno dhammadinno, yathā devadatto, brahmadatto, vaḍḍhatīti vaḍḍhamānoti.

‘May he live!’ (jīvatu), thus Jīvako. ‘May he rejoice!’ (nandatu), thus Nandako. The words Jinabuddhi, Dhanabhūti, Bhūto, Dhammadinno, and Vaḍḍhamāno are formed otherwise. Jinabuddhi is from ‘the Jina awakens this one.’ Dhanabhūti is from ‘wealth arises and increases for him.’ Bhūto is from ‘he arises and increases.’ Dhammadinno is from ‘given by the Dhamma,’ like Devadatta and Brahmadatta. Vaḍḍhamāno is from ‘he increases.’

‘Kattari ltuṇakā’ti ṇako, so ca sāmaññavidhānattā arahe sattiyaṃ sīle dhamme sādhukāre ca sijjhati, akkhāyatīti akkhāyako, ‘āssāṇāpimhi yuka’iti yāgamo, akkhātuṃ arahati, sakkoti, akkhānamassa sīlaṃ, dhammo, akkhānaṃ sakkaccaṃ karotīti attho. Kālattayepi sijjhati, pubbepi akkhāsi, ajjapi akkhāti, pacchāpi akkhāyissatīti attho. Evaṃ sesesu sāmaññavidhīsu yathārahaṃ veditabbo.

The suffix 'ṇaka' is prescribed by the rule ‘ltuṇakā in the agent sense.’ By a general rule, it is used in the senses of fitness, ability, nature, duty, and performing well. For example, one who relates is an akkhāyako (relater); the augment 'y' is inserted by the rule ‘āssāṇāpimhi yuka.’ The meaning is: he is fit to relate, he is able to relate, relating is his nature or his duty, or he relates carefully. It can be used with reference to all three times, meaning: he related in the past, he relates now, and he will relate in the future. It should be understood similarly as appropriate for the other general rules.

Itthiyaṃ-‘adhātussa ke…’ti suttena akassa assa ittaṃ, akkhāyikā-itthī, akkhāyakaṃ-kulaṃ, saṅgāyako, jānātīti jānako.

In the feminine, by the rule beginning ‘adhātussa ke…,’ the 'a' of the suffix 'aka' becomes 'i', forming akkhāyikā (a female relater). The neuter is akkhāyakaṃ (a family). A reciter is a saṅgāyako. One who knows (jānāti) is a jānako (knower).

Vikaraṇapaccayato paraṃ nāgame sati vikaraṇassa rasso, jānanako, ājānanako, vijānanako, sañjānanako.

When the augment 'na' follows the conjugational sign, the vowel of the conjugational sign is shortened. For example: jānanako, ājānanako, vijānanako, sañjānanako.

Kārite-ñāpetīti ñāpako, viññāpako, saññāpako.

In the causative: one who causes to know (ñāpeti) is an informer (ñāpako). Also: viññāpako (one who makes known), saññāpako (one who communicates).

Nāgame-ñāpanako, viññāpanako, saññāpanako, adhiṭṭhātīti adhiṭṭhāyako, adhiṭṭhāpetīti adhiṭṭhāpako, detīti dāyako, dāpetīti dāpako.

With the augment 'na': ñāpanako, viññāpanako, saññāpanako. One who resolves (adhiṭṭhāti) is a resolver (adhiṭṭhāyako). One who causes to resolve (adhiṭṭhāpeti) is an adhiṭṭhāpako. One who gives (deti) is a donor (dāyako). One who causes to give (dāpeti) is an instigator of giving (dāpako).

Ṇāpimhi yāgamo natthi, samādapetīti samādapako, ubhayattha rasso. Vidhetīti vidhāyako, pajahatīti pajahāyako, avahiyyatīti ohiyako, āssa ittaṃ iccādi.

There is no augment 'y' with the causative suffix 'ṇāpe'. One who causes to undertake (samādapeti) is a samādapako; there is shortening in both places. One who arranges (vidheti) is a vidhāyako. One who abandons (pajahati) is a pajahāyako. One who is left behind (avahiyyati) is an ohiyako. The 'ā' becomes 'i' [in the feminine], and so on.

Ivaṇṇesu-ajjhetīti [M 0.0547] ajjhāyako, mantaṃ ajjhetīti mantajjhāyako, kiṇātīti kāyako, kiṇāpetīti kāyāpako, ācinātīti ācinako, vicinako, parājayatīti pārājiko, alopo, puggalo, parājetīti pārājiko, alopo kāritalopo ca, dhammo, bhāyāpetīti bhayānako, nāgamo ādirasso ca.

Regarding roots ending in i or ī: one who studies (ajjheti) is a student (ajjhāyako); one who studies mantras (mantaṃ ajjheti) is a mantajjhāyako. One who buys (kiṇāti) is a buyer (kāyako); one who causes to buy (kiṇāpeti) is a kāyāpako. One who accumulates (ācināti) is an ācinako; also vicinako (one who investigates). One who is defeated (parājayatīti) is a pārājiko (a person who is defeated); there is no elision. One who defeats (parājeti) is a pārājiko (a rule entailing defeat); there is no elision and elision of the causative sign. One who frightens (bhāyāpeti) is a bhayānako (a frightful one); there is the augment n and shortening of the initial vowel.

Bhūmiyaṃ setīti bhūmisāyako, sayāpetīti sayāpako, pāhetīti pahiṇako iccādi.

One who lies on the ground (bhūmiyaṃ seti) is a bhūmisāyako. One who causes to lie down (sayāpeti) is a sayāpako. One who sends (pāheti) is a pahiṇako, and so forth.

Uvaṇṇesu-punāti sodhetīti pāvako-aggi, bhavatīti bhāvako, vibhāvetīti vibhāvako, lunātīti lāvako, suṇātīti sāvako-puriso, sāvikā-itthī, juhotīti hāvako iccādi.

Regarding roots ending in u or ū: that which purifies or cleanses (punāti) is pāvako, i.e., fire. One who becomes (bhavati) is a bhāvako. One who makes clear (vibhāveti) is a vibhāvako. One who reaps (lunāti) is a reaper (lāvako). One who hears (suṇāti) is a disciple (sāvako), a male; the feminine is sāvikā. One who sacrifices (juhoti) is a sacrificer (hāvako), and so forth.

Apa-pāpuṇane, pāpetīti pāpako, sampāpetīti sampāpako, upāsatīti upāsako-puriso, upāsikā-itthī, upāsakaṃ-kulaṃ, karotīti kārako, kārikā, kārakaṃ, upakārako, kāretīti kārāpako, saṅkharotīti saṅkhārako, abhisaṅkhārako, khipatīti khipako, ukkhipako, nikkhipako, khepako, ukkhepako, nikkhepako, nāgamekhipanako.

From the root ap in the sense of attaining: one who causes to attain evil (pāpeti) is an evil-doer (pāpako); one who causes to attain fully (sampāpeti) is a sampāpako. One who attends on (upāsati) is a lay follower (upāsako), a male; the feminine is upāsikā, and the neuter is upāsakaṃ (a family of lay followers). One who does (karoti) is a doer (kārako); feminine kārikā, neuter kārakaṃ. Also: upakārako (a helper). One who causes to be done (kāreti) is a kārāpako. One who constructs (saṅkharoti) is a saṅkhārako; also abhisaṅkhārako. One who throws (khipati) is a khipako; also ukkhipako (one who throws up), nikkhipako (one who throws down). Alternative forms are khepako, ukkhepako, nikkhepako. With the na augment: khipanako.

Gaṇhātīti gāhako, gaṇhāpetīti gāhāpako. Evaṃ gopako, pādamūle caratīti pādacārako, pupphaṃ ocināyatīti ocināyako, edanto dhātu.

One who takes (gaṇhāti) is a taker (gāhako); one who causes to take (gaṇhāpeti) is a gāhāpako. Similarly, a protector (gopako). One who travels on foot (pādamūle carati) is a pedestrian (pādacārako). One who picks flowers (pupphaṃ ocināyati) is a flower-picker (ocināyako); this is from a root ending in e.

Chindatīti chedako, chindako, chedāpetīti chedāpako, chindāpako, janetīti janako-puriso, janikāmātā, janakaṃ-kammaṃ, kāritalopo.

One who cuts (chindati) is a chedako or chindako. One who causes to cut (chedāpeti) is a chedāpako or chindāpako. One who begets (janeti) is a begetter (janako), a father; the feminine is janikā, a mother; the neuter is janakaṃ, generative kamma. This involves elision of the causative sign.

Jhāpa-dāhe, jhāpetīti jhāpako.

From the root jhāpa in the sense of burning: one who causes to burn (jhāpeti) is a jhāpako.

Ñapa-paññāpane, paññapetīti paññāpako.

From the root ñapa in the sense of making known: one who makes known (paññapeti) is a paññāpako.

Ṭhāpa-ṭhāne, patiṭṭhāpetīti patiṭṭhāpako.

From the root ṭhāpa in the sense of establishing: one who establishes (patiṭṭhāpeti) is an establisher (patiṭṭhāpako).

Ṇāpa-pesane[M 0.0548], āṇāpetīti āṇāpako, tudatīti tudako, santussatīti santussako, visesena passatīti vipassako, sandassetīti sandassako, dūsetīti dūsako, ādidīgho.

From the root ṇāpa in the sense of commanding: one who commands (āṇāpeti) is a commander (āṇāpako). One who goads (tudati) is a tudako. One who is content (santussati) is a santussako. One who sees with distinction (visesena passati) is an insight meditator (vipassako). One who shows (sandasseti) is a sandassako. One who corrupts (dūseti) is a corrupter (dūsako); the initial vowel is lengthened.

Pacatīti pācako, pācetīti pācāpako, āpādetīti āpādako, nipphādako, sampādako, paṭipajjako, paṭipādako, pūretīti pūrako, garupantattā na vuddhi.

One who cooks (pacati) is a cook (pācako); one who causes to cook (pāceti) is a pācāpako. One who produces (āpādeti) is a producer (āpādako); also nipphādako (an accomplisher), sampādako (one who brings to completion). A practitioner is a paṭipajjako; one who provides is a paṭipādako. One who fills (pūreti) is a filler (pūrako); there is no vowel strengthening because the preceding syllable is heavy.

Phusatīti phusako, tudādittā na vuddhi.

One who touches (phusati) is a phusako. Because the root belongs to the tud-group, there is no vowel strengthening.

Bhājetīti bhājako, bhindatīti bhindako, bhedako, kārabhedako, bhuñjatīti bhuñjako, bhojako, gāmabhojako, bujjhatīti bujjhako, bodhako, maratīti miyyako, māretīti mārako, muñcatīti muñcako, mocako, yācatīti yācako, yajatīti yājako, yuñjatīti yuñjako, anuyuñjako, yojako, payojako, yujjhatīti yujjhako, yodhako, rundhatīti rundhako, avarodhako, vacatīti vācako, ovadatīti ovādako, ovajjako, vīṇaṃ vādetīti vīṇāvādako, bherivādako, garuṃ abhivādetīti abhivādako, vidatijānātīti vedako, vindati paṭilabhatīti vindako, anuvijjati vicāretīti anuvijjako, paṭisaṃvedetīti paṭisaṃvedako, vijjhatīti vedhako, aṭṭhiṃ vijjhatīti aṭṭhivedhako, pattaṃ vijjhatīti pattavedhako.

One who divides (bhājeti) is a bhājako. One who splits (bhindati) is a bhindako or bhedako; a kārabhedako is one who breaks an agreement. One who eats (bhuñjati) is an eater (bhuñjako) or a provider of food (bhojako); a gāmabhojako is a village headman. One who awakens (bujjhati) is a bujjhako or a bodhako. One who dies (marati) is a miyyako; one who kills (māreti) is a killer (mārako). One who releases (muñcati) is a muñcako or mocako. One who begs (yācati) is a beggar (yācako). One who sacrifices (yajati) is a sacrificer (yājako). One who strives (yuñjati) is a yuñjako or anuyuñjako; one who applies is a yojako or payojako. One who fights (yujjhati) is a fighter (yujjhako) or a warrior (yodhako). One who obstructs (rundhati) is an obstructer (rundhako) or avarodhako. One who speaks (vacati) is a speaker (vācako). One who advises (ovadati) is an adviser (ovādako) or ovajjako. One who plays the lute (vīṇaṃ vādeti) is a lute-player (vīṇāvādako); a bherivādako is a drummer. One who pays homage to a teacher (garuṃ abhivādeti) is an abhivādako. One who knows (vidati jānāti) is a knower (vedako). One who finds (vindati paṭilabhati) is a finder (vindako). One who investigates (anuvijjati vicāreti) is an investigator (anuvijjako). One who experiences (paṭisaṃvedeti) is an experiencer (paṭisaṃvedako). One who pierces (vijjhati) is a piercer (vedhako); an aṭṭhivedhako pierces bone (aṭṭhiṃ vijjhati); a pattavedhako pierces a leaf (pattaṃ vijjhati).

Bahulādhikārā kammepi dissati, antare vāsīyati nivāsīyatīti antaravāsako, pasīdatīti pasīdako, pasādako vā, dīpappasādako, udakappasādako, sibbatīti sibbako, sevatīti sevako, hanatīti ghātako, gāvo hanatīti goghātako, hanassa ghāto. Haratīti hārako.

By the principle of varied application, this suffix is also seen in the passive sense. That which is worn or put on underneath (antare vāsīyati nivāsīyati) is an under-robe (antaravāsako). That which clarifies (pasīdati) is a clarifier (pasīdako or pasādako); for example, a dīpappasādako (lamp-clarifier) or an udakappasādako (water-clarifier). One who sews (sibbati) is a tailor (sibbako). One who serves (sevati) is an attendant (sevako). One who kills (hanati) is a killer (ghātako); one who kills cows (gāvo hanati) is a cow-killer (goghātako); ghāta is substituted for han. One who carries (harati) is a carrier (hārako).

Kamme [M 0.0549] – “pādehi paharīyatīti pādapahārako”ti vuttiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Titikkhatīti titikkhako, tikicchatīti tikicchako, vīmaṃsatīti vīmaṃsako, bubhukkhatīti bubhukkhako, pabbatāyatīti pabbatāyako iccādi.

In the passive sense: it is stated in the commentary, ‘That which is struck by the feet (pādehi paharīyati) is a kick (pādapahārako).’ One who endures (titikkhati) is an enduring one (titikkhako). One who treats (tikicchati) is a physician (tikicchako). One who investigates (vīmaṃsati) is an investigator (vīmaṃsako). One who is hungry (bubhukkhati) is a hungry person (bubhukkhako). One who acts like a mountain (pabbatāyati) is a pabbatāyako, and so on.

Iti akapaccayarāsi.

Thus the collection of the aka-suffix.

Ivaṇṇantarūparāsi

The Collection of Forms Ending in i

Atha ivaṇṇantarūpāni vuccante.

Now, forms ending in i are stated.

792. Dādhātvi ka. 551; rū. 598; nī. 1138.

792. After the roots dā and dhā, the suffix i.

Dā, dhāhi bhāvakārakesu ipaccayo hoti.

The suffix i occurs after dā and dhā in the sense of action or agent.

Paṭhamaṃ cittena ādīyatītiādi, taṇhādiṭṭhīhi upādīyatīti upādi, khandhupādi, kilesupādi, vidhānaṃ vidhi, vidhiyyati etenāti vidhi, nidhiyyatīti nidhi, sandhiyate sandhi, abhisandhi, paṭisandhi, sannidahanaṃ sannidhi, samādhānaṃ samādhi, samādahanti etenāti samādhi, paṇidahanaṃ paṇidhi, odhi, avadhi, upanidhi, paṭinidhi, udakaṃ dahati tiṭṭhati etthāti udadhi, mahanto udadhi mahodadhi, vālāni dahanti tiṭṭhanti etthāti vāladhi.

First, it is taken by the mind, hence ādi; it is clung to by craving and views, hence upādi; clinging to aggregates (khandhupādi), clinging to defilements (kilesupādi). Arrangement is vidhi; by this it is arranged, hence vidhi. It is stored, hence nidhi. It is joined, hence sandhi; abhisandhi; paṭisandhi. Placing together is sannidhi. Composure is samādhi; by this they compose themselves, hence samādhi. Aspiration is paṇidhi. Limit (odhi), boundary (avadhi), deposit (upanidhi), representation (paṭinidhi). Water is held and stands here, hence udadhi; the great ocean is mahodadhi. Hairs are held and stand here, hence vāladhi.

793. Ikitī sarūpe ka. 669; rū. 679; nī. 1315.

793. The suffixes i, ki, and ti in the sense of the root's form.

Dhātūnaṃ sutisaṅkhāte sarūpe vattabbe kriyatthā paraṃ i, ki, tipaccayā honti.

When the form of roots, designated as their sound, is to be stated, the suffixes i, ki, and ti occur after them in the sense of action.

Avaṇṇupantehi i, gami, paci iccādi.

After roots ending in a, the suffix i (e.g., gami, paci), and so on.

Uvaṇṇupantehi ki, budhi, rudhi iccādi.

After roots with a penultimate u, the suffix ki (e.g., budhi, rudhi), and so on.

Kehiciti, karotissa, atthissa iccādi.

After some, the suffix ti (e.g., karotissa, atthissa), and so on.

794. Sīlābhikkhaññāvassakesu ṇī ka. 532, 636; rū. 590, 659; nī. 1114, 1245.

794. The suffix ṇī in the sense of habit, frequency, and necessity.

Sīlaṃ [M 0.0550] vuccati pakaticariyā, abhikkhaṇameva abhikkhaññaṃ, punappunakriyā, āyatiṃ avassaṃbhāvī avassakaṃ nāma, sīlaggahaṇena dhamma, sādhukārāpi saṅgayhanti, etesu sīlādīsu kriyāvisesesu gamyamānesu kattari ṇī hoti. Ādantesu ‘āssāṇāpimhi yuka’iti yāgamo.

Habit is called natural conduct; frequency itself is constant repetition, a repeated action; that which will inevitably occur in the future is called necessity. By the mention of 'habit,' Dhamma and expressions of approval are also included. When these specific actions, such as habit and so on, are implied, the suffix ṇī occurs in the sense of the agent. For roots ending in ā, the augment ya is added according to the rule 'āssāṇāpimhi yuka'.

Akkhāyatīti akkhāyī, akkhāyanasīlo, akkhāyanadhammo, akkhāne sakkaccakāritā yuttoti attho. Kālattayepi sijjhati sāmaññavidhānattā.

One who proclaims is a proclaimer (akkhāyī); one whose habit is to proclaim (akkhāyanasīlo), one whose nature is to proclaim (akkhāyanadhammo). The meaning is that diligence in proclaiming is appropriate.

Avassakaṃ pana anāgatameva, dhammakkhāyī-puriso, dhammakkhāyinī-itthī, dhammakkhāyi-kulaṃ, gītaṃ abhiṇhaṃ gāyatīti gītagāyī, kappaṃ avassaṃ ṭhāssatīti kappaṭṭhāyī, saṃvaṭṭamānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ ṭhāssatīti saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī. Evaṃ vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī.

However, necessity refers only to the future: a man who proclaims the Dhamma (dhammakkhāyī), a woman who proclaims the Dhamma (dhammakkhāyinī), a family that proclaims the Dhamma (dhammakkhāyi-kula). One who frequently sings a song is a singer (gītagāyī). One who will assuredly endure for an eon is an eon-endurer (kappaṭṭhāyī). One who will endure for an incalculable period during contraction is a contraction-endurer (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī). Similarly, an expansion-endurer (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī).

Adinnaṃ ādadāti sīlenāti adinnādāyī. Tathā dinnameva ādadātīti dinnādāyī, annaṃ dadāti sīlenāti annadāyī.

One who by habit takes what is not given is an adinnādāyī. Similarly, one who takes only what is given is a dinnādāyī; one who by habit gives food is an annadāyī.

Dā-suppane. Niddāyanasīlo niddāyī, majjaṃ pivanasīlo majjapāyī, majjaṃ abhiṇhaṃ pivatīti majjapāyī, sīghaṃ yāyanasīlo sīghayāyī, sasaṅkhārena sappayogena avassaṃ parinibbāyissatīti sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Tathā asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, āyukappassa antare vemajjhe avassaṃ parinibbāyissatīti antarāparinibbāyī, āyukappapariyosānaṃ upahacca avassaṃ parinibbāyissatīti upahaccaparinibbāyī iccādi.

The root drā in the sense of sleeping. One whose nature is to sleep is a niddāyī (sleeper). One whose nature is to drink liquor is a majjapāyī (liquor drinker); one who frequently drinks liquor is a majjapāyī. One whose nature is to go quickly is a sīghayāyī (swift goer). One who will assuredly attain final Nibbāna with effort and exertion is a sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Similarly, an asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. One who will assuredly attain final Nibbāna in the middle of the lifespan is an antarāparinibbāyī. One who will assuredly attain final Nibbāna upon reaching the end of the lifespan is an upahaccaparinibbāyī, and so on.

Ivaṇṇesu-mantaṃ niccakālaṃ ajjhāyatīti mantajjhāyī, dhammajjhāyī, dhaññaṃ niccakālaṃ vikkiṇātīti dhaññavikkāyī, bhāyanasīlo bhāyī, bhūmiyaṃ sayanasīlo, bhūmiyaṃ vā niccakālaṃ sayatīti [M 0.0551] bhūmisāyī, kaṇṭake apassayanasīlo kaṇṭakāpassayī iccādi.

Among those ending in the vowel i: One who constantly recites spells is a mantajjhāyī (spell-reciter). A dhammajjhāyī (Dhamma-reciter). One who constantly sells grain is a dhaññavikkāyī (grain-seller). One whose nature is to fear is a bhāyī (fearful one). One whose nature is to sleep on the ground, or who constantly sleeps on the ground, is a bhūmisāyī (ground-sleeper). One whose nature is to lie upon thorns is a kaṇṭakāpassayī (one who lies on thorns), and so on.

Edantāpi idha vattabbā, uddhaṃ vaḍḍhanasīlo udāyī, vuddhesu apacāyanasīlo vuddhāpacāyī. Evaṃ jeṭṭhāpacāyī, jhāyanasīlo, jhāyanadhammo, jhāyane sakkaccakriyāyuttoti jhāyī, niccakālaṃ jhāyatīti vā jhāyī, pajjhāyī, ujjhāyī, nijjhāyī, abhijjhāyī, bhāyanasīlo bhāyī, tiṇaṃ abhiṇhaṃ lāyatīti tiṇalāyī, tantaṃ niccakālaṃ vāyatīti tantavāyī, palāyanasīlo palāyī, na palāyī apalāyī iccādi.

Here too, those ending in e should be mentioned. One whose nature is to grow upwards is an udāyī. One whose nature is to respect elders is a vuddhāpacāyī. Similarly, a jeṭṭhāpacāyī (one who respects seniors). One whose nature is to meditate, whose quality is meditation, who is endowed with diligent practice in meditation, is a jhāyī (meditator); or one who constantly meditates is a jhāyī. A pajjhāyī, an ujjhāyī, a nijjhāyī, an abhijjhāyī. One whose nature is to fear is a bhāyī (fearful one). One who frequently cuts grass is a tiṇalāyī (grass-cutter). One who constantly weaves thread is a tantavāyī (weaver). One whose nature is to flee is a palāyī (one who flees); one who does not flee is an apalāyī (one who does not flee), and so on.

Uvaṇṇesu-yathābhūtaṃ atthaṃ vibhāvanasīlo vibhāvīpuriso, vibhāvinī-itthī, āyatiṃ avassaṃ bhavissatīti bhāvī, sāliṃ lunāti sīlenāti sālilāvī iccādi.

Among those ending in the vowel u: A man whose nature is to explain the meaning as it truly is is a vibhāvīpuriso (an explaining man). A vibhāvinī-itthī (an explaining woman). One who will assuredly be in the future is a bhāvī (one who is to be). One who by habit reaps rice is a sālilāvī (rice-reaper), and so on.

Byāpanasīlo byāpī, kāmeti icchati sīlenāti kāmī, dhammakāmī, atthakāmī, karaṇasīlo kārī, pāpakārī, puññakārī.

One whose nature is to pervade is a byāpī (pervader). One who desires or wishes by habit is a kāmī (desirer); a dhammakāmī (lover of the Dhamma), an atthakāmī (lover of the good). One whose nature is to do is a kārī (doer); a pāpakārī (doer of evil), a puññakārī (doer of merit).

Avassaṃ āgamissatīti āgāmī. Rassatte-āgaminīratti, āgaminī-puṇṇamāsī, ācayaṃ vaṭṭaṃ gacchati sīlenāti ācayagāmī, apacayaṃ vivaṭṭaṃ gacchati sīlenāti apacayagāmī, sakiṃ avassaṃ āgamissatīti sakadāgāmī. Tathā na āgamissatīti anāgāmī.

One who will assuredly come is an āgāmī (comer). When the vowel is shortened (in the feminine): an āgaminīratti (coming night), an āgaminī-puṇṇamāsī (coming full moon). One who by habit goes towards accumulation (the round of existence) is an ācayagāmī. One who by habit goes towards de-accumulation (the rolling back of existence) is an apacayagāmī. One who will assuredly come once is a sakadāgāmī (once-returner). Similarly, one who will not come is an anāgāmī (non-returner).

Ādhānaṃ vuccati daḷhaṭṭhiti, ādhānaṃ katvā gahaṇasīlo ādhānagāhī, daḷhagāhī, dhammaṃ carati sīlenāti dhammacārī, brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ carati sīlenāti brahmacārī.

Ādhāna (establishing) is called firm standing. One whose nature is to grasp after establishing is an ādhānagāhī, a firm grasper (daḷhagāhī). One who by habit practices the Dhamma is a dhammacārī (Dhamma-practitioner). One who by habit practices the supreme life (brahmaṃ) is a brahmacārī (one who leads the holy life).

Apicettha dhammo nāma kulācāradhammo, taṃ dhammaṃ carāmīti daḷhaṃ gaṇhitvā yāva na vijahati, tāva avītikkamanaṭṭhena dhammaṃ carati sīlenāti dhammacārī nāma. Tathācaranto ca antarāvītikkamanīyavatthusamāyoge sati taṃ dhammaṃ apatamānaṃ katvā dhārento [M 0.0552] saṃvaraṇaṭṭhena dhammaṃ carati dhammenāti dhammacārī nāma, tathādhārento ca taṃ dhammaṃ attukkaṃsana, paravambhanādīhi pāpadhammehi anupakkiliṭṭhañca appicchatādīhi santaguṇehi supariyodātañca karonto pariyodāpanaṭṭhena dhammaṃ carati sādhukārenāti dhammacārī nāma.

Moreover, here 'Dhamma' means the custom of the family (kulācāradhammo). Having firmly grasped 'I will practice that Dhamma,' for as long as one does not abandon it, one is called a dhammacārī because one practices the Dhamma by habit in the sense of non-transgression. And while practicing thus, when an occasion for transgression arises, by maintaining that Dhamma without letting it fall, one is called a dhammacārī because one practices the Dhamma with restraint. And while maintaining it thus, by making that Dhamma uncorrupted by evil qualities such as self-praise and disparagement of others, and well-purified by peaceful qualities such as fewness of wishes, one is called a dhammacārī because one practices the Dhamma well in the sense of purification.

Brahmaṃ vuccati tato seṭṭhataraṃ sikkhāpadasīlaṃ, tampi gaṇhitvā avijahanto antarā ca apatamānaṃ katvā dhārento anupakkiliṭṭhaṃ supariyodātañca karonto tividhena atthena brahmacārī nāma, samādāna, sampatta, samucchedaviratīnaṃ vasena viyojetuṃ vaṭṭati, yo pana gaṇhanto tathā na dhāreti, dhārento vā upakkiliṭṭhaṃ karoti, so ekadesena atthena brahmacārī nāma.

Brahma is said to be the virtue of the training precepts, which is superior to that. Having undertaken this and not abandoning it, maintaining it in the interim without letting it fall, and making it uncorrupted and well-purified, one is called a brahmacārī in a threefold sense. It is fitting to analyze this by way of the abstinences of undertaking, attainment, and cutting off. But one who, having undertaken it, does not maintain it thus, or while maintaining it, makes it corrupt, is called a brahmacārī only in a partial sense.

Yo pana tividhena atthena mutto hutvā kadāci taṃ dhammaṃ carati, tassa caraṇakriyā tassīlakriyā na hoti, so dhammacārīti na vuccati, etenupāyena sesesu pāpa, kalyāṇabhūtesu tassīlapadesu atthavibhāgo veditabbo.

However, one who, being devoid of this threefold sense, practices that Dhamma only occasionally—his act of practice is not an act of habit. He is not called a dhammacārī. By this method, the analysis of meaning should be understood for the remaining terms denoting habit, whether they be evil or wholesome.

Brahmacārinī-itthī, visesena dassanasīlo vipassī, atthadassī, dhammadassī, piyadassī, sudassī, dussanasīlo dussīmāro, dhāraṇasīlo dhārī, iṇadhārī, chattadhārī, bhusaṃ nahanasīlo upanāhī, pariniṭṭhitapaccayekadesattā āyatiṃ avassaṃ uppajjissatīti uppādī, uppādino dhammā dha. sa. tikamātikā 17.

A brahmacārinī-itthī (a woman who leads the holy life). One whose nature is to see in a special way is a vipassī (one who sees insightfully); an atthadassī (seer of the good), a dhammadassī (seer of the Dhamma), a piyadassī (one of pleasant sight), a sudassī (one of good sight). One whose nature is to corrupt is a dussīmāro (a corrupting Māra). One whose nature is to bear is a dhārī (bearer); an iṇadhārī (debt-bearer), a chattadhārī (umbrella-bearer). One whose nature is to be very resentful is an upanāhī (resentful one). Because some of its conditions are established, that which will assuredly arise in the future is an uppādī (ariser). Uppādino dhammā (arising phenomena).

Bhara-dhāraṇe, mālaṃ niccakālaṃ bharatīti mālabhārī, bhājanasīlo bhājī, uṇhaṃ bhuñjanasīlo uṇhabhojī, attānaṃ maññati sīlenāti attamānī, attānaṃ paṇḍitaṃ maññatīti paṇḍitamānī, labhanasīlo lābhī, vacanasīlo vācī. Evaṃ vādī, atthavādī, dhammavādī, yuttavādī, muttavādī, vibhajjavādī, niccaṃ vasatīti vāsī, gāmavāsī, nagaravāsī, bhāraṃ vahanasīlo bhāravāhī[M 0.0553], dhammaṃ paññaṃ anusarati anugacchatīti dhammānusārī. Evaṃ saddhānusārī, virūpaṃ pāpapakkhaṃ paṭimukhaṃ abhiṇhaṃ sarati cintetīti vippaṭisārī, pāṇaṃ hanati sīlenāti pāṇaghātī, hanassa ghāto.

The root bhṛ in the sense of bearing. One who constantly bears a garland is a mālabhārī (garland-bearer). One whose nature is to share is a bhājī (sharer). One whose nature is to eat hot food is an uṇhabhojī (eater of hot food). One who by habit is conceited about oneself is attamānī (self-conceited). One who is conceited about being a scholar is a paṇḍitamānī. One whose nature is to gain is a lābhī (gainer). One whose nature is to speak is a vācī (speaker). Similarly, a vādī (speaker), an atthavādī (speaker of the good), a dhammavādī (speaker of the Dhamma), a yuttavādī (speaker of what is right), a muttavādī (speaker of what is spoken), a vibhajjavādī (analytical speaker). One who constantly dwells is a vāsī (dweller); a gāmavāsī (village-dweller), a nagaravāsī (city-dweller). One whose nature is to carry a burden is a bhāravāhī (burden-carrier). One who follows after the Dhamma and wisdom is a dhammānusārī (Dhamma-follower). Similarly, a saddhānusārī (faith-follower). One who frequently remembers and thinks about the disagreeable, evil side of things is a vippaṭisārī (remorseful one). One who by habit kills living beings is a pāṇaghātī (killer of living beings). The root han becomes ghāta.

Haritabbaṃ sabbaṃ harati sīlenāti hārahārī iccādi.

One who by habit takes everything that should be taken is a hārahārī (taker), and so on.

‘Kagā cajāna’nti suttavibhattiyā aghānubandhepi cajānaṃ kagādeso, samaṃ vipācetīti samavepākī-udaraggi, samavepākinī-gahaṇī, upadhi phalaṃ vipaccatīti upadhivepākinī, socanasīlo sokī, sokinī-pajā, mutto hutvā cajanasīlo muttacāgī, saṃvibhājanasīlo saṃvibhāgī, kāmasukhaṃ bhuñjanasīlo kāmabhogī, visuṃ avibhattaṃ bhogaṃ bhuñjanasīlo apaṭivibhattabhogī, yuñjanasīlo yogī iccādi.

By the rule ‘Kagā cajāna’ in the chapter on suttas, even when not followed by the affix gha, the substitution of ka and ga for ca and ja occurs. That which digests evenly is samavepākī—the digestive fire; the feminine is samavepākinī—the bowels. That in which the substratum ripens as fruit is upadhivepākinī. One whose nature is to grieve is sokī (sorrowful); sokinī-pajā (a sorrowful people). One whose nature is to give up, having been freed, is a muttacāgī (one who has abandoned freely). One whose nature is to share is a saṃvibhāgī (sharer). One whose nature is to enjoy sensual pleasures is a kāmabhogī (enjoyer of sensual pleasures). One whose nature is to enjoy wealth separately and undivided is an apaṭivibhattabhogī (one who does not share possessions). One whose nature is to strive is a yogī (one who strives), and so on.

795. Āvī ka. 532; rū. 590; nī. 1114.

795. The suffix āvī.

Āvī hoti kattari.

The suffix āvī occurs in the sense of the agent.

Bhayaṃ dassanasīlo bhayadassāvī.

One whose nature is to see danger is a bhayadassāvī (seer of danger).

Iti ivaṇṇantarūparāsi.

Thus ends the Collection of Forms Ending in the Vowel i.

Uvaṇṇantarūparāsi

The Collection of Forms Ending in the Vowel u.

796. Bhaṅgu bhīrū bhāsu assavā.

796. Bhaṅgu, bhīrū, bhāsu, assavā.

Ete saddā mahāvuttinā sīlādīsu nipaccante.

These words are irregularly formed by a general rule in the meanings of habit and so on.

Bhanja-vināse, pabhañjanasīlo pabhaṅgu-saṅkhatadhammo.

The root bhañj in the sense of destruction. That whose nature is to break up is pabhaṅgu—a conditioned phenomenon.

Bhī-bhaye, bhāyanasīlo bhīrū.

The root bhī in the sense of fear. One whose nature is to fear is a bhīrū (fearful one).

Bhā-dittiyaṃ, obhāsanasīlo bhāsu-pabhā, jeṭṭhavacanaṃ ādarena suṇāti sīlenāti assavo-putto, assavābhariyā.

The root bhā in the sense of shining. That whose nature is to illuminate is bhāsu, meaning light. One who by habit listens with respect to the words of elders is an assavo (son); an assavā (wife).

797. Vidā kū ka. 535; rū. 593; nī. 1119.

797. From vid, the suffix kū.

Vidamhā [M 0.0554] kū hoti kattari.

After the root vid, the suffix kū occurs in the sense of the agent.

Vidati sīlenāti vidū, lokavidū, paracittavidū. Itthiyaṃ paracittavidunī.

One who knows by habit is a vidū (knower); a lokavidū (knower of the world), a paracittavidū (knower of others' minds). In the feminine: paracittavidunī.

798. Vito ñāto ka. 535; rū. 593; nī. 1119.

798. From ñā with vi.

Vipubbā ñāto kū hoti kattari.

After the root ñā preceded by vi, the suffix kū occurs in the sense of the agent.

Vijānanasīlo viññū.

One whose nature is to understand is 'viññū', the discerning one.

799. Kammā ka. 535; rū. 593; nī. 1119.

799. When 'kamma' is the preceding word.

Kammupapadā ñāto kū hoti kattari.

When 'kamma' is the preceding word, the suffix 'kū' occurs from the root 'ñā' in the agentive sense.

Sabbaṃ jānāti sīlenāti sabbaññū, rattaññū, atthaññū, dhammaññū, kālaññū, samayaññū.

One who knows all by nature is 'sabbaññū' (all-knower), as are 'rattaññū' (knower of what has been experienced), 'atthaññū' (knower of the meaning), 'dhammaññū' (knower of the Dhamma), 'kālaññū' (knower of the time), and 'samayaññū' (knower of the appropriate occasion).

780. Gamā rū ka. 534; rū. 592; nī. 1118.

780. From the root 'gam', the suffix 'rū'.

Kammupapadā gamamhā rū hoti kattari. ‘Rānubandhentasarādissā’ti sabbadhātvantalopo.

When 'kamma' is the preceding word, the suffix 'rū' occurs from the root 'gam' in the agentive sense. According to the rule 'Rānubandhentasarādissā', there is elision of the final vowel of all roots.

Pāraṃ gacchati sīlenāti pāragū, vedaṃ vuccati aggamaggañāṇaṃ, vedaṃ gacchatīti vedagū, addhānaṃ gacchatīti addhagū.

One who goes to the far shore by nature is 'pāragū'. 'Veda' is said to be the knowledge of the highest path (aggamaggañāṇaṃ); one who goes to 'Veda' is 'vedagū'. One who goes a long journey (addhānaṃ) is 'addhagū'.

Iti uvaṇṇantarūparāsi.

Thus ends the section on forms ending in 'u'.

Itthiliṅgarūparāsi

The Section on Feminine Forms

Atha itthiliṅgarūpāni vuccante.

Now the feminine forms are explained.

801. Itthiyamaṇatikayakayā ca ka. 553; rū. 599; nī. 1140; ‘…kti…’ (bahūsu).

801. In the feminine gender, there are also the suffixes 'a', 'ṇa', 'ti', 'ka', 'yaka', and 'yā'.

Itthiliṅge vattabbe bhāvakārakesu a, ṇa,ti, ka, yaka, yapaccayā ca ano ca hoti.

When speaking of the feminine gender, the suffixes 'a', 'ṇa', 'ti', 'ka', 'yaka', and 'ya' occur in the sense of state or agent, and also the suffix 'ana'.

Ka[M 0.0555], a, ṇa, yaka, ya, anaiccetehi ‘itthiyamatvā’ti āpaccayo.

From these suffixes 'ka', 'a', 'ṇa', 'yaka', 'ya', and 'ana', the suffix 'ā' occurs according to the rule 'itthiyamatvā'.

Kamhi tāva-attani nisinnaṃ gūhati saṃvaratīti guhā, attānaṃ vā paraṃ vā dūsetīti dūsā-dhuttitthī.

Firstly, in the case of 'ka': that which hides or conceals one sitting within is 'guhā' (a cave). One who defiles oneself or another is 'dūsā' (a corrupt woman).

Muda-hāse, modanaṃ mudā, pamudā, sujjhati etāyāti sudhā, vasuṃ ratanaṃ dhāretīti vasudhā iccādi.

From 'mud', in the sense of joy: rejoicing is 'mudā', and 'pamudā'. That by which one is purified is 'sudhā' (ambrosia). That which holds wealth and jewels is 'vasudhā' (the earth), and so on.

Amhi-saṅkhāyanti etāyāti saṅkhā. Tathā saṅkhyā, pajānātīti paññā, ājānātīti aññā, sañjānātīti saññā, sañjānanti etāyāti vā saññā, sañjānanaṃ vā saññā, abhijānanaṃ abhiññā, paṭijānanaṃ paṭiññā, paricchijja jānanaṃ pariññā, paṭicca tiṭṭhati etthāti patiṭṭhā.

From 'amhi': that by which they reckon is 'saṅkhā' (reckoning). Likewise, 'saṅkhyā' (enumeration). One who understands is 'paññā' (wisdom). One who knows is 'aññā' (knowledge). One who perceives is 'saññā' (perception); or that by which they perceive is 'saññā'; or perceiving itself is 'saññā'. Direct knowing is 'abhiññā' (direct knowledge). Acknowledging is 'paṭiññā' (acknowledgment). Knowing by discrimination is 'pariññā' (thorough knowledge). That on which one stands dependently is 'patiṭṭhā' (support).

Thā-ṭhāne, avadhibhāvena ṭhāti tiṭṭhatīti avatthā, upādīyatīti upādā-paññatti, aññamaññaṃ upecca nissāya ca dhiyyatīti upanidhā-paññattiyeva, saddahanaṃ saddhā, saddahanti etāyāti vā saddhā, visiṭṭhaṃ katvā attānaṃ dahanti etāyāti vidhā-māno, bhāti dibbatīti bhā-nakkhattaṃ, pabhā, ābhā, nibhā, upamīyate upamā.

From 'ṭhā', in the sense of standing: that which stands as a limit is 'avatthā' (state or condition). That which is taken up is 'upādā' (a concept of grasping). That which is placed by mutually approaching and depending is 'upanidhā' (a concept of foundation). Believing is 'saddhā' (faith); or that by which they believe is 'saddhā'. That by which they, having made themselves distinct, hold themselves is 'vidhā' (conceit). That which shines or gleams is 'bhā' (a star or constellation), 'pabhā' (radiance), 'ābhā' (splendor), 'nibhā' (luster). That by which one compares is 'upamā' (simile).

Jhe-cintāyaṃ, pajjhāyanaṃ pajjhā, vajjāvajjaṃ upajjhāyati pekkhatīti upajjhā, abhimukhaṃ jhāyanaṃ abhijjhā.

From 'jhā', in the sense of thinking: pondering is 'pajjhā'. One who reflects upon or observes what is faulty and faultless is 'upajjhā' (an overseer or preceptor). Meditating towards (something) is 'abhijjhā' (covetousness).

Āsa-patthanāyaṃ, āsīsanaṃ āsā, paccāsīsanaṃ paccāsā.

From 'ās', in the sense of wishing: wishing is 'āsā' (hope). Expecting is 'paccāsā' (anticipation).

Āsa-upavesane, acchanaṃ acchā.

From 'ās', in the sense of sitting: sitting is 'acchā'.

Ikkha-dassana’ṅkesu, apekkhanaṃ apekkhā, upekkhanaṃ upekkhā, upaparikkhanaṃ upaparikkhā, icchanaṃ icchā, byāpituṃ icchā vicchā.

From 'ikkh', in the sense of seeing or observing: looking forward to is 'apekkhā' (anticipation). Looking on is 'upekkhā' (equanimity). Thoroughly examining is 'upaparikkhā' (investigation). Wishing is 'icchā' (desire). Wishing to harm is 'vicchā' (malice).

Issa-ussuyyiye, issanaṃ issā.

From 'iss', in the sense of envy: being envious is 'issā' (envy).

Īha-byāpāre, īhanaṃ īhā.

From 'īh', in the sense of striving: striving is 'īhā'.

Uchi-ucche[M 0.0556], ucchanaṃ ucchā.

From 'uch', in the sense of cutting off: cutting off is 'ucchā'.

Ela-kampane, elayatīti elā-doso.

From 'el', in the sense of shaking: that which shakes is 'elā' (a fault).

Oja-thambhane tejane ca, ojeti taṃsamaṅgine satte saṅkhāre ca samupatthambhati samuttejetīti vā ojā.

From 'oj', in the sense of sustaining and invigorating: that which sustains and invigorates beings and formations endowed with it is 'ojā' (nutriment or vitality).

Kala-saṅkhyāne, kalīyatīti kalā, khamanaṃ khamā, gajjanti etāyāti gadā, girīyati kathīyatīti girā-vācā, ghaṭīyati saṅghaṭīyati etthāti ghaṭā-yūtho, bhuso cāreti paricāretīti accharā-devī, mahāvuttinā cassa cho, jaṭatīti jaṭā, antojaṭā bahijaṭā saṃ. ni. 1.23, jiyyanti etāyāti jarā, jiraṇaṃ vā jarā, āpajjati ajjhāpajjatīti āpadā, sampajjanaṃ sampadā, uparibhāvaṃ suṭṭhu pajjanti pāpuṇanti etāyāti upasampadā, paṭipajjanaṃ paṭipadā, paṭipajjanti uparivisesaṃ etāyāti vā paṭipadā, sukhappaṭipadā, dukkhappaṭipadā, paṭisaṃbhijjanti atthādīsu ñāṇappabhedaṃ gacchanti etāyāti paṭisambhidā, atthapaṭisambhidā, dhammapaṭisambhidā, niruttipaṭisambhidā, paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā.

From 'kal', in the sense of reckoning: that which is reckoned is 'kalā' (a part). Endurance is 'khamā'. That by which one roars is 'gadā' (a club or disease). That which is spoken or uttered is 'girā' (speech). That where they assemble or gather is 'ghaṭā' (a troop). That which moves about greatly or serves is 'accharā' (a celestial nymph). And by a general rule, for 'c' there is 'ch'. That which is tangled is 'jaṭā' (matted hair); there is inner matted hair and outer matted hair. That by which beings decay is 'jarā' (old age); or decaying is 'jarā'. That into which one falls or falls deeply is 'āpadā' (misfortune). Accomplishment is 'sampadā'. That by which one attains or reaches a higher state well is 'upasampadā' (higher ordination). Practicing is 'paṭipadā' (path or practice); or that by which one progresses to a higher distinction is 'paṭipadā'; there is the pleasant practice and the painful practice. That by which one analyzes and attains distinctions of knowledge in meaning, etc., is 'paṭisambhidā' (analytical knowledge); namely, analytical knowledge of meaning, analytical knowledge of phenomena, analytical knowledge of language, and analytical knowledge of ready wit.

Bhikkha-yācane, bhikkhīyateti bhikkhā.

From 'bhikkh', in the sense of begging: that which is begged for is 'bhikkhā' (alms).

Sikkha-ghaṭane, sikkhanaṃ sikkhā, sikkhanti ghaṭenti sekkhā janā etthāti sikkhā, adhisīlasikkhā, adhicittasikkhā, adhipaññāsikkhā iccādi.

From 'sikkh', in the sense of training or striving: training is 'sikkhā'. That wherein learners train and strive is 'sikkhā', namely, higher training in virtue, higher training in mind, higher training in wisdom, and so forth.
